News.title: Crypto thieves attack man in home and threaten to kill pregnant wife's baby in 'horrific' robbery
News.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

A businessman was beaten with hammers by masked men who broke into his home and threatened to kill his heavily pregnant wife unless he transferred hundreds of thousands of pounds of cryptocurrency.

Speaking to the BBC, the couple, who want to remain anonymous, described the attack as "horrific" and said they feared for their unborn baby's life.

The attackers left in a car driven by a getaway driver after the man transferred his crypto savings.

Crimestoppers are offering a Â£10,000 reward for information in the attack, which was captured on home security footage and is being investigated by the police.

Experts say it is one of a growing type of violent theft known as a "wrench attack" targeting cryptocurrency investors.

As crypto coins have risen in value, reports of these violent robberies linked to digital assets have emerged in the UK, France and the US.

Once funds are transferred, recovering them can be extremely difficult.

The man, who the BBC is calling James, said three intruders forced their way into their Solihull home before launching an assault which lasted 45 minutes.

"The door gets pushed open, I can see gloves coming in, balaclavas," he said.

James tried to fight the men off but they hit him in the face, head and ribs with hammers.

His wife, who was seven months pregnant, was held down on the sofa by one of the criminals.

"He's got a pillow over her face," James said. "He's literally suffocating her on the sofa. I can hear her screaming, 'I can't breathe'."

The couple still had no idea what the criminals wanted until one of the men demanded James unlock his phone and hand it over.

James said the attackers appeared to know he owned cryptocurrency, but had little understanding of how to access it.

Instead, they were taking instructions from someone else connected via a live video call.

"I can hear the guy on FaceTime saying: 'Show me everything on his phone. Show me what apps he's got'," he said.

News.title: 'I was terrified': Alex Ferguson on brain haemorrhage and games that shaped his life
News.content:
"I was terrified," says Sir Alex Ferguson, one of the fiercest, most explosive and most decorated managers in football history.

The legendary former Manchester United boss is recalling the day he returned to Old Trafford for the first time after suffering a brain haemorrhage in May 2018.

Four months after emergency surgery, Ferguson - famous for his 'hairdryer treatment' when United dominated English football - was back to watch his beloved club take on Wolves in the Premier League.

The man responsible for making the dreams of United fans around the world come true for once was unsure of the reception he would receive from supporters.

"I wish I could say I was comfortable. I wasn't," Ferguson tells BBC Breakfast.

He need not have worried.

Ferguson and his wife Cathy received a standing ovation when they took their seats in the directors' box before kick-off.

"My wife was with me, and she was nearly crying," he said. "When we sat down, she said: 'That's fantastic.'"

Ferguson had been retired five years - after winning 38 trophies during 26 years in charge of United - at the time of his brain haemorrhage, aged 76.

Now three months short of 85, he says: "I'm feeling quite good despite small injuries."

The Scot has a new book coming out - 'Games of My Life'. It tells the stories of 21 defining matches in his playing and managerial career, revealing fresh insights into his journey from working-class Glasgow to dominating the English game - and Europe - as United boss.

Ferguson is thankful he is able to talk about the games that helped shape him.

"I had lost my voice; I couldn't speak," he says about the days immediately after brain surgery. "That was a frightening moment.

"I remember my grandsons coming to see me and I had lost my voice.

"Then they brought in a therapist and she started doing things like asking me to write down the names of birds, names of animals, names of rivers.

"That way my voice came back."

News.title: Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
News.content:
According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants.

Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe".

"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me.

The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around â¬1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.

Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally.

According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably.

China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran.

That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US.

And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro.

"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo.

But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market.

There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.

News.title: No more cereal at the end of the aisle? New rules in Scotland's supermarkets
News.content:
Sugary soft drinks, biscuits and some breakfast cereals have disappeared from prominent positions in Scotland's supermarkets.

The Scottish government has introduced rules meaning some products that are high in fat, sugar and salt can no longer be put in prime end-of-aisle slots, or feature as part of multi-buy offers in store or online.

The regulations will apply to the usual suspects - chocolate, crisps, biscuits and ice cream.

But it could also include kombucha, seaweed snacks, muesli and chewing gum, depending on their sugar content.

News.title: What's really going on in lymphatic drainage beauty videos?
News.content:
If she's ever feeling bloated, Abbey Alexandra has a go-to routine, using body oil and a wooden roller to perform stomach massages.

She shares before-and-after videos on TikTok, saying she feels the process leaves her depuffed and defined: "You definitely feel a lot better after, they are relaxing."

The technique is a form of lymphatic drainage massage, adapted from a medical treatment and shared as a beauty trend. Celebrity fans include Maya Jama, who shares her clinic sessions, and actress Hailey Bieber, who told Time magazine: "I swear by them."

Whether there is a physical change - or any need for one - is debatable, but fans of the massages claim they help "flatten" and "debloat" and give a "snatched waist" and "sculpted abs". But what's actually happening to their bodies?

News.title: Chris Mason: Why Andy Burnham's about-turn on Manchester City matters
News.content:
The rows circulating around Manchester City are huge, and they are only going to get bigger.

The Premier League has concluded that City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

This, clearly, matters for the club, but that is just the start of it.

It matters for Manchester, it matters for the Premier League and so, crucially, it matters for the UK's image around the world â because England's top flight is a colossal global brand. In other words, this matters whether you like football or not.

Added to all of this, Andy Burnham pitches himself as Mr Manchester and is a big football fan.

The man who was the mayor of Greater Manchester a matter of months ago is now the prime minister, and so finds himself caught up in it all at a local level, a national level and a diplomatic level.

Diplomatic, because rows will rage over the extent to which City's ownership is separate from the Abu Dhabi state. And the state is a big UK ally.

All of this is why I thought it was in the public interest to put a series of questions to Burnham about it when I spoke to him on Wednesday as the Labour Party conference concluded in Liverpool.

His comments, in his interview with me, followed by no fewer than two attempts to backtrack 24 hours later, amount to perhaps his biggest self inflicted tangle since he arrived in Downing Street in July.

He will have expected to be asked about Manchester City, but he didn't expect sustained scrutiny about it.

One particular exchange prompted a lot of interest. I asked if he was worried that Manchester City's owners from the United Arab Emirates might sell up.

It is worth quoting his answer in full.

"Well, I would be really concerned to lose them. They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester. Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene more in the process. It would be wrong for me to do that. It would be wrong, I think, to jump to a conclusion before having really studied all of the detail, but obviously it's ongoing, and because it's still contested by Manchester City, then I think it's right that I don't say much more."

His answer is revealing on several levels, and was leapt on by many in football and then by the Conservatives, who labelled them "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary".

News.title: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford incident, police say
News.content:
A UK-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with the incident at RAF Fairford, counter-terror police have said.

The 25-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London. Two properties in the area have been searched.

Five men in their twenties who were arrested near the Gloucestershire airbase on Sunday remain on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

Counter-terror police are considering "all possible angles - including foreign state involvement", the force's senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said.

"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," she said.

"I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation."

Police had initially given the dual UK-Iranian national's age as 27 and said a second man had been questioned under caution, but in a later update said that this was not the case.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. He did not provide further details, and Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

The five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after "three suspicious vehicles" were reported travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of vans near the site.

The group were aged between 23 and 25. Four live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes were carried out.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that "the hands of a foreign actor" had clearly been involved in the incident at the base, which has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the airbase for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for what it called defensive strikes on Iran.

On Thursday, the British ambassador to Iran met the country's foreign ministry at the request of the Iranian government.

News.title: Chaos, coffins and 'Claudiapatra' steal the show in Celebrity Traitors
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

One person in particular may have dominated much of this opening episode, but Claudia Winkleman's gothic arrival still caused a stir.

Carried aloft by druids in a closed coffin, the show's host arrived in a church, to greet 21 anxious-looking celebrities.

"That was quite the nap," she said as she emerged.

"Claudiapatra!" gasped model and actress Jerry Hall - spotting similarities in both grandeur and hairstyles between Claudia and Cleopatra, the Egyptian queen.

Winkleman said at the show's press launch she loved her "iconic entrance", but admitted she'd initially wanted to hide in the castle's suit of armour.

"It's like a sort of GCSE history fantasy - it was either that or the grandfather clock," she said.

News.title: Coroner warns of risk of future deaths at mental health unit where patient was killed
News.content:
On the night of Flint Cahan's death, staff on the ward were found to have been asleep on the job and on their phones for long periods.

East London NHS Foundation Trust (ELFT) says the failings identified were "wholly unacceptable" and that it has undertaken a "significant programme of work" to improve inpatient services.

The coroner's Prevention of Future Deaths report highlights 14 concerns. These include failing to carry out "timely and thorough observations" of patients, then falsifying records "in the safe knowledge that staff on duty would not report or escalate the deception".

The document also says there were delays in starting CPR on Flint Cahan when he was discovered, that staff misled the police as to what the patients had been doing on the night of the incident, and that staff colluded with each other to take two-hour unauthorised breaks.

Torres-Pena was given a hospital order with no time limit after pleading guilty to manslaughter by diminished responsibility in 2023.

The coroner also raised concerns that many of the failings had been brought up at a previous inquest he'd conducted.

"The findings in this inquest are strikingly similar to the findings of an inquest before this court in 2021, remedial measures reported in that case do not appear to have been implemented effectively by the trust", the report says.

"Findings of dishonesty on this scale are extraordinarily rare in a coronial investigation. The public are entitled to expect a clear explanation of how this was allowed to happen and what is being done to ensure it never happens again," says James Cahan, the family solicitor and Hugo's cousin.

News.title: Zack Polanski to call for three-year cap on private rent rises
News.content:
Zack Polanski is set to call for a three-year "emergency brake" on private rent increases when he opens the Green Party's conference later.

In his speech to party activists on Friday afternoon, the Green leader will seek to frame housing as a key issue of generational fairness.

He will urge the government to prevent private rents rising above whichever is lowest out of the consumer price index measure of inflation, wage growth or 2%, for three years.

According to the party, he will also argue pressure from the Greens has forced Labour into a change of political direction on some issues.

The Green Party of England and Wales is billing the gathering in Brighton as its biggest ever, after announcing earlier this year that its membership had tripled since Polanski's election as leader just over a year ago.

In his speech, Polanski is expected to say generations are having to live with their parents because of rent prices, from 19-year-olds commuting to university, 25-year-olds unable to find a job, to 35-year-olds moving back home with their partners.

"For too long, landlords have been able to hike prices way beyond wages, leaving renters forced to meet the cost to keep a roof over their heads, cutting back and back and back on everything else," he is expected to say.

A slowdown on private rent increases "would give renters vital breathing space" and give time for ministers to create a national Fair Rents Guarantee that keeps rents affordable for the future, he is expected to say.

Earlier this year, the government brought in the Renters' Rights Act under which landlords can only increase rent once a year to the property's open market rate.

Average UK monthly private rents increased by 3.5%, to Â£1,377, in the 12 months to January 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics.

The Act also means tenancies are rolling rather than fixed term, and makes it harder for landlords to evict tenants.

But Polanski is expected to argue it does not go far enough in ending "fear and uncertainty" for the millions of private renters in the UK.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies has previously warned, external that rent controls - an issue the Greens have long campaigned for - would result in "unintended consequences" including demand exceeding supply in the rental market.

However, the party's co-deputy leader Rachel Millward told BBC Breakfast most landlords were "super-earners", who were making more money than other sectors and "would be able to absorb a slight reduction in rent".

News.title: First minister demands 'new deal' for Wales, before Plaid Cymru conference
News.content:
Ap Iorwerth hosted the pro-independence first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland in Cardiff last month and jointly declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end".

In his 2,000-word letter to Burnham, ap Iorwerth made a detailed case for the transfer of powers over policing and justice, rail infrastructure and the Crown Estate, external to Wales.

He also called for "funding arrangements that are fair, needs-based and reflect Wales' demographic and economic realities".

He said that "Wales' constitutional settlement should continue to evolve to improve democratic accountability, boost growth, strengthen public services and deliver better outcomes for our communities".

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, ap Iorwerth said he was looking for "practical answers to unlock those things that we need to take Wales forward".

He said he recognised there could be "practical barriers" to how the Crown Estate was devolved, and said he was "happy to look at how we do it in a gradual way, in order to make sure that it's not just an ideological drive".

He separately suggested that he may spend extra funds that come to the Welsh government, as a consequence of more funding for social care in England, on social care in Wales.

Labour's Burnham has promised to end triple lock for pensions from 2030 to fund a new national care service.

Social care is the responsibility of the Welsh government, and how it spends its money is up to its ministers. Both Plaid and Burnham would face elections before the policy came in.

Ap Iorwerth said: "When Boris Johnson was describing his plans that would have led to a consequential [from social care], we in Plaid Cymru were able to put a plan in place at that time that would allow us to spend the consequential on social care in Wales.

"I would be taking the same approach again."

Ap Iorwerth said it was a "good direction of travel" from the prime minister, but he added: "We don't know what the consequentials will be."

Ap Iorwerth is expected to meet the prime minister, along with the first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland, at the end of the month.

Burnham had previously said he would be "open" to the idea of giving the Welsh government control over policing.

He has also said: "I have to respect the governments in the nations of the UK, and I will, and give a fair hearing to anything that is put to me."

A UK government spokesperson said: "This government is committed to building a stronger and fairer Wales in a stronger and fairer United Kingdom.

"That's why our focus is now on working with the Welsh government to empower local leaders and communities to deliver good growth and jobs in every postcode."

News.title: Bill Nighy wins best host at British Podcast Awards
News.content:
Actor Bill Nighy's reinvention as an agony uncle has earned him the award for best host at the British Podcast Awards, beating names such as Louis Theroux, Katherine Ryan and Lily Allen.

Nighy, 76, known for films including Love Actually, Living and the Underworld franchise, has now found success with what award organisers called his "irresistibly endearing series" Ill-Advised.

Billed as "a podcast for people who don't get out much and can't handle it when they do", the show sees Nighy dole out wry advice to listeners, and muse about life, music and books.

Other winners at the 10th annual British Podcast Awards on Thursday included Pete Wicks, Sophie and Jamie Laing, Peter Crouch and Alan Carr.

News.title: Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks
News.content:
In an attempt to clarify the PM's position, a No 10 spokesperson added: "He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Man City deny any wrongdoing and have until Friday to submit an appeal.

Sources told BBC Sport that City were expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than Â£830m.

The Premier League says City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

In an interview on Wednesday with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason, Burnham - who was mayor of Greater Manchester until June - said he was "not getting directly involved in the process" and that it must be undertaken independently by the Premier League.

He said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and it would be "wrong" to "jump to a conclusion".

Asked if he was worried the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, a royal and the United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister - might sell up, Burnham replied: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene more in the process, it would be wrong for me to do that."

The Tories have accused Burnham of "publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues" and questioned whether "political pressure" was being applied.

Shadow minister for sport Louie French called for the government to "keep politics out of football and ensure the Premier League's independent commission can do its job free of outside influence".

"The club face unprecedented allegations and fans are horrified by what they are reading in the papers," the Tory MP said.

"Yet Burnham is publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues. Fans will rightly ask whether political pressure is being applied here and how it relates to the owners' well-reported investments in Manchester.

"Football must be governed independently, with the rules applying equally to everyone. Fans deserve confidence that no club or owner is above those rules."

And Lib Dem MP Anna Sabine, the party's spokesperson on sport, said: "Fans of every club deserve to know the rules apply to everyone... Burnham needs to remember he's prime minister for everyone, not just Manchester."

The chairwoman of the Commons Treasury committee, Labour MP Dame Meg Hillier, wrote to HMRC on Thursday to ask for reassurance that it had "seized of the importance" of the case for any potential tax implications.

The skull of a Hong Kong socialite allegedly murdered and dismembered by her former husband and his family was found cooked in a pot of carrot and vegetable soup, a court has heard.

Prosecutors in the high-profile trial over the alleged murder of Abby Choi, a model and online influencer, alleged this week that she was killed following a bitter dispute over the sale of a luxury apartment she owned.

Choi, 28, was reported missing on 21 February 2023. Three days later, parts of her dismembered body were discovered at a rented flat in Hong Kong’s Tai Po district that had allegedly been turned into a makeshift butchery site, in a case that sent shockwaves through the wealthy financial hub.

Police found a meat slicer, an electric saw and clothing at the property, which had been rented by her former father-in-law.

Her former father-in-law, Kwong Kau, her ex-husband, Alex Kwong, and his brother, Anthony Kwong, were later arrested and accused of killing Choi following a dispute over the sale of a luxury property.

All three pleaded not guilty to murder on Wednesday.

open image in gallery Hong Kong police officers comb through garbage for the remains of murdered model Abby Choi on 28 February 2023 ( Jerome Favre/EPA )

At the start of their trial at Hong Kong’s High Court, prosecutors alleged that Kwong Kau enlisted his two sons to help kill Choi after becoming “extremely resentful and angry” over her decision to sell the flat where he had been living.

Prosecutor Charlotte Draycott SC said the dispute began when Choi sought to sell the luxury flat at the Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin in 2022. The property was valued at HK$72m (£6.9m).

The court heard that Choi had bought the flat in 2019 for HK$60m, about 17 per cent below its asking price, so that her two children with Alex Kwong could be cared for by their paternal grandparents close to Choi’s home in Kowloon Tong.

open image in gallery Abby Choi had two children with accused ( AP )

Choi registered the property in Kwong Kau’s name to avoid the significant stamp duty imposed on people who own more than one property, prosecutors said.

“The prosecution says it was her decision to do so that set off the chain of events that led to her death,” Ms Draycott said.

Private audio messages Choi sent to her mother were also played in court. In them, she described her estranged in-laws as “very unpleasant”, called Kwong Kau a “crook” and referred to his wife as a “ghost” while expressing regret over her generosity towards the family.

In one message, Choi said: “A huge amount of money was spent on that flat, and it was spent for them. To be honest, for the sake of my children, for the sake of my two children and my good heart, that’s why she can lead such a good life, right?”

open image in gallery Cordons lines are seen outside a village house where part of Abby Choi's body was found in Hong Kong ( REUTERS )

She added: “I divorced his son so many years ago, and I am still helping her son and providing for his children. Yet this kind of person is ungrateful. If she is not a ghost, what is she?”

Choi later evicted Kwong Kau from the flat, accusing him of trying to drive a wedge between her and her two children. He was then forced to share a one-bedroom flat with his elder son at Sheung Man Court, the court heard.

Prosecutors alleged that the family feud reached a tipping point in 2023, when Kwong Kau devised a plan to kill Choi so that he could keep the Kadooria flat.

The lawyer said Choi’s parents were well-off, and the family of her new partner Chris Tam was extremely wealthy. The Kwong family were not wealthy, she said.

“I mentioned the money because it was, as we understand it, the root of what happened,” Ms Draycott said.

Ms Draycott told the court that each of the three defendants had a role in the alleged murder plot, including renting a flat and driving Choi to a secluded location.

open image in gallery Police loads the refrigerator that is suspected of having been used to keep body parts of Abby Choi ( via REUTERS )

“If you find out that were the case, it does not matter which one actually killed her because they were all operating together,” she told the nine-member jury.

The case made international headlines after details emerged about the discovery of Choi’s remains. Her skull was allegedly found in a large pot containing carrots and other vegetables, while her legs were discovered inside a refrigerator at the rented Tai Po property.

Choi, who came from a wealthy family, married Alex Kwong when she was 18 and the couple had two children. They later divorced, but Choi continued to financially support members of his family, according to prosecutors.

She had two children with her second partner and regularly shared her glamorous life of photo shoots and fashion shows on social media. Days before her death, she posted about attending a Christian Dior show at Paris Fashion Week.

Police previously said they believed some of Choi’s remains had been disposed of.

“We believe [her body parts] were disposed of,” Alan Chung, a police official, said at the time.

“The suspects covered the walls of the flat with a sail, and they put on face shields and raincoats so that they would not get bloodstained by dismembering the body,” he added.

The trial, which is expected to last for eight weeks, continues, with prosecutors due to carry on outlining their case on Friday.

The Football Association says it will “take action where appropriate” in the aftermath of the Premier League’s case against Manchester City.

An independent commission found City guilty of almost all of their 115 Premier League’s charges, the majority of which related to serious breaches of the league’s financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. It found City created “sham” commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and conceal costs by more ‌than £900m over the nine-year period.

City have strongly rejected the verdict and reiterated their innocence, with CEO Ferran Soriano calling it a “Premier League conspiracy theory” in a video to members of club staff.

The club is in the process of submitting an appeal which they have until Friday 2 October to do, and could yet take the case to the High Court if the verdict is upheld.

The FA has now released a statement relating to the case and says it will “continue to monitor developments closely”.

It read: “The Independent Commission’s decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game. We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate.

“As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage. We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely.”

A sanction has not yet been decided but it has been mooted that the club could face a huge points deduction or potentially expulsion from the Premier League.

Manchester City are at threat of severe sanctions after being found guilty ( Reuters )

There has also been talk of City’s Abu Dhabi owners being removed, though UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would be “really concerned” if the club was sold as he credited the current owners with being “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”. These comments were criticised and Downing Street has since sought to clarify what Burnham said, insisting that the verdict is “serious”.

City continue to fight the verdict and stated: “The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

“The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

“The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

News.content:

A British paratrooper was killed by an explosion while helping Ukrainian troops in the war with Russia, a coroner has ruled.

Lance Corporal George Hooley, 28, died on 9 December last year after an incident that the Ministry of Defence described as a “tragic accident while observing Ukrainian forces test a new defensive capability”.

After an inquest conducted partly in secret this week, senior coroner for Oxfordshire Darren Salter revealed for the first time that the high-achieving soldier, a member of the Parachute Regiment, had died from injuries sustained in an explosion.

The location of the incident has been kept under wraps, other than that it was away from the front line.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has said that limited numbers of Armed Forces personnel are being deployed to Ukraine, to provide security for the British diplomatic presence and support the Ukrainian armed forces. But the presence of paratroopers in Ukraine was not publicly known prior to L/Cpl Hooley’s death.

Last week, the coroner rejected a media request for a public hearing of the inquest, and on Tuesday this week he reached his conclusion on his own in private.

open image in gallery Lance Corporal Hooley, 28, died in a 'tragic accident' 9 on December while observing Ukrainian forces testing a new defensive capability ( PA )

“L/Cpl George Hooley was a soldier in the British Army serving in the Parachute Regiment in Ukraine,” he recorded in the Record of Inquest supplied to the Press Association.

“On the early morning of 6/12/25 he sustained multiple injuries from an explosion while observing Ukrainian Forces test a new defensive capability away from the front line.

“He received prompt emergency medical treatment at the scene and subsequently underwent surgery but died from his injuries in hospital in Kiev on 9/12/25.”

In correspondence with PA, the coroner said he had been provided with only “limited evidence” about the circumstances and cause of the explosion, but did not elaborate on what that evidence was.

The MoD did not respond to questions about the fatal explosion, including whether the cause had been determined and if anyone had been held responsible.

Mr Salter said he received statements from L/Cpl Hooley’s Army colleagues and British Army doctors, and had also been provided with “Ukrainian documents” which set out that soldier had been treated in at least two hospital, including one in Kyiv.

He added that he found there were “no suspicious circumstances”.

When rejecting a request for a public hearing, the coroner said L/Cpl Hooley’s family “made a specific request for his inquest to be conducted in writing” which he agreed to.

open image in gallery The cortege carrying the body of Lance Corporal George Hooley passes the Memorial Garden in Carterton, West Oxfordshire, following his repatriation into RAF Brize Norton (Ben Whitley/PA) ( PA Wire )

He added that unnamed interested parties had also been consulted and agreed to an inquest behind closed doors.

“Adequate information has been obtained to answer the four statutory questions,” he said.

“Information about the precise nature of the defensive capability being tested is sensitive and would not be disclosed during an inquest.”

He called the death “sadly straightforward”, and insisted that the public interest would be served by the provision of documents after the hearing had taken place.

After his death, the MoD issued tributes for L/Cpl Hooley who had joined the Army in November 2015, joined the Parachute Regiment after being identified as a high achiever, and was an “exceptional soldier” on the verge of being promoted to Corporal.

His company commander called him “model of professionalism”, adding: “George didn’t just do his job, he excelled at it.

“A born soldier, he set the standard – the other soldiers watched to learn how things should be done, he made us all better, individually and collectively.

“He approached every task with dedication, integrity and pride.

“His colleagues will tell you that he wasn’t just part of the team, he was the character within it. The glue. The laughter. The calm voice of sense. The soldier who made the hard days easy and the good days memorable.”

The inquest was conducted “in writing” under a process which was introduced in 2022.

The MoD indicated that unanswered questions from the inquest should be directed to the coroner.

President Donald Trump has said carrying out a lethal injection “shouldn’t be very difficult” in his first public comments on the botched execution of Tennessee death row prisoner Christa Pike.

Pike, 50, remains alive but in a critical condition, her lawyer Randy Spivey said Thursday, after she survived two doses of pentobarbital during an attempt to execute her at a Nashville maximum security prison Wednesday evening.

She was due to be the first woman put to death in the state in 206 years for the brutal, “Satanic” 1995 murder of Knoxville classmate Colleen Slemmer, after a court overturned a late stay of execution. Experts say her survival is unprecedented.

Trump dubbed it an “interesting situation” when asked whether he would push for changes to capital punishment.

Pike was receiving “life-saving medical care” after her execution team went through at least seven needles while trying to find a vein in Pike’s arms to administer the lethal dose of the injection for her execution, Spivey said.

Her legal team has called the botched execution “chemical torture” while Amnesty USA and the United Nations commissioner on human rights called it “cruel.”

From what the future of AI could look like to everyday hacks, Prof Fry covers a broad range of topics, including her science-backed formula for glowing skin.

Earlier this year, Prof Fry appeared as a guest on the Table Manners podcast, hosted by Jessie and Lennie Ware. Discussing everything from food and work to family life and maths (of course), the science guru also talked about cosmetic treatments and revealed the skincare products that she actually rates.

From a hi-tech LED face mask and Korean skincare to a vitamin C serum and hyaluronic acid, a range of beauty bases were covered during the podcast.

CurrentBody LED face mask

open image in gallery ( CurrentBody )

Prof Fry revealed she uses a CurrentBody LED face mask, which is designed to tackle everything from fine lines and dullness to breakouts and redness. “Red light stuff, absolutely legit,” she told Jessie and Lennie Ware. “There are genuine peer-reviewed studies about this,” said Prof Fry, but she added that red light treatments only work at the right wavelength and if you use your mask at least five times a week.

Our beauty writers named CurrentBody’s series 2 model as their top pick in IndyBest’s guide to the best LED face masks. “It covers a larger surface area and wraps around the chin, so you can tackle ageing on the face and upper neck in one fell swoop,” said our reviewer.

After putting it to the test, beauty expert Louise Whitbread, said: “Few serums work as fast as this.” She added: “It contains 15 per cent vitamin C and 0.5 per cent ferulic acid, and is one of the most stable vitamin C formulas on the market.” You can read Louise’s full review in her guide to the best vitamin C serums.

Dyson airwrap

open image in gallery ( Dyson )

Prof Fry didn’t specify which airwrap model she uses. However, our haircare buffs have been impressed with all the airwraps released over the years. News.title: Harry Potter fans will be spellbound by this Ghent hotel haunt
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

With a delicious glance at the fairytale gothic spired turrets above us, we stepped into the dark, hushed warmth of a building that both looked – and smelled – like spells. And that, in fact, was exactly what it was: for the Harry Potter-esque 1898 Porter’s House hotel in Ghent has such exquisite attention to detail that it has even curated its own magic-inspired scent diffuser, “Freyr” – an abundance spell, comprising patchouli, amber, vetiver and myrrh.

What it smelled like to me, however, was a love potion. For this boutique, otherworldly experience didn’t feel like it was for first-year wizards-in-training, heaving bags of luggage (and brooms) onto platform 9 and 3/4. And while families are welcome (there is a Porter’s family suite, complete with terrace, sauna and plunge bath), I personally wouldn’t bring my kids along – because this hotel is sexy. The vibes are cozy, luscious honeymoon, perfect for couples who appreciate something darker and more sensuous; the perfect complement to a winter wedding (or, dare I say, Halloween...?).

open image in gallery 1898 Porter's House double bed – you won't want to get out... ( 1898 Porter's House )

It’s impossible not to feel mysterious (and, I’ll admit, turned on) when surrounded by dark wood and earthy, deep-red hues. Even the hallway doors are, the hotel manager Damien Brunin told me, painted “midnight black”; the housekeeping trolleys specially commissioned to blend in with the rich, heavy curtains, plush carpets, wooden beams and exposed wrought iron structures in the ceiling, which are the same as those on the Eiffel Tower.

Over in the main building that makes up the neighbouring 38-room heritage hotel 1898 The Post, there are secret doors where you must twist a button to open them; an “honesty bar” complete with hidden library, vintage radio and view of the river outside; and a cocktail bar called 1898 The Cobbler (which beats the Leaky Cauldron, hands down).

open image in gallery 1898 Porter's House The Cobbler – Leaky Cauldron, eat your heart out... ( 1898 Porter's House )

There’s also an illusory double stairwell that gives you the impression of walking downstairs (yet you find yourself back on the second floor), a relic of the main building’s past persona as a post office, and an enormous spiral staircase. “We have already ordered 200 floating candles for this staircase for Halloween,” Brunin casually tells me. Hogwarts Great Hall, eat your heart out...

For more from Vix, sign up to her Independent Women newsletter – a weekly dose of smart, sharp and unflinching stories on the issues that matter most.

No, much as my kids might have wanted to join me – and are perfectly catered for in the luxury family suites – I’m afraid that my visit to the latest extension to bougie, boutique hotel brand 1898 (the four-roomed, newly-refurbished, heritage townhouse luxury of 1898 Porter’s House, which opened on 1 September) on this occasion is strictly adult-only.

How else to truly and ostentatiously (it’s pricey, so pretty much perfect for a special and romantic anniversary weekend treat) enjoy the huge wet room with twin rainforest waterfall showers, and the copper ice plunge bath on a private terrace, where you can shimmy out of your hotel robe and into the water without fear of being overlooked (I did exactly that) armed with a glass or three of Champagne?

Kids are welcome, yet 1898 Porter’s House feels like it’s for grown-ups. Specifically: grown-ups who, like me, have an affinity for Morticia Addams, Dracula and Bellatrix Lestrange; fans of Harry Potter, certainly – who have all grown up. It’s much more “Cursed Child” than “Philosopher’s Stone”, even if the staff (kind, sweet, polite) are on the young side.



open image in gallery 1898 Porter’s House feels like it’s for grown-ups ( 1898 Porter's House )

What makes Porter’s House so special are the trimmings. Luxury Parisien beauty and cosmetics house Guerlain is known for being discerning – but never more so than with the brands it chooses to partner with. Guerlain usually won’t collaborate with more than one hotel per city, Brunin tells me – and it wasn’t a surprise to hear that 1898 Porter’s House was its choice for Ghent, its bottles strewn carefully throughout the pure marble bathroom suites.

From the hidden tech in the rooms (the only snag we noticed was how difficult it was to find the right light switch), to the fairylights on the terrace; the home-made negronis and manhattans in potion bottles on the antique writing desk; the carefully chosen coffee table books (one on flowers, one on the Queen) that are changed and rotated every month – and the incredible, 80-item “choose your own” breakfast in the comfort of the Cobbler lounge at “The Kitchen” – my real wonder was why I hadn’t been to Ghent before now.



open image in gallery An 80-item breakfast feast awaited us at 1898 Porter's House ( 1898 Porter's House )

After all, it is barely four hours door-to-door from St Pancras via Eurostar, making it the perfect (and perfectly romantic) sustainable travel option. And with some CityCards from Visit Ghent giving us access to a guided boat tour where we saw Ghent the way it must have looked in the 11th century – when it was the second major medieval port after Paris – not to mention some achingly beautiful willow trees (where, legend has it, if you kiss your loved one you’ll be together for a lifetime); plus entry to see the restored Ghent Altarpiece Painting by Hubert van Eyck and Jan van Eyck ... well – what more could you really wish for?

If it’s high-end Michelin-starred food, then cracking a wand and yelling “Accio” in the direction of Lys D’Or would definitely do the trick, but for me, the really memorable evening came courtesy of “grapes and plates” natural wine bar Chubby Cheeks. It was one of the best meals of not just my weekend, but possibly my life. A “taste explosion” was how I explained it, breathlessly, to my boyfriend.

That’s who I chose to travel with, you see – and I’d advise you do the same. The thing about 1898 Porter’s House is that you need to go with someone you love and desire, because love and desire runs through it like day and night (or Lumos and Nox).

If only I could flick my wand and conjure up a Portkey to take me back...

News.title: What’s the no-spend challenge and could it help you reset your financial habits?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

In a world where we are constantly bombarded by advertising urging us to “spend, spend, spend” – the viral no-spend challenge can help us resist mindless consumerism.

It’s not just about turning an old-fashioned skill like thriftiness into a social media challenge, but also a way for people to understand the impulse triggers that make them press that “spend” button, and help them break that cycle.

Louise Hill, founder of GoHenry, the pocket money and financial education app for kids and teens, explains, “The no-spend challenge is a financial reset which is when you commit to spending zero money on non-essential items for a set period.

“It shows you where you spend your money, so that you take more accountability for your purchases. It creates a really clear categorisation in your mind about what your true ‘needs’ are versus your ‘wants’.”

open image in gallery

Hill also sees it as a “good way to exercise a really important muscle – your money skills muscle”. She adds, “By learning to prioritise your spending and delaying instant gratification, it’s a really useful way of testing yourself and taking back control. Turning it into a challenge is a fun and interesting way to do it – it’s a more positive way of saving money.”

GoHenry’s Hill explains the rules…

Set a time duration

It’s important to treat this exercise as a circuit breaker rather than an extreme lifestyle trend – or you’ll fall off the wagon.

Hill advises, “I would start with a weekend, or maybe a week, but many people seem to be setting themselves a challenge for doing it for a month, which I still think is quite hardcore but can help if major savings need to be made.”

She adds, “You must be clear to yourself and family and friends how long you’re doing this for before you start.”

Ban non-essential items

Invest at least £100 in Stocks or ETFs of your choice. Get fractional shares worth £50! Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Invest at least £100 in Stocks or ETFs of your choice. Get fractional shares worth £50! Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

This is the tough bit and probably a good time to go through expenditure with a fine-tooth comb and decide whether things like subscriptions count as non-essential.

“You need to decide your categories of essentials and non-essentials,” says Hill. “But I would simplify that into ‘needs’ and ‘wants’ – that will help you guide your spending. If you categorise it into your needs, you’ll probably get a shock at how much of it is non-essential.”

She explains the basic differences: “Essentials or needs are rent or mortgage payments, essential groceries, utility bills, transport and debt payments.

“While non-essential or wants are eating out, online shopping, clothes, entertainment, buying extras for your house and takeaway coffees.”

open image in gallery Louise Hill (PA)

Tricks to avoid spending

• Use up surplus food in the fridge and the kitchen cupboards.• Meal prep on Sunday and bring packed lunches to work.• Use surplus food apps such as Olio and Too Good To Go.• Wait for 72 hours before buying something.• Go for a ‘walk and think’ after trying on clothes in a shop.• Rather than meet at a pub, host a games night at home.• Meet friends for free leisure activities like walks in the park and picnics.• Use the library rather than buy books.• Delete online shopping accounts to make it difficult.• Remove saved credit cards from your phone.

Spotting impulse triggers

open image in gallery

The instant gratification of spending activates the brain’s pleasure circuits and releases dopamine – which is why you feel good after splurging on a new coat.

But Hill advises, “Waiting builds patience and decision-making discipline, and if you get to the end of a month without spending anything on non-essentials, that will give you a huge sense of achievement rather than just a quick buzz.”

She makes the point, “This is not about removing all pleasure but making you more mindful about what adds value to your life and what you actually want to spend your money on.”

And it might be worth keeping a mental note of your “almost purchases” to help you understand why you’re spending in the first place – whether it’s emotional or out of boredom.

The immediate bonus

It’s important to have a job for your saved cash so it doesn’t just get frittered away the following month. Unless you have a debt to pay off, it could be used to build an emergency fund, or moved into a high interest savings account rather than left in a current account.

Hill says, “It’s best to always immediately move money into a savings pot so you can see the results as you save. And have a plan to do something with it so you can feel the benefit of all your hard work.”

open image in gallery

The long-term benefits

The extra cash always comes in handy, but Hill believes this exercise will reset future financial habits. She says, “This might have started as a TikTok challenge but if it’s getting people to think about whether they truly need to spend money, then it’s a really useful exercise, especially in a cost-of-living crisis.

“And even when they relax the reins, most people will find they spend less. If they manage the challenge for a month, future spending patterns will be different because they will be more mindful about where they spend their money.”

News.title: FTSE 100 tumbles amid bond market sell-off
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepare for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing 0.2pc growth in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The figure was much worse than analysts had forecasts, with most expecting prices to remain steady.

Over the course of the year to September, the rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc, which was the weakest rate since December 2025.

The value of the average home has fallen to £274,251 over concerns the Bank of England is on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Polanski urges Miliband to block Rosebank oil field over Israel links | Green leader claims North Sea project is a test of Foreign Secretary’s proposed sanctions regime

2) Netherlands ditches wealth tax over exodus fears | Dutch PM scraps plan to target paper profits, instead introducing a more convention capital gains levy

3) Diesel crisis deepens as UK’s biggest refinery shuts for 10 weeks | Fears of squeeze on supplies after fuel costs rise higher than £2 per litre

4) Debt-ridden France branded ‘the new sick man of Europe’ | Investors hope the European Central Bank sees the struggling country as ‘too big to fail’

5) Britain blocks foreign lawyers after surge in south Asian applicants | Bar Standards Board halts scheme unless candidates have already secured a position

What happened overnight

The cost of government borrowing edged higher in Asia as soaring energy costs sparked inflation fears.

Bond yields, a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money, surged in September as investors brace for a period where interest rates stay higher for ​longer.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year Treasury notes hit 5.31pc, the ‌highest level since mid-June 2007. The 10-year yield gained 87 basis points in the July-September quarter, the biggest quarterly rise since 1994.

Market focus has been on how long US Treasury yields stay above the psychologically important 5pc level, while some investors even contemplate the possibility of yields breaching 6pc.

Yields in Japan have climbed to multi-decade highs too, while those in Germany, France and Britain have all hit 17 to 19 year peaks.

On Thursday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government ​bond yield was at 3.11pc, not far from the 30-year high it hit last week.

Asian technology stocks rose after a boost from AI chipmaker Micron, ​although US bonds struggled ‌after their sharpest quarterly sell-off in more than three decades as inflation risks from elevated energy prices linger.

Stalling peace talks between the US and Iran to end the seven-month-long war in the Middle East have kept crude prices aloft.Brent futures surged 42pc in the July-September quarter.

The high-stakes earnings from Micron, a key supplier to AI bellwether Nvidia, signalled strong demand for AI memory chips, with financial commitments under long-term supply agreements at $32 billion, up from $22 billion in June.

That helped push tech-heavy stock markets in Asia higher. Japan’s Nikkei jumped over 3pc, and South Korea’s Kospi reversed earlier losses to gain 1.7pc. Taiwan’s stock benchmark was 0.8pc higher.

News.title: Chewing tobacco killed 250,000 people in one year, study shows
News.content:
Chewing tobacco killed around a quarter of a million people in 2023, with use of the product remaining stubbornly high, according to research.

The smokeless tobacco is particularly popular in south Asia that is placed between the cheek and lower gum. It is flavoured and sometimes sweetened, and users often spit out unwanted juices while chewing. It is often viewed as safer than smoking but it is a major cause of stroke, as well as head and neck cancer.

Chewing tobacco is different to white snus or nicotine pouches, which contain no tobacco. These white pouches are also made up of flavourings and sometimes sweeteners, and deliver a hit of nicotine through the lining of the mouth.

Despite a successful fight against smoking over the last few decades, rates of chewing tobacco use have fallen little and it has often been overlooked in tobacco control efforts, researchers point out. In a study published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in the US estimate that 241 million people aged 15 years and older used chewing tobacco in 2023.

Researchers looked at data on use in 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 and found that there was no significant decrease in the number of users of chewing tobacco over that period. And in 24 countries there was a significant uptick in the number of people using the product. Researchers estimate that about one in five men and one in 10 women in south Asia chewed tobacco in 2023.

Bangladesh has seen the biggest increase in the number of people using the product with 15 million new users between 1990 and 2023. Nepal, Madagascar and Yemen also saw increases in the number of users.

In India 105 million people chew tobacco regularly, accounting for just over two thirds of users globally. Historically, Indians would chew paan, tobacco in its raw form which was mixed with betel leaf and areca nut, a mild stimulant. But the use of chewing tobacco exploded in the 1980s when manufacturers began grinding these into a powder and selling them in packets known as gutkha. This was banned in 2012 but is still widely available. Chewing tobacco is also popular in Pakistan, China and Vietnam.

News.title: Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
News.content:
Dame Esther was a vocal supporter of the Assisted Dying Bill, claiming in March that most people “want and need” the right to end their own lives.

When the bill was defeated in the House of Commons in September, as MPs voted 286 to 270 against the legislation, she called it a “tragic day”. The bill would have allowed those with less than six months to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives.

In 2024, she said that she had joined the Dignitas assisted-dying clinic in Switzerland.

Writing for The Telegraph at the beginning of September, Rebecca Wilcox, Dame Esther’s daughter, said her mother was “too ill now to travel to Dignitas as she had planned and paid for”.

Earlier this month, Dame Esther said in a statement that it was too late for her to “buzz off” to the clinic in Switzerland and said Britain’s current laws on assisted dying are “messy and cruel”.

In a final message shared by her family, the presenter said she had been “immensely lucky” for the support she had received from the public, which she said had enabled her “to live such a long and happy life”.

She added: “Sadly, all good things come to an end, as they say. So I particularly wanted to say goodbye and thank you so very, very much. Perhaps I will see you eventually, on the other side. I do hope so. With very good wishes, as ever, Esther.”

News.title: Eight tips for improving your laptop’s performance (and save your sanity)
News.content:
MacBooks and Windows laptops both have modes intended to maximise battery life. Low Power Mode (Mac) and Power Saver (Windows) should be avoided if you want peak performance.

On a Mac, you’ll find the Low Power Mode switch in Settings > Battery. For the best experience, set this to Never, but remember to change it back if you need your MacBook to last longer.

On a Windows laptop, there are two controls you need to consider. Both are found in Settings > System > Power & Battery.

Energy Saver mode uses multiple tactics to reduce battery consumption, including lowering maximum power. Switch this off, and you have access to Power Mode controls.

Your options are Best Power Efficiency, Balanced and Best Performance. While Balanced is the default, I was able to unlock up to 33 per cent more power by playing around with these settings using my own laptop.

To make matters more complicated, some laptops have their own performance modes. Many Asus laptops have MyAsus or Armory Crate, for example. Lenovo has the Vantage app, Dell has MyDell, and MSI laptops have MSI Center.

3. Stop applications from opening on start-up

If your laptop is slow when it first starts up, it may be because a whole bunch of apps have been given the green light to wake up with it.

Some applications such as antivirus software are critical, but most can be toggled off. As an example, I make sure apps such as Spotify, Steam and WhatsApp don’t open on startup; I only launch them when I need them.

On a MacBook, you can see which apps have this permission in Settings > General, under Open at Login. Select an app entry and click the “minus” button to remove it.

On a Windows laptop, you’ll find the list of start-up apps in Settings > Apps > Startup. Each entry has a little on/off slider.

4. Free up storage space

News.title: Why the UK medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks
News.content:
The UK’s medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks, experts have warned, with the NHS dependent on a system where much of the world relies on a handful of countries for its drug supplies.

India and China are the backbone of the global medicines market, manufacturing around two-thirds of the world’s active pharmaceutical ingredients. This leaves countries exposed to factory shutdowns, natural disasters, geopolitical tensions, shipping disruption and sudden changes in the price or availability of raw materials, experts told The Telegraph.

“We rely now more than ever on other countries to make sure we can get access to the medicines that the vast majority of people take,” said Dr James Davies, director of research and insights at Community Pharmacy England.

Nearly all the active ingredients in the UK’s most widely used medicines are made overseas, around 80 per cent of them in China and India, leaving the NHS exposed to shocks thousands of miles beyond its control.

The resilience of Britain’s medicine supply has eroded gradually in recent years, as global instability has placed growing strain on the supply chains it depends on.

“We’ve seen more global turbulence in general,” said Dr Davies. “It’s not unique to the UK, but it’s affecting countries across Europe, across the Western world, with the Iran war, with difficulties flying things over Ukraine and Russia, and challenges with shipping in the Red Sea.”

In the UK, shortages have been reported across a wide range of products, including antibiotics, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder medicines, epilepsy treatments, hormone replacement therapy, and some diabetes medicines.

The drugs most at risk are the cheapest and most widely used – statins, blood pressure pills and antibiotics – taken by millions of people and manufactured in China and India at huge scale and minimal cost.

“Some antibiotics are almost exclusively made in China,” said Dr Davies. “For some of the blood pressure medicines, they’re more likely to be made in India. But across the board, those two are where most of the raw ingredients for those active pharmaceutical ingredients come from.”

News.title: Fraudster jailed for 41 years over Pakistani nurse scam in Saudi
News.content:
A fraudster who sent 92 Pakistani nurses to Saudi Arabia on fake documents in an elaborate scam to provide workers for short-staffed Gulf hospitals has been jailed for 41 years.

Ghulam Zulfiqar Ali used forged experience certificates, created fake verification QR codes and phoney employment platform IDs.

Ali was being paid by the Saudi authorities to find staff, but also charged genuine Pakistani nurses who wanted a job overseas, in a racket that has caused major embarrassment to the Pakistan’s authorities.

Gulf nations including Saudi Arabia are experiencing a severe shortage of nurses, compounded by rapid population growth, a rising burden of chronic diseases, and heavy dependence on nurses from abroad.

The World Health Organization (WHO) forecasts a global shortfall of 4.5 million nurses by 2030, and recruiting nurses for developed countries is a lucrative trade.

The 91 women were all genuine nurses, but did not meet the criteria for the “Nurse Highly Qualified” visa category under which they were sent.

When the Saudi authorities realised the fraud they deported all the nurses.

Syed Shehzad Nadeem Bukhari, director of Pakistan’s Federal Investigation Agency, told the Telegraph: “They lost both their money and their employment, and the incident caused serious embarrassment to Pakistan internationally.”

Investigators found that between October 2022 and September 2023, a Pakistani employment firm called M/S Sahou Manpower obtained permissions for the recruitment of 108 nurses for a Saudi-based manpower company, to work in hospitals under the visa category “Nurse Highly Qualified”.

The investigation found the Saudi employer bore all recruitment costs, including visa processing fees and air tickets.

It paid the Pakistani recruiting firm between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,100 (GBP 830) per candidate. However, Ali was also demanding between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,000 (GBP 750) from each nurse.

Investigators found the candidates were genuine nurses, but did not meet experience requirements and were given fake certificates.

Meanwhile Ali had not uploaded their details to Saudi systems designed to verify and check qualifications and give each applicant a QR code. Instead he provided them with faked QR codes and verification platform IDs.

Ali was convicted of cheating, two counts of forgery and emigration offences.

He was given 41 years imprisonment by the special court in Rawalpindi. He was also fined £1,904 and ordered to pay £25,031 compensation – £272 to each of the 92 nurses.

His accomplice, Ghulam Fareed, was given three years’ imprisonment and a £544 penalty.

Nasreen Begum, one of nurses, told the Telegraph: “We are thankful to FIA for compensation. Most of us have genuine qualifications as nurse-midwives, licenced practical nurses, clinical nursing assistants and a lady health visitor but our documents weren’t verified and that landed us in a difficult situation.”

Zeenat Khan, another victim of the fraud, said she had opted to take a job in Saudi Arabia because she was jobless despite having nursing qualifications.

She said: “I have three kids and wanted to give them a good education. Now, I hope to get back my money,” she said.

Swera Ali said she had been working in a private hospital in her native Lahore, Punjab province, but received only £50 a month and performed 16 hours duty.

She said: “My parents took a loan from relatives to facilitate me, but my hope of making money from an overseas job was short-lived when they deported us after less than a month.”

Mr Bukhari added: “The investigation established that their nursing diplomas were genuine. The fake QR codes and fake [employment platform] IDs were created by the accused, and the experience certificates were forged by the visa agent without the knowledge of the nurses.”

News.title: How vaccines and antibiotics can beat some cancers
News.content:
At least one in eight cancers worldwide are caused by viruses and bacteria, according to a new study published in The Lancet.

An estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 – out of a total of 20 million recorded worldwide – were caused by common infections, almost all of which could have been prevented with treatments such as antibiotics or vaccines.

Almost half of infection-linked cancers, around 760,000 cases, were caused by H. pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach, researchers from the International Agency for Research on Cancer found.

The pathogen, which is typically ingested through contaminated food and water and is carried by around 60 per cent of the world’s population at any given time, can remain relatively undetected in the gut for between 20 and 40 years without causing any symptoms.

If left untreated, it can trigger chronic inflammation in the stomach and cellular mutations that, in some cases, lead to gastric cancer.

Cases of stomach cancer linked to H. pylori are particularly common in East Asia, where roughly 80 per cent of the population carries the bacterium. This is due in part to the prevalence of a more aggressive strain of the pathogen, known as CagA, which is endemic to the region.

East Asian diets – which typically include salty, pickled or smoked foods – can also damage the stomach’s protective lining and accelerate the inflammatory processes that can contribute to stomach cancer, researchers have found.

While H. pylori infection is treatable with a course of antibiotics, its symptoms often mimic those of other digestive problems and can be difficult to distinguish without testing.

This means the infection can remain undetected for years, allowing inflammation and damage to progress.

Cees-Rein van den Hoogenband told sportnieuws.nl: “That has a huge medical impact. Everyone can see that from the large number of injuries, both nationally and internationally.

ARSENAL have outlined their plans to evolve the Emirates Stadium in a meeting with the Arsenal Advisory Board.

Club chiefs have put a pin in any plans for a “huge scale masterplan” and are instead looking to build on improvements already made to the stadium in recent seasons.



The Gunners explored redeveloping the Emirates in recent years, given the huge demand for tickets and their 60,000-seat capacity starting to fall behind a number of their close rivals.

But any potential project would likely be extremely costly and could even mean the club might need to find a temporary home while construction was underway.



Now, in a meeting with chairman Josh Kroenke and CEO Richard Garlick, the club said they plan on “building on improvements” already made.

Safe standing will extend to 6,650 fans in the North Bank next season.

One of the changes Arsenal are committed to making is the addition of 5G mobile connectivity for fans inside the stadium, which has been a persistent issue for supporters for years.

The club expects the signal to improve before the end of the season.

Sports.title: Until Man City are punished the Premier League will be a farce and a cloud will hang over the tainted competition
Sports.content:
Next

THERE are 33 rounds of matches left until the Premier League season ends on May 30.

Over the course of those 240 days, we’ll have another transfer window and dozens of domestic and European cup fixtures, too.



And every time Manchester City take to the pitch or are involved in a player transaction it will be accompanied by suspicion, disgust, anger.

How can football fans — and moreover the Premier League — just carry on as normal as we come to terms with one of the greatest sporting scandals ever, complete with its “sham” deals?



City’s top brass have made it abundantly clear their tactic is to draw this out for as long as legally possible, perhaps in the hope the Prem backs down or is pressured into a compromise over the severity of future sanctions.

It is impossible to know how long it will take but nobody in their right mind can accept the possibility that City may end the season as champions.



Just imagine how you’d feel if Enzo Maresca’s men are holding the Premier League trophy aloft at the Stadium of Light on the final day of the season.

To carry on as if it’s business as usual until we reach the point when sanctions are finally imposed doesn’t just stick in the craw, it dumps all over the integrity of the competition.

It diminishes it to such an extent that it becomes almost meaningless.

Until they are punished, and in all likelihood relegated, the Prem will be nothing short of a farce.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

It won’t just be their trophies that get the asterisk treatment — it’ll be every goal and every point for the rest of the campaign.

The English footballing world is a different place now than it was eight days ago, before the initial reports of the astonishing guilty verdicts came to light.

When the first leaks emerged in November 2018 and the Prem announced in February 2023 that City were charged with 115 breaches of the rules, there was outrage — but the show carried on as usual.

Now, everything has changed. The extent of their offences is laid out in black and white.

Can any of us truly trust what we are seeing on the pitch for the remainder of this season?



The confidence of every fan — the regular matchgoers and those who pay through the nose for TV subscriptions to Sky, TNT or Amazon — has been shattered.

Not to mention supporters of those ambitious clubs who have bent over backwards to play by the rules.

As long as City remain in the league, unpunished, a cloud will hang over the season, the competition itself tainted.

What are Man City charged with? THE Premier League claim Man City hid £900m in 'sham' deals across a nine-year period. They were found guilty on 114 of the initial 115 charges – with the number now up to 130 charges – which fit into six categories… Failing to give accurate financial information over sponsorship revenue, related parties and operating costs between 2009-10 and 2017/18. Total charges: 50

Failing to provide full details of managerial remuneration between 2009/10 and 2012/13. Total charges 8

Failing to provide full details of player remuneration between 2010/11 and 2015/16. Total charges 12

Failing to comply with Uefa Licencing and Financial Fair Play regulations between 2013/14 and 2017/18. Total charges 5

Breaching Premier League Profitability and Sustainability rules between 2015/16 and 2017/18. Total charges 25

Failing to co-operate with the Premier League investigation between 2018/19 and 2022/23. Total charges 30

Total charges: 130

While the Premier League must be commended for having the b***s to see this investigation through, they must also shoulder some of the blame.



The League’s “regulation light” approach in the 2000s effectively allowed a nation state with bottomless reserves of wealth to buy into the league.

We all know what awaits City on the terraces for as long as they remain a top-flight club — they are going to hear it, non-stop, until their punishment is meted out.

It’s funny how these things work out but it really is a tremendous twist of fate that their first game back after this shameful guilty verdict sees City away at Liverpool.

The club who probably suffered most at the hands of the sky blue cheats have every right to be beyond outraged.

If the Kopites don’t turn Anfield into a seething cauldron a week on Sunday, they never will.



And what are opposition players going to do? Will teams refuse to shake their hands?

Clearly, the scandal has nothing to do with City’s squad.

You can only imagine how uneasy the players must feel about the whole situation.

There have been reports that suggest City knew this verdict was coming down the track back in July.

With a host of potential sanctions at the Prem’s disposal, including transfer bans, is it merely a coincidence they went on such a big spending spree this summer?



Everything they do from now on will be questioned, so the only way this season can avoid descending into shambles is to bring the saga to a conclusion as soon as possible.
