In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Boxing chief Turki Alalshikh calls out Dua Lipa in bizarre rant about pop sensation during Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua press conference
Sports.content:
Boxing chief Turki Alalshikh calls out Dua Lipa in bizarre rant about pop sensation during Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua press conference

Boxing chief Turki Alalshikh has claimed that Dua Lipa has refused to perform at the Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua super-fight in a bizarre tirade against the pop sensation during the launch press conference.

On Wednesday evening, Britain's two most iconic boxers of the last two decades went face to face for the first time since their eagerly anticipated clash was announced last week.

Ahead of the press conference, Alalshikh, who was lauded by Fury, Joshua and many others during the evening for financing the fight, was invited to speak about how the 'Battle of Britain' came to be.

New York's Madison Square Garden and Wembley had previously been billed as potential venues for the 'super' heavyweight clash, but it has since been confirmed that the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Wales, will host the contest.

During his explanation of how the venue was eventually decided, Alalshikh took a swipe at Dua Lipa in the process.

He said: 'I will be honest today, I know that London wouldn't give me the stadium until 2am, and I know that Dua Lipa will not perform in the stadium, because she doesn't like boxing, and maybe she doesn't like me.'

Turki Alalshikh went on a bizarre tirade during Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua press conference

The boxing chief claimed that Dua Lipa has turned down the chance to perform ahead of the long-awaited bout

Dua Lipa's representatives have been approached for comment by Daily Mail Sport.

Alalshikh went on to also explain the financial losses that staging the bout in Britain has led to.

He added: 'Nobody questioned me about UK. I love the British people, I try to deliver everything for them. Put yourself in my shoes; there's a situation to lose $70million (£52.8m); the best is to have it in a good time zone.

'I have two reasons, and I know London won't deliver it; they won't give me the stadium until 2am... Wales delivered it; it's still the UK, the town of Ryan Giggs, let's do it.'

Anthony Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn has been vocal about his and the two-time heavyweight world champion's desire to have the fight staged in the UK.

The chairman of Matchroom took his moment on stage at the British Airways ARC to thank the British boxing community for applying the 'pressure' to ensure the fight is played out on British soil.

Fury and Joshua faced off for the first time ahead of their super fight on Wednesday evening

'I'm excited,' Hearn said. 'Turki, I know we've fallen out, but I promise you this'll be the greatest night you've ever had in boxing.

'On a serious note, when we talked about this fight, you envisaged it for British boxing. This guy (Joshua) has changed boxing in this country. So has Tyson Fury. We are the envy of the boxing world.

'We can't stage it anywhere else. Thank you to the British public for putting the pressure on. We couldn't do it, we failed.'

Sports.title: Ricky Hatton left £30MILLION estate after his tragic death, new figures reveal, as son Campbell claims family are 'completely in the dark' amid dispute over late boxer's finances
Sports.content:
Ricky Hatton left £30MILLION estate after his tragic death, new figures reveal, as son Campbell claims family are 'completely in the dark' amid dispute over late boxer's finances

Ricky Hatton reportedly amassed a £30million fortune before his death last year, though uncertainty remains over how the boxing legend's estate will be distributed.

Hatton, who died aged 46 last September, won multiple world titles before using his fight earnings to build a business empire worth more than £20million, with at least another £10m tied up in property investments, according to The Sun.

Trustees were appointed to manage Hatton's estate after he took his own life in September last year.

However, sources close to the family claim communication with the trustees has since broken down, with one describing the situation as a 'complete mess', according to an earlier report in The Sun.

It was thought Hatton had intended for his fortune to pass to his three children, Campbell, 25, and daughters Millie, 14, and Fearne, 12. However, a year after his death, the family are still waiting to learn how and when the estate will be distributed.

Campbell told The Sun on Wednesday: 'My family is still completely in the dark. We’ve had no involvement in my dad’s finances for over 15 years.'

Hatton, who died aged 46 last September, won multiple world titles before using his fight earnings to build a business and property empire

It was thought Hatton had intended for his fortune to pass to his three children, Campbell, 25 (above), and daughters Millie, 14, and Fearne, 12

During his successful boxing career, Hatton used his fight earnings to finance a string of businesses, many of them linked to property investments in his hometown of Hyde, as well as in Leicestershire, London and Kent.

One source said Hatton was 'determined to ensure that he had a financial legacy from his incredible career'.

'Everyone who knew and loved Ricky would give anything to have him back. But during his life he's done a great job of providing for the people he loved the most, his children,' the source added.

Earlier this month, the Daily Mail reported that Hatton's house had been sold for £1.5m this year after £350,000 was knocked off the original asking price.

The house, where Hatton was found in September last year, was put up for sale shortly before his death for £1.85million but was later taken off the market following his tragic death.

The mansion then went back on offer for £1.75million, then £1.65million before it was sold for £1.5million.

It was described by the estate agent as being a 'landmark modern residence offering luxury, space and unrivalled lifestyle features'.

It said that the five-bedroom six-bathroom property, which was built in 2010, had been 'impeccably designed'.

Earlier this month, the Daily Mail reported that Hatton's house had been sold for £1.5m this year after £350,000 was knocked off the original asking price

One source said Hatton was 'determined to ensure that he had a financial legacy from his incredible career'

Hatton put his own stamp on the property, decorating it with personal touches including a traditional telephone box in the garden and an array of Manchester City memorabilia. Among its more unusual features are seats salvaged from the club's former Maine Road stadium.

It has extensive landscaped grounds with greenbelt views, plus a leisure suite with a heated indoor pool and jacuzzi.

A private gym and cinema room complement a games room and bar area, which is separated from the pool by a striking glass wall.

The principal bedroom suite features a walk-in dressing room, a luxurious en suite bathroom, a crushed-velvet chaise longue and dark patterned wallpaper.

Elsewhere, the property offers multiple reception rooms and expansive open-plan living areas centred around a high-specification, dark-panelled kitchen.

Situated in the sought-after area of Gee Cross in Greater Manchester, the estate is equipped with advanced security features, including CCTV.

The estate agents said: 'This is a rare opportunity to acquire a truly outstanding home in one of the North West's most prestigious and sought-after residential locations.'

For confidential support, call Samaritans on 116 123, visit samaritans.org or visit thecalmzone.net/get-support.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua press conference LIVE: Heavyweight rivals trade insults and clash over Eddie Hearn
Sports.content:
Right, that's it for today.

The first presser is over and now we have two months to wait until we see both Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua go face-to-face again.

Let's hope the next time they face off and have words, it's a bit more fiery and feisty. That was all too nice for me.

Anyway, thanks for joining us for this live coverage and I will see you all very soon.

Goodnight.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua reveals that Tyson Fury's estranged uncle has joined his camp ahead of £150m mega-fight as Gypsy King claims: 'I've not spoken to him for years'
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua made the startling revelation that he has joined forces with Tyson Fury's uncle, Peter, ahead of their eagerly-anticipated super-fight in Cardiff in December.

Never has the calling of a sporting press conference agitated as much, if not more, attention than the event itself.

Without putting Fury and Joshua into the same room in London on Wednesday evening there would have been no chance of them sharing a ring in Cardiff two months from now.

Never has a promo prompted so many startling revelations, either. We might never have known that Fury’s estranged uncle is advising AJ on how to prevent Tyson beating him. Traveller families are usually bonded by such fierce loyalties that we can only wonder about the tensions around the camp fire.

‘Not to worry,’ said the Gypsy King about the defection. ‘I haven’t spoken to him for years.’

Nor might we have learned that Joshua took a mind-blowing pay cut in order to haul the Battle of Britain back home from the clutches of New York.

Even though the ritual stare down was lengthy the chatter was amicable and ended in smiles

When they took to the stage there were very few of the histrionics which are the trademark of most of Tyson Fury’s ticket-selling appearances

How much of a purse deduction? ‘Twelve figures’ declared his promoter Eddie Hearn. That’s £10million at least.

AJ shrugged and cited another fringe benefit picked up during the maelstrom of doubt as to whether this fight between a pair of British world heavyweight champions would ever take place. He also added Fury’s former trainer Ben Davison to his team.

Joshua said: ‘Ben’s pinpointing details which will make the difference on the night.’

Fury replied: ‘Ben can’t put muscles on that suspect chin.’

He could not resist reminding everyone that Davison has just returned from Las Vegas where he presided over Conor Benn’s two-round devastation by America’s great Latin hope, Ryan Garcia.

When they took to the stage there were very few of the histrionics which are the trademark of most of Fury’s ticket-selling appearances.

Instead he advertised ‘probably the greatest fight boxing’s ever seen if you factor in the commercial aspect'.

Which includes the US$150million split equally between the two of them as they put an end to 12 years of public waiting for this fight.

Joshua said: ‘Both of us want to do British boxing proud.’

Even though the ritual stare down was lengthy the chatter was amicable and ended in smiles with Fury inviting Joshua to ‘a pint of Guinness as soon as the fight over, win lose or draw'.

Well, they are ten weeks away from them putting on their fight faces.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White
Sports.content:
It's on. At last. Finally. Confirmed by the almighty Turki.

Reconfirmed by the late, late word sent out that the face to face stare down between our two heavyweight titans will definitely take place at a press conference launch this Wednesday.

The fight that almost got away. AJ versus the Gypsy King. So close to being another of boxing's lost jewels that we almost gave up hope.

May the lords of the rings be praised.

Whether or not Dana White, the American interloper from UFC cage fighting who is demanding a share of the action, is present despite the protestations of Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn, who won the battle for this fight to take place if not at Wembley but not as far, far west of London as New York.

Anthony Joshua v Tyson Fury has been rescued for the British fight fans, by Cardiff. Although like the 70-odd thousand in the Principality Stadium the TV majority will have to stay awake into the wee small hours on the Friday night of December 11.

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will face each other down at a press conference on Wednesday

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on December 11 in Cardiff with the showdown set to begin at 2am so Netflix subscribers can stream it at peak time in America

Fury against Joshua was almost the fight that got away, with the heavyweights now set to sort out differences that should have been settled a decade ago

First bell about 2am so that the tens of millions of Netflix subscribers can stream at peak time in America.

Assuming they buy into this as being a mega fight for all time. Or are satisfied that it is a spectacle unto itself.

Maybe a world heavyweight title adding spice to the occasion. Maybe not. Maybe just two good old Brits sorting differences that should have been settled a decade ago.

And why not? Fury and Joshua may be past their prime but they are not yet the walking dead.

They have enough fight left in their late 30s to put on a show.

And a future to fight for. For the winner there can be challenges to meet from the new generation of champions and a few million dollars more to add to the 75 million each will receive as an early Christmas present.

Always assuming no more spanners are thrown into these on-off-on works.

Good luck to both. Even more so to the Welsh constabulary who will have to deal with all those fans spilling out into darkened streets on what will already be a typically wild Friday night in Cardiff.

Sports.title: For Scottish boxing, the cupboard is bare. All that remains are memories of better times
Sports.content:
Given the endless nonsense that continues to surround the Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua fight, it’s no surprise that it has dominated all the recent headlines in boxing.

Will they? Won’t they? Does anyone even really care any more? Is it happening in the UK? America? Saudi Arabia? Maybe on the moon? For a gazillion dollars?

It felt like a degree of certainty had been reached last week with the announcement that the fight will go ahead at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff in December.

That was until Dana White, the UFC supremo and one of the fight’s chief promoters, said only a few days ago that he ‘doesn’t know’ if it will go ahead.

Perhaps we will get a clearer picture tomorrow afternoon, with Fury and Joshua set to face-off at a media conference in London.

Either way, this tiresome circus act involving two fighters long past their prime continues to be pretty much the only thing anyone is speaking about in boxing right now.

Josh Taylor is dominated by Jack Catterall in Leeds as his ring supremacy is left in ruins

Nathaniel Collins had been Scotland's biggest hope until he suffered two successive defeats

Taylor's rise to the top of the fight game was an incredible achievement that will long be lauded

It perhaps escaped your attention, then, that Scotland’s Nathaniel Collins was back in the ring last weekend. Quite an important fight it was, too.

Taking on European featherweight champion Liam Davies in Birmingham, this was supposed to be Collins’ comeback fight after he lost to Spain’s Cristobal Llorente in Glasgow in April in their world title eliminator.

It did not go well. Collins was floored in the first round and never really recovered, before his trainer put a stop to it all and said enough was enough at the end of the seventh round.

There was a sadness to it all. Not only that Collins had suffered a second successive defeat, but also in terms of the wider implications for himself and for Scottish boxing as a whole.

The defeat to Llorente at The Hydro had been the first loss of Collins’ career. It had been a tough night, albeit not disastrous. There was a chance to bounce back and come again.

But, in terms of challenging at world level, he now looks further away than ever. The same would surely apply to Scottish boxing as a whole after this latest blow.

Not so long ago, Scottish boxing felt like it had a pulse. Josh Taylor climbed the mountain and was, in his pomp, one of the best pound-for-pound fighters on the planet.

The Tartan Tornado put together one of the greatest runs by any British fighter in history to become our first undisputed world champion in the four-belt era. Achieving that in just 18 fights was truly phenomenal.

When Taylor’s career then fizzled out due to a combination of burn-out, inactivity and promotional mismanagement, it had been hoped that Collins would be the next cab off the rank.

The late Ken Buchanan won multiple titles at lightweight and fought between 1965 and 1982

The Nightmare, as he’s known, was supposed to be the fighter who kept the lights on and continued to fly the flag in the post-Taylor era.

That’s not to say he was ever going to be quite as good as Taylor. That always looked unrealistic. But there was genuine hope that Collins could at least be a contender for a world title.

The brutal yet stylish manner in which he dismantled fellow Scot Lee McGregor at The Hydro in May 2025 gave the look of a fighter with all the credentials to go on and box at world level.

But the defeat to Davies in Birmingham last weekend has surely ended that conversation. In the post-Taylor era, the cupboard is depressingly bare for Scottish boxing. Completely and utterly empty.

No one is selling out arenas in Scotland. No one is forcing their way on to Sky Sports and the likes. No one is even close to holding box-office appeal or appearing on pay-per-views.

The amateur and club scene are still doing their bit. The numbers are OK, even if a lot of people use boxing clubs as fitness classes these days rather than having any desire to actually enter a ring.

But when you speak to people involved with boxing clubs across Scotland, the majority of them all share a similar concern.

Plainly, that we have no one even remotely close to following in Taylor’s footsteps and fighting at the top level of the sport. The outlook is bleak.

Listen, Scotland is a relatively small country. We do not have an endless pool of talent. Boxing is not a mainstream sport like football or rugby.

The two successive defeats for Collins have signaled a barren period for Scottish boxing

Kids learn to play football in various different ways; at school, at coaching sessions, or with a club. Maybe even down the local park or on the streets in some very rare and old-fashioned instances.

Rugby is a non-negotiable for those in private education. Even golf now has far more reach and appeal with the younger generation than boxing.

With the awareness around long-term brain damage now greater than ever, you can hardly blame any parent if they aren’t overly enthused by the idea of their kids being involved in a sport where they get punched in the head.

When a generational talent like Taylor comes along and then leaves, the gap is enormous. There is no conveyor belt of world-class operators waiting in the wings.

Sadly, it also now appears that Scotland can’t even offer up any fighters in the bracket just below world level either.

Collins has already come through a serious health scare – a life-threatening twisted bowel caused by infant scar tissue – that put much more than just his boxing career at risk. He has shown heart. No one questions that. He gave it a good go.

But his latest defeat is emblematic of the wider malaise that continues to be so prevalent across Scottish boxing as a whole.

There have been lean times in the past. After Ken Buchanan and Jim Watt, there were quiet periods. After Scott Harrison’s turbulent reign at featherweight the scene thinned out again until Ricky Burns and then Taylor arrived.

Cycles exist. The problem now is that the cycle feels stuck in the downward phase with no obvious sign of it moving back up again.

Where is the next boxing superstar in Scotland? It is beginning to feel like the sport is dying a death. That is the uncomfortable truth.

When Collins fought Llorente at The Hydro in April, it wasn’t even close to being a sell-out. The whole top tier of the arena was closed. Make of that what you will.

And that was a world title eliminator involving the guy who was supposed to be our next big hope. Taylor himself has acknowledged the lack of young fighters breaking through.

The Tornado’s retirement left a void. Collins’ latest defeat has made it wider and deeper. The Hydro still stands ready for big nights, but it’s hard to see a major promoter going back there any time soon.

The Scottish public still loves a fighter who will dig in and go to war. But the fighters of genuine world-class pedigree are simply not here at present.

These are the lean years. The barren stretch. And that should worry anyone who cares about the sport north of the border.

The cupboard is bare. The stars have gone. Until someone steps forward and proves otherwise, Scottish boxing is living on memories of Taylor and on nostalgia about some of the other great names of the past.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury enrolls in drug testing programme after Anthony Joshua threatened to boycott London press conference ahead of £150m Cardiff bout
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury enrolls in drug testing programme after Anthony Joshua threatened to boycott London press conference ahead of £150m Cardiff bout

Tyson Fury has now enrolled in the Voluntary Anti-Doping Association (VADA)'s testing programme ahead of his blockbuster showdown with Anthony Joshua, his camp has confirmed.

The development comes just 24 hours after Joshua threatened to boycott Wednesday's first press conference in London unless Fury could prove he had entered the VADA testing pool.

Joshua had already enrolled, while Fury's camp maintained that the terms of their agreement gave him longer to do so.

But with the first face-to-face meeting between the two heavyweights this Wednesday, Fury has now completed his enrolment and provided his whereabouts to VADA.

Fury's manager, Spencer Brown, told Playbook Boxing: 'We are enrolled in VADA. We are enrolled in VADA. Just to confirm that.'

Asked about the timing of Fury's enrolment, they added: 'He did it a bit earlier than when the fight was announced. In our contract, we had more time, but you know, it doesn't matter. We've done it. We've done everything we've been asked to do. Everything.'

Tyson Fury has agreed to join a drug testing programme after Anthony Joshua threatened to boycott their press conference

The Gypsy King's manager also explained that enrolment and testing are separate stages of the VADA process.

Asked whether Fury had already been tested, they said: 'No, you have to enrol first, don't you? That part of it's all been done, then the testing comes second.'

Brown stressed that the nature of VADA's programme means fighters are not given advance warning of when testers will arrive.

'You could be tested in a week, you could be sitting there on your toilet and they knock on the door,' he said. 'That's the way they work. They don't tell you a time. They don't say we're coming round tomorrow. That's the way. That's why it works.'

The dispute had threatened to become an unwanted subplot to a fight more than a decade in the making.

Joshua's camp had raised concerns after it emerged that the two fighters had different timelines under their respective contractual arrangements, with promoter Eddie Hearn subsequently making clear that he expected Fury to enter the programme.

There is now another significant issue to resolve before December 11: exactly when the fight will take place.

The heavyweight blockbuster will be staged at Cardiff's Principality Stadium and streamed globally by Netflix, with organisers targeting the US primetime market. The main event is expected to take place in the early hours of Saturday morning in Britain, with a ring walk potentially as late as 2am.

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on Friday December 11. The pair are set to meet for a press conference on September 30

Brown has now revealed that the precise timing is still being negotiated and made clear that he does not want the fight to start at 2am.

'I think 2am is far too late,' he said.

'I think that the general public in England will want to watch it in the pubs, the clubs, you know, round each other's houses. There'll be a party atmosphere, and I just think it needs to be earlier. Simple as that.'

Brown added: 'It's all in negotiation at the moment, but it shouldn't be at 2 o'clock in the morning. I certainly wouldn't like to sit there at 2 o'clock in the morning, would you?'

And Brown also questioned the experience for the thousands of fans expected to attend in Cardiff.

'I think 99 per cent of the people will probably tell you that if you're in the stadium, you don't want to be sitting in the stadium till 2 o'clock in the morning, freezing your nuts off.'

The late start has been driven by the fact Netflix is looking to maximise its US audience, while Cardiff's Principality Stadium was selected after the proposed venues in London could not accommodate the required late finish.

The venue can accommodate the late finish, but the event's licensing arrangements have also required negotiation because of the proposed early-hours schedule.

Fury and Joshua are due to meet for the first time in public since their long-awaited fight was officially confirmed at Wednesday's press conference in London.

The bout, which will be contested at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on December 11, is the culmination of years of failed negotiations between the former world champions.

Both men have won their respective comeback fights this year, clearing the way for the long-awaited all-British heavyweight showdown.

Now, with Fury's VADA enrolment confirmed, attention can turn back to the build-up and whether organisers can find a start time that works for both the global Netflix audience and the British fans inside and outside the stadium.

Sports.title: Dana White admits he 'doesn't know' if Tyson Fury's fight with Anthony Joshua will go ahead after Gypsy King claimed rival wants to pull OUT of the £150m bout amid Eddie Hearn's feud with promoter
Sports.content:
Dana White has cast doubt over Tyson Fury's heavyweight blockbuster against Anthony Joshua, admitting that he has 'no idea' whether the £150million showdown will go ahead on December 11.

The battle between British boxing's biggest names was plunged into jeopardy over the weekend, with Fury claiming his arch rival 'wants to pull out' of the fight amid a dispute between White and Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn.

Fury's claim made for a dramatic escalation, with the pair announcing their Cardiff bout just over 24 hours earlier.

White, who runs Zuffa Boxing alongside Saudi Arabia's boxing supremo Turki Al-Sheikh, has been billed as the main promoter for the heavyweight showdown and had fought for the contest to take place in New York City.

Hearn, who successfully wrestled the fight back to Cardiff, has claimed that the contract Joshua signed stipulates that White cannot be involved in the contest and threatened crunch talks with broadcaster Netflix over White's attendance at Fury and Joshua's press conference on Wednesday in London.

That warning appears to have thrown the event into chaos, with Fury claiming Hearn's 'ego' is presenting a major stumbling block in the long-awaited bout taking place.

Dana White has admitted he has 'no idea' if Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua will go ahead

Tyson Fury announced on Saturday that Joshua 'wants to pull out' of the December 11 contest

White, whose involvement has been criticised by sections of the British boxing public, was grilled by the media in a cagey press conference on Saturday night, where he labelled the bout a 's***show' while conceding he has 'no idea' if the contest will take place.

'I don't know. The guy who is supposed to be helping the fight has been hurting the fight the entire time. He hasn't done the fight any favours. I don't know anybody who is more full of s*** than Eddie Hearn.'

When asked whether he would step aside to allow the fight to go ahead, White said: 'That's not up to me. I'm involved in the f***ing fight.

'If Eddie Hearn really cared about this f***ing fight — first of all the fight would've happened a f***ing long time ago, one. Number two, he could finance the thing himself.

'Listen, this whole thing's a s***show right now. We'll all know a lot more in the next three, four days, see how this thing plays out.'

White's comments follow Fury's expletive-laden Instagram video, in which he labelled Joshua and Hearn 'cowards'.

He said: 'Breaking News: Anthony Joshua and Eddie Hearn are trying to pull out of this fight they are saying he is not going to fight now.

'They're little s*** house cowards, mainly to do with Eddie Hearn's ego, he's making up a million different things and threatening that "we're not going to fight" you little coward.

Fury and Joshua have been on a collision course for 15 years but a fight has never transpired

Fury and Joshua's fight was due to take place on Friday December 11. The pair are set to meet for a press conference on September 30

'AJ pull your finger out you white flag, yellow-bellied coward. You know now we're coming home, now I'm coming home the Gypsy King is coming back to the United Kingdom to thrash you in front of all my fans in Wales.'

Fury went on to call Joshua a 'body-building sausage'.

He also claimed that boxing supremo Turki Al-Sheikh is now looking to find a new person to fight Fury at 'the drop of a hat'.

Fury continued: 'So I hope [Hearn and Joshua] are happy you little cowardly b*******, I've never seen anything like [Hearn and Joshua] you pure s*** houses and this is mainly to do with Eddie Hearn's ego. What a little p****.'

The 38-year-old then posted a mocked up poster of himself and light heavyweight champion David Benavidez, hinting that the 29-year-old American could replace AJ in the Cardiff contest.

It is understood that both men are set to pocket around £75million for arguably the biggest bout to be staged on British soil, if it goes ahead.

Sports.title: Vasseur calls for Ferrari unity: Pointing fingers would be "big mistake"
Sports.content:
Ferrari team boss Fred Vasseur has welcomed the public backing of his bosses and called on his team to remain united rather than point fingers and get distracted by outside noise.

While Ferrari has enjoyed an upturn in form under the new 2026 regulations, Vasseur's position returned to the centre of media speculation earlier this week. The cause was an interview in The Times in which former Red Bull F1 chief Christian Horner suggested the Ferrari job would be a dream role, albeit without suggesting he was actively seeking it.

But the comments were enough to spark a media frenzy, especially in Ferrari's home country Italy, which prompted the team to release a statement at the behest of Ferrari president John Elkann and CEO Benedetto Vigna, backing Vasseur.

"This is not just related to the story in The Times of Mr Horner, but in general, there is a lot of speculation about Fred," the statement said. "So again, we have confidence in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so. And the position is clear, but not just now. We already confirmed in the past.”

With Ferrari's drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc also backing their boss on Thursday, Vasseur said he welcomed the support and hoped a sense of relative calm could return to Maranello as the team focuses on finishing the season strongly and advancing the 2027 car and power unit projects.

"When you see the noise and all the rumours in the press all the week, as a team we need to work in serenity and it was absolutely not the case," Vasseur said in a press conference at F1's Bahrain Grand Prix, exceptionally held in Malaysia. "I think the statement, it was mandatory to do something or it would have been the same this weekend. Honestly, the big issue we have today is the stability, the serenity in the team, the focus that we need to have and not to have this kind of question all day."

Fred Vasseur, Ferrari Photo by: Jayce Illman / Getty Images

While handing Vasseur his strongest vote of support yet, Hamilton suggested the structure around the Frenchman could use some tweaking, although he refused to go into details.

"There is a structure that's been there for some time; whether or not that needs looking at moving forward... There are changes that I would make, but I'm not going to talk about what those are," the seven-time world champion said. "Toto [Wolff] is in a different position to Fred and the structure's a lot different. So, that's all I can say on it, really."

But Vasseur didn't feel there was an organisational issue at Maranello and said it would be a "big mistake" to point fingers. Improving his squad's inner workings is a continuous process.

"On the comment of Lewis, I think it would be a mistake to finger-point someone or something," Vasseur said. "In the good moments, we are winning as a team. In the bad moments, we are suffering as a team. And I don't want to speak about a single individual or whatever. Honestly, I think it would be a huge mistake to start to not be unified.

"We had a good beginning of the season. For sure it's not enough, we want to get more, we want to win more, we want to win the championship. But at the end of the day, we had a positive start. We are struggling the last couple of races, but we are hoping to come back soon with development and to be back on the pace."

Sports.title: F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Verstappen pips Russell to top FP1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen topped opening practice for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia aboard a highly competitive 2026 Red Bull Formula 1 car in an uninterrupted session at Sepang.

The four-time world champion posted a 1m37.520s to go 0.383s quicker than second-placed George Russell of Mercedes, with Verstappen’s team-mate Isack Hadjar completing the top three on a 1m38.303s.

It came on F1’s first visit to Sepang in nine years – Verstappen won the last race there in 2017 - which is hosting the Bahrain Grand Prix on behalf of the Sakhir circuit due to the ongoing Middle Eastern conflict.

So with next to no recent data of the Malaysian track, it was little surprise to see teams rush out in the early moments of FP1 with the medium tyre largely being the preferred choice.

It saw Russell go quickest of the medium runners in the opening 30 minutes, setting a 1m38.932s that was 0.522s quicker than team-mate Kimi Antonelli – but there were some outliers.

That included both Red Bull cars, which chose the soft tyre from the off, allowing Verstappen to set the early pace with a 1m38.883s, 0.049s quicker than Russell in second.

Hadjar had a trickier time of it sitting seven tenths off the Dutchman, having at times been caught out by the low-grip nature of Sepang such as an understeer moment at the final hairpin.

But grip was not the only thing to contend with, as drivers had to adapt to the hot and humid conditions of the Southeast Asian country given temperatures hit 32C.

“This is the craziest I’ve ever been in my life with temperatures,” claimed Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto, who was 2.631s off the pace during the opening half of the one-hour session.

“Even more than Bahrain in FP1.”

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

Drivers nevertheless dealt with it, and the final 30 minutes started with Hadjar lowering his team-mate’s benchmark to a 1m38.303s, just as more teams fitted the soft compound.

So lap times kept tumbling: Ferrari pair Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton went 0.064s and 0.287s off Hadjar respectively, before Russell took the top spot with a 1m37.903s.

The upgraded W17 was therefore looking fast, but so was the RB22 – last weekend it took its first double podium of 2026 – as Verstappen soon went 0.383s quicker with a 1m37.520s.

That lap was set with 25 minutes remaining, yet the closing moments saw drivers go back onto the harder compounds, working through various testing programmes ahead of the weekend.

The top three of Verstappen, Russell and Hadjar therefore remained as it was, with fourth going to Leclerc (+0.847s) and championship leader Antonelli taking fifth on a 1m38.580s.

Antonelli just seemed to have a scrappier time of it – struggling to find the pace that has allowed him to dominate the 2026 campaign – and in FP1 he split the Ferrari duo.

So Hamilton took sixth with a 1m38.590s, 1.070s off Verstappen, with Pierre Gasly’s 1m38.715s putting him seventh for Alpine after he took the fastest first sector.

Racing Bulls duo Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad, plus Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg, completed the top 10 in a disappointing session for McLaren, who finished 11th and 12th.

Oscar Piastri was 1.756s off the pace, 0.017s quicker than reigning world champion Lando Norris.

Sports.title: Colapinto handed extra grid penalty at F1 Bahrain GP
Sports.content:
Alpine driver Franco Colapinto is set for an additional grid penalty at Formula 1's Bahrain GP in Malaysia after taking a new Mercedes V6 engine.

Colapinto was set for a five-place grid drop at Sepang, which he carried over from last weekend as a punishment for causing a collision with Pierre Gasly and Lando Norris in Baku.

The Argentinian will now be demoted further for taking a fifth Mercedes internal combustion engine for the year, exceeding the annual allowance of four units.

It is understood that because Colapinto is already losing five places on the starting grid anyway, making a recovery to the points difficult, Alpine felt it was worth introducing a new Mercedes V6 here to minimise the damage. Colapinto will now receive an additional 10-place penalty, with a total of 15 places likely meaning a start on the back row.

Alpine is embroiled in a tight battle with Racing Bulls for fifth place in the constructors' championship, having been dealt a blow by Colapinto's Baku accident as Racing Bulls capitalised. Instead of gaining ground on Racing Bulls, Alpine's deficit grew to 15 points in the Azerbaijani capital.

Photo by: Alex Pantling / LAT Images via Getty Images

Colapinto's team-mate Gasly is also due a new power unit over the next few races, but Alpine has not yet decided when it will introduce the new engine and take a grid penalty.

In Malaysia, Racing Bulls rookie Arvid Lindblad will also take a penalty for taking a new engine, turbocharger and exhaust, demoting him to the back of the grid, while Red Bull's Isack Hadjar goes back five places for taking his seventh V6 engine of the year.

Sports.title: Mercedes introduces new floor, sidepods for F1 Bahrain GP
Sports.content:
Mercedes has revealed its updates for Formula 1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, introducing a vastly reworked floor and new sidepods as it seeks to increase its control in both 2026 championships.

The W17 has been the class of the field so far in 2026, although has faced competition from Ferrari, McLaren, and Red Bull intermittently throughout the season.

Although none of them has been able to produce a concerted effort to challenge Mercedes and its drivers in either the drivers' or constructors' standings, the Silver Arrows is nonetheless keen to keep up development.

The floor updates touch on the floor board, leading edge, rear corner, and the main underbody area – including the diffuser area – while the rear half of the sidepod bodywork has also been revised.

Here, Mercedes has moved away from the undercut sidepod geometry used since the start of the season – and since adapted by other teams – for a ramped profile.

The change in sidepod geometry demonstrates something of a shift in Mercedes' approach to flow management at the rear of the car, albeit without straying too far from the inwash characteristics presented in the previous design.

Comparison of Mercedes' old (below) and new (above) sidepods Photo by: Jake Boxall-Legge/Eric Le Gaillot

With the old-spec design, Mercedes used an undercut to prioritise inwash flow around the Coke bottle section of the car. The new version still does this, but now uses a ramp along the top surface to pull the flow downwards too to enhance the simultaneous downwash towards the top of the diffuser.

By doing this, the team is intending to increase the pressure field in this area, therefore enhancing the pressure differential between the top surface and the air within the diffuser volume. As such, downforce increases.

The changes to the floor board are also quite noticeable, featuring a rework to the three horizontal elements. The upper 'slat' now features a lower leading edge, albeit ultimately resolving in the same angular trailing edge as the older design.

However, there are now two vertical pieces behind this, which offer more flow guidance to the wake shed off the front tyre. These help to condition the flow and bring it outwards, while the horizontal pieces continue to flick airflow upwards to help clear the wake away from the car and allow clean flow to be channeled around the sidepods.

Comparison of Mercedes' floor boards Photo by: Jake Boxall-Legge/Eric Le Gaillot

The team has also reworked the rear suspension fairings and the winglets implemented within the rear wheel drums to further enhance the changes to the floor and sidepod bodywork, as it aims to improve rear-end downforce around the car.

This is Mercedes' first large-scale update package since May's Canadian Grand Prix; the team opted to delay its car build ahead of 2026 to implement as many of its winter developments as possible. This ensured the W17 was a few steps ahead of its rival cars at the start of the season, but left the team with fewer parts in the pipeline for the opening rounds.

"We think it's a good step, purely because it's been so long since we last brought an upgrade," said George Russell, who won for the team last time out in Baku to close the gap to Kimi Antonelli in the drivers' championship to 66 points.

"It's quite abnormal to have an upgrade back in May and then only again almost in October. So as an individual upgrade step, it's large, but in a normal season it's just sort of a normal trajectory where you would have expected from a May to an October upgrade package.

"I'm hoping it's going to propel us back to the front on these types of circuits, which have been more challenging for us in the past six races."

Mercedes will run in Malaysia with a teal and black livery to recognise its title partner Petronas, Malaysia's national oil company and the official fuel supplier to all Mercedes-powered teams on the grid.

Sports.title: The unpredictability to expect for F1's one-off return to Sepang in 2026
Sports.content:
Malaysia's Sepang circuit is making a one-off return to the Formula 1 calendar as a proxy host for the Bahrain Grand Prix, bringing challenges both familiar and new.

The hot and humid conditions, along with the daily late-afternoon rain downpour, act as a Proustian madeleine for those with previous experience of this venue. For others – including most of the drivers on the grid – these are conditions they have only read about.

Sepang occupies a significant place in F1 history since it signalled grand prix racing's aggressive expansion eastward under the Bernie Ecclestone regime. This was the first of many grand-scale facilities with statement architecture, paid for by governments who wanted to put their countries on the map.

It also set the template for the kind of track designed by the architect who came as part of the package: Hermann Tilke. His belief was that wide tracks with long straights followed by sharp corners would facilitate overtaking organically by provoking drivers to make mistakes. Tilke's detractors describe his genre as bland and failing to deliver on the promise of overtaking.

The downside of state backing is that political winds change. In Malaysia, ticket prices set beyond the reach of most locals – just one would cost the average person's monthly wage – meant largely empty grandstands year-in, year-out.

Not the advert the country wanted. In 2017, after 18 years as a fixture on the calendar, Malaysia terminated its hosting deal a season early.

There are certainly more fans this year than used to be the case at this venue Photo by: Getty Images

For Sepang's cameo appearance in 2026, the F1 cars are entirely different so there are many unknowns. Only the ambient heat and humidity, and the abrasiveness of the track surface, are well understood.

At least one driver has likened the track surface to sandpaper. Built to withstand the harsh weather and provide quick drainage, the aggregate has a very open texture.

Tyres produce grip through a process known as hysteresis. Rubber is a viscoelastic material: unlike a fully elastic substance, it doesn't immediately spring back fully to its original shape once compression forces are removed. As a tyre rotates, the outer layer is compressed against the track surface and some of the kinetic energy is lost as heat as the material tries to return to its original state.

The rougher the surface, the higher the temperatures. For this reason it's expected that tyre degradation will be more of a factor here than other tracks this season. That will come as some relief after an Azerbaijan Grand Prix which was a nailed-on one-stop race, even with the soft tyre.

Interestingly, while Pirelli has leaned towards the harder end of its compound family, it hasn't brought the hardest tyre of all. Instead the choices from hard to soft are the C2, C3 and C4 – just one step harder than in Baku.

Sepang's layout, with long straights and sharp corners, is likely to be relatively deterministic in the way the teams will approach energy harvesting and deployment – potentially along similar lines to China, where there was plenty of the so-called ‘yo-yo racing' fans and drivers dislike. But there are some suggestions this may not actually be the case.

"We come to an incredible circuit now," said Fernando Alonso, who claimed his maiden F1 pole position at Sepang in 2003.

"It's going to be sad, the middle sector, because we cannot use the battery there – if not, you don't have [sufficient charge] for the three consecutive straights, you know, from Turn 14 to the last corner, then last corner to Turn 1, Turn 2 to Turn 4, you have to use the full 100% battery on those three straights, so the rest is just charging the battery."

A much younger Fernando Alonso claimed his maiden pole position here at Sepang in 2003 and finished on the podium with first-time winner Kimi Raikkonen Photo by: Getty Images

So the cars are likely to be quite slow through the middle sector as a result – but anyone who uses electrical boost to snatch an overtake will pay for it at the end of the lap.

When deploying the electrical motor, the current cars put quite savage amounts of energy through the rear tyres, so the likelihood of damaging them by causing the surface temperatures to spike is as worrying for the engineers as the longer-term effects of thermal degradation. This will also affect how the teams approach deployment here.

"I think the big difference on this circuit compared with other so-called yo-yo circuits is the tyre overheating," said George Russell.

"So circuits such as Melbourne, Silverstone, Monza, there wasn't actually that much tyre overheating from the surface. Canada as well. So that kind of allowed the drivers to stay a little bit closer within that one second [which grants access to additional power through overtaking mode].

"Even in Baku it was quite cool, the drivers could stay close. Whereas here, surface overheating is going to be a huge thing. You'll be overheating the tyres even on the outlap of a qualifying session, which may make it more challenging to follow closer and to re-attack once you've been overtaken. But that's a total unknown currently."

After several races with little or no degradation, channelling teams into broadly similar strategies, this venue could generate some strategic variety. If so, it would have something in common with the track which usually hosts the Bahrain Grand Prix, another one with a rough surface hostile to tyre life.

This may also be the first proper outing for F1's wet-weather tyres. Here there are more unknowns, given the long-standing fears that the new intermediate tyre is a little too hard, and prone to not warming up quickly enough.

"It will be a good test for sure if it rains," said Carlos Sainz. "A good test for the regulations also because I think with all the issues we have with downshifts, with harvesting, power, variability, corner to corner, the wet is going to be a challenge for sure.

"Both from a tyre standpoint – from what I heard from people that have run them, this year's wet tyre and inter-tyre are difficult – plus the power unit factor [ie large delivery of torque in slippery conditions], it will be for sure a good test."

In 2009 the race start was moved to a later time of 15:00 local, as it will be this year, and a downpour caused the race to be stopped early. When conditions didn't improve, the restart was aborted Photo by: Getty Images

In Malaysia you can reliably bet on a torrential downpour at around 4 o'clock in the afternoon. Sometimes it arrives early; sometimes it clears up quickly, in which case the heat will dry the track quite quickly.

But there are circumstances where it can be raining but, owing to the heat drying the track surface, not wet enough even for intermediate tyres. This was the case in the 2009 running of the Malaysian Grand Prix.

Most people remember that because it was one of the relatively few races in F1 history to have been red-flagged and not restarted before the full race distance was completed. The race start was put back to 15:00 local that year for the co nvenience of European TV viewers, so a drenching was virtually inevitable – and it should have figured in the thoughts of those who scheduled the race at the same time this year.

But what many people forget is that for at least 10 laps before the rain turned biblical, those who had made an early swap to wet tyres suffered as their tyres overheated. Still, given the general lack of running on Pirelli's wet-weather rubber this year, this area remains an unknown.

"The only thing I remember from Japan [where he tested the wet tyres] is that the tyres have zero grip," said Isack Hadjar. "It would make the racing very dangerous with a lot of water. So, I would definitely welcome any competitive session to be a rain session and qualifying. But at the moment, for the race, with all this energy, I think it would create a bit of chaos.

"I don't think we're much ready for that. But definitely qualifying – why not?"

Sports.title: Why Norris apologised to Colapinto after Baku comments
Sports.content:
Reigning Formula 1 champion Lando Norris says he issued a public apology to Franco Colapinto to help calm the waters as his calls for a race ban sparked an online backlash.

Norris slammed Colapinto for causing a pile-up at last weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, calling for a race ban for the Argentinian driver.

The McLaren driver soon reached out to apologise to Colapinto for going too far with his comments straight after the incident, but not before his outburst had triggered another torrent of online abuse directed at him from corners of Colapinto's fanbase.

As a result, Norris decided to also issue a public statement to help calm the waters, although he stressed Colapinto was the only partner that needed apologising to.

"It was more for the wider audience," Norris said on Thursday in Malaysia. "I said what I wanted to Franco and he's the only one really that I need to share my opinion and my apology with.

"I don't need to do it on social media, but at the same time there was obviously a lot of that noise and stuff in the background and I thought it was only sensible to announce or show that I made that apology. I accept that I was in the wrong."

Norris said his chat with Colapinto "didn't need to be very long" as they both accepted blame for their respective wrongdoing in Baku.

"I apologised to him for some of the things I said that were wrong, and he apologised to me for the incident, which is good," Norris explained. "I like Franco a lot, he's a very nice guy, we always talk on our track walk, on our drivers' parades and things like that, so I have a lot of time with him. We were both just apologising to each other, so nothing more than that."

But while accepting he went too far with his comments, he regretted how his post-race comments triggered so much abuse and hoped social platforms could do more to stamp toxic behaviour out.

Franco Colapinto, Alpine, Lando Norris, McLaren, Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT images via Getty Images

"Sadly, that's what we and a lot of sports deal with," he said. "Some of it's down to just passion and that's what you always have in sports, and I think you kind of will always have. I think you see a lot more of it because social media is such an easy thing to share your opinions on.

"And to a certain extent I completely respect it. But obviously, to the extent of online abuse, death threats, all of those things are way too far beyond being a fan of a sport or a driver or athlete, whatever it is. I think there's a line.

"It just highlights the fact that social media platforms, sports need to do more, maybe the athletes need to do more to stop this kind of stuff from happening. Because some people can deal with it much better than others."

But Norris, who has significantly scaled back his own social media usage, said the episode would not discourage him from speaking his mind in the future.

"Well, it depends," he pondered. "I should never have said some of the stuff that I said, so I get why some people might have been upset.

"But I think I'm always happy in general to speak my mind. I know I'm not able to please everyone and you're never going to have everyone on your side, so I think that's normal and that's life."

Sports.title: Ocon fighting for his F1 future - but is adamant he deserves to stay
Sports.content:
This week the Haas Formula 1 team confirmed what had long been mooted in the paddock: Esteban Ocon will be leaving at the end of the current 2026 season. But the man himself has designs on staying in F1.

“My focus is on Formula 1,” he said in Malaysia. “That is clear, that's where I belong, that's where I want to be. So I'm not going to look elsewhere.

“But you never know what can happen in Formula 1. As you guys know, things move every two seconds. So I'm still working on trying to find a solution for next year.

“For now, our focus is that and to do well on track. I think we've done pretty well in the last races and, for me, that's the best way to show that I still deserve to be in Formula 1.

“Of course, I need the car [to be competitive], which we didn't have for many, many races, including last year. So if we have that, it should work, as it did in Baku, as it did in Madrid. We'll see.”

Ocon has had two up-and-down seasons at Haas after moving from Alpine, where he spent five years before falling out of favour with the latest management regime, headed by Flavio Briatore. He won the 2021 Hungarian Grand Prix for Alpine from eighth on the grid, holding on tenaciously to track position he gained by threading through the first-corner carnage triggered by Valtteri Bottas.

His problem is that, to paraphrase the famous Henry Wadsworth poem There was a little girl, when Ocon is good, he's very good indeed – but when he's bad, the results are highly sub-optimal. At Haas he has struggled with a car riddled with inconsistencies, but team-mate Oliver Bearman has generally wrangled better results from the same machinery and invested less energy in complaining about them.

Oliver Bearman, Haas, Esteban Ocon, Haas Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

As an independent team, Haas is among the least well-funded on the grid, so it has often fallen behind over the course of a season through being unable to add significant performance through updates. Last year it got off to an unfortunate start when the VF-25 car suffered unexpected aerodynamic oscillations at high speeds, and was unable to run the low rear ride heights required to maximise ‘ground effect’.

Ocon also complained regularly about instability under braking which came and went unexpectedly. After Friday practice in Abu Dhabi last year, for example, he told Canal+ he “felt like a rookie who's never driven an F1 car”. But for the following days the issues absented themselves and Ocon qualified eighth, then raced to seventh.

“For the past 10 races we should have been performing like that,” he said afterwards. “We clearly missed out on something. It leaves a bittersweet taste.”

Missed opportunities have been a recurring theme throughout the 2026 season as the VF-26 has also been bedeviled by inconsistencies. At several races Ocon has alluded to the car performing differently, with measurable shifts in aerodynamic load, after routine strip/rebuild operations with the same components.

At Monza he chuckled in the media ‘pen' post-qualifying when Autosport suggested he should hire an exorcist.

But it's understood that the team began to feel Ocon wasn't taking enough responsibility for those occasions where he underperformed relative to his and the car's potential – even though Bearman has found his own car to be inconsistent. Ocon has a directness which can be interpreted as undiplomatic at best, combative at worst.

And yet it was precisely this quality for which he was hired.

“No, I don't think that has anything to do with that,” said Ocon when asked if he was in effect being punished for the car's issues.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Joe Portlock / LAT Images via Getty Images

“I've just been doing my job trying to get the cars to where they should be. And at the end of the day, it has benefited everyone in the team because we see the result of the hard work that we've put in, and me pointing the fingers at the current issues.

“Obviously, I was the first one to experience that. So it took us a few races to realise that it was actually there. But we all realise since quite a while now that this has happened. And it's clear in everyone's mind, in the engineering office. So those are not the reasons.”

The most likely candidate to replace Ocon at Haas is Rafael Camara – who, like Bearman, is a member of Ferrari's young-driver programme. He also brings some sponsorship, although this is understood to be a side benefit rather than the principal reason for bringing him aboard.

The only potentially vacant race seats for Ocon are at Cadillac, where both Sergio Perez and Bottas have options for next year which are yet to be taken up. There is also a possibility of taking a test driver role at Aston Martin with a view to moving up when former Alpine team-mate Fernando Alonso eventually hangs up his helmet.

“I'm not going to say I go here or there,” said Ocon. “I keep working with the team, trying to do well, and I will assess the options later in the year.

“But as I told you guys, you know, everything can happen in Formula 1. And I want to be on the grid next year, for sure.”

Sports.title: Hamilton strongly backs Vasseur amid Horner to Ferrari links
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari Formula 1 boss Fred Vasseur "really is the guy to take this team in the right direction" amid destabilising rumours around his future.

Just over one year on from the last barrage of rumours around his future, which were quelled by signing a new contract, Vasseur's future has been under increased scrutiny again.

A recent interview with former Red Bull chief Christian Horner in The Times, meant to promote the upcoming release of his memoir, was construed as him angling for Vasseur's job when Horner was asked about his requirements for accepting an F1 return. That would generally involve some sort of ownership stake, with one exception.

"I did 21 years sitting on the pitwall. I don’t need to go back to that. At this stage in my life, there’s only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership,” Horner said.

“Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It’s the dream. And arguably it’s the sleeping giant of Formula 1.”

Christian Horner, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Horner's comments, and the subsequent buzz they caused in Italy, frustrated Vasseur, because they caused more unnecessary distractions than the team is already dealing with on a daily basis. “We are not working in perfect serenity, if that is the question,” he said.

“For me, first, but for everybody on the team, for the media, for 50% of the questions about this, I think it's a bit of a frustrating situation. Mr Horner is looking for a job – that everybody knows – everywhere."

While Horner wasn't implying he was looking to replace Vasseur, though the media attention that followed won't have harmed his book's PR campaign, Ferrari is unwillingly finding itself on the defensive again. And following a team statement earlier this week that its leadership of Ferrari president John Elkann and CEO Benedetto Vigna remains fully behind Vasseur, seven-time world champion Hamilton has now given his team boss his strongest vote of confidence yet.

"I think Fred has the full backing," Hamilton said in Kuala Lumpur ahead of this weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. "You can see they've obviously switched out lots of different people in Fred's role but Fred is a fantastic leader. He really is the guy to take this team in the right direction.

"There are also people above Fred and it's not about one person. Fred has led the team. He's helped make changes in this past year. He's helped us get to second in the constructors' championship, that's a huge step from last year."

Frederic Vasseur, Ferrari Photo by: Jayce Illman / Getty Images

Hamilton added it was "frustrating" to deal with the air of negativity circling the team, which he noticed was more volatile at Ferrari than at other teams on the grid who are performing worse.

"For me, it's frustrating to see all the negativity because you see other people making mistakes and no one really says too much about them," he pointed out. "We either make the same mistake or are not perfect and we know we're not. It's 10 times worse for some reason for Ferrari. But that's also to be expected given that it's the best brand here, it's the most iconic by far."

Hamilton, who experienced a different leadership structure at his long-time team Mercedes, did acknowledge that he felt Ferrari's way of working was worth looking at, though he preferred to keep his exact ideas private.

"There is a structure that's been there for some time, whether or not that needs looking at moving forward. There are changes that I would make, but I'm not going to talk about what those are," he said.

"Toto is in a different position to Fred and the structure's a lot different. So, that's all I can say on it, really."

Sports.title: Hadjar, Colapinto and Lindblad to take grid penalties in Malaysia | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Three Formula 1 drivers will take grid penalties for this weekend’s race in Malaysia after their teams changed parts of their power units.

Isack Hadjar , who finished on the podium last weekend, will take a five-place grid penalty as Red Bull have swapped his internal combustion engine. Hadjar will use his seventh ICE of the season.

Franco Colapinto will take a further penalty on top of the five-place grid drop he received for colliding with Pierre Gasly and Lando Norris in Azerbaijan. Alpine have fitted his fifth different ICE, moving him beyond the maximum allocation, which incurs a 10-place grid drop, meaning he will be moved back a total of 15 places.

Racing Bulls have replaced Arvid Lindblad’s ICE, turbocharger and exhaust this weekend. As he has taken his fifth example of each, Lindblad receives a 30-place grid penalty. F1’s regulations state this means he will be moved to the back of the grid.

Cadillac have also fitted a new ICE and turbocharger to Valtteri Bottas’s car, but he is still within his maximum allocation of components and therefore does not incur a penalty.

Sports.title: Verstappen quickest in first session as drivers encounter “insane” tyre degradation | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The last Formula 1 driver to win a grand prix in Malaysia was quickest in the first practice session for nine years at the Sepang circuit.

Max Verstappen again demonstrated Red Bull’s recent resurgence in form as he set a quickest time of 1’37.520.

As pre-event predictions of high tyre degradation on the abrasive track came true, Verstappen spent the entire session on soft rubber, preserving his stock of harder compounds for later in the event. George Russell used one set each of the softs and mediums as he set the second-fastest time in the upgraded Mercedes, almost four tenths of a second slower than Verstappen.

“Tyre degradation is insane” acknowledged Charles Leclerc as he set the fourth-fastest time of the session behind Verstappen’s team mate Isack Hadjar.

Mercedes introduced a significant upgrade for their car, which is also sporting a special livery this weekend. Championship leader Andrea Kimi Antonelli, who like his team mate is making his first visit to Sepang, went fifth-quickest ahead of Lewis Hamilton.

Both McLaren drivers were also experiencing the Sepang International Circuit for the first time and had a poor start to practice. Both finished the opening session outside the top 10.

All four Red Bull-Ford-powered cars appeared in the top 10. The Racing Bulls pair occupied eighth and ninth behind Pierre Gasly’s Alpine. Nico Hulkenberg completed the top 10 for Audi.

Sports.title: Norris calls for “respect and humility” after “death threats” on social media | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lando Norris says people posting death threats on social media in reaction to his collision with Franco Colapinto last week went “way too far.”

The reigning world champion explained why he apologised to Colapinto, and again in public, for the critical remarks he made after the Alpine driver took the pair of them out of last week’s race. Norris called for Colapinto to be banned and said he did not deserve to be in Formula 1.

“I don’t normally think I get caught up in the heat of the moment, but this was certainly one of the cases where I think I did,” said Norris. “For me, the most important thing was to speak to Franco about it.

“He’s the only guy that I want to direct something to and care about in this situation and that’s what I did. So I spoke to him already Sunday night, as soon as I could.

“And of course, I then put the post out later in the week to apologise, to let everyone know that I did it, because there was also the rest of the world that I felt like I owed the apology to.

“As drivers, we all get along. Franco is a good friend of mine. I get on with Franco very well. He always means well. He’s a very good guy.”

Alpine also criticised the reaction to the collision on social media. The team and others have spoken out several times on the issue of social media abuse over the past year, often in response to incidents involving Colapinto.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Norris said the series needs fans who are enthusiastic but never abusive.

“The thing is, you see this in every sport. And I certainly support big fan bases and having great fans and all of that. I think it’s great and it’s normal that you support [some] people and don’t support [other] people. I think you get that in every sport.

“But there’s obviously a certain level of how far you take that. And especially on social media, people are happy to hide behind keyboards and that type of thing, but I think abuse always takes things too far, death threats are certainly one thing that takes things way too far.

“We want passionate fans, we want people who love our sport, we want to cheer for drivers and things like that. You don’t need to cheer for everyone, I certainly don’t think I’m gonna get all the fans, you’re not going to win over all of the fans, things like that. But there’s just a level of respect and humility I think people should have. We all make mistakes.

“One of those things was me making a mistake last weekend, but there’s a level of things and as a community we need to understand how we can make it better, not just in Formula 1 and on social media, but in every sport because sadly it’s the thing that happens around the world everywhere.”
