The satellite launched today is a prototype that Beals called "a very minimal test" to make sure the chips can run in space. A SpaceX rocket carried it into orbit, and Planet will get it up and running. Beal said Google will then fire up and test the TPUs. The goal is for the mission to be operational for a year.

toggle caption i Google

Brandon Lucia, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, said the idea sounds "very sci-fi," but much of the technology has been proven at a research level.

Still, there are huge challenges. Heat is a big one. Computer chips get hot, and on Earth the heat can be dissipated with wind or water. That's not possible in the vacuum of space.

"In a satellite in particular, using more power to do the computations means dumping more heat into the confined environment inside of the satellite," Lucia said.

In its blog post, Google called cooling the chips "a crucial research challenge," and outlined some of the approaches it's working on, including using a combination of pipes and radiators to wick heat away from the chips.

Beal said the radiators are one of the heaviest components on the current mission — a drawback because heavier objects are more expensive to launch — and his team is working on ways to cool chips more efficiently.

Lucia points out that there are also major questions about upkeep. When a chip malfunctions in a terrestrial data center, or something goes on the fritz, a technician can walk in and fix it. That's harder when the data center is circling hundreds of miles above Earth.

Sponsor Message

"Those all have their cost and complexity amplified by a factor of 10, maybe a factor of 100. And so there has to be a big payoff," Lucia said.

And there are environmental questions, too. While space data centers would run on solar power, the rockets that launch them run off of carbon-based fuels. And eventually they will re-enter earth's atmosphere, potentially adding pollution as they burn up.

Elon Musk has said that space is the "only way to scale" data centers to meet future demand for AI. But the economics are still a question mark. Launches are costly, repairs are difficult, and communication by laser across hundreds of miles and through Earth's atmosphere is slower. And it will take constellations of many satellites to equal the computing capacity of a terrestrial data center.

Beals said he and his small team think about these questions a lot. "It doesn't help a lot if this is technically possible, if it's always going to be too expensive to be practical," he said.

He added that it is difficult to know when space-based data centers will be economically viable. "I don't see this being something where it's cheaper to do this in the next five years. I think it will take longer than that," he said.

And he doesn't think that space data centers will replace terrestrial data centers any time soon. "I think that there are going to be use cases that make more sense to do on Earth and use cases that make more sense to do in space," Beals said. "In the really-long run, perhaps the set of things you do in space gets larger and larger until that's where most of the compute is happening. But I think for a long time you'll have both coexisting."

The whole project, he said, is a "moonshot."

Sponsor Message

"It's going to take a long time," he said. "It's not going to be a completely straightforward journey."

Google is a financial supporter of NPR.

World.title: A judge permanently dismisses former Olympian's Reflecting Pool charges
World.content:
A judge permanently dismisses former Olympian's Reflecting Pool charges

toggle caption i Mark Schiefelbein/AP

A judge has dismissed with prejudice the government's vandalism charges against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn. That means federal prosecutors cannot refile them in the future, despite President Trump's public demands to do so.

In fact, as D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman explained in a 26-page ruling released Thursday, the case should be permanently closed in large part because of the "political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers."

Sponsor Message

"While the prosecutors admit that the evidence indicates that he committed no crime, the President's statements create a risk that Mr. Hearn will be prosecuted nonetheless, either because the current United States Attorney and her assistants will eventually yield to his public pressure campaign or because the President will replace them with prosecutors more likely to carry out his wishes," wrote Edelman, an Obama appointee.

Hearn, 67, was arrested at the Reflecting Pool in June, around the time its multimillion-dollar new blue lining started noticeably peeling off in chunks. He was charged with one felony count of property destruction and quickly indicted by a grand jury, though he pleaded not guilty.

In late July, however, with a trial start date — and the prospect of up to 10 years in prison if convicted — looming, Pirro's office abruptly asked the judge to drop the charges against Hearn and three others altogether.

Citing new reports from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, federal prosecutors admitted that the Reflecting Pool damage was, in fact, "the result of botched installation and not vandalism."

Trump disagreed, and publicly urged Pirro to revisit the case — which Thursday's ruling prevents.

When asked for comment, the White House referred NPR to three of Trump's Truth Social posts from August, blaming the Reflecting Pool damage on vandals and disagreeing with U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro's decision to drop charges against Hearn in the first place.

toggle caption i Mark Schiefelbein/AP

Neither the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. nor the Department of Justice returned NPR's requests for comment in time for publication.

Sponsor Message

Hearn's lawyers — Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann, Steve Levin and Michael Bromwich — celebrated the ruling in a joint statement, calling it "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice."

"This case never should have been brought in the first place," they said. "This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American."

The soft-spoken Maryland resident quickly became a cause célèbre for the many Americans captivated by the Reflecting Pool saga, which some saw as a referendum on the Trump administration itself.

In an August interview with NPR, Hearn described his experience as "Kafkaesque" and "Orwellian," but said he was buoyed by the support he'd received from within and beyond his community.

"With the power of the law, the power of the courts, and my wonderful team, I feel very well equipped … to bring democracy back to me," he said.

Trump's public pressure campaign

Trump railed against Pirro in the days and weeks after she dropped the charges, saying she had "choked" and "folded like an umbrella" — and didn't rule out firing her. He continued to blame the damage on vandalism and wrote on social media that anyone who disagreed "should go back to Law School."

"Most concerningly," Edelman wrote, during that time, the president also leveled increasingly personal attacks against Hearn and his legal team.

"U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro should re-visit her hastily made decision, especially since it turned out that the 'gentleman' involved is a big player in ActBlue, a disgraceful fundraising SCAM, and is represented by a TRUMP DERANGED SLEAZEBAG, Political Hack Lawyer, Norm Eisen," Trump wrote in early August, in one of the social media posts the White House directed NPR to on Thursday.

It's against that backdrop that Hearn's legal team has been lobbying the judge to dismiss the charges with prejudice, to prevent the same case from being revived. The Trump administration, on the other hand, sought to leave that door open.

Sponsor Message

Edelman's Thursday ruling offers a peek into the government's argument — and then dismantles it.

toggle caption i Rod Lamkey/AP

Edelman wrote that when asked in court what kind of hypothetical new evidence might prompt prosecutors to revisit the case, an unnamed assistant U.S. attorney "waxed philosophical, musing, 'I don't know what the future may bring. None of us do.'"

He says prosecutors could not provide any specific examples of such evidence, and "admitted that the government was no longer even investigating the case."

"Given its own description of the existing evidence and the circumstances of this case, the development of contrary evidence seems practically inconceivable, and the possibility of a future meritorious prosecution strikes the Court as fanciful," Edelman concluded.

Hearn's lawyers say Thursday's ruling allows him "to move forward with his life as he deserves."

The Reflecting Pool, which was drained after July 4th, remains empty and fenced off for repairs, with no public timeline for completion.

World.title: AI data centers: How much are ratepayers on the hook for?
World.content:
AI data centers: How much are ratepayers on the hook for?

toggle caption i Stephen Maturen/Getty Images North America

Ahead of the midterm elections, Congress is scrambling to show that it understands voter concerns about AI data centers and their potential impact on electricity rates. But answering the question of how much of those costs will be shouldered by residential utility customers is surprisingly difficult to answer.

That uncertainty is at the heart of a growing fight on Capitol Hill, as lawmakers advance competing proposals aimed at protecting ratepayers in a debate that often belies the complexity of the underlying economics.

On Capitol Hill this week, Republicans have been trying to push through the Ratepayer Protection Act , sponsored by Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted. The bill would have state utilities consider holding "large-load" customers responsible for the increased costs.

Sponsor Message

Husted is in a heated reelection campaign against Democrat Sherrod Brown, who lost his Senate seat in 2024. Brown has made Husted's past support of data centers in Ohio a major campaign issue. The bill easily passed the House in September with strong bipartisan support.

Senate Minority Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer opposes the measure, saying its protections for ratepayers are voluntary. Instead, Schumer is promoting the GRID Savings Act, a similar bill authored by New Mexico Democrat Sen. Martin Heinrich, which he says has more teeth.

Several other data center and AI-related bills are at various stages in the legislative process.

The cost of AI is showing up in customers' bills

The question of how much of the energy and grid costs are being borne by ratepayers is a complicated one and has no universal answer, experts tell NPR. They say it varies by utility and state, but that in the end residential electricity customers will pay for a share of the AI buildout.

By one estimate , Maryland customers, for example, pay somewhere around $168 to $216 more per year on their electricity bills primarily due to the data center boom.

"We're talking tens to hundreds of millions of dollars [of infrastructure] that are being built by these local utilities," says Connor Waldoch, co-founder and chief strategy officer at Grid Status, which focuses on making electricity-market data easier to access and understand. "In many cases, it is just ultimately going to end up in customers' bills."

Sponsor Message

Tracking the impact of data center growth on residential bills isn't easy, however. How much of the increase is passed on to residential customers and when, depends on utilities' power-purchasing contracts, retail rates and regulatory decisions about who pays, according to Lucy Qiu, a professor at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland.

PJM is a regional transmission organization that coordinates the electricity grid and wholesale power market across 13 states and the District of Columbia. It supplies power to Northern Virginia, home to the largest concentration of data centers in the world. PJM's Independent Market Monitor estimates that data centers have cost their 67 million ratepayers about $29 billion over roughly the past two years.

"Everyone pays those costs," says Ari Peskoe, director of the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative. "They're spread across the region to every business and resident that has an electricity meter."

toggle caption i Nathan Howard/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

How to determine who the grid infrastructure benefits?

Data center growth can push up wholesale costs of energy by increasing demand. This determines how much generating capacity utilities and regional grid operators need to secure, Qiu says. There are also costs with building new power lines, substations and other infrastructure to connect data centers to the grid. Determining how much of that exclusively serves data centers — and how much also benefits other customers — is part of the difficulty in determining who gets the bill, she says.

"It really depends on the scale of the upgrade and also how utilities are doing the accounting of that different share, whether it's being used solely by the data centers or also being shared by other customers," Qiu says.

No "single, clean number"

Even so, "a single, clean number" that applies nationwide is just not possible, Harvard's Peskoe says, because "a lot of the data about how much particular data centers are paying is hidden behind non-disclosure agreements."

Sponsor Message

Those NDAs have become a major sore spot on the local level, as residents opposed to new data centers call out local officials for the secrecy that has surrounded many deals. A study last year by the University of Mary Washington found that NDAs had been signed in 80% of Virginia localities where there were existing, approved or proposed data centers.

In an email to NPR, Jeremy L. Slayton, a spokesman for Dominion Energy, which serves Loudoun County, Va., home to about 250 data centers, said, "We recover costs for distribution and transmission infrastructure from customers."

"These assets are core to the reliable electric service we provide our customers. All costs we recover from customers are reviewed and approved by the Virginia State Corporation Commission," he said, referring to the independent state agency that regulates public utilities.

Added costs of building out in a hurry

There is still another factor at play, University of Maryland's Qiu says. The data center industry is in a hurry and waiting for new power-generation technologies doesn't seem to be in the cards. As a result, to meet the demand, utility companies will likely need to opt for less efficient power plants and those costs will be passed onto consumers over time, as well.

One other consideration is optics, Waldoch of Grid Status says. Big customers like AI data centers pay less per kilowatt hour for power than residential customers do. Think of it as a volume discount. In the current environment where 70% of Americans are worried that data centers will increase their electricity bills, Waldoch says, "If you're saying, hey, this data center is actually paying a lot less for electricity than you are, even though it matters much less to them ... it's not like that's palatable for a lot of people at this point."

Benefits of the AI buildout

But not all price increases in recent years are linked to data centers, Qiu says.

Sponsor Message

"The fuel cost ... is a very important factor," she says and some of those new substations and power lines were going to need to be replaced anyway due to things like extreme weather events.

Qiu also notes that the U.S. power grid needs upgrades to accommodate higher demand for things like electric vehicles. The AI boom "can accelerate the upgrade of the grid infrastructure," she says.

There's also evidence, Qui says, that resiliency — the ability to survive high-impact events such as extreme heat and to recover from outages — is better for people living near data centers due to the robust infrastructure those facilities require. "So if there's a data center, it actually helps … improve the local grid reliability [and] reduce the power outages," says Qui.

World.title: New York Attorney General Letitia James made special prosecutor in Cornell rape investigation
World.content:
New York Attorney General Letitia James made special prosecutor in Cornell rape investigation

toggle caption i Spencer Platt/Getty Images

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has appointed the office of New York Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor in the investigation into allegations of a gang-rape at Cornell University.

"Newly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney not to prosecute an alleged sexual assault on Cornell University's campus in October 2024," Hochul said in a statement.

"This has, in turn, undercut my faith, and the public's faith, in the district attorney's ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time," she added, explaining why she was appointing James.

Sponsor Message

The woman who alleges she was gang raped by fellow Cornell University students in 2024 clearly stated in her statement to police two years ago that she was sexually assaulted.

That's according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, who confirmed to NPR that his client told investigators, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," citing transcripts from Jane Doe's sworn statement in 2024.

NPR asked Giuffra to specifically confirm on the record to NPR that his client made this exact quoted statement regarding her assault. His response by text: "Yes she did."

This is in contrast to statements from the local prosecutor, who claimed on Monday that Doe never stated she was raped. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NPR local station WSKG on Wednesday that he had not read the full account of her detailed statements to investigators where she repeatedly described being assaulted.

NPR asked Cornell if campus police provided the DA with all of the information from their investigation, including her repeated statements about being assaulted. The university did not respond to the request for comment.

CBS News New York reported Wednesday on a transcript of an interview between the Cornell University Police Department investigator and the alleged victim. NPR has not been able to obtain a copy of these transcripts.

Sponsor Message

Van Houten said in Monday's statement that in the 2024 statement taken by Cornell University police, Doe "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."

No criminal charges were ever filed against the seven men Doe alleges drugged and assaulted her for several hours in October 2024.

Van Houten told NPR member station WSKG on Wednesday evening that he was in the process of getting the interview transcript from Cornell. He told the station over email that he doesn't know when he will get the transcript from the university "or if Cornell will resist turning it over."

"If it's factual, we absolutely should have been informed about what Jane Doe said to police that was not in her six-page statement," he told WSKG.

Van Houten said earlier this week that his office is reexamining the case.

He added that particular transcript is part of the confidential Title IX investigation Cornell launched into the alleged assault.

In mid-September, Doe filed a lawsuit against the seven men who she alleges assaulted her two years ago. Cornell was also named in the lawsuit.

Following the onslaught of public backlash against Cornell and the local prosecutor, the school said Wednesday night that it will bring in an outside counsel to conduct an independent probe into the handling of the case.

Discrepancies mount

Since Tuesday, Cornell has directed the public to an FAQ page on the rape allegations.

The university has maintained that Cornell University Police investigated the case thoroughly and that the school held its own Title IX investigation, which resulted in suspensions and expulsions. Cornell has not specified how many students faced punishments, or of what nature. It noted in the FAQ: "Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students, and the university is therefore unable to make a public statement regarding any other disciplinary response."

Sponsor Message

WSKG found that as of Wednesday, the university has changed its FAQ. And it has quietly removed a sentence stating that the Cornell police "shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office."

Previously, the FAQ read: "The Cornell University Police Department investigated the matter in 2024 and shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, which is the established protocol if the department believes it is possible a crime has occurred."

But by Wednesday afternoon, WSKG found that statement had been edited, and any mention of Cornell police sharing "all investigatory information" with the district attorney had disappeared from the page.

"The Cornell University Police Department is a unit of the university, and its officers are sworn Tompkins County deputy sheriffs whose duties include the enforcement of law and order on Cornell property," the new statement reads. "This incident occurred in Cornell's jurisdiction."

WSKG reported that Cornell University did not respond to its questions about these changes.

Students at the university have expressed outrage and deep disappointment toward school officials for their handling of this case. The Cornell University Student Assembly held a public hearing on Thursday afternoon demanding "institutional accountability" from their school.

"We stand unequivocally with survivors of sexual violence, and we remain committed to ensuring that their voices are not only heard, but met with action," the organization said in a statement on Instagram.

Probes into Cornell's handling of the case to begin

Late Wednesday, the school confirmed to NPR that it is bringing in an outside counsel to hold an independent examination of the alleged gang rape.

University officials told NPR they have no further details about how the investigation will play out. Previously, Cornell strongly defended how it handled the case when Doe first reported the incident to school officials two years ago.

Sponsor Message

In addition to appointing James to investigate the case, Hochul said in a video posted on X that she's considering new legislation to tighten sexual assault laws across the state.

"While we have some of the toughest laws on sexual assault on college campuses right here in New York, I think we can do better," she said. "This culture has to stop. And it will stop here in the state of New York."

Kate Bartlett and WSKG's Aurora Berry contributed reporting.

World.title: New space station crew launches from Florida on SpaceX's Crew Dragon capsule
World.content:
New space station crew launches from Florida on SpaceX's Crew Dragon capsule

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Fla. — Despite concerns about thunderstorms and gusty winds, SpaceX launched four people on NASA's Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station.

The Falcon 9 rocket leaped off the launch pad at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station and soared northeast, over the Atlantic Ocean. It will take the capsule about eight hours to catch up with and dock to the space station. The four crew members will spend up to six months living and working aboard the outpost before returning home.

The crew includes two NASA astronauts. Commander Jessica Watkins, a geologist, is making her second trip to space, previously launching to the space station on the Crew-4 mission in 2022, and totaling 170 days in space (She was the first Black woman to serve on the space station, and has the most time in space of any Black woman). Pilot Luke Delaney, a naval aviator, is making his first trip to space. He's from DeBary, Fla., around 50 miles from the Space Coast.

Sponsor Message

"I did grow up pretty close to here," he said ahead of his flight. "I got to watch Space Shuttle launches, and now I'm going to get to see it from a little bit different perspective."

Deltona High School — where Delaney attended — declared Thursday "Luke Delaney Day" as students gathered outside to watch him take flight.

Mission specialists from Canada and Russia are joining the crew. Canadian Space Agency's Joshua Kutryk and Roscosmos' Sergey Teteryatnikov are both making their first trip to space.

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Their capsule is named Grace and is the fifth and final Dragon spacecraft built by SpaceX. It's only made one trip to the space station, ferrying four private astronauts on the Axiom Ax-4 mission.

The mission name is similar to a well-known NASA mission in history: Apollo 13. An explosion just 55 hours into that mission in 1970 crippled the Apollo 13 crew's spacecraft, and NASA raced to find a solution to bring the crew home safely.

While not superstitious themselves, the members of Crew-13 incorporated elements of the Apollo 13 mission into their mission patch, remembering the ingenuity and bravery that saved that crew.

"I think it really represents what we can do when we're faced with extremely challenging and dire circumstances," said NASA's Dana Weigel. "I give the crew a lot of credit for giving the nod to Apollo 13 and kind of giving credit to that and representing that in the mission patch that they chose."

Sponsor Message

The Crew-13 members will spend their time on the space station performing maintenance on the orbiting lab and conducting science experiments – some even on the crew themselves. They'll work on a stem cell investigation that will help researchers better understand the treatment of Parkinson's disease, investigate crop production in space to prepare for long-duration missions, and test new medical equipment for monitoring crew health.

The mission was delayed in August after a leak of oxidizer was detected on the Dragon capsule during processing. NASA and SpaceX pushed the mission from a mid-September launch to find and fix the issue.

"It took a lot of effort, time, [and] many, many hours in determined troubleshooting to put us on the right path for launch," said Lori Glaze, NASA's head of human spaceflight.

Crew-13 will relieve members of the Crew-12 mission, which launched to the station in February. They'll make the trip back to Earth next week, splashing down off the coast of Southern California.

This mission is SpaceX's 13th operational mission for NASA, and 14th total for the agency. (SpaceX launched a test flight carrying two astronauts to the station in 2020.) The company has flown additional private missions to space as well, both to the space station and orbital missions. NASA's current administrator, Jared Isaacman, funded and flew two of those missions before taking the agency's top job.

World.title: Hidden cameras show some stores unlocking speed limits on e-bikes, selling e-scooters that go up to 120 km/h
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Whether it's children cruising down a suburban street, drivers delivering food downtown or a daredevil taking their need for speed to the highway, electric bikes and electric scooters are becoming more common across Canada.

A new hidden camera investigation by Marketplace shows how some stores are selling e-scooters and e-bikes with top speeds much higher than provincial speed limits and with recommended rider ages younger than provincial regulations allow.

Most provincial traffic laws limit e-bikes and e-scooters to 32 kilometres per hour or less. Age restrictions, meanwhile, vary across the country, ranging from 12 to 18. The territories and some provinces have no minimum age to ride.

That means it is mostly up to local police services to enforce these rules at a time when the number of injuries caused by these vehicles is climbing yearly, and public calls are growing for stronger, consistent rules nationwide and better enforcement .

Marketplace visited some of Canada's most well-known big box and specialty shops in the Greater Toronto Area — Amego, Emmo, EZbike, Best Buy, Canadian Tire and Costco — that sell popular brands. The undercover journalists tested how easy it is to find an e-bike or e-scooter that either had a maximum speed or age recommendation contravening Ontario limits.

In Ontario, e-scooter and e-bike riders must be at least 16. E-scooters cannot travel faster than 24 km/h on a flat surface, and e-bikes cannot travel faster than 32 km/h, according to provincial laws.

10 of 12 stores exceeded Ontario limits

Of the 12 stores journalists visited undercover, salespeople at six stores told us or showed us how to bypass built-in speed limits.

While most stores reminded us of Ontario rules, 10 stores sold e-bikes or e-scooters with maximum speeds beyond Ontario limits.

Stores are allowed to sell the e-bikes no matter how fast they go, but Michael Pasquali, founder of the Canadian Electric Bicycle Association (CEBA), says it's "heartbreaking."

"Shops that are selling products that are way beyond the legal limit, they're putting a lot of people in danger."

Seven stores also had e-scooters for sale with manufacturer-recommended rider ages under 16, though some medical experts say e-bikes and e-scooters are too unsafe for anyone under 16.

Watch the full Marketplace investigation on Friday, Oct. 2, on CBC-TV and YouTube.

"It's not just a toy; it's a motorized vehicle," said April Kam, an emergency physician at McMaster Children's Hospital in Hamilton.

"We're seeing kids who are presenting with brain bleeds, with abdominal injuries, solid organ injuries."

Recently released data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information shows 150 people ages 15 and under were hospitalized for falls involving an e-scooter in the 2025-2026 fiscal year across Canada, compared to 54 the year prior. That's an increase of roughly 178 per cent — and reflects a steady year-over-year increase for the last three years.

The number of head injuries related to e-scooters has also increased, from 50 in the 2022-2023 fiscal year to 157 in the 2025-2026 fiscal year. Fractures, dislocations and or muscle and tendon injuries have more than doubled in that same period, with 544 last fiscal year.

The Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program released its own survey in August and found 10 children have died from using devices like e-scooters and e-bikes in 2025.

Meanwhile, sales for the electric rides have more than quadrupled in Canada since 2019, with roughly 372,000 e-bikes and 76,000 e-scooters sold so far this year, according to Statista.

Marketing to kids 'deceiving' parents, doctor says

The youngest age recommendation the Marketplace journalists found was at Canadian Tire — a Razor e-scooter that hits a maximum speed of 16 km/h and is recommended for children who are eight or older.

"That just boggles my mind. Kids at this age don't necessarily have the developmental ability to maneuver these motorized vehicles," said Kam, who is also president of the Canadian Paediatric Society's emergency medicine section.

"It's very concerning that there's this huge market for selling children these motorized vehicles, essentially, and deceiving the parents and family, marketing them as toys."

WATCH | Doctor says kids 16 and under shouldn't ride e-bikes, e-scooters : Doctor says kids 16 and under shouldn't ride e-bikes, e-scooters | Duration closed caption 1:51 April Kam, an emergency physician at McMaster Children's Hospital in Hamilton, says e-bikes and e-scooters are vehicles, not toys.

Razor, the manufacturer of that particular e-scooter at Canadian Tire, said in a statement its device meets U.S. safety guidelines that say eight-year-olds can operate slow-moving motorized vehicles.

The company said its e-scooter is safe when properly used, isn't meant to be on public roads and that riders should follow local laws.

In statements to Marketplace, Best Buy, Canadian Tire and Emmo said customers should follow local laws. Best Buy said rules for e-bikes and e-scooters are evolving and that it tries to keep product information updated.

Costco didn't comment on Marketplace's findings.

E-bike stores can modify speed controls

At an EZbike location in Richmond Hill, a salesperson told undercover journalists it sells e-scooters that can reach 120 km/h — a speed that could get you a ticket on most highways.

At other stores, some e-bikes have their speed limited to 32 kilometres, adhering to Ontario's rules. But when asked if they modify vehicles, a salesperson at an Emmo location in Toronto said yes, they could modify a bike to go up to 150 km/h for off-road use.

"That's horrible," said Pasquali, of CEBA, who owns his own e-bike store in Hamilton.

Emmo and the company that operates the Emmo stores Marketplace visited said in a statement that a product's technical capabilities should not be confused with what's allowed on the roads.

But as an employee at an Emmo in Vaughan, Ont., described it: bypassing the speed limiter is "just like a toggle switch."

WATCH | E-bike stores can modify speed control: E-bike stores can modify speed control | Duration closed caption 2:53 Undercover CBC journalists visited 12 stores selling e-bikes and e-scooters across the Greater Toronto Area. Salespeople at six stores told them or showed them how to bypass built-in speed limits on the vehicles.

Passing on that kind of advice is "extremely unethical," Pasquali said.

"If you're showing consumers how to push a button and make it faster or offering to modify it to go faster with the caveat that you keep it off road, well, that's technically right. But most consumers aren't doing that, right?"

A salesperson at an Amego store in North York, Ont., went a step further, unlocking the 32 km/h speed limit in front of undercover journalists and revving the motor, showing the e-bike exceeding the speed limit and saying it could hit a top speed of roughly 50 km/h.

Amego said in a statement it does not offer or perform modifications, and its salesperson likely exaggerated the top speed.

EZbike didn't comment on Marketplace's findings.

Mom wants change after son's devastating injury

Amy Richards, of St. John's, became one of those parents pleading for change after watching her son spend 102 days in the hospital after losing control of his e-scooter.

Jayden King, 14, was riding his e-scooter on a quiet street in May when he hit a speed bump and lost control.

King's mom says he was wearing a helmet at the time of the accident but suffered a traumatic brain injury. He spent 21 days in a coma and had to have part of his skull surgically removed due to brain swelling. Once he's healthier, King will have to undergo another surgery to get the rest of his skull put back in place, Richards said.

WATCH | Mom wants change after son's devastating e-scooter injury: Mom wants change after son's devastating e-scooter injury | Duration closed caption 2:30 Amy Richards of St. John's wants stronger e-bike and e-scooter legislation after her 14-year-old son crashed an e-scooter in May.

He learned to walk, talk and eat again but still lives with a long list of issues, including memory loss.

"I can't remember nothing in my whole life," King said. He says there's not a chance he'll ride an e-scooter again.

Newfoundland and Labrador has no rules governing e-bikes or e-scooters, but a spokesperson for Government Services said in a statement that it has consulted the public and is looking at changes to the Highway Traffic Act to include micro-mobility devices.

Richards said it should have happened a long time ago, and no one under 16 should be able to ride one.

"We need to protect our children. That should come first and foremost," she said.

Pasquali says the federal government needs to step in and stop the sale and importation of e-bikes and e-scooters that can be modified with the flick of a switch.

Safety is top priority, federal minister says

Canada's Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon told Marketplace in an interview in late September that he has heard stories of people being injured riding e-bikes and e-scooters, and he wants to talk to his provincial counterparts about how to respond.

Most of the legislation governing e-bikes and e-scooters is provincial, he said, and there is "impetus" for provinces and municipalities to act.

But, MacKinon also said the federal government needs "to absolutely consider what we will do in terms of regulating the safety of those devices."

"We'll always work with safety in mind. Safety is our principal priority."

World.title: What Cornell's alleged rape case and the Hockey Canada trial's striking parallels reveal
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article references sexual assault and may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

An intoxicated woman. A sexual encounter. A group message that invites other men to join. In the fallout, allegations of sexual assault, questions regarding consent and the response of elite cultural institutions under the microscope.

If it feels like you've heard this story before, it's because you likely have.

Several legal experts note there are some striking similarities between the alleged gang-rape case unfolding at Cornell University this week, and last year's Hockey Canada sexual assault trial in London, Ont., which saw all five players acquitted.

"It just seemed like yet another example of a group exploiting a vulnerable person," lawyer Karen Bellehumeur, who represented the survivor known as E.M. in the 2025 Hockey Canada trial, told CBC News about the Cornell case.

"When a group is involved, it's particularly abhorrent."

The Cornell case recently came under the spotlight after the victim, known in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16 alleging the Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed "the Cornell 7."

Jane Doe alleges they plied her with ketamine and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024, and that one of the frat brothers sent a Snapchat message inviting other members to join them.

Lawyer Karen Bellehumeur, seen in July 2025, says the Cornell case now in the spotlight is 'yet another example of a group exploiting a vulnerable person.' (Nicole Osborne/The Canadian Press)

None of the fraternity members have been criminally charged, and the lawsuit claims the accused only faced temporary suspensions and "were afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays" to the university — an allegation Cornell denies. Cornell also says some of the students were expelled after an internal disciplinary investigation.

On Monday, after intense backlash, the Tompkins County district attorney announced he was reopening the investigation.

By Thursday evening, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she’d lost faith in the Tompkins County district attorney's ability to handle the case and was appointing a special prosecutor to oversee the investigation.

Hochul said she had signed an executive order giving the office of New York Attorney General Letitia James responsibility for the investigation.

In the 2025 Hockey Canada sexual assault trial, five former World Junior hockey players were charged with sexually assaulting a woman, known as E.M. due to a publication ban, in a hotel room in June 2018. One of the men sent a text message to the team inviting them to come to his room to "be in a 3-way quick."

All of the so-called "Hockey Canada 5" were found not guilty. The NHL reinstated them. One was recently signed by the Edmonton Oilers.

The broader themes in the two cases are "strikingly significant," said Melanie Randall, an associate professor of law at Western University in London, Ont., who researches gender-based violence.

"Institutional failures, inadequate investigations, an inappropriate focus on what she did and not what they did, misunderstandings of consent — it's all there," Randall told CBC News.

WATCH | What we know about the Cornell 7 lawsuit: 'Cornell 7' lawsuit: What we know | Duration 2:53 Alumni are threatening to pull funding, celebrities are lashing out and people are boycotting institutions associated with Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., after an alleged gang rape ignited the internet. The case came into the spotlight after the victim, known in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging the private Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed 'the Cornell 7.' She alleges they drugged and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024. WARNING: This video may affect those who have experienced sexual violence or know someone affected by it. It also contains vulgar language.

Not a coincidence, lawyer says

The parallels between the two cases are more than a coincidence, Toronto lawyer Gillian Hnatiw, a legal expert in gender-based violence and sexual assault, told CBC News.

Both cases involve exclusive organizations of men — a fraternity at a prestigious university and an elite hockey team — where it's alleged that no one stepped in to stop a woman from being harmed, Hnatiw said, calling it "a continuation of locker room culture."

"The fact that there are these communities where as men they feel comfortable not just speaking in this way but inviting their friends to participate in this event, raises serious cultural concerns for me," Hnatiw said.

"This strikes with Hockey Canada as well, that it seems like not an exceptional thing that one of their teammates sent out a group chat saying come to this room, there's a girl you can have sex with."

Supporters of the woman known as E.M. rally outside a London courthouse on July 24, 2025, during the trial of five former junior hockey players accused of sexual assault. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

The Cornell lawsuit, filed in New York Supreme Court and viewed by CBC News, alleges the assault happened on campus at the Chi Phi fraternity house. It included an image of an alleged Snapchat message sent at 1:42 a.m. to members of the fraternity, claiming there was "free pussy."

It also included some of the purported responses from the accused, including, "like you can walk in and whip it out." CBS further reports that later on, one of the fraternity brothers texted the chat to ask "Shop still open?" and the response was "Yea."

"The texts … speak volumes to the kind of misogynist mentality that saw her body as something they had a right to access," Randall said.

And it's the same mentality and the same idea as what we saw with the Hockey Canada texts, she added.

"'There is a woman available to you.' This is the message that went from one man to the rest."

Misunderstood trauma responses

Another root problem both these cases share is how little people understand trauma responses, said Bellehumeur, the lawyer who represented E.M. in the Hockey Canada trial.

"My concern for Jane Doe is that it appears there was an initial statement taken by her, and it's different than what she said later and in her civil lawsuit, and I think much is going to be made of that difference," Bellehumeur said.

On Monday, Tompkins County district attorney Matthew Van Houten said the original investigation in 2024 didn't result in criminal charges in part because Jane Doe did not, in her initial sworn statement to campus police, make any allegations of being gang-raped or drugged.

"On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual," he said.

Jane Doe's lawyer has since disputed Van Houten's claim that she did not report the incident as a rape.

The Chi Phi fraternity house, where the assault is alleged to have happened, is shown at Cornell University on Monday. (Heather Ainsworth/The Associated Press)

This was also an issue in the Hockey Canada trial, where E.M. was scrutinized for her differing statements and for acting permissive and compliant in the hotel room, with defence arguing the men couldn't have known she didn't consent.

Survivors often initially don't understand their own trauma reactions, Bellehumeur said. Any time there's a perceived lack of control and fear, the brain automatically causes involuntary reactions the victim herself may not understand, she added.

"She may ask herself, 'Why didn't I leave? Why did I acquiesce?'" Bellehumeur said.

Researchers have explained trauma responses can include: fight, flight, freeze and fawn. In the latter, the response involves trying to please or placate the perpetrator in order to stay safe during the assault.

This is a persistent misunderstanding, Randall said, where people think that if a woman doesn't consent, she will fight back or say no. But in reality, in many of these situations, women feel threatened, fearful, incapacitated, and in the case where a group is involved, outnumbered.

"You figure out what you need to do to survive and get through it," Randall explained.

WATCH | A look at text messages and consent at the Hockey Canada trial: Text messages and consent at the Hockey Canada sex assault trial | Duration 3:24 Closing arguments in the sexual assault trial of five former world junior hockey players are being presented in court on Monday. All five players have pleaded not guilty. Part of the evidence includes text messages between the accused as a group and also to the complainant. CBC News spoke to several lawyers who aren’t involved in the trial to see how the messages may or may not factor into the judge’s decision.

'Pretty close to doomed'

And then there's the issue of consent. In the Hockey Canada trial, much of the case hinged on what E.M. did and didn't consent to after a night of drinking.

Legal experts say the same will be true for Jane Doe if the Cornell case goes to trial. But that case is further muddied by current New York law, which makes a distinction between sexual assault victims who became intoxicated voluntarily and those who were given intoxicants without their consent or knowledge.

Only the latter can be considered "mentally incapacitated" and therefore unable to consent. As a result, it can be more difficult to bring certain rape charges in a case when the victim chose to consume intoxicants, according to experts and advocates cited by Reuters.

The lawsuit claims that Jane Doe had consumed about 10 alcoholic beverages before heading to the fraternity house the night of her alleged assault, where she was allegedly pressured into snorting ketamine several times — including snorting a line off the penis of one of the accused.

People walk in Ho Plaza at Cornell University on Monday. The alleged on-campus assault raises questions about when an intoxicated person becomes unable to consent. (Heather Ainsworth/The Associated Press)

The legal experts CBC spoke with agreed Jane Doe has a long, onerous road ahead of her, especially if criminal charges are laid and she goes to trial.

"I wish the best for her, but I know it won't be easy," Bellehumeur said.

And like the Hockey Canada trial's outcome, if the Cornell case goes to trial, "I think it would be pretty close to doomed," Hnatiw said.

But, she added, "there are a lot of parallels between the two cases that I think we can learn from, if not legally, then sociologically."

World.title: The Black Sea is the most dangerous it's been since the start of Russia’s war. And it's choking global grain
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Mykola Lupar and his crew head out on a navy patrol boat from the Ukrainian Black Sea port of Chornomorsk, the 29-year-old commander can usually count the time they spend on the open water in minutes, before rushing back to shore.

The heavy machine guns aboard can’t offer much protection from Russian jet-powered drones launched from Crimea, especially when they are trying to board a vessel rocking in the churning waves.

“We are trying to find some windows in time between Russian attacks to patrol, to search for mines and some explosive materials,” Lupar said.

“It’s very dangerous. For the merchant fleet, I would say there’s almost no chance to stay safe in our waters.”

A screenshot from a video taken by Mykola Lupar, a patrol boat commander, of a sea drone captured by a Ukrainian patrol vessel. (Mykola Lupar)

After nearly five years of war, maritime analysts warn that the conflict in the Black Sea is the most intense it has been since the early days of Russia’s full-scale invasion, which began on Feb. 24, 2022.

Since mid-July of this year, strikes on commercial vessels have escalated dramatically as Russia seeks to halt Ukraine’s exports and bludgeon its economy, while Kyiv has tried to blunt Russia’s ability to fund its war by striking vessels connected to Moscow’s shadow fleet and some of its port infrastructure.

According to Ambrey, a British-based firm specializing in global maritime risk, there were more than 210 strikes on commercial vessels between July and the end of September.

It attributed 125 of those strikes to Ukraine and 88 to Russia. The strikes have not only elevated the risk across the entire Black Sea, but have also eroded the export capacity of both countries, sparking concerns about the global grain supply.

A woman looks toward the Russian-flagged cargo ship OMSKIY-107, which was attacked off the coast of Russia, drifted and ran aground off the shore of Sile district in Istanbul, on Sept. 3. The 108-metre vessel was damaged in a drone attack near the Russian port of Novorossiysk before its crew abandoned ship in lifeboats. (Cem Taylan/AFP/Getty Images)

Together, Russia and Ukraine account for roughly a quarter of the world’s wheat exports, and analysts estimate that their combined exports are down 60 per cent from last year.

Efforts, including those led by Turkey, to secure a limited truce in the Black Sea have so far failed. While both Russia and Ukraine are looking for alternative routes for their exports, the attacks on shipping and ports are already leading to a rise in global wheat prices, which could spike further.

“It’s not only a Ukrainian problem. This is a problem for the whole region,” said Dmytro Barinov, president of the Ukrainian Ports Association.

“The price jumps at the gas station and everybody feels the lack of fuel. And here, believe me, very soon — October, November latest — everybody will feel the shortage of food in our region, unfortunately.”

Throughout its full-scale invasion, Russia has routinely attacked Ukraine’s ports and ships, including the port of Izmail, which lies on the Danube River and borders Romania.

But since July, Moscow has ratcheted up its attacks. Russia’s Defence Ministry insists it is targeting only military assets, and after it struck a cargo vessel in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk on Thursday, officials accused the ship of supplying the military.

'It’s not only a Ukrainian problem. This is a problem for the whole region,' said Dmytro Barinov, president of the Ukrainian Ports Association. (Angela Johnston/CBC)

Barinov insists that Russia is hitting purely civilian ships and points to a missile strike on a vessel named the Golden Leo, which was near the port of Odesa in July. Ten people were killed in the strike, which Ukrainian officials said was carrying corn.

He describes Russia’s attacks as akin to hunting because merchant ships are slow, can’t manoeuvre quickly and don’t have military defences.

“It’s like hunting for an elephant from a helicopter,” he said in an interview with CBC News in Odesa.

Russia launched three cruise missiles at the Golden Leo as it was 'leaving the combat zone with a cargo of grain,' the Ukrainian navy said in a statement. Ten people were killed. (AFP/Getty Images)

But Ukraine, too, has been striking Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, which are connected by the Kerch Strait, east of Crimea.

In August, when Ukraine launched a massive missile and drone strike against the Russian port of Novorossiysk, it hit a naval base and damaged two major grain export terminals.

The strikes by both sides have prompted London-based insurers to expand the area of the Black Sea they consider high risk, as vessels are being hit farther south in the sea. There has also been a significant increase in the number of unexploded ordnance. According to Ambrey, more than 50 were found outside Russian and Ukrainian waters so far this year.

Back in 2022, the UN and Turkey worked to secure an agreement known as the Black Sea Grain Initiative to keep commercial vessels transiting to Ukrainian ports. But after a year, it fell apart when Russia refused to renew it.

In the wake of that, Ukraine established its own shipping corridor, where vessels would reach its ports by first travelling along the coastlines of Turkey, Bulgaria and Romania before reaching Ukraine.

But that route has now also been disrupted by Russia’s widespread attacks.

WATCH | Escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports are making shipping risky: Escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports is making shipping risky | Duration closed caption 2:18 Escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships in the Black Sea have made getting crucial exports like wheat out of Ukraine much riskier. Russia claims it only hits military targets.

Caitlin Welsh, director of the Global Food and Water Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, says that after Russia first launched its full-scale invasion, global food prices reached an all-time high not factoring in inflation. Now, she says, the difference is that a significant chunk of Russia’s export capacity is offline as well.

“Now it’s not just Russia attacking Ukraine, it’s Ukraine also attacking Russia, and those things are happening at the same time,” she said in a Zoom interview with CBC News.

Recent figures from the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization say world wheat prices are up 15 per cent from last year, driven in part by disruptions in the Black Sea.

“Prices are already increasing, and I think we can expect grain prices, especially wheat prices, to continue to increase.”

Welsh isn’t sure that prices will rise to 2022 levels, but does note that the turmoil in the Black Sea is happening at the same time as other global shocks, including the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz and the compounding effects of El Niño, which brought drought to global wheat-producing regions, creating further food insecurity.

For Ukrainians in Odesa, who took advantage of a relatively drone-free sky on Tuesday afternoon to visit the windswept shore near the port, the absence of ships moored offshore is noticeable.

“It is really concerning,” said 20-year-old Iryna Kostina.

“Our country has a lot of grain, a lot of agriculture, and it’s basically going to be a bad situation for everyone.”

World.title: Amid the push to build Canadian, a Quebec train factory is booming
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For Claude Michaud, the increasingly loud buzz of machinery, welding and ringing steel is a source of optimism at the train factory where he has worked for much of the past 34 years.

The Alstom plant in La Pocatière, Que., a community of about 6,000 people, has endured waves of layoffs and uneven production over the past two decades. But amid a wave of new Canadian projects, the plant is expanding its factory floor and preparing to hire more staff.

"There's pride in building trains at home for people here in Canada," Michaud said in French. "It's a positive change."

Alstom, a French company whose Americas headquarters is in Saint-Bruno-de-Montarville, Que., is seeing a rise in orders amid a push by all levels of government to buy Canadian. The company completed its acquisition of Bombardier's rail-building division in 2021.

Claude Michaud, the union president, has worked at Alstom, formerly Bombardier, for the last 34 years. His father, spouse, father-in-law, brother-in-law and niece have all worked at the plant. He says there's a sense of pride in building trains for Canadians. (Alexandre Silberman/CBC)

The company is building rail cars for Vancouver's SkyTrain, subway trains for the Toronto Transit Commission and vehicles for a new Quebec City tramway. It will soon begin work on a $4.7-billion contract to build long-distance passenger cars for VIA Rail.

In La Pocatière, 140 kilometres northeast of Quebec City, the plant has long been one of the region's largest employers and an economic driver. But it became heavily dependent on export projects, often for the United States.

The number of employees at the plant — more than 1,000 in the 1990s — fell to about 150 in 2021, according to Alstom and the union. The decline threatened the economic viability of keeping the facility in operation. Now, there are about 550 employees and the company is preparing to grow.

Alstom's plant is one of the largest employers in La Pocatière, a community of about 6,000 people located 140 kilometres northeast of Quebec City. (Louis-Marie Philidor/CBC)

A shift toward buying Canadian

Olivier Marcil, Alstom's vice-president of public affairs for Canada, said increasingly protectionist manufacturing policies in the U.S. effectively closed the door to the market south of the border.

The U.S. Federal Transit Administration Buy America policy requires projects receiving federal funding to use materials and final products, including buses, trains and ferries, manufactured in the United States. The threshold of percentage of domestic components was raised between 2016 and 2021.

"When you look at the megatrend that we've experienced over the last decades — the United States were asking a lot from manufacturers to build local, right? While Canada was not asking anything," he said.

"If everybody's protecting their industry, everybody's nurturing their industry — Canada must come at par with those and do the same."

Olivier Marcil, vice-president of public affairs for Alstom in Canada, at the company's prototype centre in Saint-Bruno-de-Montarville, Que. Marcil says Buy American protectionist policies for transit hurt Canadian-based manufacturers. (Alexandre Silberman/CBC)

Rebuilding manufacturing capacity

Dan Breznitz, a professor at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, said there are challenges to restoring manufacturing in sectors such as rail.

He said Canada needs to be more strategic about which industries it chooses to invest in as part of a return to manufacturing.

"We have to find the people, we have to find the manufacturing, we have to find the other factories that produce everything that you need to make rail," said Breznitz, who studies how innovation and government policy affect industries.

"The problem is, if you don't do it for 20 to 30 years you lose the skills."

Frédéric Platteeuw, Alstom's site manager for La Pocatière, said the facility is undergoing a major transformation to be able to build long-distance train cars for VIA Rail. (Alexandre Silberman/CBC)

Nearly a decade of work

For Alstom, the VIA Rail project will generate manufacturing work for nearly a decade, with additional employment supported by a 15-year agreement for technical support and spare parts.

The new long-distance train cars will be built in La Pocatière, with final assembly in Thunder Bay.

Frédéric Platteeuw, Alstom's site manager in La Pocatière, said the facility will have to scale up and adapt to focus entirely on the contract for the Crown corporation.

"It's a real challenge, such a project, because it will push us to rethink all the layout," he said. "To optimize our surface, to optimize our work, to develop new technology."

For employees like Michaud, the new contract signals a long-awaited shift from the federal government. As a union leader, he pushed for years for the federal government to introduce Canadian-content requirements for trains.

A major blow came in 2018, when a $989-million contract for VIA Rail's Quebec City-Windsor corridor fleet was awarded to German company Siemens, which built the train cars in California.

Michaud followed in the footsteps of his father, who built the first cars to roll out of the plant for the Montreal Metro. He said it's refreshing to see the plant, where other members of his family work, come back to life with Canadian projects.

"We see that the government is finally listening," he said. "A dollar invested in Quebec and in Canada is money that stays in our country."

World.title: What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hi, it's Johanna. For almost two decades, I've been talking about climate change through the weather we experience every day. But after spending Climate Week in New York with fellow meteorologists from across North America, one thing is clear: this job is getting deeply personal.

This week:

What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week

The Big Picture: Progress on the world's nature goals

Mycelium with your meatballs? How one Vancouver company is farming fungi to combat meat costs

What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week

Grabbing a quick moment outside the WNYC radio studio before heading in to record. (Johanna Wagstaffe/CBC)

I was invited to join a closed-door workshop in New York City during Climate Week called "Beyond the Forecast: How Trusted Weather Voices Can Help Communities Understand Climate and Extreme Weather." Hosted by the Clinton Global Initiative in partnership with the Eleven Eleven Foundation, the session offered a rare space to talk openly with other broadcast meteorologists about how we communicate climate change.

I mean, this is my bread and butter. For almost two decades, I've been talking about climate change through the everyday weather we experience. I've been grateful to have the support, platforms and formats at CBC to do just that.

Even so, there is a distinct weight to this work — seeing the data play out in real time, knowing the severity of a storm's impact before it hits, and navigating how politicized the term "climate change" has become. Stepping into my new role as the host of CBC's climate podcast What on Earth?, the timing couldn't have been better for this gathering.

Finding common ground in New York

Arriving in New York, I loved being recognized by fellow Canadians at Newark Airport — climate advisers from Vancouver headed to the same gathering. It was a nice reminder of why these conferences matter. Bringing people together (despite the carbon footprint of travel) creates a momentum you can't replicate virtually.

Walking from the subway up 5th Avenue toward the conference centre on my first day, I instinctively fell into the fast-paced ebb and flow of the city street. I credit my former Toronto days for my defensive walking skills, but adopting that rhythm makes you feel immediately plugged in. This trip was going to be all about feeling part of something bigger.

Fuelling the Climate Week hustle with an essential New York slice. (Johanna Wagstaffe/CBC)

The workshop itself was one I won't soon forget. Nearly every major meteorologist I've watched on U.S. networks was there (plus Bill Nye!). Our scheduled two-hour session ran long — after all, we talk for a living — but it was deeply cathartic. Hearing forecasters from Fox News to CNN to ABC, alongside scientists and policy-makers, open up about the shared challenges of communicating climate risk felt like a rare moment of unity.

Here are a few takeaways I can share:

1. The connection between weather and climate is undeniable — but the pushback is real

Underlying every discussion in that room was one overarching reality: we are all trying to talk about climate change as station scientists.

The science behind extreme weather is indisputable. But for television forecasters attempting to bring that science into daily broadcasts, the pushback from audiences can be tough — and deeply emotional. While I've been lucky enough to avoid the absolute worst of it, let's just say you never truly develop a thick skin. And knowing what lies ahead when forecasting a devastating storm carries a real weight.

Between sessions, I raced from Midtown down to SOHO to record in the studios at WNYC (New York public radio) — a fun moment of solidarity, hopping from one public broadcaster's home base to another. But the conversation I recorded hit home sharply. I spoke with forecaster Chris Gloninger, who made the difficult decision to leave his TV news career after facing severe harassment and a death threat simply for explaining climate links on air.

But Chris's story was a stark reminder that serving as a trusted voice often comes at a high personal cost. To go "beyond the forecast," weather communicators need more than just thick skin — we need strong community support to keep having these vital conversations safely.

Connecting with forecaster Chris Gloninger during Climate Week in New York. (Johanna Wagstaffe/CBC)

2. U.S. and Canadian TV live in different broadcast universes

I attended the workshop alongside only one other Canadian: my friend Mark Robinson from The Weather Network, who I went to meteorology school with! Being there together highlighted how much the U.S. and Canada have in common, and also just how differently our two media markets operate.

American broadcast TV remains deeply traditional, with millions of viewers still tuning in to local 6 o'clock newscasts every night. For U.S. forecasters, that means trying to cram complex climate attribution science into a lightning-fast, two-minute weather window between commercial breaks.

Reunited with fellow Canadian weather broadcaster and storm chaser Mark Robinson from The Weather Network. (Johanna Wagstaffe/CBC)

At CBC, as the media landscape has shifted, we've chosen to experiment with meeting audiences where they are. Beyond dedicated space on podcasts like What On Earth? and digital platforms, our local TV markets frequently carve out extra airtime specifically to connect the dots between severe weather and climate change. Having that room to explain why a heat wave or atmospheric river is happening is something I was reminded not to take for granted — because in a tight TV hit, context is often the first thing left on the cutting-room floor. But as more U.S. newsrooms experiment with climate-dedicated segments and digital extras, the potential to inform communities is huge. It shows that when we give trusted weather voices room to breathe, audiences gain a far better understanding of the world shifting around them.

Stepping out of those closed-door rooms in New York, I was reminded that connecting those dots on air isn't always easy, and it certainly isn't always comfortable — but as extreme weather becomes our daily reality, it's a conversation we're more committed than ever to having.

— Johanna Wagstaffe

Old issues of What on Earth? are here . The CBC News climate page is here .

Check out our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode : When a meteorologist took a job in Iowa, he was excited to make his forecasts matter to viewers by bringing in climate impacts that were relevant to their lives, like rising costs and energy independence. But then the backlash began, escalating to a death threat.

He's not the only one. At climate week in New York City, a group of meteorologists gathered to share stories about speaking to often polarized audiences. When facts become political, how can climate change's frontline communicators stick to the science?

What On Earth? drops new podcast episodes every Wednesday and Saturday. You can find them on your favourite podcast app or on demand at CBC Listen . The radio show airs Sundays at 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Check the CBC News Climate Dashboard for live updates on record-breaking weather and current conditions across the country. Set your location to find out how today's temperatures compare to historical trends.

Reader feedback

Last week, we told you about a unique air quality meets wearable art project that's trying to bring awareness about dangerous pollutants especially when we can't see them.

Edwina Hylton wrote in with an important point: "In the eventuality that the device shows serious pollution, what is the person wearing the device supposed to do? Fine to know things are bad, but if there isn't a reasonable alternative, what is the point in collecting the information?"

While not always equitable or within reach, some experts we've spoken to over the years have said awareness gives a power of choice to take action , like wearing a mask or moving indoors.

And, for some, like reader Maureen Moffat, awareness is a click away. She writes, "I check the air quality daily on the net. Easy."

Got questions, comments, or just want to share something? Write us at whatonearth@cbc.ca (and send photos there, too!)

The Big Picture: Progress on the world's nature goals

Four years ago, Canada welcomed negotiators from around the world to strike a historic deal on protecting nature. The conference was supposed to be in China, but it was 2022 and the COVID-weary government there had decided not to host.

So the meeting reverted to Montreal, which hosts the secretariat of the UN treaty that governs biological diversity, and I jumped on a train to go cover it. Canada led negotiations to land a new global target : protecting 30 per cent of lands and oceans by 2030. And it decided to lead by example by embarking on its own ambitious conservation agenda.

Here's a map of Canada's protected spaces. Canada has protected about 14 per cent of its lands and 15.5 per cent of its oceans so far.

And a new assessment says there's progress internationally — the world will reach 27 per cent protection on land by 2030. For oceans, protection will only reach 12 per cent. I spoke to Steven Guilbeault, Canada's former environment minister and the guy who helped land that deal in Montreal, about why we are falling short — and also why he's still optimistic countries will ramp up the fight against biodiversity loss.

— Inayat Singh

Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

A man in Squamish, B.C., has put his Halloween zombie decoration out early — to keep bears out of his garbage bins. See how the bears are responding in this CBC News video .

Kids are being toilet trained later and later. That's costing parents in money spent on diapers and time spent on additional gross diaper changes. But it's also creating a lot more plastic waste. A new study calculates the environmental cost, and offers some solutions .

Mountainous, densely populated Japan doesn't have many places to put large solar farms, but it has found a solution in a type of infrastructure that proliferated in the economic boom of the 1980s and is now disused .

A new study shows electric trucks are becoming cheaper to operate than their diesel counterparts and how quickly the savings can outstrip the higher up-front cost in some European countries .

Canada's Building Canada Strong Act is supposed to speed up infrastructure projects. But it could also dismantle environmental safeguards that protect Canadians and prevent wildlife from extinction, despite the federal government claiming otherwise , environmental groups tell CBC's David Thurton and Olivia Stefanovich.

Mycelium meatballs? How one Vancouver company is farming fungi to combat meat costs

Vancouver-based company Maia Farms has figured out a way to grow and harvest mycelium — the hidden, underground root-like networks of fungus that give rise to mushrooms. (Monia Blanchet/Radio-Canada)

If fermented liquid fungus from a bioreactor doesn't sound like your idea of a delicious meal, the folks at Maia Farms say, don't knock it 'til you've tried it.

The Vancouver-based company has figured out a way to grow and harvest mycelium — the hidden, underground root-like networks of fungus that give rise to mushrooms.

"The bioreactor allows us to control the environment in which the mycelium are grown," said chief innovation officer Sean Lacoursiere.

"It allows us to keep everything moving and grooving and it also allows us to aerate and provide all the oxygen that the mushroom will need."

WATCH | Company argues mushrooms could help lower skyrocketing meat costs for restaurants: Company argues mushrooms could help lower skyrocketing meat costs for restaurants | Duration closed caption 2:02 Meat is one of the biggest costs facing restaurants and data shows prices are only going up. Diners are increasingly seeing those expenses being reflected in menu prices. A Vancouver company is trying to make meat go further by blending it with mushrooms.

The result is a food product that can be mixed with different protein sources to add bulk and enhance a meal's nutritional profile.

While mushroom products are often used in meat substitutes, one of Maia's target markets is the meat industry itself.

"We can add a lot of nutritional, taste and texture benefits while reducing the amount of meat that's required," Lacoursiere said.

The offering couldn't be timelier for restaurateurs and other food retailers struggling to keep costs down as the price of meat soars.

According to Canada Beef, retail beef averaged $28 per kilogram in April, up 15 per cent from a year ago and close to a record high.

Maia Farms' director of food science and innovation Karen McAfee said mycelium could replace between 25 and 40 per cent of the meat in items like sausage rolls, meatballs and burger patties.

"It can help retain moisture… it can also help with the high level of umami flavour," she said.

Better for the planet

The benefits of hiding mushrooms in your meat go beyond the financial.

"From our estimates, we produce around two kilograms of carbon dioxide per kilogram of material," Lacoursiere said.

According to a 2024 report by the Canadian Roundtable for Sustainable Beef, one kilogram of consumed boneless beef in Canada produces 32.8 kilograms of carbon dioxide.

The same amount also requires 1,912 litres of water, almost four times the 500 litres Maia reports in its process.

"I don't think people really comprehend just how much of a difference this type of product can make," he said.

Finding consumers

While meat alternatives are readily available in Canadian supermarkets, sales in the sector have been declining for several years .

Lacoursiere is hoping Maia has what it takes to buck the trend.

"The whole goal of our company here is to produce mycelium at large scales, at a very cost competitive level. And we're already seeing that," he said.

As for the "ick" factor?

"It's an oyster mushroom. It's been eaten for hundreds, if not thousands of years. It's delicious. We just found a way to grow it in a submerged liquid state."

— Ruby Cornish

Thanks for reading. If you have questions, criticisms or story tips, please send them to whatonearth@cbc.ca.
