What happened at Green Hill

The shooting happened late on Friday, 25 September, in Green Hill, a community just outside Kingstown. “On arrival, officers discovered two bodies lying on the public road,” the Royal St Vincent and the Grenadines Police Force said.

Another victim was found inside a parked vehicle and a fourth on nearby land, the police statement said. Three of the dead were from Green Hill and one from Paul’s Avenue in Kingstown, iWitness News reported.

The injured included a 16-year-old and a 17-year-old student. Two of the wounded were treated and discharged and two remained in hospital on Sunday, Global News reported.

Police recovered 40 shell casings, Deputy Prime Minister St Clair Leacock said.

“Violence has no part in our society,” said acting police commissioner Trevor Bailey. Police were also checking whether another killing on Saturday was linked.

The government’s response

Friday told NBC Radio the government was “putting in place a comprehensive plan to deal with crime and violence, especially violent crimes”. He listed immediate security in affected areas, the root causes of youth violence and the flow of illegal guns into the region.

Leacock, who is also national security minister, went further on NICE Radio.

He said he would ask Barbados, through the Regional Security System, for “soldiers from the Barbados Defence Force” if he had to. “I’ll do it,” he said.

The Regional Security System is a defence pact among eastern Caribbean states.

Leacock also cited more than 120 new police recruits and a rapid-response unit. Two extra coast guard vessels and FBI help with forensics are part of the plan.

“You can’t arrest yourself out of criminal behaviour,” he added, calling on churches, families and schools to play a part.

Worries about tourism

The killings made international news, including on CNN and the BBC. “We have had some very bad press, very terrible international headlines,” Leacock said.

Tourism Minister Kishore Shallow set up a “damage control team”, iWitness News reported. It is led by Shafia London, head of the tourism authority.

Opposition leader Ralph Gonsalves rejected claims that his Unity Labour Party had fuelled the foreign coverage. His party governed for 24 years until its defeat in 2025.

The prime minister in court

Separately, Friday and Foreign Minister Fitzgerald Bramble were cross-examined in the High Court in Kingstown on 29 September, before Justice Gertel Thom. The petitions were filed by Carlos Williams and Luke Browne, Unity Labour Party candidates defeated in the 2025 election.

They argue that both men were disqualified from running under Section 26 of the constitution because they also hold Canadian citizenship.

Outside the court on Thursday, 1 October, Friday backed his lawyer Anand Ramlogan, who called the petitions “disingenuous”. “And I would add sour grapes and sore losers,” Friday said, iWitness News reported.

What comes next

Police have asked anyone with video, photographs or information to come forward. In the petition case, “we have to do the submissions in November, and then the judge … [will] … make her decision,” Friday said.

A mass shooting of this scale remains rare in St Vincent: the last comparable attack was more than three years ago. Even a ruling against Friday and Bramble would not end the NDP’s majority: it holds 14 of the 15 elected seats.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Green Hill in St Vincent?

Green Hill is a residential community just outside Kingstown, the capital of St Vincent and the Grenadines, on the main island of St Vincent.

Is it safe to visit St Vincent and the Grenadines?

The government says visitors remain welcome and has set up a team to reassure travellers. The Green Hill shooting took place in a residential area outside Kingstown; travellers should follow their own government’s current advice.

What is the Regional Security System?

It is a defence and security pact among eastern Caribbean states that lets members share troops and police. St Vincent’s security minister said he would ask Barbados for soldiers through it if needed.

Why is the prime minister in court?

Two defeated opposition candidates argue that Prime Minister Godwin Friday and Foreign Minister Fitzgerald Bramble were disqualified from running in 2025 because they also hold Canadian citizenship. Final submissions are due in November; the High Court has not yet ruled.

World.title: Uruguay Prosecutor Denies Ex-Senator Gandini Access to 260-Kilo Drug Case
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

URUGUAY · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The country Uruguay, a nation of about 3.4 million between Brazil and Argentina, is usually ranked among South America’s cleanest democracies. Drug money near a party payroll draws unusual attention there.

— The background Operation Trazador seized more than 260 kilos of drugs and ended with three convictions. One of those convicted, Pablo Leiva, was a paid aide to a councillor in Jorge Gandini’s National Party faction.

— Why now Leiva regularly paid bills at a payment outlet owned by Gandini’s wife. Gandini, a former senator who now sits on the ports authority’s board for the opposition, asked to see the case file.

— What happened Drug prosecutor Angelita Romano refused, saying Gandini “is neither under investigation nor a victim”, El Observador and Montevideo Portal reported on 1 October 2026.

— Who is who Gandini leads Por la Patria, a faction of the opposition National Party. His wife, the accountant Laura Scalabrino Muga, owns the payment outlet.

— What it means for you No authority has accused Gandini or his wife of wrongdoing. The refusal applies a standard secrecy rule, not a finding about them.

— Still open Where the separate money-laundering inquiry leads, and how the National Party deals with the councillor who employed Leiva.

A Uruguay drug prosecutor has refused to let Jorge Gandini, a former National Party senator, see the investigation file of Operation Trazador. The case ended with three drug-related convictions, including that of a paid aide in Gandini’s own political faction.

Prosecutor Angelita Romano said Gandini “is neither under investigation nor a victim” in the case, El Observador reported on 1 October 2026. Only suspects, victims and their lawyers may see such files.

What the prosecutor decided

Romano, who heads the first-shift drug prosecution office, cited the rules on preliminary investigations. Those proceedings “shall be reserved for third parties outside the procedure”, her reply said.

She added that the file stays reserved even after an investigation ends. Victims, suspects and their defence lawyers, by contrast, have free access, she wrote, as quoted by El Observador.

Montevideo Portal confirmed the refusal and its grounds. The prosecution service’s own rules say complainants who are not victims cannot see the file either.

Why Gandini asked

Gandini wrote to Romano the week before, saying he and his wife had been “publicly mentioned as linked” to the case. Neither had been contacted or summoned by any authority, he said.

“I am convinced that I am entitled to see that file, to defend my honour and my family’s,” he wrote. He made the request personally, without a lawyer.

Gandini, a former senator, now sits for the opposition on the board of the National Ports Administration. That state body runs Uruguay’s public ports, including Montevideo.

How his name came up

Pablo Leiva was a paid aide to Gonzalo Gómez, a Montevideo councillor from Por la Patria, the National Party faction Gandini leads. He was dismissed after his conviction.

Leiva received two years and six months for laundering drug money and for trafficking ammunition. The operation seized more than 260 kilos of drugs, valued at about US$2 million, El Observador reported.

Leiva paid bills at a franchise of a payment-collection network owned by Gandini’s wife, as well as at other outlets. At a press conference on 22 September, Gandini said: “We have nothing to hide.”

He said Leiva was a local regular who paid two social-security receipts for two construction firms, and did not change money there. “We are not responsible for any illicit activity,” he added, saying neither he nor his wife knew Leiva.

What comes next

The money-laundering prosecutor, Enrique Rodríguez, opened a new investigation on 28 September into how the gang moved its cash. It looks at exchange houses and bill-payment offices; no politician has been charged.

The National Party has separately referred councillor Gómez to its ethics committee. The refusal does not mean Gandini is under suspicion; it applies a rule that closes files to outsiders.

Nor does it settle what the file contains, or what parts of it have reached the press. The reports of 1 October carried no response from Gandini to the refusal.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Jorge Gandini?

He is a veteran politician of Uruguay’s opposition National Party and a former senator. He leads the Por la Patria faction and sits on the board of the state ports authority for the opposition.

Why was he denied access to the file?

Uruguay’s rules keep preliminary investigation files reserved for third parties. Only suspects, victims and their lawyers may see them, and the prosecutor said Gandini is neither a suspect nor a victim.

Is Gandini accused of any crime?

No. Neither he nor his wife has been summoned or charged. His name came up because a convicted aide in his faction paid bills at a payment outlet his wife owns.

What was Operation Trazador?

It was a police and prosecution case that seized more than 260 kilos of drugs and led to three convictions, including the laundering conviction of the aide Pablo Leiva.

World.content:

CUBA · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The country Cuba is a one-party communist state in the Caribbean. A deep economic crisis has brought long blackouts and food shortages, frequent subjects of critical posts online.

— The background Anna Bensi, full name Anna Sofía Benítez Silvente, is a 21-year-old content creator from Alamar, in eastern Havana. Since September 2025 she has posted videos about blackouts, inflation, low pay and food shortages.

— Why now In March her mother filmed a police officer who came to their home with a summons, and Bensi posted the video. The officer later filed a private criminal complaint.

— What happened On Thursday 1 October the Havana East Municipal People’s Court found both women guilty of offences against personal privacy and image. Each received two years of “limitation of liberty”.

— Who is who The co-defendant is her mother, Caridad Silvente Laffita. Their lawyer is Roberto Ortega; Judge Zamira Marrero Morgado presided.

— What it means for you The sentence is not prison. It restricts movement and residence, and their lawyer says it includes a ban on leaving the country.

— Still open The written ruling, due in about 15 days, and whether the women appeal. They have 10 working days after notification.

Anna Bensi, a 21-year-old Cuban content creator who criticises the government online, was convicted in Havana on Thursday 1 October. Her mother was convicted with her, over a video of a police officer that Bensi posted in March.

The court sentenced each woman to two years of “limitation of liberty”, a penalty served outside prison. “This really is an injustice,” Bensi told reporters after the hearing, the news agency EFE reported.

Who Anna Bensi is

Bensi’s full name is Anna Sofía Benítez Silvente; “Bensi” is the name she uses on social media. She lives in Alamar, a district of large housing blocks in the Havana East municipality.

She trained as a dental-prosthetics technician. In September 2025 she began posting about blackouts, inflation, low wages and food shortages, the daily face of Cuba’s economic crisis.

She describes herself as a Baptist Christian and an anti-communist, Periódico Cubano reported.

From a doorstep video to a trial

On 10 March 2026 a police officer came to the family’s home to deliver a summons. Her mother, Caridad Silvente Laffita, filmed him as he showed his identity card, and Bensi posted the video.

According to the court, the footage captured the officer’s name, identity number, photograph and address.

Thousands of comments followed. Some contained “offensive, degrading and threatening words against the officer and his relatives”, according to a court statement reported by CiberCuba.

Both women were charged on 25 March and placed under house confinement with a ban on leaving the country. On 9 April they received a visit from the then US chargé d’affaires in Havana, Mike Hammer.

On 13 April the Havana provincial prosecutor’s office closed the case. On 6 July Bensi said it had been reopened after the officer filed a private complaint, Periódico Cubano reported.

A trial set for 17 September was postponed. It finally took place on 1 October at the Havana East Municipal People’s Court, sitting in Cojímar.

What the sentence means

The offence falls under Article 393 of Cuba’s penal code. It covers acts against personal and family privacy, a person’s image and voice, and identity data.

In August, Periódico Cubano reported a possible range of two to five years in prison.

“Limitation of liberty” is served without detention. The women must obey the law, appear in court when summoned, and not move house or leave their province without permission.

Their lawyer, Roberto Ortega, told EFE that a person serving it “leads a normal life”. The law’s rules still apply, he said, “such as the ban on leaving the country”.

According to Bensi, the complainant’s lawyer had asked for a two-year prison term for her. The court imposed the non-custodial sentence instead.

The government’s case and the reactions

The court said both sides had appointed lawyers and that the trial respected “constitutional rights and due process at all times”. Bensi’s sister said only one witness was allowed in, CiberCuba reported.

The Ministry of the Interior posted a message that did not name the case. “A court case is not decided on social media,” it said.

“Filming is not a crime; spreading it without consent can be,” the ministry added.

The US Embassy in Havana posted: “Thinking differently is not a crime.”

The legal-aid group Cubalex argued that filming officials on public duty is legitimate. In its view, Article 393 should not apply to state agents.

At least two religious activists were detained on their way to the court, CiberCuba reported. About 30 religious representatives sang outside, according to EFE.

What comes next

The verdict was given orally. Ortega said the written ruling will follow in about 15 days.

The women then have 10 working days to appeal, to the Havana Provincial People’s Court.

The ruling does not send either woman to prison. It does leave them under court supervision for two years and, according to their lawyer, unable to leave Cuba.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Anna Bensi?

Anna Bensi is the social-media name of Anna Sofía Benítez Silvente, a 21-year-old Cuban content creator from Alamar in eastern Havana. She posts videos criticising blackouts, inflation, low pay and food shortages.

Why was she convicted?

In March she posted a video, filmed by her mother, of a police officer delivering a summons. It showed his name, identity number and address. A Havana court found both women guilty on 1 October of offences against privacy and personal image.

Is Anna Bensi going to prison?

No. She and her mother each received two years of “limitation of liberty”, a non-custodial sentence. It restricts movement and residence, and their lawyer says it includes a ban on leaving Cuba.

Can the verdict be appealed?

Yes. The written ruling is expected in about 15 days. The women then have 10 working days to appeal to the Havana Provincial People’s Court.

World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

PARAGUAY · SCIENCE

Key Facts — The country Paraguay is a landlocked South American country between Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia, known abroad for soybeans, beef and the Itaipú hydropower dam it shares with Brazil.

— The background Its first satellite, GuaraníSat-1, was developed with Japan’s Kyushu Institute of Technology, assembled in Japan and launched in 2021.

— Why now GuaraníSat-2 is the first Paraguayan satellite designed and assembled in Paraguay. It took three years and more than 40 professionals and students.

— What happened It lifted off on a SpaceX rideshare with more than 100 other satellites from Vandenberg, California, on Thursday 1 October 2026 and was put into orbit.

— The numbers The satellite measures 30 by 10 by 10 centimetres, about the size of a loaf of bread. It weighs under four kilograms and should work for about two years.

— What it means for you If you are a radio amateur, it will relay data for your community. For Paraguay, it is a test bed for a planned Earth-observation satellite, GuaraníSat-3.

— Still open Whether the satellite has unfolded its solar panels and made contact with its ground station in Asunción; the first reports did not yet confirm it.

Paraguay’s second satellite, GuaraníSat-2, has reached orbit on a SpaceX rideshare, SNT television and the newspaper Hoy reported on 1 October. It is the first Paraguayan satellite designed and assembled inside the country.

The nanosatellite took three years and more than 40 engineers, technicians and students to build. It will test solar panels and a computer chip, and help study a weak spot in Earth’s magnetic field.

What reached orbit

GuaraníSat-2 measures 30 by 10 by 10 centimetres and weighs less than four kilograms. It lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, on Thursday 1 October, on a SpaceX mission carrying more than 100 satellites.

The rocket climbed for about ten minutes, and the satellite was released about an hour after lift-off. Once free, it should unfold its solar panels and contact the Spacelab ground station at the National University of Asunción (UNA).

SNT called the launch a source of national pride that “marks a new chapter in the space history of Paraguay”. The project brought together more than 40 professionals and students over three years, the channel said.

What the satellite will do

Its main jobs are technical tests. It will try out solar panels developed by an Italian company and relay data for the amateur radio community.

It also carries a microchip from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, previously used on missions to Mars, to process and store images.

Researchers from UNA’s engineering faculty will use it to measure the South Atlantic Anomaly. That is a zone of weaker magnetic field that covers parts of Paraguay and Brazil.

The mission should last about two years, Hoy reported. The satellite will then lose altitude slowly and burn up in the atmosphere, so it leaves no debris in orbit.

From built in Japan to built at home

Paraguay’s first satellite, GuaraníSat-1, was developed with Japan’s Kyushu Institute of Technology and launched in 2021. It was assembled in Japan; its successor was built in Paraguay by engineers trained on that first project.

Japan remains a partner: GuaraníSat-2’s environmental tests took place there in 2025. Japan has also granted Paraguay US$24 million for a space technology centre at the university.

“What we want, from Paraguay, is to have autonomy and no longer depend on other countries,” said Esteban Fretes in September 2025. He directs research projects at the Paraguayan Space Agency (AEP) and was speaking to Paraguay TV.

What comes next

The first milestone is contact with the ground station in Asunción, which the first reports did not confirm. Months of tests on the panels, the chip and the magnetic measurements would follow.

Lessons from the mission will feed into GuaraníSat-3, planned for Earth observation. In 2025 the agency named crop monitoring as a goal; GuaraníSat-2 itself is a test platform, not an observation satellite.

The launch does not give Paraguay its own rockets, and a satellite this small does not provide internet or television. What it builds is skill: a country whose first satellite was assembled abroad now has home-built hardware in orbit.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is GuaraníSat-2?

It is Paraguay’s second satellite and the first designed and assembled in the country. The nanosatellite measures 30 by 10 by 10 centimetres, weighs under four kilograms and was launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission.

What will GuaraníSat-2 do?

It will test solar panels from an Italian company and a NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory microchip, relay data for radio amateurs and help measure the South Atlantic Anomaly, a weak zone in Earth’s magnetic field.

How long will the satellite stay in space?

About two years. It will then lose altitude gradually and burn up on re-entry, so it does not leave debris in orbit.

Who built Paraguay’s first satellite?

GuaraníSat-1 was developed with Japan’s Kyushu Institute of Technology, assembled in Japan and launched in 2021. GuaraníSat-2 was built in Paraguay by engineers trained on that project.

Sources: SNT, “GuaraníSat-2 ya está en el espacio”, 1 October 2026, Última Hora, 1 October 2026, EFE via Diario Libre, 1 October 2026, Hoy, 1 October 2026, Hoy, Paraguayan Space Agency interview, 15 September 2025. World.title: Honduras Plans Cybersecurity Law for Congress by End-2026, Regulator Says
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

HONDURAS · TECHNOLOGY

Key Facts — The country Honduras, in Central America, is still drafting a cybersecurity law. It has also not joined the Budapest Convention, the main international treaty on cybercrime.

— The background Phishing, messages with links that steal personal data, is one threat the regulator cites. Most attacks come from abroad, which the regulator says makes them hard to prosecute.

— Why now On 29 September prosecutors and the Supreme Court said they will ask Congress for new cybercrime offences. Two days later the telecoms regulator set out its own plan.

— What happened On 1 October 2026 a Conatel commissioner said a draft cybersecurity law could go to Congress by the end of 2026.

— Who is who César Cáceres of Conatel works with the ITU, the United Nations telecoms agency. The plan includes a state cyber-incident response centre.

— What it means for you Nothing changes yet, as the law is still a draft. The regulator’s warning about text messages with links applies now.

— Still open The draft text, the cost of the response centre and when it will open have not been published.

Honduras’s telecoms regulator says a draft cybersecurity law could be ready and sent to the National Congress by the end of 2026. César Cáceres, a commissioner of the National Telecommunications Commission (Conatel), gave the timeline on 1 October, the newspaper Tiempo reported.

The plan also includes a state centre to detect and respond to cyber attacks. Neither the draft law nor a budget for the centre has been made public.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

What the regulator announced

The proposed law aims to strengthen the state’s ability to prevent, investigate and respond to cyber attacks, Cáceres said. It is part of a national cybersecurity strategy that Conatel is preparing with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU).

“We hope that by the end of the year we can have it ready and sent to Congress,” he told HCH television. “But above all, we are working hard to set up a centre (…) to respond to cybersecurity attacks.”

He described phishing as a present danger, on which Conatel works directly with the phone companies. “There are people who send messages with links for people to open, and that is where they capture the information,” he said.

A response centre for the state

The centre would be what specialists call a CSIRT, a computer security incident response team. Such teams watch for attacks, coordinate the response and help restore systems.

Cáceres said it would guard databases that “cannot be hijacked”, including the central registers of personal data. It would also cover security, defence and the country’s critical infrastructure.

He gave no date for the centre to open, no budget and no staff numbers.

Why the Budapest treaty matters

Conatel is also working on certifications that would let Honduras join the Budapest Convention. The 2001 treaty, drawn up by the Council of Europe, sets common rules for prosecuting cybercrime and sharing evidence across borders.

“The attacks are not local; most are international,” Cáceres said. Because Honduras has not joined, he added, it lacks a mechanism to pursue such crimes internationally.

A second track on cybercrime

The regulator’s plan runs alongside a separate push by the Public Ministry, the prosecution service, and the Supreme Court. On 29 September they said they will ask Congress to modernise the criminal law on cybercrime, Tiempo reported.

Their proposal would add new offences, with priority for human trafficking and child sexual exploitation through online platforms, and online fraud. It would also tighten the rules on electronic evidence in investigations and trials.

That initiative followed Honduras’s participation in the 15th United Nations Crime Congress in Abu Dhabi. There, the Honduran delegation reached agreements with the Cybersecurity Council of the United Arab Emirates.

What comes next

Both proposals must still reach Honduras’s single-chamber Congress, where lawmakers can change them. Conatel’s target is the end of 2026; the prosecutors and the court have given no date.

The announcement is a plan, not a law, and it places no new duties on companies or users today. Cáceres did not link it to any specific recent attack on state systems.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Conatel?

Conatel, the National Telecommunications Commission, is the state body that regulates telecommunications in Honduras.

What is a CSIRT?

A computer security incident response team detects cyber attacks, coordinates the response and helps systems recover. Honduras plans one to protect state databases and critical infrastructure.

Has Honduras joined the Budapest Convention on cybercrime?

Not yet. Conatel says it is working on the certifications needed to join the 2001 treaty, which helps countries cooperate against cybercrime.

Sources: Tiempo, 1 October 2026 (quoting César Cáceres on HCH); Tiempo, 29 September 2026.

World.title: Guyana Charges Man Over Two Surinamese Men Missing Since 29 August
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

GUYANA · SURINAME · CRIME

Key Facts — The countries Guyana and Suriname are neighbours on South America’s north-east coast, divided by the Corentyne River. Small boats carry people across it outside the official ferry.

— The background Siegello Lorenzo van Dalen, 28, and Derryl Danillo Bont, 29, left home in Suriname on 28 August. They were last seen the next day in Nickerie, about to cross to Guyana by boat.

— Why now Police in both countries reported them missing on 19 September. On 29 September residents of a village near Guyana’s capital blocked a police search with fires.

— What happened On 1 October 2026 a Guyanese court charged Jimmol Murphy, 33, with abducting both men at Rosignol, in eastern Guyana, on 29 August.

— The numbers Bail was set at GY$1 million (about US$4,800). The offence carries up to five years in prison.

— What it means for you The case is a reminder that informal river crossings between the two countries sit largely outside official control.

— Still open The men have not been found. His lawyers say he was elsewhere, and the case returns to court on 19 October.

A Guyana court has charged a 33-year-old man with abducting two missing Surinamese men who set out by boat on 29 August. Jimmol Murphy appeared at the Fort Wellington Magistrates’ Court on Thursday, 1 October 2026, and was granted bail.

The men have not been found, and the police have not said what happened to them. The case centres on a family from Vigilance, a village east of Georgetown, the capital.

The charge

Murphy, of Vigilance, is accused of abducting Siegello Lorenzo van Dalen, 28, of Saramacca, and Derryl Danillo Bont, 29, of Wanica. Both districts lie west of Paramaribo, Suriname’s capital.

The offence allegedly took place at Rosignol, on the west bank of the Berbice River, on 29 August. Waterkant described Murphy as a driver and contractor.

Magistrate Shareefah Parks granted bail of GY$1 million (about US$4,800), Demerara Waves reported. Murphy appeared by video link and was not required to plead to the indictable charge.

He must hand over his passport and report to the police Major Crimes Unit every Friday, the Surinamese news site Waterkant reported. The case continues on 19 October.

The maximum penalty is a fine of GY$750,000 (about US$3,600) and five years in prison. Conversions use the Bank of Guyana’s 1 October rate of about 209 Guyana dollars per US dollar.

The defence

Murphy’s lawyers, led by Siand Dhurjon, said he was “in between Houston and Greater Georgetown at the material time”. Houston is a community on the southern edge of Georgetown, not the American city.

They argued that investigators had not contacted witnesses who could confirm that alibi. They also said the two men “might have happily left Guyana through its porous borders”.

Dhurjon was assisted by the lawyers Mark Waldron and Meshon Persaud, Demerara Waves reported.

How the case unfolded

The two men left their homes on 28 August in a Toyota Vitz heading for Nickerie, Suriname’s western district on the border. On 29 August they were seen leaving the car at Clara Sluice to travel to Guyana by boat.

Suriname’s police and Guyana’s police reported them missing on 19 September. A day later Guyana’s deputy police commissioner, Wendell Blanhum, said there had been no sightings in Guyana.

“Searches were conducted and several persons were questioned. No useful information was obtained,” the Guyana police said at the time.

Police later said the men “were last seen alive when they joined a white vehicle registered in his wife’s name”. The vehicle belonged to the wife of Mark Cromwell, Murphy’s brother, Demerara Waves reported.

On 29 September residents of Vigilance blocked a police search of Cromwell’s house with burning debris. A lorry was set on fire.

Officers met hostile resistance when they tried to put out a fire threatening utility poles, Kaieteur News reported. Cromwell’s wife and brother were held in custody.

Who Mark Cromwell is

Cromwell, known as “Demon”, is a former policeman. In June 2025 the US Treasury placed him under sanctions over alleged cocaine trafficking.

The Treasury accused him of moving tons of cocaine to the United States, Europe and the Caribbean. He has not been charged in Guyana, according to Demerara Waves, and he is not charged in this case.

What comes next

Murphy returns to court on 19 October, while police in both countries continue to search for the two men. The two men have now been missing for more than a month.

Police in both countries have asked anyone with information to come forward; in Guyana the emergency number is 911.

A charge is not a conviction, and Murphy has not entered a plea. The reports reviewed by The Rio Times do not mention any charges in Suriname, where the men lived.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who are the missing Surinamese men?

Siegello Lorenzo van Dalen, 28, of Saramacca, and Derryl Danillo Bont, 29, of Wanica. They were last seen on 29 August at Clara Sluice in Nickerie, preparing to cross to Guyana by boat.

Who has been charged?

Jimmol Murphy, 33, of Vigilance, East Coast Demerara, was charged on 1 October 2026 with abducting the two men at Rosignol on 29 August. His lawyers say he was elsewhere at the time; he was granted GY$1 million (about US$4,800) bail.

Have the men been found?

No. As of 2 October 2026 police in Guyana and Suriname had not found the men or said what happened to them.

How do people cross between Suriname and Guyana?

The official route is the ferry across the Corentyne River. Small boats also cross from the Nickerie area outside the official route, as the two men planned to do.

Sources: Demerara Waves, Demon/Diamond’s brother charged with abduction of Surinamese men, 1 October 2026, Waterkant, 33-jarige man aangeklaagd voor ontvoering van twee vermiste Surinaamse mannen, 2 October 2026, Demerara Waves, Vigilance villagers block search, 29 September 2026, Kaieteur News, Unrest at Vigilance after police arrest Mark Cromwell’s wife and brother, 29 September 2026, Demerara Waves, No sighting of missing Surinamese men in Guyana, 20 September 2026, Bank of Guyana, exchange rates as at 1 October 2026. All retrieved 2 October 2026.

World.title: Ecuador Has 40 Days to Seek Extradition of Blackout Suspect Freed in Spain
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

ECUADOR · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The country Ecuador, a dollarised Andean nation of about 18 million people, suffered long daily power cuts during a drought in 2024. Emergency power contracts signed then are now in court.

— The background In the Progen, or “Blackout”, case, prosecutors say the state paid advances of more than US$104 million for 49 generators that did not work as promised. Thirty people are charged.

— Why now Interpol arrested José Walther Manrique Suárez, one of the defendants, in Spain on 30 September. A Spanish judge released him after a hearing on 1 October, his defence said.

— What happened Ecuador has 40 days from the arrest to send Spain a formal extradition request, which a lawyer quoted by El Comercio puts at around 8 or 9 November.

— Who is who Manrique, 47, owns Astrobryxa S.A., a subcontractor of the US firm Progen Industries. He and his wife, co-defendant Karla Saud, applied for asylum in Spain on 10 July.

— What it means for you No quick handover is coming. While the asylum claim is pending, Spain cannot deliver him to Ecuador, even if a court approves extradition.

— Still open Whether Ecuador files in time, how Spain rules on asylum, and whether the case’s move to new judges in Quito keeps his detention order alive.

Ecuador now has 40 days to ask Spain formally to extradite José Walther Manrique, a suspect in a major blackout-era corruption case. A Spanish judge released him on 1 October, a day after Interpol arrested him.

His defence confirmed the release after a court hearing, the newspaper El Comercio reported. Neither El Comercio nor other Ecuadorian reports mention any conditions attached to it.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Why he walked free

Interpol detained Manrique on 30 September, as Interior Minister John Reimberg announced. El Comercio says he was held under an international notice to locate him for extradition. Spanish law requires a detainee to see a judge within 24 hours, a lawyer told El Comercio.

That judge decides whether the person stays in custody or goes free, possibly under supervision.

In Manrique’s case, the arrest did not lead to a handover, his defence said. Ecuador’s National Court of Justice had not yet sent the formal request.

The news site Ecuadorinmediato also reported the release, citing his lawyer. The Rio Times reported the arrest on 1 October.

The 40-day clock

Ecuador has 40 days from the arrest to file the request through diplomatic channels. José Elías Cárdenas, a lawyer interviewed by El Comercio, puts the deadline at around 8 or 9 November 2026.

Ecuador’s new extradition law has been in force since 7 August 2026. The request must come from the president of the National Court and go through the Foreign Ministry.

It must include the detention order, a summary of the facts and the relevant laws.

There is a complication at home.

The case against former energy minister Antonio Gonçalves has been dismissed. As a result, the proceedings move from the National Court to criminal judges based in Iñaquito, in Quito.

According to Cárdenas, the new judge must take up the case and keep Manrique’s detention order in force. That order is what supports the extradition request.

Why asylum blocks a handover

Manrique and his wife, Karla Saud Calero, applied for international protection in Spain on 10 July 2026. They say a commercial dispute became political persecution and that their family received threats.

The asylum claim does not stop the extradition process, El Comercio reports. But it legally prevents Spain from handing them over while the claim is pending.

If Spain refuses asylum, the handover could be reactivated, although the defence can appeal. A refusal would not mean automatic extradition either, because Spanish courts can reject the request on other legal grounds.

The case behind it

Prosecutors added Manrique to the case on 24 August as an alleged co-author of embezzlement of public funds. His company, Astrobryxa, worked as Progen’s subcontractor on emergency power plants at Quevedo and Salitral.

The contracts between CELEC, the state power company, and Progen totalled US$149.1 million for 49 generators. Prosecutors say the machines were used, technically incompatible and did not work.

Saud says Progen did not pay all it owed. She says her firm was the first to sue it in the United States.

The 30 defendants are awaiting a preparatory trial hearing.

What comes next

Once Ecuador files, Spain’s government reviews the request and the National High Court holds a hearing. Spain’s Council of Ministers steps in at the final stage, and the defence can appeal at several points.

Cárdenas says there is no fixed timetable, and the process could take several months or more than a year. Manrique’s release does not mean the charges in Ecuador have been dropped, and it does not end the extradition.

It does mean Ecuador must move fast on paperwork while changing judges. The prosecution’s figures remain allegations that no court has yet tested at trial.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Progen case?

It is an Ecuadorian corruption case over emergency power contracts signed during the 2024 electricity crisis. Prosecutors say state power company CELEC paid advances of more than US$104 million to the US firm Progen for 49 generators that did not work as promised.

Was José Walther Manrique released in Spain?

Yes. A Spanish judge ordered his release after a hearing on 1 October 2026, a day after his Interpol arrest, his defence said. No conditions have been reported.

Can Spain extradite him to Ecuador?

Only after Ecuador files a formal request, which it must do within 40 days of the arrest. His pending asylum claim currently prevents Spain from handing him over.

How long could extradition take?

There is no fixed timetable. A lawyer quoted by El Comercio says the process could last several months or more than a year, depending on the asylum claim and appeals.

Sources: El Comercio, Manrique released in Spain, 1 October 2026, El Comercio, extradition explainer, 1 October 2026, Ecuadorinmediato, 1 October 2026. All retrieved 2 October 2026.

World.title: PSU objects to Troy Gabb as Acting PSC Chair, cites political commentary; appointment revives controversial DFC-era history
World.content:
PSU objects to Troy Gabb as Acting PSC Chair, cites political commentary; appointment revives controversial DFC-era history

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Public Service Union of Belize (PSU) has formally objected to the appointment of Troy Gabb as Acting Chairperson of the Public Services Commission (PSC), saying his record as a political commentator and his past public positions raise concerns about confidence in the body responsible for appointments, promotions and discipline in the public service.

In a statement issued today, October 1, the PSU said Gabb, a weekly commentator on Love FM, has “repeatedly shown hostility toward trade unions,” opposed PSU positions on public policy and sharply criticized public officers. The Union further described him as widely perceived to be politically partisan. Those characterizations are the PSU’s stated position.

The Belize Gazette of July 23 confirms that Governor General Dame Froyla Tzalam appointed Gabb to act as Chairperson of the PSC effective July 20, 2026, while substantive Chairperson Diana Price-Murillo is on leave.

But Gabb is no stranger to controversy involving public institutions.

He previously served as Chief Executive Officer of the Development Finance Corporation (DFC) during a period that later became the subject of extensive Senate scrutiny and a Commission of Inquiry over questionable loans, securitization arrangements and other transactions at the state-owned lending institution.

During Senate hearings in 2004, Gabb was questioned about DFC’s large portfolio of non-performing loans. He acknowledged at the time that roughly 35% of DFC’s loan portfolio was non-performing, while senators questioned the institution’s due diligence surrounding major borrowers, including the Novelo’s Group.

Gabb was again called before the DFC Commission of Inquiry in 2007, where he faced questions concerning a number of major transactions, including the Novelo loans, DFC’s involvement in the Mahogany Heights deal, transactions involving companies associated with former DFC chairman Glenn Godfrey and a multimillion-dollar transaction involving the Belize Bank and Government.

One of the more personally controversial issues raised during those hearings concerned a San Pedro property Gabb acquired from DFC for $15,000. Contemporary reporting on the inquiry said commissioners placed its value at approximately $68,000, meaning the purchase price was roughly $53,000 below that valuation. Gabb was questioned about the transaction during his testimony.

The inquiry also heard testimony that, during Gabb’s tenure, certain DFC administration or legal fees were waived or varied in selected cases, with commissioners questioning what authority existed for the CEO to exercise that discretion.

Gabb defended his stewardship of the DFC and challenged aspects of the inquiry and forensic audit, arguing that adverse findings had been prepared without first allowing him an opportunity to respond and questioning the legality of the forensic auditor’s appointment.

Justice Herbert Lord’s subsequent report concluded more broadly that wrongdoing had occurred in the operations of the DFC during the period investigated. That finding concerned the institution and transactions examined by the Commission and should not, by itself, be read as a finding that Gabb personally committed a criminal offence.

Against that history, the PSU says it also opposes Gabb being reappointed as a member of the PSC when his current term expires in November 2026.

“Building a strong Public Service begins with confidence and trust in the Commission,” the Union said.

The PSU has written to Minister of the Public Service Henry Charles Usher outlining its concerns and has called for future PSC appointments to be persons with public-service knowledge, integrity and standing who command the respect of both public officers and the wider public.

The Union also extended best wishes to Price-Murillo and said it hopes for a speedy resolution of the circumstances surrounding her leave and her return to office.

World.title: Sentencing delayed again for cops convicted over filming viral sex video of couple having sex
World.content:
Sentencing delayed again for cops convicted over filming viral sex video of couple having sex

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two police officers convicted of wilful oppression for recording and circulating a video of a couple engaged in a sexual act during the COVID-19 pandemic will have to wait a little longer to learn their fate after their sentencing was adjourned again on Thursday.

Police Corporal Jason Shaw and Police Constable Leslie Martinez appeared before High Court Justice Derick Sylvester for sentencing, but the matter could not proceed because reports previously ordered by the court were still outstanding.

Justice Sylvester therefore adjourned the matter to Monday, October 5, 2026.

Shaw and Martinez were unanimously convicted on July 17 by a nine-member jury after less than two hours of deliberation. The five women and four men on the jury found both officers guilty of wilful oppression.

The case stems from an April 5, 2020 incident in which the officers recorded a couple engaged in a sexual act inside an abandoned building in Belize City. Prosecutors said the video was subsequently shared in a police WhatsApp group known as “Loyal Group” before spreading publicly and causing humiliation to the couple.

The July proceedings were a retrial. An earlier trial ended after the jury was unable to reach the required verdict, and the matter was later transferred to Justice Sylvester.

A third police officer, Anthony Villamil, had originally been charged alongside Shaw and Martinez, but prosecutors later withdrew the charge against him and granted him immunity in exchange for his testimony.

Shaw and Martinez remain awaiting sentencing and are due back before the High Court on October 5.

World.title: Khris Rosado sentencing delayed again in fatal crash that killed Police Constable Arcenio Cus
World.content:
Khris Rosado sentencing delayed again in fatal crash that killed Police Constable Arcenio Cus

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The sentencing of businessman Khris Rosado for causing the death of Police Constable Arcenio Cus has been postponed again, this time until Monday, October 5, 2026.

Rosado appeared before High Court Justice Derick Sylvester on Thursday morning for what was expected to be his sentencing hearing, but the matter was adjourned. Justice Sylvester apologized for the delay and indicated that efforts would be made to conclude the matter at the next appearance.

Rosado, the owner of Thirsty Thursday, pleaded guilty on June 16 to causing death by careless conduct in connection with the July 28, 2025 traffic collision on the Philip Goldson Highway that claimed the life of 38-year-old PC Cus.

His sentencing had initially been scheduled for June 30 but was postponed to October 1 after his attorney, Dr. Lynden Jones, requested an adjournment because he was engaged in another matter outside the district.

Police said Cus, who was from Silver Creek Village, was travelling toward Belize City on a motorcycle when a black vehicle entered his lane and collided with him between miles six and seven of the highway. Cus suffered severe head and abdominal injuries and later died.

Investigators later detained Rosado at his Ladyville residence, where police located a damaged 2009 Honda Ridgeline believed to have been involved in the collision. A post-mortem found that Cus died from multiple blunt-force traumatic injuries sustained in the crash.

Rosado was initially charged with five offences, including manslaughter by negligence, causing death by careless conduct, driving without due care and attention, failure to stop and render aid, and failure to report an accident. The matter ultimately proceeded in the High Court on the causing-death-by-careless-conduct charge, to which he pleaded guilty.

He is now scheduled to return before Justice Sylvester on Monday for sentencing.

World.title: Gian Teck pleads guilty to sex with 14-year-old girl after Crown Counsel Kirk Brown presents damning evidence
World.content:
Gian Teck pleads guilty to sex with 14-year-old girl after Crown Counsel Kirk Brown presents damning evidence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Just 16 days after celebrating his 22nd birthday, Gian Teck of Maskall Village was remanded to the Belize Central Prison on Thursday after changing his plea to guilty in a High Court trial for Unlawful Sexual Intercourse (USI) with a 14-year-old minor. Teck, who stood trial before Justice Nigel Pilgrim in a judge-alone matter without a jury, conceded to defeat on the fourth day of proceedings after Crown Counsel Kirk Brown, prosecuting on behalf of the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), presented damning evidence and the testimony of the victim.

The trial, which commenced on Monday, September 28, 2026, hinged on the testimony of the virtual complainant, which was delivered in camera behind closed doors. According to agreed facts presented in court, the incident occurred on the night of Monday, June 5, 2023, when the 14-year-old victim visited Teck—who was 18 at the time—at his home.

The minor arrived on her bicycle, and the two went inside where Teck undressed her and engaged in sexual intercourse before she left around 1:00 a.m. the following morning. A medical examination conducted on June 29, 2023, by a doctor confirmed hymeneal tears classified as grievous harm, and during a caution interview that same day, Teck admitted to police that he had sexual intercourse with the minor three times at his residence, leading to his formal arrest on June 30, 2023.

This conviction comes months after Teck managed to avoid prosecution on separate sexual assault charges. On January 28, 2026, two counts of unlawful sexual intercourse against Teck were discontinued in the High Court before Justice Candace Nanton when the Crown entered a nolle prosequi after a victim from a May 2024 incident refused to testify, though Justice Nanton cautioned Teck at the time that the matter could be recalled in the future.

Following his guilty plea on Thursday, Justice Pilgrim revoked Teck’s bail and remanded him to the Belize Central Prison. Teck, who was represented in court by attorney Javier Williams, is scheduled to return to court on October 22, 2026, where Justice Pilgrim will hear mitigation pleas before handing down his sentence.

World.title: Kareem Anderson, charged for punching down 2 women, set free after nine months on remand without psychiatric evaluation; mother died while he was in prison
World.content:
Kareem Anderson, charged for punching down 2 women, set free after nine months on remand without psychiatric evaluation; mother died while he was in prison

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 27-year-old Belize City man who spent approximately nine months on remand without receiving a court-ordered psychiatric evaluation has been ordered released from the Belize Central Prison after the Chief Magistrate dismissed the charges against him.

Kareem Anderson had been charged with common assault and harm in connection with separate attacks on two women in Belize City in late 2025, but the court had never taken a plea from him because of concerns about his mental state.

The Chief Magistrate noted on Wednesday that Anderson had remained behind bars for months while still awaiting an evaluation and that there was no clear indication when one could be completed.

His family reportedly could not afford a private psychiatric assessment, which can cost thousands of dollars, and the court was told that the absence of an available government psychiatrist had further delayed the process.

Given the length of time Anderson had spent on remand and the uncertainty surrounding the evaluation, the Chief Magistrate dismissed the charges and ordered that he be released as soon as possible.

Anderson had been accused of attacking two women in separate incidents captured on surveillance footage. One victim, sanitation worker Kendra Hamilton, was reportedly struck while cleaning a Belize City street, while 69-year-old Barbara Austin was allegedly punched as she walked along a sidewalk and fell to the ground.

The case also took a tragic turn while Anderson was incarcerated.

His mother, Jacqueline Elizabeth August, 54, died on August 8, 2026, while he was still on remand. Anderson’s sister, Monique, said he has not yet been told of their mother’s death and did not attend her funeral.

She said the family now faces the difficult task of breaking the news to him after his release.

Monique, who has reportedly helped care for Anderson for several years, said she expects to collect her brother from prison by Friday.

The dismissal means the allegations against Anderson will not proceed to trial at this time.

World.title: Raymond Moody granted $800 bail to seek psychiatric evaluation but remains behind bars after failing to post bail
World.content:
Raymond Moody granted $800 bail to seek psychiatric evaluation but remains behind bars after failing to post bail

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man whose theft arraignment was previously halted because of concerns over his mental state has been granted bail so he can seek a psychiatric evaluation, but remains at the Belize Central Prison after being unable to post the required bail.

Raymond Moody, 33, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday, where he was offered bail in the sum of $800 with one surety of the same amount.

Moody has been in custody since late August, when his arraignment on a theft charge had to be stopped after he reportedly appeared disoriented and gave the court several different names while showing uncertainty about basic personal details including his age, date of birth and address.

At that time, Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison ordered that Moody undergo a psychiatric evaluation before the court proceeds with the matter.

More than a month later, however, the evaluation has reportedly still not been completed.

The court has now granted Moody bail in the hope that relatives can assist him in obtaining a private psychiatric assessment so it can be determined whether he is fit to enter a plea.

Moody was unable to secure the $800 bail and was therefore remanded back to the Belize Central Prison.

The theft charge has not yet been formally put to him.

Police allege that on August 26, 2026, Moody stole a dark blue Samsung cellphone valued at $650, property of Tarique Campbell.

He is expected to return to court in December.

World.title: Family demands answers after child knocked down outside school in designated safe zone
World.content:
Family demands answers after child knocked down outside school in designated safe zone

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Santa Elena resident Britney Guerra and her family is seeking answers after her 5-year-old niece was reportedly knocked down this week by a motorcycle in front of Santa Elena Primary School in Santa Elena.

“The person operating the motorcycle is a 15-year-old boy.

When we spoke with the police, we were told that the child cannot be arrested because of his age and that he is supposed to be charged. However, as of now, we understand that he has still not been charged, and we are very concerned because the same child is still riding a motorcycle and was seen delivering food at Santa Elena Primary School on September 30th,” Guerra explained.

“We are not trying to harass or attack a 15-year-old child. We simply want answers, accountability, and reassurance that our children are safe around the school,” she added.

The family is reportedly seeking the police assistance in dealing with this matter.

World.title: Ladyville man admits attacking brother with pint bottle; court seeks help for drinking problem before sentencing
World.content:
Ladyville man admits attacking brother with pint bottle; court seeks help for drinking problem before sentencing

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 24-year-old Ladyville man who admitted attacking his own brother with a pint bottle while drunk is out on bail pending sentencing, as the Chief Magistrate has ordered intervention from the Community Rehabilitation Department after he acknowledged having a drinking problem.

Bryan Salvatierra, a gas vendor from Ladyville, pleaded guilty to aggravated assault upon his brother, Henry Salvatierra.

According to the court facts, Henry reported that on September 28 he was lying on a sofa at home when Bryan allegedly approached him aggressively, insulted him and threatened to stab him.

Their mother reportedly intervened and separated the brothers, after which Henry called 911. Before police arrived, Bryan allegedly returned with a bottle and again threatened his brother.

When the Chief Magistrate asked Bryan what had caused the confrontation, he reportedly replied, “nothing,” before acknowledging that he had been drinking.

The court was also told that the incident was not the first time Bryan had behaved aggressively while intoxicated.

Because aggravated assault carries the possibility of a substantial prison term, the Chief Magistrate ordered a pre-sentencing report through the Community Rehabilitation Department before determining his punishment.

A social worker is expected to interview Bryan, his brother and other relatives, including their mother, as part of the assessment. The court indicated that the report could help determine whether rehabilitation or other intervention may be appropriate before sentencing.

Salvatierra was granted bail of $3,000 with one surety in the same amount. He must report to the Ladyville Police Station every Wednesday and remain at least 100 feet away from his brother and any prosecution witnesses.

He is scheduled to return to court on October 26, 2026.

World.title: No fallout
World.content:
DESPITE concerns from some

quarters over the slow spending

of Hurricane Melissa donations,

permanent secretary in the Ministry of

Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Sheila

Sealy Monteith says the Jamaican Diaspora

has not raised any complaints about how

its contributions are being used.

Sealy Monteith told Parliament’s Internal

and External Affairs Committee on Thursday

that the ministry had “many opportunities”

to receive feedback from the Diaspora but

had not received any indication of concern. The assurance

came against the backdrop

of concerns about the pace

at which millions of dollars

donated following Hurricane

Melissa have been utilised.

Category 5 Melissa left

immense damage after

slamming into Jamaica’s

south-western coast on

October 28, 2025 and swept

across western and north-western parishes.

During the committee’s deliberations with the ministry,

Opposition Member of

Parliament Dr Kenneth Russell

raised the Auditor General’s

finding that only about 1.7 per

cent of the donated funds had

been used months after the

contributions were made.

“Has the ministry, one,

received any feedback from

the members of the Diaspora

and the donors about the slow

use of their contributions? And

secondly, is the ministry concerned about the reputational

risks done to the country and

the effect it will have on your

ability to raise funds should

a similar situation recur?”

Russell queried.

Sealy Monteith responded

that the ministry had not seen

evidence of a decline in confidence in Jamaica’s ability to

handle international support.

“We have used the strength

of our diplomacy to ensure that

countries who wish to contribute are enabled to contribute,

that we are able to record it.

We are providing direction

for them, and we pass them

on to the relevant authorities.

We have not received any

indication to date that there

has been a loss of confidence

in our abilities to use it,” she

revealed.

The permanent secretary

stressed that the Ministry of

Foreign Affairs and Foreign

Trade’s role is primarily to facilitate international assistance,

rather than to determine how

the funds are ultimately spent.

She said the ministry works

with other government entities

to ensure that countries and

other contributors wishing to

assist Jamaica are able to do so

and are directed to the relevant

authorities.

Sealy Monteith also suggested that the pace at which contributions are absorbed and

deployed must be considered

in the context of the capacity

of the receiving authorities to

use the support.

“I think people understand

also that when support comes

in, it requires the ability to be

able to assimilate and to use,

and that comes over time as

well,” she said.

“So, if you’re asking me

whether there’s been a fallout

of interest and solidarity, I have

not seen that. We continue

to be a preferred guest on

many agendas, and Minister

[Kamina Johnson Smith] had

a schedule in New York last

week that was head-turning

because everybody wants

Jamaica to be at the table, to

sit on our committees, to be

there,” she added

World.title: TALL TASK!
World.content:
JAMAICA will be looking to get back on track in the Concacaf Nations League when they face hosts El Salvador in San Salvador tonight at 9:00 pm Jamaica time.

The Reggae Boyz started their campaign with a 3-2 win against Guatemala at the National Stadium in Kingston last Friday. But three days later, they lost 1-0 to Honduras at the same venue.

Now, Jamaica face two away games in four days. After playing El Salvador, they travel to take on Honduras again on Monday.

Suriname lead Group B with six points from two games. Four teams — Guatemala, Honduras, Jamaica, and El Salvador — are tied on three points each, while Martinique sits at the bottom without a point.

Jamaica made five changes to their starting line-up against Honduras, but the team still struggled with energy levels.

Interim Head Coach Rudolph Speid says fatigue hurt the team early in that match.

“The people who started the last match, we repeated them,” Speid said in the press conference on Monday. “We were a bit lethargic, and that allowed Honduras to dominate the game in the first half, especially.”

The home loss puts extra pressure on the team as they head into two tough away matches.

“The loss to Honduras is a setback for us,” he said. “It means that we have to win our remaining games to qualify straight from this stage. So, it’s going to be tough, and we’re going away, which makes it even harder for us.”

Speid also mentioned defensive problems that need quick fixing before facing El Salvador.

“There’s a lot of things — almost everything that we need to improve on,” he said. “Our pressing wasn’t good against Honduras, but even when we dropped into a low block, Honduras still found ways through. Maybe we were just too wide apart, and we have to play much tighter.”

With games coming four days apart and travel involved, Speid hinted at making changes to keep the team fresh.

“We have a big squad, and it is possible that we might have to allow other players who have more energy to play,” he said. “We’ll have to rotate, and that’s something we’re going to look at.”

Tajay Grant, Jamone Lyle, Kyle Ming, and Ramone Howell have been added to boost the squad for this trip.

El Salvador also enter this match with three points from two games. They opened with a 3-1 win over Martinique before a 6-0 loss away to Guatemala on matchday two.

Playing at home at Estadio Cuscatlán, El Salvador will be eager to recover and take advantage of their home crowd.

Jamaica are undefeated in their last five meetings against El Salvador, with one win and four draws. The most recent match was a 1-1 draw in Kingston during World Cup qualifying in March 2022.

Winning away at Estadio Cuscatlán has proven difficult for the Boyz. Their last two trips to San Salvador in World Cup and Nations League qualifying ended in a 1-1 draw in November 2021 and a 2-0 loss in March 2019.

World.title: JTA president-elect rushed to hospital following two- vehicle crash in Trelawny
World.content:
Scenes from a two-vehicle crash in Duncans, Trelawny, on Thursday afternoon that left President-elect of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association (JTA), Dr Maureen Mullings-Nelson, injured.

TRELAWNY, Jamaica — President-elect of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association (JTA), Dr Maureen Mullings-Nelson, was rushed to hospital on Thursday afternoon after sustaining multiple injuries in a two-vehicle crash on the Duncans main road in Trelawny.

The crash, which occurred about 3:30 pm, involved two Honda CR-V motor vehicles.

Mullings-Nelson was a passenger in one of the vehicles, which was travelling from Montego Bay, St James, towards Kingston after a JTA Central Executive meeting at the Sea Gardens Hotel.

The Jamaica Observer understands that Mullings-Nelson sustained multiple injuries and was taken to hospital for treatment.

The driver of the other Honda CR-V reportedly suffered minor injuries. It was not immediately clear whether the driver of the vehicle in which Mullings-Nelson was travelling was physically harmed.

The crash resulted in a lengthy traffic pile-up along the roadway as emergency personnel responded to the scene.

Members of the Jamaica Fire Brigade and the Jamaica Constabulary Force were among those who responded.

Further information on Mullings-Nelson’s condition were not immediately available.

World.title: ‘A me kill Taneka’: Detective testifies Ruddock confessed to Pathways killing
World.content:
Taneka Gardener was allegedly murdered on the orders of Kevin Smith at Kingdom Restoration Ministries in Albion St James.

A detective constable a few moments ago testified that murder accused Andre Ruddock confessed to him that he killed 39-year-old Taneka Gardner at the Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in Albion St James.

Gardner was killed on October 17, 2021, as part of what has been described as a human sacrifice ritual at the church.

Ruddock is alleged to have cut her throat on the instructions of his now-deceased pastor, Dr Kevin Smith, who allegedly told Gardner that her blood was unclean and therefore she had to die. The pastor allegedly asked her if she believed he could bring her back to life if she was killed. After she repeatedly said she believed, her throat was cut, allegedly by Ruddock after another man hesitated to carry out the pastor’s order to slash her throat.

Both Ruddock and Gardner were members of Smith’s flock.

The detective constable took the witness stand for the first time in the Home Circuit Court murder trial of Ruddock in downtown Kingston. He is the seventh witness to take the stand.

The detective explained that when he arrived at the scene around 11:00 pm he was pointed to two men in handcuffs who were sitting on the ground by a big gate leading to the church. One of the men was identified to the detective as Kevin Smith. The other man was identified to him as Andre Ruddock. The only sort of clothing both had on was underwear.

After receiving certain details regarding the incident, the cop led Ruddock away from the pastor and took him inside the building, where he allowed him to put on some clothes. He proceeded to caution him by telling him that he was not obliged to say anything unless he wished to do so, but that anything he said would be taken down in writing and could be used against him in a court of law.

According to him, Ruddock decided that he had something he wished to say and allegedly began to spill the beans.

“I took him away from where he was by the gate. I allowed him to put on some clothes because he was in underpants…He immediately started talking, saying, ‘a me kill Taneka, mi naa go tell you no lie and mi ago tell you everything weh happen’.

“I asked him how he killed Taneka, and he said, ‘mi cut har neck’. I asked him why he cut Taneka’s neck, and he said, ‘mi get instructions fi do it. I asked him who instructed him, and he didn’t respond, but he was looking in the direction of the big gate where I took him from,” the detective said.

The prosecution team, comprising Latoya Bernard and Carolyn Wright, will continue the examination-in-chief of the witness. In the meantime, Ruddock’s attorneys Anthony Williams and Venice Brown are listening attentively as they prepare to cross-examine the detective constable.

World.title: Water crisis deepening
World.content:
JAMAICA’S water crisis is deepening, with 107 of the National Water Commission’s 405 reserve systems dipping into drought territory, even as several parishes continue to face strict water restrictions. In the meantime, Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda has put Jamaicans on warning for even tighter water restrictions come Monday, as the country continues to grapple with worsening drought conditions.

Some communities could be getting day-on, day-off supply as the crisis deepens, with rainfall projections for drought-affected parishes looking bleak for the months ahead.
