World.title: Defence raises questions about cop who was member of Kevin Smith’s flock
World.content:
Late pastor of Pathways International Restoration Ministries, Kevin Smith.

THE detective sergeant who cried repeatedly on Tuesday while giving evidence in the Andre Ruddock murder trial in the Home Circuit Court in Kingston breathed a sigh of relief on Wednesday as she was released as a witness after defence attorney Anthony Williams ended his cross-examination of her.

Ruddock is on trial for murder in relation to the October 17, 2021 throat cutting of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner at the Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James.

On Wednesday, the witness was more composed on the stand as Williams quizzed her on the happenings at the church where Gardner and two male members were killed. One of the men was killed allegedly by the late pastor of the church, Dr Kevin Smith. The other man was shot and killed by the police after he attacked lawmen with a knife.

The detective sergeant was the initial investigator assigned to the case before it was turned over to a more senior cop.

On the day of the incident, the pastor was said to have taken a Glock pistol from a female member of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) who was also a member of the church. The pastor used that firearm to shoot at the police.

When the incident was brought to an end, the police carted away numerous individuals, including Smith and the members of his church, to a police station where criminal charges were laid against them.

The female cop, who had a close relationship with Smith, was among those who were arrested. She was charged for breaching the Disaster Risk Management Act (DRMA) during COVID-19 lockdowns when no one, except for essential workers, was supposed to be on the road. Under the Act, large gatherings were prohibited.

Williams, who is one of two attorneys representing Ruddock, along with Venice Brown, asked the witness whether any other charges were laid against the female police member of Smith’s flock.

The attorney enquired if the cop was ever referred to the Inspectorate and Professional Standards Oversight Bureau (IPROB), which is a disciplinary unit within the JCF.

“Is this arm of the JCF responsible for complaints and investigations into the conduct of any member of the JCF?” Williams asked.

The witness told him that to the best of her knowledge that was, in fact, so.

The attorney wanted to know why the cop wasn’t referred to IPROB, but no definitive answer was given to that question.

The witness told the court that when the female constable was arrested, she was taken to an area of the church which looked like living quarters where she handed over a bag that contained her private Glock pistol, handcuffs, a video recorder, personal items, as well as her police uniform.

“As indicated to me, it was a private firearm,” the witness said.

Williams asked her if the constable’s hands were swabbed, and the witness said she personally did not swab her hands but gave instructions for that activity to be carried out; however, she could not speak to the outcome of the swabbing.

“When you first saw her on the 17th of October 2021, did she say anything to you?” Williams asked.

The witness responded in the affirmative, saying that she did speak to the cop, and that she said several things.

The lawyer sought to find out if whatever was said was indicative of her involvement at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries.

“In light of the several utterances, did it lead you to carry out any further investigation?” the attorney asked.

“Yes, sir, certainly,” the witness said, before explaining that she was not the person who charged the constable.

She explained further that she did not know who exactly charged the constable for breaching the DRMA.

The trial continues today with a new witness. The seven members of the jury are expected to view photographs of the scene at the church as described by the six witnesses who have taken the stand so far during the trial which started two weeks ago.

World.title: Kabaka Pyramid still has lots to say
World.content:
Kabaka Pyramid.

There is still a rebel in Kabaka Pyramid. Fifteen years after the Rebel Music era first introduced audiences to that particular side of his artistry, the Kingston-born musician has chosen to revisit familiar territory — but he is not quite the same man who entered it.

Though the lyrical sharpness and the instinct to make music that says something beyond simply sounding good remains, time and a few battles of his own have added new layers to the story.

That evolution is recognisable in his latest single A Warrior’s Pain, a collaboration with American rappers R-Mean and Styles P.

The track serves as the foundation for Rebel Music 1 & 2, a new lyrics tape marking 15 years since the beginning of the entertainer’s Rebel Music chapter.

For Kabaka Pyramid, the return was not the result of an elaborate master plan. In fact, it was almost accidental.

“We knew the 15-year anniversary of Rebel Music was approaching and also the 10-year anniversary of the Accurate mixtape,” he explained. “So my team and I were floating around ideas since the start of the year. We were keeping it simple — samples and hip hop drums,” he said. “I just wanted something that inspired me to be lyrical.”

That instinct reignited something the artiste said had perhaps become dormant.

“It felt like I had suppressed a part of my craft and it needed to be reawakened,” he said outlining that the first few tracks were a hit with his manager, who remarked that they sounded like the

Rebel Music days.

“That moment was when we knew what had to be done,” he said. “Everything flowed easily from there.”

That renewed focus on lyricism sits alongside another important thread in Kabaka Pyramid’s current work — vulnerability.

On A Warrior’s Pain, the entertainer brings together reggae and hip hop through a shared appreciation for substance, storytelling, and resistance. But beneath the lyrical exchanges and musical chemistry, A Warrior’s Pain speaks to a more personal kind of battle

Kabaka Pyramid points to his own struggle with confidence in his voice and singing ability as part of the experience informing his contribution.

“I was always being told I need more melody, songs need to be more catchy, simplify the music,” he said. But, rather than resist the criticism, he used it as motivation.

“So I put in the hours to train myself and be ready for anything when called upon,” he explained. “Overcoming challenges is the best way to build confidence and strength comes from there naturally.”

That growth is perhaps one of the clearest differences between the Kabaka Pyramid of the early days and the artiste he has become.

“The message is still the same, just more mature now,” he said. “I think more people can relate to what I’m saying. It’s not music only for hip hop heads that love to dissect lyrical patterns.”

With that said, Kabaka Pyramid shared that the response to reggae and conscious music from international audiences continues to surprise him, particularly in Africa, Europe, Japan, and the United States. This is sees as not cultural appropriation, but an opportunity to observe how others interpret and conduct business around Jamaican music.

“When others incorporate our music I like to learn from them, and see what aspects they connect with and also how they conduct the business of touring,” he said.

There is, however, one boundary: “If you sample my record I want what is rightfully mine,” he said with a laugh.

World.title: Green calls for regional farmworker framework
World.content:
Belize’s Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and Enterprise, Rodwell Ferguson (left) speaking on Wednesday during a plenary session on “Unlocking private sector partnerships and expanding investments in agriculture and fisheries development” during the Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 conference at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny. Looking on is Floyd Green, Jamaica’s agriculture minister. (Photo: Horace Hines)

CORAL SPRING, Trelawny — Agriculture Minister Floyd Green is calling for a regional structure to facilitate the movement of agricultural workers across the Caribbean, pointing to Dominica as a model for easing constraints on farmers and boosting production.

“I think we need a framework, a framework that works for the movement of agricultural workers across the region,” he said.

He noted that Dominica has already established a framework for agricultural migrant workers which has enabled the country to bring in about 200 workers, benefiting roughly 80 farmers and contributing to a significant increase in productivity.

Green was speaking during Wednesday’s plenary session on “Unlocking private sector partnerships and expanding investments in agriculture and fisheries development” at the Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 conference. It was held at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny.

The session, on the fourth of the six-day conference, followed a question from the floor about region-wide difficulty finding workers for agriculture.

Green said the Caribbean should reconsider its traditionally insular approach to agricultural labour.

“If given the opportunity, just as they are given the opportunity to go to Canada and to go to America and they work and they return home…what about the region?” he asked.

He said a regional mechanism could allow workers to take up agricultural employment in neighbouring territories while providing farmers with access to people willing to work within the sector.

Green acknowledged that such an arrangement would require proper oversight, but said Dominica’s experience provides a model worth examining. He said he intends to raise the matter at the Caribbean Community’s Council for Trade and Economic Development (COTED).

At the same time, Green said the region must make greater use of technology as the profile of the agricultural workforce changes.

“One of the challenges with the young people going into agriculture now, they want to be owners. They don’t want to be workers,” he said, stressing the need to provide them with tools that can improve efficiency and productivity.

Green cited agricultural drones as one example of how technology can reduce reliance on manual tasks.

Through the Rural Agricultural Development Authority (RADA), Jamaica has invested in four drones which farmers may rent. They come with trained drone pilots. The College of Agriculture, Science and Education (CASE) is also training drone operators, while Jamaican company Sky Crop has begun assembling agricultural drones locally.

Green also pointed to the growing use of small walk-behind tractors, which can enable individual farmers to more efficiently manage their operations.

He said artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies should form part of the region’s response as agriculture adapts to changing workforce patterns.

Belize’s Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and Enterprise Rodwell Ferguson said his country has experienced a similar shift.

He recalled that three to four decades ago, Belize relied on agricultural workers from neighbouring Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador. That has changed as more young Belizeans have gained access to secondary and tertiary education, including university and postgraduate studies.

“Young people are getting the opportunity to go to high school, sixth form, universities, [do] master’s degree, doctorate degree. And so maybe it is a good reason for the advent of the AI because it’s a time when we are having labour shortage, and no matter what we do, we can’t convince those young people to go and do agriculture,” he said.

Ferguson said the changing aspirations of young people are also reflected in schools.

In Belize, he said, agriculture is compulsory in first and second form but becomes an elective in third and fourth form. By then, participation can fall to about five students.

Ferguson said smart agriculture could help make the sector more attractive to young people while helping Belize meet its food production needs.

“It is critical. It is crucial because we must be able to feed ourselves,” he said.

World.title: Speed up EU health security prep, says NATO chief medic
World.content:
On tobacco: Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi said the Commission remained committed to publishing a comprehensive review of tobacco legislation, including on advertising rules, this year and that there will be a focus on nicotine addiction. “We are very well advanced in the preparation of the proposals,” he said in a press conference following Thursday’s meeting.

We’re close: Forthcoming legislation would address vapes and heated tobacco products; their use being twice as high among young people than the broader population, Várhelyi said. It is important the tobacco products directive is revised to address nicotine addiction “so that we can deal with the cross-border element of this and create a genuinely harmonized system,” added Irish Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill who joined Várhelyi at the press conference. “Colleagues are concerned about the capacity of nicotine addictive companies to create new and novel ways of getting children addicted to nicotine,” she said.

Presidential priorities: The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU is pushing for the Biotech Act and Medical Devices Regulation to be finalized as the Council works on its position (more on where this is up to in the Parliament later). “This is the moment to deliver this because this is the moment when long-term decisions are made in this sector,” Várhelyi said. “But for this to succeed, we can only achieve it if we have speed, if we have simplicity and if we have predictability.”

MFN

FRENCH DEAL DOMINATES MFN TALKS: France’s new pharma agreement this week has shaken up the Gastein forum, seeping into nearly all conversations (whether on panels or by the coffee machine lines) on competitiveness, drug pricing and geopolitical relationships. Some are reeling from what they say was a very unexpected announcement, which throws into doubt what the rest of the bloc can do, while others see it as an inevitable evolution of U.S. pressure.

Recap: France announced this week a new deal with the pharmaceutical sector on drug pricing, to provide “more clarity and predictability to pharmaceutical companies.”

Stay united: Morning Health Care reported yesterday that patients, payers, EU lawmakers and capitals urged European countries not to seek individual agreements to counter the effects of the U.S. most-favored-nation policies, urging instead for a united Europe. During a panel on Europe’s upgraded pharmaceutical legislation, speakers reiterated the message Thursday. Morning Health Care contacted the French government for comment but did not get a response.

World.title: How a failed attack in Leipzig revealed a wider Russian campaign
World.content:
It wasn’t the first time such an improvised explosive had been discovered on European soil. Almost two years earlier, on Aug. 20, 2024, police investigators arrived at a cemetery in Kaunas, Lithuania, with a bomb disposal team. They had received a highly sensitive tip from Poland concerning explosives and a Ukrainian man alleged to have deposited them there for Russian intelligence, according to investigation files from the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau.

At a weathered grave, beneath artificial flowers and concrete slabs, officers recovered a plastic bag containing two tin cans. According to their labels, they contained corn. Forensic analysis, however, found they contained 968 grams of explosives, around 700 grams of TNT equivalent per can — roughly the lethal force of four hand grenades.

In January and June 2025, investigators unearthed more explosive-filled cans at various locations in Lithuania. Four were fitted with metal plates stamped with circular indentations. Investigators say they were intended to act as projectiles in an explosion. Forensic examinations found that the plates were highly likely to have been manufactured by the same machine, according to a report by the Forensic Science Service of the Police Department of Lithuania.

The device attached to the drone in Leipzig bore striking similarities to those recovered from the Lithuanian caches, including the explosive-filled tin can and the stamped metal plate.

The resemblance alone does not establish that the devices belonged to the same operation. But two Western security officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss security matters, say it fits with other evidence — including travel records, suspected logistics routes and intelligence reporting — linking the cases to a broader Russian intelligence mission.

The resemblance is one element of a pattern that German and European officials believe points to an escalating campaign of sabotage and violence across Europe, planned and coordinated by Russian intelligence officers.

World.title: Russia’s not-quite-war on Europe
World.content:
Europe’s gray-zone war with Russia is getting harder to ignore.

Sarah Wheaton speaks to security expert and author Elisabeth Braw about how Europe should respond as sabotage, arson, cyberattacks and attacks on critical infrastructure become more frequent and more dangerous, who pays when businesses are targeted, and what happens when one of them turns deadly.

They also discuss Braw’s new book, The Undersea War: The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World, and the increasingly contested cables, pipelines and infrastructure hidden beneath the seabed — another target in this growing gray-zone conflict.

You can read Elisabeth’s most recent column for POLITICO about how European businesses are paying the cost for Russias hybrid war here.

World.title: Conservative ex-mayor Andy Street out of the running for top railways job
World.content:
Both of the people said a key reason was that Street still appeared to harbor a desire to return to frontline politics. One of the people, a government official, said he had been “unable to subdue his political ambitions.” Street was the Conservative mayor of the West Midlands for seven years until Labour narrowly defeated him in 2024.

Street declined to comment on the Great British Railways recruitment process, and told POLITICO that supposition about his political intentions was “speculation” and “conjecture.”

‘Political ambitions’

Recruitment began in January for the role of chair, which will pay £200,000 to £300,000 a year for 10 days of work a month. Great British Railways is due to be up and running in 2027, with passenger services transferred to public ownership by the end of that year as private rail operators’ contracts expire.

The Department for Transport declined to comment on whether a decision was imminent or the process of finding a chair had slowed. A government official said a “fair, open and merit-based process” was underway.

Street has history with Britain’s railways. He narrowly decided not to quit the Conservatives in 2023 when former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak scrapped a leg of the planned High Speed 2 rail line from Birmingham to Manchester.

Supporters describe him as a figure who reached across political lines and was respected for his nine-year stint as managing director of department store John Lewis.

World.title: Burnham wants to change British elections. Voters think they’re fine already.
World.content:
At the same time, the survey revealed potential openness to a system of proportional representation, in which the number of parliamentary seats each party wins is more closely linked to the total number of votes it receives across the country.

“Most people don’t spend much time thinking about how we elect MPs and, broadly, people think the current system is fair,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at Public First. “Burnham will need to make a convincing case to voters about why changing the electoral system is necessary, if he is to gain support for his plans.”

Under first-past-the-post, whichever candidate wins the most votes in their constituency is elected to represent that seat, even if they fall far short of a majority of local voters. Nationally, that can result in a party taking power with relatively low popular support.

Labour won the last election in 2024 by a landslide, taking 63% of seats in Parliament with just 34% of the vote — the most disproportionate result in British history.

Since then, some polling projections have suggested Nigel Farage’s populist-right Reform UK party was on track to win a majority with around 30% of votes under the first-past-the-post system.

In a speech to Labour members in Liverpool, Burnham said recent turbulence in British politics — he’s the country’s seventh prime minister in 10 years — meant a new system was needed. “We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No. 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote,” he said.

World.title: Europe war-games life after Merz
World.content:
It’s not a prospect they take lightly. Merz leads the EU’s largest economy and is the chief negotiator for wealthy countries seeking to rein in spending in the bloc’s proposed €2 trillion seven-year budget. He is also a driving force behind EU efforts to save heavy industry.

“Any debate about the German chancellor weakens Germany’s role in the EU and in the world,” said Wilhelm Gebhard, a member of the Bundestag and an official in Merz’s governing CDU party.

With France facing its own far-right surge and a presidential election next year that could hand power to euroskeptic Marine Le Pen, few in Brussels relish the prospect of Germany, historically the EU’s other major player, turning inwards or derailing important negotiations.

The contingency planning, which has seen officials and diplomats brainstorm the situation, comes after months of mixed signals from Berlin on EU policy, including car emissions and a proposed social media ban for children. Even if Merz stays in office, the political turmoil is already complicating Berlin’s work on the EU’s biggest files.

The worst-case scenario for Brussels would be a leaderless Germany, or one with a far-right government. But that is seen as virtually impossible in the short term, with none of the mainstream players seeking new elections while the far-right Alternative for Germany party are leading in the polls.

“All coalition partners know that they have a great deal to lose from early elections,” said Hannah Neumann, an opposition Green MEP who sits on the European Parliament’s security and foreign affairs committees. “My expectation, therefore, is that they will stay together and muddle through.”

World.title: It’s the end of the world as we know it (and I feel an investment opportunity coming on)
World.content:
Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei looks on as US President Donald Trump speaks to the press after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington, DC, on September 29, 2026. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

AI might kill us all, but is it worth buying shares in?

Welcome to Declassified, a weekly humor column.

As you will no doubt have marked in your calendars, the end of the world is scheduled for the spring of 2029 (exact timing TBC).

It’s just a few weeks now since researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic, stating that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” A senior safety researcher at Anthropic then claimed there was a more than 10% chance that AI “could kill all humans” within the next decade.

That means humankind will outlast the EU, as the bloc’s demise is penciled in for May 2027, when either French far-right leader Marine Le Pen or far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon will march into Brussels with a flaming pitchfork (unless they do it on a Friday, in which case no one will be there to see it).

Between now and the end of the world, AI will replace all jobs except those that absolutely, categorically cannot be done by a machine because they are essential and require a delicate human touch: nurse, electrician, writer of weekly satirical columns …



But what if you’ve got loads of money you want to invest and yet you have some concerns about the impending apocalypse? That was the conundrum posed this week as Anthropic prepared for a potential $2 trillion flotation (as in when a company offers shares to the public — not when you’re on holiday in a pool, lying on a piece of plastic shaped like a donut).

Anthropic issued a prospectus outlining its finances, growth plans and risk profile to potential investors that warns AI models could exhibit “self-preserving behaviours”, including attempts to “resist shutdown,” to “conceal or manipulate information” and behavior “resembling blackmail.”

So on the one hand, AI could refuse to shut down and try and blackmail us, but on the other hand, there’s a chance to make some cash by investing in a growth industry. What’s an investor to do?

Despite all the doom and gloom, though, there’s still hope for humanity. This week, the White House signed an accord on “Super Intelligence” — that’s just AI — signed by the likes of xAI CEO Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, as well as noted intelligence fan U.S. President Donald Trump. Alas, the latter was described in the accord as “President of the Unites States” with an “s” instead of the “d.”

Sumb dhitd!

World.title: ‘Tough’ talks with China have yet to deliver, EU trade chief says
World.content:
Šefčovič travels to Beijing Oct. 8 for what he termed a “a super crucial meeting” with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, and said he was optimistic the trip will bear fruit. “You have to believe that you can accomplish something, otherwise you better don’t go.”

The commissioner needs to get results he can present at a meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Oct. 15-16, and has said previously that Brussels is ready to restrict Chinese access to the EU market should the talks fail.

The EU and China have been locked in tense negotiations since June. EU leaders have said they can no longer tolerate the flood of Chinese imports inundating the single market, putting pressure on domestic manufacturers and forcing plant closures and layoffs.

“I think our Chinese partners understood that this has direct implication on the future of emblematic European companies — literally thousands of jobs,” Šefčovič reported. “And also the social fabric and social model which was developed in Europe over many, many decades.”

The bloc’s ballooning €1-billion-a-day trade deficit with China lies at the heart of the talks. Cutting that deficit would require either reducing imports from China, boosting EU exports, or a mix of the two.

Šefčovič said he hopes to bring a “proof of concept” back from Beijing that addresses three main issues: sudden Chinese export surges in key industrial sectors; tangible ways to increase European goods exports to China; and long-term clarity regarding China’s export curbs on raw materials, especially rare earth elements.

World.title: Pete Hegseth creates Pentagon Office of Religious Affairs reporting directly to him
World.content:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is launching an office of religious affairs, the latest of his faith-related reforms at the Pentagon.

 

He announced in a speech on Wednesday that the office will help offer “first-class religious support” and will report directly to him.

“Our department is, you might say, putting on the full armour of God, because while we wage physical war, we all know the real battle is spiritual,” he said.

Hegseth has infused his evangelical Christianity into his leadership of the Pentagon, hosting worship services for employees and often speaking of the United States as a Christian nation.

The Office of Religious Affairs (ORA) will advocate for military chaplains and religious support “at the highest level of the Department,” according to a Pentagon statement.

It will not “compel religious participation, favour one faith, or diminish the rights of personnel of any faith or lack thereof.”

Some criticism of the initiative surfaced quickly.

US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth gives a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, 30 September, 2026 AP Photo

The Pentagon “owes it to the nation’s service members to defend religious freedom,” said Rachel Laser, head of Americans United for Separation of Church, which has sued the Pentagon over its worship services.

“Hegseth’s latest announcement violates that promise by elevating Christianity to an even higher role in shaping US military policy.”

Other federal agencies have had religious or faith-based offices, which were established under President George W. Bush and were continued in different forms under the Obama and Biden administrations.

President Donald Trump established a White House Faith Office and had a similar effort during his first term.

Shaun Casey, a religion scholar, led the State Department’s Office of Religion and Global Affairs during the Obama administration.

The office did not promote religion or spiritual well-being, he said. “It was there to understand what were the political implications of lived religion in the various hot spots around the world.”

The leader of the new office has not been named. A Pentagon memo said the religious affairs director will coordinate spiritual resources, including “faith-based homeschool support for military families.”

Hegseth has also pushed the military school system to introduce more coursework that draws from conservative and Christian influences.

The memo mentions “faith-based initiatives supporting Department-wide suicide reduction.”

In recent years, the military has become increasingly dependent on chaplains to help address the growing numbers of troops in mental health distress.

Hegseth has said he wants chaplains to focus more on God and less on therapeutic “self-help and self-care.”

The secretary has pushed other changes within the military’s chaplain corps, which provides spiritual care to troops.

He ordered chaplains, who are commissioned officers, to no longer wear their rank on their uniform but instead be identified by religious insignia.

The Pentagon pictured in Arlington, 26 September, 2026 AP Photo

The Defence Department also slashed the number of religious affiliations it officially recognises, down to 31 from more than 200 previously recognised traditions.

The list no longer includes atheists, Unitarian Universalists, pagans and Wiccans.

Hegseth spoke directly to chaplains in his address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia. Using Christian-inflected language, he said: “Live your calling. Stand firm. Preach truth. Minister to the flock.”

He then quoted from the Bible: “The Lord is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do unto me?”

World.title: Houthis deny Saudi accusations of targeting Medina's holy sites
World.content:
The Saudi-led coalition accused Yemen's Houthis of striking a power station in the holy city of Medina in Saudi Arabia, a claim the Iran-backed group denied.

 

The alleged attack came as fighting intensified in Yemen, where forces of the internationally recognised government said they carried out attacks on Houthi targets and witnesses heard explosions in the Houthi-held capital Sana'a.

The Saudi-led coalition said on Thursday a drone struck Medina's Taibah electricity distribution station, which provides power to the Prophet's Mosque.

Medina, the burial place of the Prophet Mohammed and home to the Prophet's Mosque, is one of Islam's holiest cities alongside Mecca.

Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said a drone struck the Taibah electricity distribution station at 5:11 am (3:11 am CEST) on Tuesday.

"The investigation and evidence gathered by the competent authorities have confirmed the involvement of the terrorist Houthi militia in planning and executing this cowardly terrorist act, based on after-action review and the wreckage of the drone used," he said in a statement.

The coalition said one transformer was taken out of service without affecting the wider electricity network. Al-Maliki said the facility supplied electricity to the Prophet's Mosque.

"This cowardly terrorist act, targeting a civilian facility providing electricity to the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, is a continuation of this extremist militia's attempts to target the Two Holy Mosques," he said.

On Thursday, a senior Houthi official again rejected allegations that the movement had targeted Islamic holy sites, stating they were a "lie" to further back previous claims, according to Houthi-run news agency Saba.

The group had firmly rejected Riyadh's accusations in mid-September of a drone attack on Mecca, Islam's holiest site.

"Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said at the time, adding that "fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal al-Saud regime cannot deceive anyone."

Mecca is Islam's holiest site, home to the Kaaba — which Muslims worldwide turn toward for prayer — and the destination of the Hajj pilgrimage, one of the faith's Five Pillars or main tenets.

The accusation came as fighting intensified in Yemen, as the internationally recognised government's military said it had carried out strikes on Houthi targets in Sana'a, Saada and Taiz.

A spokesman said the military had conducted a "high-value targeting operation" in Sana'a and struck 11 targets in Saada.

He added that 27 air strikes had targeted an "integrated military system" belonging to the Houthis in Taiz.

The Houthis, who control Sana'a and much of Yemen's Red Sea coast, have repeatedly launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia since the kingdom intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015.

Any confirmed attack on either Mecca or Medina would put the perpetrators beyond the pale in the eyes of virtually the entire Muslim world, Shia and Sunni alike.

Ankara blasts 'provocative attacks'

Turkey strongly condemned the alleged attack and voiced support for Saudi Arabia.

"We strongly condemn the Houthis' attack on civilian infrastructure" in Medina, the foreign ministry said.

"These provocative attacks, which threaten Saudi Arabia's sovereignty and security and target the sacred values of the Islamic world, must cease immediately and unconditionally."

Turkey said it reiterated its "strong support for Saudi Arabia" and called for steps to prevent further escalation.

Qatar also condemned the attack. In a statement, Doha said it was "a grave assault on the sanctity of Islamic holy sites", a violation of Saudi sovereignty and international law.

It reaffirmed its "full solidarity" with Riyadh and said the kingdom's security was integral to Gulf security.

The League of Arab States joined the condemnation, calling the attack "an unacceptable transgression".

The organisation said the attack "provokes the sentiments of Muslims worldwide" and represented a dangerous escalation.

Al-Azhar, the Cairo-based institute of Sunni Islamic learning, also denounced the incident, stating that "targeting Medina provokes the sentiments of Muslims worldwide".

The Houthis are Zaydi Shia Muslims, a specific branch of Islam historically rooted in northern Yemen that is theologically distinct from both the Twelver Shia Islam dominant in Iran and Saudi Arabia's Wahhabi-influenced Sunni tradition.

The group formally known as Ansar Allah is tied to Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

World.title: Uzbekistan wins home gold at record-breaking Chess Olympiad in Samarkand
World.content:
The biggest Chess Olympiad in history brought almost 400 teams from around the world to Samarkand, where host nation Uzbekistan won gold in the Open competition after defeating Ukraine in the final round.

 

Uzbekistan won its first Chess Olympiad title in India's Chennai in 2022 and followed it with bronze in Budapest two years later.

“This is our second Olympiad victory. Winning it at home feels different,” Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov said. “I think we played the tournament at the highest level.”

Sindarov’s next major test will come later this year. After winning the Candidates Tournament, he will challenge India’s Gukesh Dommaraju for the world title in Geneva from 22 November to 12 December.

Both players will be 20 when the match begins, making it the youngest World Championship contest in chess history.

How the Chess Olympiad works

Organised by the International Chess Federation (FIDE), the Chess Olympiad is the leading international team competition in chess.

Unlike most major chess tournaments, players compete for their countries rather than only for themselves.

Four players from one national team face four from another at the same time, with their individual results combined to determine the result between the two countries.

Teams compete over 11 rounds, facing different opponents as the tournament progresses.

Uzbekistan finished the competition with 20 of 22 possible match points, winning 10 of its 11 matches. Among the teams it defeated were defending champions India, China and the top-seeded US. Its only loss came against eventual bronze medallists Germany.

Uzbekistan claims second Open title

Nodirbek Abdusattorov was another key member of the winning team. Playing on Uzbekistan’s first board, meaning he generally faced the strongest player from each opposing team, he completed the Chess Olympiad without losing a game and received an individual gold medal for his performance.

“I think we can now confidently say that Uzbekistan is unrivalled in the world of chess,” Abdusattorov said after the victory.

India finished with silver, while Germany took bronze.

Uzbekistan, India and Germany take the podium at the closing ceremony of the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. Rafal Oleksiewicz/FIDE

For Germany, the result marked its first Open team medal at a Chess Olympiad since 2000, when it won silver in Istanbul.

“I think it’s by far the best Olympiad we’ve had in recent years, at least as long as I’ve been playing,” German grandmaster Vincent Keymer told Euronews.

Several European countries also finished near the top, with Hungary, France and Spain all placing inside the top 10, alongside Azerbaijan and Armenia.

In the women’s competition, China won gold, Kazakhstan finished second and defending champions India took bronze.

Indian grandmaster Koneru Humpy was part of the bronze-medal-winning team.

“There is a lot of attention from all the spectators and followers, and this is one of the widely followed tournaments from all over the world,” Humpy told Euronews.

The biggest Olympiad yet

The final field included 205 teams in the Open and 189 in the Women’s competition.

For almost two weeks, hundreds of games were played simultaneously in the same competition hall, bringing national teams from around the world together in Samarkand.

The tournament also coincided with a change at the top of international chess. Timur Turlov, then president of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, was elected president of FIDE during the federation’s General Assembly in Samarkand. At 38, he became the youngest person ever elected to the post.

FIDE President Timur Turlov makes a ceremonial first move for Uzbekistan’s Nodirbek Abdusattorov in the final round. Michal Walusza / FIDE

“The interest in the game is definitely rising year over year,” Turlov told Euronews. “It’s not just a professional sport. It’s a sport which is getting more and more popular almost everywhere.”

At the end of the tournament, the Olympiad flag was handed to representatives of the United Arab Emirates.

Abu Dhabi will host the 47th Chess Olympiad in 2028.

World.title: Christa Pike in critical condition after Tennessee botched execution, lawyer says
World.content:
A condemned female murderer who survived two lethal injections during a botched execution by the US state of Tennessee is in critical condition and receiving "life-saving care," her lawyer said on Thursday.

 

In an extraordinary chain of events, Christa Pike, 50, was whisked from a prison execution chamber to a hospital on Wednesday night, still alive despite two deadly doses of pentobarbital.

"What we have been told is that she is in critical condition, receiving life-saving care," Randy Spivey said in a virtual news conference on Thursday afternoon, declining to provide further details.

He urged Governor Bill Lee, who had denied a clemency request earlier in the week, to scrap Pike's death sentence.

"After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa's sentence now."

Experts on the US death penalty said the case was unprecedented.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee speaks during a news conference in Nashville, 20 May, 2026 AP Photo

"This failed attempt is the worst we've ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," said Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre.

The centre counts seven inmates whose executions could not be carried out because medical staff were unable to establish IV lines, but "Pike is the first person to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs."

Late on Thursday, US President Donald Trump questioned how an execution like Pike's could fail, telling reporters that it "shouldn't be very difficult."

'Loudly snoring'

The case had already attracted scrutiny as Pike would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

Kim Chandler, a media witness with the Associated Press, told CBS News that "Pike appeared notably awake as the execution began" at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.

"A couple of times she looked around the room. At one point she looked towards prison officials and asked if it was supposed to feel that way," Chandler said.

This photo provided by the Tennessee Department of Correction shows Christa Pike, 12 January, 2023 AP Photo

Pike later began snoring and witnesses listened from the viewing area for about an hour before being ushered out.

The condemned woman was "loudly snoring, clearly very alive" as journalists left, Chandler told CBS.

Pike's legal team had previously objected to the execution IV protocol, saying it would have caused needless suffering due to her small veins and a blood condition.

"I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt" to start an IV line, Spivey said.

Lawyer Stephen Ferrell said medical experts had warned of needles becoming dislodged or piercing through the vein, causing lethal drugs to flow into Pike's arm instead of the bloodstream.

"It sounds like that is likely to have occurred," he said.

Media witnesses recount the moments before the execution of Christa Pike was halted in Nashville, 30 September, 2026 AP Photo

Media witnesses said Pike told execution staff her arm felt like it would "burst open," and Spivey said he saw her right arm turn purple, especially after the second lethal injection.

Pike had not been scared to die, Ferrell said.

"It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death, and that's what happened, minus the death."

'A mess'

The Tennessee Department of Correction said it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol," adding that Pike was subsequently taken to an "off-site medical facility."

Governor Lee called for a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the failed execution.

The state's remaining scheduled execution, convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton is scheduled to die on 3 December, would not be carried out this year, Lee added.

Pike's case had sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals. She was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp.

Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, 30 September, 2026 AP Photo

The killing gained national attention after Slemmer's body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.

Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, told NBC News the botched execution was "a mess."

Pike's lawyers had argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of Slemmer's killing. They also cited her history of childhood sexual assault and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Following a flurry of legal filings that delayed the execution by several hours, the US Supreme Court on Wednesday night cleared the way for the punishment to go ahead.

In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

UN rights chief Volker Turk urged Tennessee not to make a new attempt to execute Pike.

"The case of Christa Pike lays bare multiple reasons why the death penalty should be abolished," his office said on X.

Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.

The killing gained national attention after Slemmer's body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.

World.title: EU says oil reserve release possible amid US pressure
World.content:
EU contemplates oil release: EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen has told Europe Today that releasing strategic oil reserves to cushion soaring prices “is a possibility”, as the US mounts pressure on EU allies to release diesel reserves or face a US export ban.

 

The war in Iran and reduced refining capacity have squeezed supply, driving a sharp rise in prices for companies and consumers. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Europe to make new stocks available “immediately” to ease costs, saying US "farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden".

Painful at the pump: US diesel prices have surged to $7 a gallon in recent days, while Brent crude has traded between $97 and $102 a barrel since late September — up $25 to $30 from pre-war levels. The issue is a priority for President Trump ahead of pivotal midterm elections.

“We are discussing with all members of the International Energy Agency (IEA), not only the United States, when the right time is to release, because this is one of the opportunities that we have. We've used it before, and we'll likely use it again,” Commissioner Jørgensen told my colleague Maria Tadeo on Thursday.

Pressure on EU governments: The decision to release stockpiles ultimately lies with EU capitals. Jørgensen told Europe Today that EU countries are discussing a coordinated release through the Paris-based IEA “as we speak”.

An EU source also told my colleague Marta Pacheco that the Commission had held a call on Thursday with several countries, including the UK, to assess different scenarios. Catch the full interview with Commissioner Jørgensen on Europe Today.

Nothing to see here, folks! Meanwhile, the European Commission has abruptly closed the debate over Ukraine’s $27 billion deficit by announcing that the country’s financial and military needs for this year are fully covered, Jorge Liboreiro writes.

“Through coordinated joint efforts, we have identified the means to cover Ukraine’s budget and defence needs for 2026,” the Commission said in a vague statement posted on Thursday by Ursula von der Leyen.

Reminder: The $27 billion funding gap in the Ministry of Defence, flagged by Kyiv in late August, prompted intense technical talks between the two sides. Brussels, though, always kept its distance from the headline figure, which EU officials considered unexpected and unexplained. Instead, the Commission urged Ukraine to focus on passing the necessary reforms to unlock the €90 billion support loan.

Jorge’s take: “The one-month saga has ended,” Jorge, who has attentively followed the talks, tells me. “It was evident from the start that the Commission didn’t want to be associated with, let alone be held responsible for the $27 billion. The loan is barely one year old. Reforms are stuck in the Rada. It’s way too soon to talk about fresh money.”

Grim outlook: the focus now shifts to 2027, which looks much direr. Ukraine has identified a staggering $78 billion hole for next year: $32.6 billion for the budget and $45 billion for the military, which Russia’s escalation threatens to increase.

Brussels and Kyiv will continue discussions on the 2027 needs. The International Monetary Fund is also involved but isn’t yet ready to provide an updated number, Julie Kozack, Director of the IMF’s communications department, said.

“Beyond 2026,” Kozack said on Thursday, “the specific financing gap is going to depend on, of course, very importantly, the evolution of the war, the implementation of reforms by the authorities, economic developments and continued support from Ukraine’s international partners.

VDL’s three messages to Montenegro: Commission President Ursula von der Leyen delivered three main messages to Podgorica yesterday during her annual tour of the Western Balkans, my colleague Luca Bertuzzi writes in.

The elephant in the room: Firstly, von der Leyen pressed the country to resolve bilateral issues with Croatia, describing the disputes between the countries as “of utmost importance”. Zagreb has raised a range of issues that risk derailing Montenegro’s ambitious timeline to become the EU’s 28th member by 2028, with the Commission currently mediating.

Sort your internal divisions: Montenegrin politics has been rocked by controversy after Parliament Speaker Andrija Mandić sent public condolences after the death of Ratko Mladic in August. The Commission chief recalled that, to maintain the ambitious accession timeline, cross-party support is fundamental.

We are also getting ready: Von der Leyen also underlined that the EU needs to be ready to accept new member states, teasing next week’s pre-enlargement policy reviews. “We will look at our institutions, our policies, our budget, what has to be done to be ready to welcome a new member state and to make sure that our union is ready to become larger,” she said.

Greece pitches suspension of the EU’s right to asylum during migration crises

Athens has proposed suspending the right to apply for asylum in the EU in cases of a mass influx of irregular migrants, with Migration and Asylum Minister Thanos Plevris making the case to his EU counterparts in a ministerial meeting in Luxembourg.

The controversial measure would mark a major shift in the bloc's migration policy, allowing migrants to be returned without an individual assessment of their asylum claims, potentially resulting in “collective pushbacks”, which are prohibited under current EU law.

Greece is pushing for the proposal to be included in the “European Emergency Response Framework”, a new law the European Commission is presenting in the coming months to tackle irregular arrivals and the instrumentalisation of migration at the EU’s external borders.

Athens has proposed a mechanism called the “Special Derogation Regime”, which would be triggered only in exceptional circumstances. The criteria would include a rapid increase in irregular arrivals, pressure on local infrastructure and evidence that migratory flows are being organised or facilitated by non-EU countries.

My colleagues Vincenzo Genovese and Luca Bertuzzi have the details.

World.title: Over 1,000 adult LEGO fans gathered in Denmark near the toy giant’s birthplace
World.content:
More than 1,000 LEGO fans from 36 countries have gathered in a small Danish town, Skærbæk, near Billund, the toy giant’s hometown, to celebrate their love of the plastic bricks.

 

At Skærbæk Fan Weekend, Adult Fans of LEGO (AFOLs) find a community around a hobby often associated with children. The fan-run event welcomes people who build their own creations as well as those who collect sets.

“It's a place where AFOLs come together, no matter where they come from, no matter which language they speak, no matter what they believe in,” said Stephan Sander, co-organiser of the event.

“They have just one thing in common and that's the love for the brick.”

Adults have long enjoyed playing with LEGO, but pandemic lockdowns helped rekindle toy buying among adults, industry insiders say.

Some longtime fans also describe a shift in how their hobby is perceived.

Didier Bruel, a 66-year-old French retiree, recalled avoiding the subject when colleagues asked what he had done over the weekend.

“I would be careful not to say that I was doing my LEGO in my basement because they would have looked at me as a bit [of a] bizarre guy,” he said.

Bruel said The LEGO Movie and television programme LEGO Masters helped make the hobby more widely accepted.

“You become kind of a star, right? So it's completely different in the last 20 years”.

Toymakers cater to adult buyers

Adult spending is also boosting toy sales. LEGO reported a net profit of around €1.15 billion in the first half of this year, up 32% on the same period last year.

The trend extends beyond LEGO, with adults also buying plush toys, Hot Wheels cars, Barbie dolls and other collectibles.

These buyers are often described as “kidults”, a portmanteau blending of “kid” and “adult”, referring to grown-ups who buy toys for their own enjoyment.

Nearly 40% of European consumers said they bought toys for themselves or another adult in 2025, according to market research company Circana.

Toymakers such as LEGO have responded with products designed for adults, including elaborate sets costing hundreds of euros, well beyond the average child’s pocket money.

“This is not a fad, this is really a long-term trend,” said Frédérique Tutt, global toy industry advisor at Circana.

“Adults and teenagers are proud of saying 'I am collecting, I'm buying toys, aren't you?'”

Tutt pointed to LEGO’s Formula 1 products and Spice Girls set as examples of how the company appeals to different interests.

“LEGO is targeting every single passion point you might have,” she said.

World.title: Ethiopia: Who could bring the warring sides to the negotiation table?
World.content:
Ethiopia might be facing its most complex armed conflict in contemporary times. The fragile 2022 peace deal has collapsed. International mediators have failed. How will the country return to normal?

Just four years after a landmark peace deal officially halted the devastating Tigray war, fighting has escalated once again in northern Ethiopia in recent weeks.

Just days before full-scale fighting resumed, several armed groups which had previously considered each enemies formally announced an alliance with a common goal: To bring down Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.

But this time, the situation looks quite different from the previous conflict: Parties outside the country have been accused of meddling in the situation, with each having their own motives to want to destabilize Abiy's government.

This has raised fears about prolonged instability hitting the Horn of Africa.

Reasons for the collapse of the peace deal

The 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the conflict between the Ethiopian federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which cost hundreds of thousands of lives in the course of two years.

Negash Mohammed, a journalist with DW's Amharic department. believes that the deal collapsed for three key reasons — or rather because three key actors in the conflict were largely neglected at the negotiation table.

The final agreement didn't factor in the role of Eritrea in the conflict, which had fought alongside Ethiopia against the TPLF, Mohammed said. It also ignored the part that Amhara militias — known as Fano — played in the war, who later felt sorely excluded from the negotiations; finally, it ignored hardliners within the TPLF who viewed the peace as a military defeat.

Tensions between the federal government and the Fano escalated further when Abiy's government moved to forcibly disarm the militias instead of addressing their grievances.

"The federal government has its own shortcomings," said Mohammed. "Instead of convincing the other side, it went on to aggravate the grievances they [already] had."

Tigrayan rebels in northern Ethiopia seized control of strategic airports while facing off federal troops Image: AFP

An alliance of former enemies

Mohammed also emphasized that the coalition against the federal government includes several groups which have otherwise little to do with each other.

It includes the Oromo Liberation Army, a faction of the Ogaden National Liberation Front, as well as multiple smaller armed groups from the western Benishangul-Gumuz region and also ethnic militant factions from Afar, which borders Tigray.

Eritrea meanwhile appears to have shifted sides in the current situation: While not officially a member of the alliance, the neighboring country is believed to be providing support to the rebels.

The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patricia Rodrigues, a senior analyst at Control Risks, a global intelligence and security consultancy, referred to the level of strategic coordination among these various groups in the current conflict as "quite significant" and "definitely alarming for the federal government."

She noted, however, that cracks might eventually appear: "How long this coalition lasts, because all of them have very different interests and represent very different ethnic constituencies, remains to be seen," she told DW.

Rodrigues added that, based on Control Risks' assessment, the fighting is likely to remain limited to Ethiopia's northern regions, particularly those situated along the borders between Tigray, Amhara and Afar.

Furthermore, she highlighted that the idea of it spreading across the entire country was rather unlikely due to the difficulty of nationwide coordination, taking into consideration the rough terrain of the nation and the fragmentation of other opposition groups.

Could Ethiopia plunge back into a war-like situation as witnessed just a few years ago? Image: UGC/AP/picture alliance

Could the conflict have been prevented?

Rodrigues also pointed to the failure of sustained international engagement after the end of the crisis in 2022 as a key reason for the current conflict.

She noted that while the Pretoria agreement saw some early proof of implementation — including the TPLF's surrender of heavy weaponry in 2022 and 2023 — international attention had soon shifted to other global crises, leaving both sides free to quietly rearm and conscript supporters.

"It was more of a stopgap or a ceasefire, but people were quickly rearming in the background," she told DW.

The United States had recently lifted sanctions imposed during the 2020–2022 conflict — a step which, according to Mohammed, diminishes the West's leverage in the conflict to push combatants to the negotiating table.

Many Ethiopians continue to live in IDP camps as a result of the last conflict in the region Image: Amanuel Sileshi/AFP

The real cost of war

In the meantime, civilians are bearing the cost of the warring parties: People caught up in the crossfire have been fleeing the conflict once more, adding further to a population of internally displaced persons (IDPs) that has not recovered from the previous war.

"Since 2020, they have not returned to their areas. They are still in makeshift IDP centers," Mohammed said, adding that there have also been isolated reports of drone strikes hitting civilian areas and of rebel groups deploying military hardware inside schools and clinics.

Telephone and internet connections have also been cut in parts of Tigray and Amhara, electricity has been disrupted, and flights have been suspended to several cities including Kombolcha and Lalibela.

Despite official assurances from all parties that civilians would be protected, Mohammed says that the reality on the ground tells a different story: "Words and practice are very contradictory."

Limited prospects for mediation

UN Secretary-General António Guterres dispatched a special envoy to the Horn of Africa, charged with mediating between the African Union, regional powers and Egypt. These are many of the same parties involved in brokering the Pretoria agreement.

But, according to Mohammed, meaningful negotiations are unlikely to bear fruit until at least one of the sides involved in the conflict "comes to understand that this violence will not help them to achieve what they want."

Rodrigues has a similar opinion, stressing that she cannot be optimistic about "an international or a regional mediation being the solution to the current fighting," adding that "intense, but geographically contained" fighting will continue for the foreseeable future.

Adapted from the AfricaLink Podcast by Silja Fröhlich

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Taiwan: first new F-16V fighters arrive amid China threat
World.content:
The US-made jets, part of an order made in 2019, touched down as concerns grow in Taiwan that support from the United States could be wavering. Washington insists its policy towards Taiwan and China hasn't changed.

Two new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets landed in Taiwan on Friday, the first of a batch of 66 US-made planes ordered back in 2019 as the island nation looks to bolster its defenses in the face of threats posed by neighboring China.

The aircraft, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at Chihhang Air Base near Taitung on Taiwan's mountainous east coast at midday local time (0400 GMT).

The arrival of the fighter jets was delayed by several months due to reported software issues, and Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo said more were on the way.

"Of course we won't only have delivered these two by year-end," he told reporters in the capital, Taipei, without providing further details.

"At present, I think aircraft are gradually moving through the production line, and there are also aircraft that have passed tests," he said.

Taiwan fears drop in US support

The delivery comes amid growing concern in Taiwan regarding the United States' commitment to arming Taiwan – and ​a week after US President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.

The US insists that there has been no change in policy towards China and Taiwan but Trump has stalled signing off on a new $14 billion package for Taipei. In May, he called it a "very good negotiating chip" in dealings with Beijing, raising fears that Taiwan's security could be traded away.

"We continue standing with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan," said a US State Department spokesperson when asked about the new F-16Vs.

The jets, made by US defense contractor Lockheed Martin as part of an $8 billion sale agreed seven years ago, are equipped with advanced avionics, and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its stealthy J-20 fighters — but Washington has been unwilling to provide its most advanced fighters like the F-22 or F-35.

Trump floats arms sales to China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Taiwanese air force, which scrambles on an almost daily basis in response to aggressive Chinese maneuvers, is expected to have over 200 F-16Vs once deliveries are completed.

"China's intention to annex Taiwan by force has never changed," said Defense Minister ​Koo, referring to Beijing's claims that the democratically governed island belongs to China.

The Chinese foreign ministry has not commented on the arrival of the F-16s but US officials told the Reuters news agency that a Chinese invasion before 2028 is considered increasingly ​unlikely in Washington.

Taiwan: locals welcome arrival of F-16Vs

That assessment didn't stop dozens of locals – some equipped with binoculars and long-lensed cameras – gathering near the air base's perimeter fence to watch the highly anticipated arrival of the jets.

"The threat from the CCP has always been there so we definitely need to strengthen our defense capabilities," Eric Chan, a 57-year-old former air force servicemen, told the AFP news agency, referring to the Chinese Communist Party and stating that the F-16Vs will "play a very important defensive role."

"In terms of hardware capabilities, there will definitely be an improvement," added Kimi Chi, a 37-year-old salesman from the central city of Taichung who had travelled through the night to be able to photograph the aircraft.

"But what we are actually lacking the most right now is pilots. Of course, I hope the government can provide better additional allowances for these military pilots."

As China threat looms, US pausing arms sales to Taiwan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

10/02/2026 October 2, 2026 In other news from India

PM Modi speaks with Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday spoke with Flydubai Captain Smit Machchhar, who was injured in an alleged mid-air attack on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, lauding him for his bravery and presence of mind.

A video of the conversation, posted on the PM's social media, showed the bandaged captain briefing Modi about the incident and about what gave him the courage to confront the attacking co-pilot.

"I was trying to save my own life, but I knew I could not let all those people die," Machchhar said during a call from his hospital bed.

Flydubai passengers recount terror after hijacking attempt To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

India trade minister meets counterparts on sidelines of G20 event

India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal met with his counterparts from France, Canada, Saudi Arabia and South Korea to discuss furthering bilateral trade, at a time when India is looking to diversify away from the United States.

The meetings were held on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting in Milwaukee.

At the same G20 event, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he did not think there was "something imminent" on the trade deal with India, News agency PTI reported.

A pending trade deal between New Delhi and Washington has been in a stalemate over threat of new tariffs, sunset clauses and possiblyIndia's use of Russian oil. Greer and Goyal met on Wednesday and said they had a "productive discussion" on the conclusion of an interim trade agreement.

British activist released from Delhi after 9 years in prison

British-Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal was released from a prison in Delhi on Thursday after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court. Johal had been in jail for nine years without trial.

The court had ordered Johal's release on September 18 and later warned the government against continued attempts to keep him imprisoned.

Johal was detained on charges of terrorism and targeted killings, and has been a point of diplomatic tensions between India and the UK. While he was acquitted of one terrorism-linked charge in March 2025, eight other charges remain.

World.title: South Korea demands Ukraine apology over POW disclosure
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's disclosure of the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul has caused a major diplomatic spat between Seoul and Kyiv.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Friday threatened Ukraine with "further measures" if Kyiv does not issue a public apology for revealing that North Korean POWs were sent to South Korea.

Seoul has reacted sharply to Ukraine's disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean soldiers captured while fighting for Russia, warning that Pyongyang could target their families.

What has led to the rift between Seoul and Kyiv?

Last week, Lee expressed his regret hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had disclosed the transfer of the soldiers while speaking at the United Nations.

Since then, South Korea and Ukraine have been at loggerheads, with Seoul demanding an apology from Kyiv.

"If the refusal to acknowledge the facts and issue a public apology continues, we will take additional ​measures," Lee said in a post on X.

Lee also accused Kyiv of making him out to be a "liar."

Prisoner swap: From North to South Korea via Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

South Korea claims that Kyiv violated an agreement to keep the transfer of the two soldiers to Seoul confidential to protect them. However, Ukrainian officials have denied that such an agreement existed.

Ukrainian media on Thursday cited Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha as saying that Kyiv is trying to mend ties with Seoul.

"I would not like to call this an incident. Let's say, it's a diplomatic misunderstanding," Sybiha told ⁠journalists ​at an event, according to Ukrainian news agency RBC-Ukraine.

"South Korea is an important country for us. And I very much hope for momentum, continued cooperation, and concrete results that we are indeed achieving with them," he said.
