World.title: Fugitive opposition politician granted safe passage to return to Poland against prosecutors’ wishes
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Warsaw court has approved a request from Marcin Romanowski, a fugitive former government minister who has been on the run for almost two years, to receive safe passage back to Poland. Romanowski is believed to currently be in the pro-Russian Moldovan breakaway region of Transnistria. Although Polish prosecutors have long been seeking Romanowski’s return, they opposed his request for safe conduct, arguing that he cannot be trusted to comply with its terms given that he has repeatedly sought to evade the law. Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, has already announced that prosecutors will appeal the court’s decision, which he claims was issued by an illegitimately appointed judge and in violation of regulations. Nie ma i nie będzie bezkarności dla ludzi Zbigniewa Ziobry. Prokuratura złoży ZAŻALENIE na decyzję o wydaniu listu żelaznego dla Marcina Romanowskiego. Spójrzmy prawdzie w oczy: kto jednoosobowo próbuje zapewnić nietykalność człowiekowi podejrzanemu o gigantyczne nadużycia w… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 30, 2026 Romanowski served as deputy justice minister in the former Law and Justice (PiS) government between 2019 and 2023. After PiS lost power, prosecutors sought to bring charges against him for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served in government, including participating in an organised criminal group. However, Romanowski fled Poland in December 2024 and was granted asylum by Hungary, which was then ruled by Viktor Orbán, a conservative ally of PiS. When Orbán lost power earlier this year, Romanowski went on the run, and for months his location was unknown. In August, it emerged that Romanowski had sent a letter to Poland requesting safe passage to return. The document indicated that he was in Tiraspol, the capital of Transnistria, a region that sought to break away from Moldova in the 1990s and is now effectively under Russian control. Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that, based on intelligence sources, Poland is now “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia https://t.co/mdvmJpkFf7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 18, 2026 At the time, the spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, Przemysław Nowak, said that there were “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland. He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”. However, on Wednesday, Warsaw’s district court approved Romanowski’s request. A spokeswoman for the court said that the decision had been made as “previous methods used [to secure Romanowski’s return] were ineffective” and safe passage would “allow the case to be clarified”. The politician’s lawyer, Bartosz Lewandowski, said that safe passage meant his client could not be detained in Poland and that a European Arrest Warrant against him, which applies in other EU countries, would no longer be valid. ❗️Sąd Okręgowy Warszawie wydał @RomanowskiPL list żelazny, uchylając środek zapobiegawczy w postaci tymczasowego aresztowania od momentu uprawomocnienia się orzeczenia❗️ Mój Klient na terytorium Polski nie będzie mógł być zatrzymany i tymczasowo aresztowany, a ENA „upada”, jeśli… — Bartosz Lewandowski (@BartoszLewand20) September 30, 2026 In a subsequent justification for the ruling, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily, judge Konrad Mielcarek wrote that Romanowski had pledged to “voluntarily return to the country”. Conditions for his safe passage include Romanowski reporting to the court and prosecutors at designated times and places, not leaving his declared place of residence, and not seeking to obstruct the criminal proceedings against him. The judge said that prosecutors had failed to provide adequate arguments as to why Romanowski’s request should be denied. He also found that Romanowski had not obstructed proceedings against him, but had merely exercised available legal remedies. The fact that Romanowski had fled Poland does not count against him, argued the judge. In fact, “the very nature of safe passage is to provide a person residing abroad with a legal guarantee…in exchange for voluntarily submitting to the jurisdiction of Polish authorities”. The judge also clarified that safe passage is neither a “reward” nor a “privilege” and that, given that evidence in the case is already secured and Romanowski no longer has influence over justice ministry officials, the risk of tampering is low. The National Prosecutor’s Office immediately issued a statement declaring its opposition to the ruling and its intention to appeal. It noted that there had been no confirmation that Romanowski really is in Tiraspol and that the suspect had repeatedly sought to evade the law. “These circumstances do not provide assurance that the suspect will comply with the conditions of the letter of safe conduct,” wrote the prosecutors, who also pointed to the fact that Romanowski had admitted to using travel documents issued under a false identity. Żurek, meanwhile, noted that Mielcarek is one of the so-called “neo-judges”, appointed by a judicial body rendered illegitimate by PiS’s reforms. There are legal doubts about the status of such judges and the rulings issued by them, some of which have been overturned on that basis. In his statement, the justice minister also argued that, under the law, safe passage cannot be issued without a prosecutor’s consent. Lewandowski, however, cited examples of case law that he said disproved this. He also noted that prosecutors had not filed any motion to recuse Mielcarek from the case. Prokurator ocenia dzisiejsze postanowienie Sądu o wydaniu podejrzanemu Marcinowi Romanowskiemu listu żelaznego jako niezasadne. Na postanowienie to prokurator złoży zażalenie. Sąd może wydać list żelazny, jeżeli podejrzany przebywający za granicą złoży oświadczenie, że stawi… — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) September 30, 2026 Romanowski served in the justice ministry when it was led by Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of PiS, who is also wanted by the Polish authorities on suspicion of 26 crimes relating to his time in office. Like his deputy, Ziobro also obtained asylum in Hungary. When Orbán lost power, Ziobro fled to the United States, reportedly with help from a senior Trump administration official. Poland has requested that Ziobro be extradited, though that process could take years. Both Ziobro and Romanowski deny committing the crimes they are accused of and claim that they are being pursued as an act of “political revenge” by the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. World.title: Speaker of Polish parliament signs off on service dog’s retirement after eight years of “exemplary” service
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. After eight years of service, Cobra, one of the first dogs to serve in the security force of Poland’s parliament, has retired. To mark the occasion, the speaker of the lower-house Sejm, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, personally informed Cobra of the decision. “An application for transfer to retirement?” said Czarzasty, sitting opposite the extremely well-behaved Cobra in a video published by the Sejm. “Impeccable reputation. No disciplinary punishments. You’ve never barked in the Sejm,” he read from her files. “OK, signed. As of tomorrow, you are free.” Cobra idzie na emeryturę! 🐕‍🦺 Decyzję o przejściu w stan spoczynku przypieczętował podpisem Marszałek Sejmu @wlodekczarzasty. 😉 Psy Straży Marszałkowskiej to ważny element systemu ochrony Sejmu. Czuwają nad bezpieczeństwem wszystkich osób w gmachach pozostających w zarządzie… pic.twitter.com/dKRvHOlKxe — Sejm RP🇵🇱 (@KancelariaSejmu) September 30, 2026 On a more serious note, the Sejm pointed to the vital role played by dogs in the so-called Speaker’s Guard (Straż Marszałkowska), which is responsible for security in parliament. “They watch over the safety of all people in the buildings managed by the chancellery of the Sejm,” they wrote, thanking Cobra for eight years of “exemplary” service and wishing her well on her “well-deserved retirement”. Two weeks ago, the Sejm announced the arrival of a new dog, Otik, who would serve as part of the Speaker’s Guard. He has worked alongside Cobra and another canine colleague, Hela, until now. State broadcaster TVP reports that Cobra was one of the first dogs to enter service in the Speaker’s Guard. It notes that dogs serving in the force are eligible for retirement after reaching the age of nine. Their handler has the option of taking in the dog after it retires, or they can nominate another person to care for the animal. The chancellery of the Sejm then continues to cover the costs of any veterinary care that the dog requires. It has not been revealed where and with whom Cobra will spend her retirement. In 2021, Poland’s government moved to introduce retirement benefits for dogs and horses who had served in the police force, border guard and fire service, providing them with support after they finished working. The following year, that was extended to the prison service. World.title: Inflation hits 4% in Poland as fuel prices surge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s inflation accelerated to an annual rate of 4.0% in September, up from 3.4% a month earlier, driven primarily by higher fuel prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the end of Polish government subsidies that kept down prices at the pump. The development means that inflation has now risen above the upper bound of 3.5% set by the National Bank of Poland (NBP), which aims to keep the figure at 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Analysts say that an interest rate hike by the NBP is now more likely. The new preliminary inflation figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that prices in September were 4% higher than a year earlier, the fastest rise since June 2025. On a monthly basis, prices in September were up 0.7% from August. The rise was caused in particular by the price of fuel for private transport, which was up 36.1% on a year earlier and 9.2% from the previous month. Energy prices also rose, with electricity, gas and other fuels up 4.9% year-on-year and 0.9% month-on-month. To shield consumers from the energy crisis triggered by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Poland has twice introduced temporary measures to curb petrol station prices, including daily price caps and cuts in VAT and excise duty. The system was in place from March to June and again during the the last two weeks of August. The government has been under pressure from the opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to reintroduce the subsidies. However, it argues that Nawrocki’s decision to block a proposed windfall tax on fuel companies makes the measures harder to fund Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices provided some offset, falling 0.5% from a year earlier, although they edged up 0.1% from August. Analysts, however, expect food prices to rise later in the year to reflect lower agricultural yields. According to GUS’s own estimates, also published on Wednesday, the grain harvest came in 5% lower compared to the last season. This will, in turn, “push the CPI index higher in the coming months”, wrote Erste Bank. The breach of the upper end of the central bank’s inflation target and the 4% threshold could influence the stance of the NBP’s Monetary Policy Council (RPP), prompting it to hike rates, added Erste Bank analysts. Inflacja CPI we wrześniu w górę do 4,0%r/r (ING: 4,2%; konsensus: 4,1%). Wyraźny wzrost cen paliw (36,1%r/r) odpowiada już za ok. połowę wzrostu cen w ujęciu rocznym. Zahamowanie spadków cen żywności m/m. Inflacja bazowa prawdopodobnie w dół do 3,0-3,1%r/r, co oznacza że wciąż… pic.twitter.com/AqdIXBthFl — ING Economics Poland (@ING_EconomicsPL) September 30, 2026 Economists at ING Bank Śląski, meanwhile, expect the first rate hike – after a series of nine cautious cuts between September 2023 and March 2026 – to come in early 2027. “The RPP may opt to wait, leaving interest rates unchanged in October, with discussions on potential monetary policy tightening beginning in November following the release of the NBP’s new projections,” they wrote on X. Poland’s benchmark interest rate currently stands at 3.75%, down from a peak of 6.75% reached during the country’s last tightening cycle in 2021-2022, when policymakers were grappling with persistent inflation fuelled by the post-pandemic recovery and the war in Ukraine. Inflation peaked at 18.4% during that period.

World.title: US ambassador inaugurates planned Polish-American Centre at Kraków’s Kościuszko Mound
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The US ambassador to Poland, Thomas Rose, has launched a planned new Polish-American Centre to be established in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city. Rose symbolically laid a cornerstone for the new facility and announced a $150,000 (577,000 zloty) grant to restore and preserve the site. The centre, whose website describes it as a “home for all Polish-American initiatives in Poland”, will be established alongside the famous mound in Kraków created in honour of Tadeusz Kościuszko, a hero of both the Polish and American struggles for independence in the 18th century. Proud to announce a $150,000 AFCP grant to help restore and preserve the future site of the Kościuszko Mound’s Polish American Center — a living symbol of the friendship between our two nations. Under @POTUS, we remain committed to preserving the shared history that binds the… pic.twitter.com/5atStUIid2 — Ambassador Tom Rose (@USAmbPoland) September 29, 2026 “This is a tremendous opportunity for me, on behalf of President Donald Trump and the American people, to celebrate what I consider the most important relationship the United States has with Europe today,” said Rose at the ceremony on Monday. “America is fortunate to have many, many good friends around the world. But we have no better friend in Europe,” he added, quoted by broadcaster RMF. Together with Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska, the speaker of Poland’s Senate, he laid a cornerstone for the new centre and announced the $150,000 grant, which comes from the Ambassadors’ Fund for Cultural Preservation, a programme run by the US State Department. “Tadeusz Kościuszko is a symbol of the historical bond between Poland and the USA,” declared Kidawa-Błońska. “There is no better place for the Polish-American Centre than Kraków and the mound commemorating a hero of both nations.” Tadeusz Kościuszko to symbol historycznej więzi między Polską i USA. Nie ma lepszego miejsca dla Centrum Polsko-Amerykańskiego niż Kraków i kopiec upamiętniający bohatera obu narodów. Niech powołane dziś Centrum dobrze służy naszym relacjom, które budujemy od 250 lat 🇵🇱🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/8nOkCYDLfD — Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska (@M_K_Blonska) September 29, 2026 Kościuszko’s Mound was established in Kraków in 1823, following the pattern of two prehistoric mounds that already existed in the city. It honours Kościuszko, a military officer who had fought against Russian rule over Poland and in the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War. Construction of the new Polish-American Centre is being supported by the Kościuszko Mound Committee in Kraków in partnership with USA250PL, the platform for celebrations in Poland of this year’s 250th anniversary of the American Declaration of Independence. The Kościuszko Mound Committee has long been engaged in efforts to preserve the mound against partial collapses caused by heavy rain. Polish hydraulics manufacturer PONAR Wadowice is also listed as a partner of the new centre. The facility says it “will serve as a living symbol of friendship, understanding, and transatlantic cooperation”, providing “a welcoming space for dialogue, creativity, and exchange”. The centre will house event spaces, conference rooms, and offices. In June, the centre acted as a patron of a United States–Central and Eastern Europe Connection Weekend at Kraków’s Jagiellonian University. Next year it plans a commemoration of the Battle of Saratoga, where Kościuszko designed fortifications that contributed to the American victory. Poland has long looked to the United States for support and as an example during its struggle for independence over the last two centuries, including during the period of partitions in the 19th century, the reestablishment of the Polish state after the First World War, and during the later decades of communist rule. Since the fall of communism, the US has become Warsaw’s most important security partner – including establishing its first permanent military garrison, named Fort Kościuszko, in Poland in 2023. The US has opened its first military garrison in Poland, and its first anywhere on NATO's eastern flank. "This is a historic moment," says Poland's defence minister. "We have been striving for years for this word 'permanent' and it has now become fact" https://t.co/knJEcqv4MB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 21, 2023 Last week, President Donald Trump, in a virtual address to the Polish-American Congress (an entity unrelated to the new centre in Kraków), praised his Polish counterpart Karol Nawrocki, a close Trump ally, and described himself as a “great friend of the people of Poland”. Shortly before that, Nawrocki had expressed confidence that a planned new US military base in Poland would soon be confirmed, and suggested that it would be named Fort Trump. World.title: EU court rejects Poland’s request to suspend implementation of Mercosur trade deal
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Court of Justice of the European Union has rejected a request from Poland to suspend the implementation of the EU’s recently launched free trade agreement with the Mercosur bloc of South American countries. The CJEU found that the Polish government had failed to prove its claims that the trade deal would cause serious harm to European farmers, consumers or the environment. #ECJ: Order in Case C-460/26 R Poland v Council: should the implementation of the Council’s decision authorising the provisional application of the EU-Mercosur interim trade agreement be suspended pending the Court’s ruling?#CJEU #Mercosur pic.twitter.com/ocb4I4PsE8 — EU Court of Justice (@EUCourtPress) September 29, 2026 Poland has long been critical of the agreement, in particular over the potential negative impact that imports of agricultural products from Mercosur, which includes Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, could have on Polish farmers, who have repeatedly protested against the deal. In January, Poland failed in a bid to block the agreement at the European Council, where 21 of the EU’s 27 member states voted in favour of the deal. Although the agreement has not yet received final ratification – still requiring approval from the European Parliament and national parliaments – it nevertheless went into provisional force on 1 May. Shortly afterwards, Poland submitted a complaint to the CJEU, calling for implementation of the agreement to be suspended. It argued, first of all, that the process through which the deal had been provisionally implemented violated the EU’s treaties. Second, it claimed that liberalising trade in agricultural products without imposing the same production standards in both the EU and Mercosur created a risk of harm to human and animal health, the environment, the income of farmers, and the functioning of the market in the EU. Poland has filed a complaint to the European Court of Justice against the EU's free-trade deal with the South American Mercosur bloc that recently went into provisional force. It wants the agreement to be suspended until the court issues a ruling https://t.co/wE7DIbDazU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 However, on Tuesday, the CJEU announced that it had dismissed the application to suspend the agreement, finding that “Poland has not provided any concrete evidence to establish the likelihood and imminence of serious and irreparable damage”. The court pointed out that agricultural products from Mercosur could already be imported to the EU before the free-trade deal, and that they were and continue to be subject to food safety and health regulations similar to those for products manufactured in the EU. It also noted that the new trade deal includes tools allowing the EU to bar products that do not meet standards, including emergency measures in the case of a serious threat to human, animal or plant life. Finally, the CJEU said that Poland’s “general and abstract claims” regarding potential harm to farmers and markets did not include “any evidence capable of establishing, with a sufficient degree of probability, that the implementation [of the agreement]…will cause disruption”. In response to the court’s decision, the Polish government’s spokesman, Adam Szłapka, immediately blamed the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) administration, which was in power in Poland from 2015 to 2023. Szłapka said that the details of the Mercosur deal had been agreed during that period and that PiS had “failed to secure Polish interests in any way”. He argued that it was the current government which secured the addition of last-minute safeguards intended to protect farmers. The spokesman also noted that Polish agricultural exports to the Mercosur bloc have actually increased under the new agreement while imports from there have fallen, showing that “Polish farmers are profiting from this”. Rząd i Premier Tusk najpierw mówili, że umowa UE-Mercosur będzie „bezpieczna dla polskich rolników”. Potem nie potrafili zbudować koalicji blokującej w Radzie Europejskiej – choć polityka europejska jest domeną rządu. Politycy KO, PSL i Lewicy nie potrafili nikogo przekonać.… https://t.co/EqOJr4sneP — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) September 29, 2026 However, Marcin Przydacz, the head of the foreign policy office of President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, argued that the CJEU’s decision showed the impotence of the current pro-EU government. “The government and Prime Minister Tusk first said that the EU-Mercosur agreement would be ‘safe for Polish farmers’. Then they failed to build a blocking coalition in the European Council,” wrote Przydacz. “In the end, under pressure from public opinion in Poland, they filed a complaint with the ECJ. [It was] so weak that they lost the request for interim relief,” he added. “Ineffective policy and ineffective government.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Prague Passengers Can Now Request Czech or English Speaking Bolt Drivers
World.content:
Bolt has introduced two new ride categories in Prague that allow passengers to request drivers who speak either Czech or English.

The new options are available at the same price as a standard Bolt ride.



They are open to drivers of any nationality who can communicate in the relevant language at a level suitable for everyday conversation.

Czech-speaking passengers who are less comfortable communicating in English can request a Czech-speaking driver, while foreign residents, tourists and business travellers can choose a driver who speaks English.

Bolt already provides automatic translation for communication between passengers and drivers within its app. Booking information, addresses and messages can therefore be translated automatically. The new categories are designed to cover situations in which communication takes place outside the app, particularly during the journey itself.

The company said the new options are already available in Prague, where it has enough partner drivers who meet the language requirements.

Drivers can choose whether to participate in the new categories. They may offer rides in Czech, English, both languages or continue driving exclusively in the standard category.

Participation is voluntary.

Passengers will see the two new options directly in the Bolt app. The Czech-speaking category is identified by an icon featuring the Czech flag, while the English-speaking option uses an English flag icon.

World.title: Pegasus Airlines Completes Acquisition of Czech Airlines and Smartwings
World.content:
Pegasus Airlines has completed its acquisition of Czech Airlines and the Smartwings Group, marking a major change in the ownership of one of the Czech Republic’s most established aviation businesses.

The Turkish low-cost carrier announced the completion of the transaction on Thursday, October 1, following the approval of the relevant regulatory authorities and the fulfilment of the required closing conditions.



The deal brings together Pegasus Airlines and the Czech-based Smartwings Group, creating an aviation group with a combined fleet of more than 175 aircraft.

The two airlines also have firm orders for a further 140 aircraft.

For passengers in Prague and across the Czech Republic, Smartwings will continue to operate under its existing brand. Its day-to-day operations, customer relationships and service are expected to remain in place, while the company will gain access to new opportunities for expansion and development through its new ownership.

Pegasus expands further into Central Europe

Founded in 1990, Pegasus Airlines has operated as a low-cost carrier since 2005. The airline currently serves 161 destinations in 57 countries from its main hub at Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen Airport and other bases in Türkiye.

Its network covers Europe, the Middle East, North Africa and Asia, making the acquisition an opportunity to strengthen Pegasus’ presence in Central and Eastern Europe.

Smartwings, meanwhile, operates a network of around 80 destinations across 20 countries. The group has a particularly strong position in the Czech leisure travel market, with scheduled and charter services as well as private flights and special flights for international companies and organisations.

The Czech airline has been operating under the Smartwings name since 1998, while the Czech Airlines (ČSA) brand is one of the oldest names in European aviation.

The combined business is expected to benefit from the complementary networks of the two airlines. Pegasus brings a large international network and experience with the low-cost model, while Smartwings has an established customer base and strong relationships with tour operators in the Czech Republic and wider Central European market.

Pegasus said that Smartwings will continue operating under its established brand following the completion of the acquisition.

Pegasus carried a record 43.3 million passengers in 2025 and operates one of Europe’s younger aircraft fleets.

World.title: Ibiza Is Coming to Prague: A Night of DJs, Lasers and Tropical Vibes
World.content:
On April 17, 2027, OX Club in Prague will transform for one night into an Ibiza-inspired party featuring DJs, immersive visuals and tropical-themed spaces.

The Sound of Ibiza event will bring British DJ and producer Daxson, Dutch DJ and producer Laura Van Dam, Czech DJ Lucca and DJ TiGi to one stage.



The night will combine electronic music with a full immersive laser show, acrobatic performances above the dancefloor and Ibiza-inspired décor throughout the club.

There will also be a dedicated Sunset Experience for photos and social media, as well as a Chillout Zone with its own DJ programme and mentoring by Pavel Bidlo.

Daxson has performed at major festivals and clubs including Creamfields, EDC, UNTOLD and Ministry of Sound, while also creating several anthems for Transmission Festival. Laura Van Dam has appeared at Tomorrowland, Ultra, EDC, Sziget and Ushuaïa Ibiza and has built a following with her melodic techno and trance sound.

DJ Lucca, one of the country’s best-known electronic music artists, has performed alongside international names including Carl Cox and Paul van Dyk.

The event will also feature competitions for an iPhone and other prizes. An Ibiza Beach Outfit is suggested, although the dress code is optional.

With a capacity of 1,000 people, Sound of Ibiza aims to recreate the atmosphere of the famous Mediterranean party island in the centre of Prague for one night.

Tickets went on sale on October 1. Party packs are also available.

The event has no age restriction. Tickets are available through GoOut.

World.title: The Prague Post’s First Issue Goes Online 35 Years Later
World.content:
The Prague Post has launched a digital archive marking 35 years since the publication of its first issue.

October 1, 2026, marks the 35th anniversary of the newspaper’s debut.

Founded in 1991, The Prague Post was Czechoslovakia’s longest-running English-language weekly newspaper.



The newly launched archive begins with that very first issue, which is available to read in full, browse online and search by text.

A new issue will be added each week, corresponding to the same week 35 years earlier.

The project will allow readers to follow the political, social and cultural changes of the early 1990s through the newspaper’s coverage, much as readers did at the time.

The Prague Post Archive is also active on Facebook and Instagram, where updates about newly digitized issues and the project will be shared.

The archive is administered by Modrá sova z.s., a nonprofit English-language library and learning center in Loužnice, where The Prague Post’s physical archives are housed.

Issues published between 1991 and 1994 have already been scanned and processed.

Around two decades of additional issues remain to be digitized, making the project a long-term and costly undertaking. Modrá sova has independently funded the digitization work since the project began and is now inviting organizations and individuals interested in supporting the project to contribute through the archive’s website.

The archive will also continue to handle requests from people looking for specific articles and welcomes visitors by appointment.

For more information, contact Mimi Fronczak-Rogers at [email protected] or +420 721 518 385.

World.title: Halloween Trick-or-Treat for Charity to Return to Prague on October 22
World.content:
A Halloween charity event will bring children and families to several Prague neighbourhoods on October 22, combining trick-or-treating with fundraising for SOS Children’s Villages.

The Halloween Trick-or-Treat for Charity will take place from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. across Vinohrady, Vršovice, Žižkov, Prague 15, Holešovice and Barrandov.



The concept is simple. Children dressed in Halloween costumes and accompanied by their parents will visit participating host locations, which can include cafés, restaurants, shops, confectioneries, schools, children’s centres and other businesses or organisations.

The participating locations will remain a secret until children register for the event and receive a special map showing where they can go trick-or-treating.

At each location, children will make a contribution of at least CZK 10 to a sealed collection box supporting SOS Children’s Villages. In return, they will receive a sweet treat before continuing to the next location.

Last year’s event attracted more than 1,100 registered participants and raised CZK 296,157 despite rainy weather.

The entire amount was donated to SOS Children’s Villages, which has supported children, families, young people and foster carers in the Czech Republic for more than 50 years.

How it started

Dinah Spritzer-Richter and several of her friends organized the first American Halloween in Prague for her two children in 2017. The event has supported charity from the very first year, with the proceeds going to help children in SOS Children’s Villages.

Dinah sees the charity side as just as important as creating a joyful and memorable experience for the kids.

How to take part

Families who want to participate can register in advance and then use the secret map to find the participating locations on October 22.

Children are encouraged to come in costume and bring enough coins to make contributions at the individual stops.

Businesses and organisations can also join the event as hosts. Each host is asked to prepare sweets, add some Halloween decorations and wear at least part of a costume or Halloween accessory.

Hosts must be available for at least two hours between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m.

The organisers will provide the collection boxes, while hosts provide the sweets for visiting children.

World.title: Prague Study Reveals How Much Waste Tourists Leave in the City Center
World.content:
Specialists from Prague City Hall and the Institute of Circular Economy (INCIEN) have analyzed the contents of public waste bins in central Prague, finding that about one ton of rubbish is discarded on Wenceslas Square every day.

The latest analysis was carried out to examine how the composition of waste changes with the seasons and fluctuations in tourist traffic.

A similar measurement was conducted during the winter, providing a basis for comparison.



Beverage packaging made up roughly one-third of the waste collected from bins on Wenceslas Square. Cans and plastic bottles were among the most common items.

Another third consisted of disposable food-service items, particularly cups. The remaining third was made up of general household waste.

Researchers also found waste originating from businesses in the surrounding area, including cafes and shops. Some household rubbish appeared to have been left by tourists staying in apartments rented through short-term accommodation platforms.

Food waste was another recurring part of the findings. Partially eaten food was frequently found in the bins, with trdelník pastries among the more common examples.

The summer analysis gives Prague authorities a clearer picture of the waste generated in one of the city’s busiest public spaces during the peak tourist season and allows them to compare the results with the winter survey.

World.title: Prague Hospitals Warn of Critical Blood Shortages
World.content:
Several hospitals in Prague are reporting critically low blood supplies, prompting the Czech Ministry of Health to urge people to donate blood in the coming days.

The shortage is affecting more than individual blood groups. Hospitals and transfusion centers in several parts of the Czech Republic are reporting a broader decline in available supplies, with some facilities nearing the minimum levels needed to maintain safe operations.



The situation differs from one region to another. Some transfusion centers still have adequate reserves, while others are short of particular blood groups or are approaching critical levels.

The shortage also extends to individual blood components. In Prague, the Institute for Clinical and Experimental Medicine (IKEM) is currently seeking more platelet donors regardless of blood type.

People planning to donate are advised to check the latest information on the website or social media channels of their chosen transfusion center before visiting.

Why hospitals need more donors

Hospitals depend on regular blood donations not only during emergencies but also for planned medical treatment.

Blood is routinely needed for surgery, childbirth and the treatment of patients who require repeated transfusions. This includes some cancer patients whose treatment can interfere with the body’s production of blood cells.

Blood donations are also essential in cases of severe complications during childbirth. Heavy blood loss can become life-threatening within a short period, and an adequate supply of donated blood can be critical to saving the lives of mothers and newborns.

The demand for blood can increase during the summer and holiday period, when hospitals continue to perform scheduled procedures while also dealing with more injuries and traffic accidents. At the same time, the number of people coming to donate tends to fall as residents leave the country or travel elsewhere.

Number of donors continues to decline

Official figures indicate that the Czech donor base has been shrinking. Around 348,000 people donated blood last year, down from 362,000 the previous year.

Transfusion centers are also losing older regular donors as they reach the age limit, while the number of younger people replacing them has not been sufficient.

In the Czech Republic, adults can generally donate blood until the age of 65, provided they weigh more than 50 kilograms. Additional eligibility restrictions may apply, including for people who have recently travelled to countries where certain infectious diseases are present.

Donating blood in the Czech Republic is voluntary and free of charge. Donors are entitled to time off work on the day of their donation, while some health insurance companies provide additional benefits or rewards for regular donors.

World.title: Bangkok Gears Up for the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings
World.content:
All eyes are on Thailand as the country prepares to host the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) Annual Meetings, also known as the 2026 Annual Meetings or AM2026 Thailand.

Running from 12-18 October 2026, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, the event will mark Thailand’s second time hosting the meetings, following its first in 1991. This will make Thailand one of only three nations to have hosted the IMF–WBG Annual Meetings twice.



The IMF–WBG Annual Meetings, held for two consecutive years in Washington D.C. and every third year in one of the 191 member countries, serve as a gathering of top economic figures from around the world. By covering a broad range of issues, the meetings aim to strengthen global financial stability, combat poverty, and ensure inclusive economic growth and job creation.

Thailand’s selection to host again in 2026 highlights how the country has advanced over the past three decades in terms of its institutional progress, economic resilience, and sustained engagement with international partners. As host, Thailand brings decades’ worth of experience in economic transformation and regional leadership to the table.

The “Olympics of Finance”

Often dubbed the “Olympics of Finance,” the meetings are set to attract more than 15,000 participants, including finance ministers, central bankers, economists, business leaders, civil society representatives, and journalists from the IMF and World Bank’s 191 member countries, including the Czech Republic.

The Annual Meetings will be held under the theme of “Thailand’s New Horizons: Empowering People, Building Resilience”. Therefore, the meetings will focus on enhancing people’s potential and creating opportunities, with the goal of fostering a financial and economic system that is safe, sustainable, and inclusive.

Under the theme, the government plans to showcase four policy priorities it believes are increasingly relevant in an era marked by geopolitical fragmentation, economic volatility, and demographic change. These are indeed the issues that warrant serious conversation and sincere collaboration among the global community and all stakeholders to address them in the most efficient way:

Digital Transformation : The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems.

The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems. Connected Economy : A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored.

A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored. Climate Finance : The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change.

The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change. Longevity Economy: The final priority seeks to turn the challenges of ageing populations into new sources of economic growth.

Alongside these focus areas, the Bank of Thailand plans to unveil the “Bangkok Blueprint,” an international framework developed jointly with the IMF and the World Bank aimed at combating digital financial fraud and strengthening trust in the digital economy.

Readiness in All Aspects

According to the Fiscal Policy Office, Thailand’s overall readiness has been assessed at “Grade A” following months of coordination between the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Thailand, and the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings Secretariat.

Preparations extend beyond the conference venue. Authorities have developed contingency plans for traffic management, emergency responses, and arrangements for high-level foreign officials. A working group has also been established to address cybersecurity matters.

Beyond Tourism: A Regional Economic Capital

Beyond its long-established reputation as a world-renowned tourist destination, the 2026 Annual Meetings offer Thailand an excellent opportunity to present another dimension of the Kingdom to the international community.

AM2026 reinforces Thailand’s standing as a trusted international partner while highlighting its growing role as a regional economic capital and a hub for finance, investment, policy innovation, and multilateral dialogue in Southeast Asia. Having said that, countries and companies vying for economic and business opportunities cannot overlook Thailand and its potential to become an important impetus for their long-term prosperity and growth.

(Source material and reporting courtesy of Thailand NOW)

World.title: Former Hungarian economy minister Márton Nagy moves to Switzerland, report says
World.content:
Márton Nagy, a former minister in former PM Viktor Orbán’s government, has reportedly moved to Switzerland and has been working for a Zurich investment bank since the summer.

Márton Nagy, who served as Hungary’s national economy minister before the April 2026 election, has moved to Switzerland and has been working for a Zurich-based investment bank since the summer, Válasz Online reports.

According to the publication, Nagy has made it clear to people in his close circle that he has permanently left Hungarian politics. He is also reportedly no longer in regular contact with the leadership of Fidesz, which is now in opposition.

Válasz Online reached Nagy by telephone, but he declined to comment on the reports. His former ministry has not been reported as confirming the move either.

Nagy reportedly cuts ties with Hungarian politics

The reported departure is notable because Viktor Orbán recently referred to Nagy’s intellect in a speech in Kötcse. The remarks could have suggested that the former minister is still part of the strategic circle around the former prime minister. However, Válasz Online’s sources say Nagy has now definitively moved away from Hungarian politics.

According to the publication’s background conversations, the decision followed a serious health crisis last year. Nagy was reportedly in immediate danger to his life in July 2025 and subsequently underwent major surgery at the Városmajor Heart and Vascular Centre in Budapest.

One of his distant relatives told Válasz Online that Nagy had already wanted to leave politics at that point, but circumstances prevented him from doing so. Just days after the April 2026 election, Nagy also deactivated his Facebook page.

From government minister to Zurich investment banking

Nagy served as national economy minister in Orbán’s government before the 2026 election. He had previously held senior economic positions and became one of the most prominent figures in the government’s economic policy.

His reported move to Switzerland comes amid a wider departure of former government figures from frontline Hungarian politics. Former foreign minister and foreign economic affairs minister Péter Szijjártó announced in July that he would give up his parliamentary mandate and take a position at Chinese carmaker BYD.

Meanwhile, Viktor Orbán’s daughter Ráhel Orbán and her family moved to the United States in 2025 after she was admitted to an American university. Her children began the 2025/2026 academic year there. Nagy himself was also recently reported by 24.hu to have appeared on a South Korean holiday island during one of his official trips.

World.title: Tisza Party support falls sharply, but Magyar Péter’s party still dominates new poll
World.content:
Support for Hungary’s governing Tisza Party has dropped nine percentage points since May, while Fidesz and Mi Hazánk have both gained ground, according to a new survey by 21 Kutatóközpont.

The Tisza Party remains well ahead of its rivals despite a significant decline in support since May, according to a fresh poll by 21 Kutatóközpont.

Among voters able to choose a party, 60% said they would vote for Péter Magyar’s party, down from 69% in May. However, the September figure is still higher than the 56% share the Tisza Party received in the April parliamentary election among voters in Hungary.

The poll was conducted by telephone between 28 and 30 September, with 1,000 people surveyed. The sample is representative of the Hungarian population, with a margin of error of approximately ±3 percentage points for the full sample.

Fidesz regains some support as Tisza declines

The poll also recorded a modest recovery for Fidesz, which increased its support among party-choice voters from 23% in May to 26% in September. However, this remains well below the party’s 36% support in the same category around the April election, according to 21 Kutatóközpont.

The biggest increase was recorded by Mi Hazánk. Its support almost doubled, rising from 6% in May to 11% among voters who said they could choose a party. The remaining parliamentary and non-parliamentary parties collectively account for 3%, with the Democratic Coalition (DK) the strongest of them at 1%.

Tisza still has a huge lead among committed voters

The gap is even wider among voters who say they would definitely participate if an election were held this Sunday. In this group, the Tisza Party stands at 62%, compared with 26% for Fidesz and 10% for Mi Hazánk. All other parties together account for 2%.

According to the analysis cited by 24.hu, the nine-point decline in Tisza support and five-point rise for Mi Hazánk represent substantial changes when viewed over several months. However, they accumulated over the four months since the May measurement rather than occurring in a single month.

The research also notes that the unusually high 69% recorded for Tisza in May may have been the more exceptional result, rather than the current 60%.

Tisza leads in the full population too

Looking at the entire population, the Tisza Party has 51% support, followed by Fidesz at 23% and Mi Hazánk at 9%. A further 2% would choose another party, while 15% either could not name a party or did not wish to choose one. Compared with May, Tisza’s support has fallen by nine percentage points, while Fidesz has gained three points and Mi Hazánk four.

The findings broadly follow the direction of another recent poll. A Medián survey published in late September put Tisza at 64% among both party-choice voters and those certain to vote, while Fidesz stood at 26% and 27% respectively.

World.title: Hungarian house prices soar over 10% in a year – But then came a sharp quarterly drop
World.content:
Hungary sees one of the EU’s sharpest annual house price increases, but the latest quarter brought an unexpected turn.

House prices in the European Union rose 4.7% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, Eurostat reported Thursday. Prices increased 1.2% compared with the previous quarter. In the euro area, house prices rose 4% annually and 1.1% quarterly. Annual growth slowed from 5.1% in the EU and 4.6% in the euro area in the first quarter.

Portugal recorded the strongest annual increase at 16.5%, followed by Bulgaria at 15.5% and Lithuania at 14.3%. Finland, Luxembourg and France registered annual declines.

Other substantial annual increases included Slovakia at 13.6%, Croatia at 12.7%, Spain and Romania at 12.1% each, Latvia at 11.4% and Hungary at 10.2%. Prices fell 2.7% annually in Finland, 2.2% in Luxembourg and 0.8% in France, according to Anadolu Agency.

On a quarterly basis, Lithuania posted the largest increase at 5%, followed by Bulgaria at 4.5% and Romania at 4.4%. Latvia recorded a quarterly rise of 3.9%, Portugal 3.6%, Estonia 3.5%, Spain 3.4%, Austria 3.3%, Slovenia 3% and Denmark 2.8%.

Hungary and France recorded quarterly declines of 1.4% and 0.8%, respectively.

World.title: PM Magyar demands apology from priest after he attacked Tisza voters in sermon
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has called on the Catholic Church to publicly distance itself from priest Zoltán Osztie after he strongly criticised Tisza voters during a Mass and called the party morally corrupt.

Priest attacks Tisza voters during Mass

Catholic priest Zoltán Osztie has come under fire after making strongly political remarks about Tisza Party voters during a Mass in Feldebrő on 26 September. In the sermon at St Martin’s Church, Osztie questioned how Christians could vote for Tisza, describing the party as a “morally deeply corrupt” group that would destroy the country.

He also said that people who identified as Christians but voted for Tisza “understood nothing” of the Gospel. He criticised what he described as support for “lies, immorality and hatred”, and referred to the political group as “unbelieving, immoral and treasonous”.

Osztie also said he was proud that there were no Tisza voters around him and said he wanted that to remain the case.

According to Telex, the priest has previously made political statements. In July, he spoke at a demonstration near the Sándor Palace without authorisation from the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest. At that event, he discussed, among other topics, the influence of global powers and BlackRock, as well as Pride and what he described as communist and fascist terror.

If you missed it: Scale of deficit inherited by Magyar government is now official: EUR 7.6 billion in the red

Magyar demands public response and apology

Magyar shared an excerpt of the more than 13-minute sermon on Facebook on Thursday and called on the Catholic Church to immediately and publicly distance itself from Osztie’s remarks.

The prime minister said Osztie had previously made what he considered inappropriate political statements, but argued that the latest comments were particularly problematic because they were delivered as part of a sermon inside a church.

Magyar said criticism itself was not the issue, but argued that neither believers nor non-believers should have to listen to a Catholic priest speak about them in such terms during a Mass. He said he understood that the Catholic Church did not share Osztie’s views, but nevertheless expected the Church to make its position public. He also said he expected Osztie to apologise.

Magyar added that he valued the social, educational, cultural and religious work carried out by churches in Hungary. He called on people not to respond with anti-Church comments, stressing that his criticism was directed at the priest’s remarks rather than at the Church as a whole.

Osztie has previously drawn criticism over political activity

Osztie has attracted attention for his political involvement before. In July, he spoke at a demonstration organised near the Sándor Palace in support of then-President Tamás Sulyok and against a constitutional amendment proposal by Tisza. The speech was not made with the authorisation of the Esztergom-Budapest Archdiocese.

Osztie has also regularly celebrated Masses attended by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, including a Mass held for Orbán’s birthday in May. Magyar’s latest intervention comes shortly after his visit to the Vatican, where he met Pope Leo XIV in September.

World.title: Hungary’s central bank probe summons former and current governors
World.content:
A parliamentary committee investigating the use of public funds by Hungary’s central bank has summoned former governor György Matolcsy and current governor Mihály Varga for questioning.

Former and current NBH governors to appear before committee

A parliamentary committee investigating alleged abuses surrounding the operation of the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) has decided to summon former governor György Matolcsy and current governor Mihály Varga.

The ad hoc committee voted unanimously to summon Matolcsy, who headed the central bank between 2013 and 2025. The decision to summon Varga, who succeeded Matolcsy as governor in 2025, was approved with five votes in favour, no votes against and one abstention.

The committee’s chairman, Attila Csőszi of the governing Tisza Party, said the decisions would formally require both men to appear and give oral testimony. The next committee meeting is expected to take place in three to four weeks. Csőszi told state news agency MTI that the committee plans to question Matolcsy and Varga on several occasions.

György Matolcsy. Photo: National Bank of Hungary

Committee requests data from NBH foundation

The committee also voted to request data from the Pallas Athene Domus Meriti Foundation, one of the foundations established by the central bank. The request was approved with five votes in favour, one abstention and no votes against.

The parliamentary committee was established to examine the use of public funds and alleged abuses linked to the operation of the NBH. Its work is expected to focus on the central bank and entities connected to it.

If you missed it: Central bank chief on the scenario for introducing the Hungarian euro

Several former officials already questioned

The committee has already begun questioning figures connected to the NBH case. On Thursday, it spent more than three hours questioning Erik Bánki and Lajos Kósa. The committee has previously said that it intends to identify and summon the key figures involved in the case. Further hearings are expected to include Matolcsy’s son, Ádám Matolcsy, among others.

Matolcsy served as NBH governor from 2013 until 2025. Varga was Hungary’s economy minister from 2013 to 2018 and finance minister from 2018 to 2024 before taking over as central bank governor in 2025.

World.title: India and Hungary deepen academic and cultural ties through new MoU
World.content:
Nālandā University, Rajgir, India, and Dharma Gate Buddhist College, Budapest, Hungary, have entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to promote and strengthen academic, educational, cultural and scholarly exchanges and cooperation between the two institutions.

The MoU provides a framework for cooperation between the two institutions with a view to strengthening their intellectual ties and developing academic collaborations across a diverse range of disciplines. It reflects the shared commitment of both institutions to promoting mutual understanding, goodwill and greater institutional linkages between India and Hungary.

Under the MoU, the two institutions will explore and promote cooperation in a range of academic areas, including joint research supervision, joint teaching programmes, post-doctoral research, joint conferences and symposiums, academic publications, and exchange of faculty, research fellows and students. The cooperation will also include exchange of publications and mutual access to academic literature and materials, as well as other activities that may be mutually agreed upon.

The MoU will provide opportunities for enhanced interaction among academics, researchers, faculty members and students of the two institutions, thereby facilitating the exchange of knowledge, ideas and academic expertise. Such exchanges are expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of India’s rich intellectual, educational and cultural heritage in Hungary and further strengthen academic connections between the two countries.

If you missed it: India and Hungary strengthen cooperation in Ayurveda through establishment of Academic Chair at Széchenyi István University

The collaboration also provides an important platform for advancing scholarly engagement in areas relating to Buddhist studies and the broader intellectual and cultural traditions associated with India. Through joint academic activities, research and educational exchanges, the partnership is envisaged to contribute to the promotion of knowledge and greater appreciation of the shared historical and cultural linkages between India and Hungary.

The MoU builds upon the longstanding and multifaceted relations between India and Hungary, particularly in the fields of education, culture, scholarship and people-to-people exchanges. It underscores the importance attached by both sides to strengthening institutional and academic linkages and promoting greater cooperation in areas of shared interest.

The Embassy of India in Budapest will continue to facilitate and support initiatives that promote closer institutional linkages between India and Hungary, particularly in the areas of education, scholarship, culture and research. The collaboration between Nālandā University and Dharma Gate Buddhist College adds a significant academic dimension to these efforts and is expected to foster sustained interaction among scholars, researchers and students, while further advancing the longstanding bonds of intellectual and cultural exchange between the two countries.

World.title: Kremlin warns Hungary’s ‘unfriendly steps’ could hurt economic ties with Russia
World.content:
Vladimir Putin’s spokesman has said Moscow hopes Hungary will continue its economic cooperation with Russia, while warning that Budapest’s recent actions could affect bilateral ties.

Kremlin hopes Hungary will continue economic cooperation

The Kremlin hopes “reason will prevail” in Hungary and that Budapest will continue its economic cooperation with Russia, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Thursday. His comments came just hours after Russia announced that it was expelling 10 Hungarian diplomats in response to Hungary’s decision in September to expel 10 Russian diplomats.

Peskov said the Hungarian government had so far been cautious and had not taken what he described as “rash steps” concerning economic cooperation with Russia. He said Moscow therefore remained hopeful that the two countries could continue working together economically. At the same time, however, Peskov did not rule out a deterioration in economic relations.

“Unfriendly steps” by Budapest could have an impact on economic cooperation, he said, according to Russian state news agency TASS.

Russia responds to diplomatic expulsions

Hungary expelled 10 Russian diplomats in early September. The Hungarian authorities did not publicly identify the diplomats, but the move came amid concerns over Russian intelligence activity. Russia announced its response on Thursday, ordering 10 Hungarian diplomats to leave the country.

This dispute marks another strain on relations between Budapest and Moscow, although Peskov’s comments suggest the Kremlin does not currently want the dispute to spill over into economic cooperation. The remarks also come against the backdrop of important changes in Hungary’s foreign and energy policy.

Russian oil company still linked to potential NIS deal

According to Telex, Peskov’s comments may also be significant in light of the ongoing possibility that Russian oil company Gazprom Neft could sell its stake in Serbia’s NIS oil company to Hungary’s MOL. NIS operates Serbia’s only oil refinery, and the future of Gazprom Neft’s stake has become complicated by sanctions imposed on Russia. Gazprom Neft has nevertheless remained open to selling the stake to MOL. The deal has not yet been completed.

Meanwhile, Hungary has also been exploring energy cooperation with other European partners. Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán recently held talks with Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže, with the two countries agreeing to restart foreign and security policy consultations that have been suspended since 2019.

The Russian embassy in Budapest responded with a sarcastic social media post after the talks, questioning whether Hungary had found its “new strategic energy partner” in Riga.

World.title: Hungary backs tougher EU return rules, bloc approves new system for migrants without right to stay
World.content:
Hungary has voted in favour of new EU rules designed to make the return of people without a legal right to stay more effective, including stricter measures and the possibility of return hubs outside the bloc.

EU approves new return framework

The Council of the European Union has given its final approval to new rules governing the return of non-EU nationals who have no legal right to remain in the bloc.

Hungary was among 23 of the EU’s 27 member states to vote in favour of the regulation on Thursday, Telex reports. Spain voted against it, while Belgium abstained. Denmark and Ireland did not vote because of their respective opt-outs in the area of justice and home affairs.

The new rules are intended to strengthen the EU’s common approach to returns and complement the bloc’s Migration and Asylum Pact. According to the Council, around two in three people who are ordered to leave the EU do not actually do so. The new framework is intended to give national authorities more tools to enforce return decisions.

Stricter obligations for those ordered to leave

Under the new system, people who receive a return decision will be required to leave the member state concerned and cooperate with the authorities.

Failure to comply can result in sanctions, including financial penalties, reduced benefits and allowances where permitted under national law, or the withdrawal of incentives intended to encourage voluntary return. Criminal sanctions may also be possible where national legislation provides for them.

Authorities will also have greater powers to impose measures such as reporting requirements, restrictions on leaving a designated place of residence, financial guarantees and electronic monitoring.

In certain circumstances, people may be detained for up to two years, with an additional six months possible where justified. National authorities may also carry out investigative measures, including searches and seizures, when necessary to prepare for or secure a return.

The rules provide for particularly strict measures for people considered to pose a security risk. These can include longer detention and, where justified and proportionate, an indefinite entry ban.

If you missed it: 10 Chinese guest workers and 37 bunk beds found at former restaurant building in Szeged

Return hubs could be established outside the EU

One of the most significant elements of the new framework is the possibility of establishing so-called return hubs in non-EU countries.

Under agreements with third countries, people who have received a return decision could be transferred to such a centre outside the EU. A return hub could serve either as the final destination or as an intermediate stage before the person is returned to their country of origin.

Such agreements can only be concluded with countries that respect international human rights standards and international law, including the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to a country where they face a serious risk of persecution or other serious harm. Unaccompanied minors are excluded from these arrangements.

The idea of external return centres has already faced legal and practical difficulties. Italy, for example, has attempted to establish similar facilities in Albania, although the scheme has encountered legal challenges.
