World.title: Who’s behind Trillanes’ trial withdrawal? He won’t say Escudero, but calls him out
World.content:
SPEAKING OUT. Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV holds a press conference at Club Filipino in San Juan City on October 2, 2026, where he presented his findings on the alleged ill-gotten wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV doesn't explicitly disclose what he means when he says the prosecution is being pressured over his testimony, but he still can't resist taking a swipe at the trial's presiding officer

Listening to former senator Antonio Trillanes IV’s press conference is an exercise in reading between the lines.

Trillanes, fresh from his removal from the prosecution’s witness lineup in Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial, consistently faced questions from the media on the identity of the individuals who orchestrated his eventual withdrawal.

The veteran politician dodged these questions over and over, yet in the same breath repeatedly took a swipe at one person: presiding officer Chiz Escudero.

At first, Trillanes didn’t want to give reporters a juicy soundbite on the “pressure” subject.

“I would have wanted to address that, but it would be a distraction from the main issue that we want to discuss, which is more important,” Trillanes said in Filipino on Friday, October 2. When asked if the pressure was coming from the senator-judges, he quipped, “No comment.”

Relentless journalists didn’t drop the subject, prompting Trillanes to eventually take a swipe at Escudero, without explicitly naming him.

“It’s this simple: The prosecution requested that certain people be subpoenaed. My name was on the list. The subpoenas came back, and I was the only one missing. Does the impeachment court have that kind of power? Does the presiding officer have the power to say, ‘Not this one yet’? That is the question. They don’t have that power. Because this is the prosecution’s strategy,” Trillanes said.

“Let us suspend our judgment, but let’s call him out,” he added.

Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV holds a press conference at Club Filipino in San Juan City on October 2, 2026, where he presented his findings on the alleged ill-gotten wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte.

For the record, Escudero had suggested that the prosecution present witnesses from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) and the banks first in their unexplained wealth case against the Vice President before calling Trillanes to the witness stand.

It was a peculiar week of the trial at the Senate, though, marred by a sudden cancellation of a trial day, deferment of the presentation of the AMLC witness, and lead prosecutor Jinky Luistro’s abrupt withdrawal of Trillanes’ name from its lineup, to the surprise of even some of her colleagues in the panel, based on our candid conversations with them.

Letting go of Trillanes has its pros and cons for the prosecution and even the former senator. It’s a risky move to present a witness who has a fraught history with senator-judges, although his testimony would have been potentially explosive and highly interesting to the general public.

For Trillanes, a court appearance may have limited what he could actually say due to — as he points out — the constant objections by the defense team. He argued the objections were unnecessary and could have been stopped by Escudero himself.

“If the person presiding over that were competent, the presentation of evidence should be liberal. Because what you want is the truth. This isn’t a criminal trial where someone gets sent to jail,” Trillanes said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Dive into Spanish cinema (and more) with this year’s ‘Película>Pelikula’ lineup
World.content:
No Spanish fluency required! Find your next watch based on your mood, interests, and the kind of story you want to see

You know that feeling when you’re itching to watch a movie, but end up spending 30 minutes scrolling through your streaming platform instead? Now, imagine having 23 movies to choose from – in the cinema, on top of that.

Welcome to PELÍCULA>PELIKULA, a celebration of the 25 years of the Manila Spanish Film Festival. This year’s edition brings together films from Spain, Latin America, and the Philippines that range from dramas and documentaries to animation, comedy, and shorts.

Running October 4 to 11, you can catch the (free!) screenings at Instituto Cervantes Intramuros on October 4 and Power Plant Cinema 2 from October 5 to 11. Films are shown in their original languages and with English subtitles.

If 23 titles feel like homework, here’s your cheat sheet: pick a film based on what you’re in the mood for.

If you want something introspective

Start with Los domingos (2025), a Spanish drama directed by Alauda Ruiz de Azúa. The film follows 17-year-old Ainara, whose life and beliefs are thrown into question, making it a good pick if you like coming-of-age stories that leave you with something to think about after the credits.

The film is also one of the most recognized titles in this year’s lineup, earning the most nominations at Spain’s 40th Goya Awards.

Play Video

Another option is Maspalomas (2025), which explores identity, aging, and the possibility of starting over. The film is part of the festival’s Premios Goya on Tour, a special selection of seven recent Spanish productions presented in partnership with the Spanish Film Academy.

If you want a friendship story

The Room Next Door (La habitación de al lado) follows Ingrid and Martha, two old friends who reconnect after years apart. As they spend time together, they find themselves confronting illness, complicated relationships, and difficult choices.

Directed by Pedro Almodóvar, the film stars Julianne Moore and Tilda Swinton and is part of the festival’s Goya-focused selection. And if you’ve never seen an Almodóvar film before, this could be a good place to start.

Play Video

If you want something intense

For a more visceral movie night, try Sirāt, directed by Oliver Laxe.

The film follows a father and his son as they search for the son’s missing sister in Morocco, eventually becoming involved with a group of ravers traveling through the desert. It is one of the seven Goya titles in the festival and was among the most-nominated films at the 40th Goya Awards.

If that darker mood is what you’re after, keep going with Los Tigres, directed by Alberto Rodríguez, another Goya selection.

Play Video

If you’re an animation fan

L’Olívia i el terratrèmol invisible (Olivia and the Invisible Earthquake) brings 12-year-old Olivia into a new neighborhood after her family is forced to leave their home. With the help of friends and a little adventure, she learns to navigate a major change in her life.

For a story filled with action and fantasy, Gigantes: una aventura extraordinaria brings three friends together on a mission to save their town from a devastating storm.

Both are part of La Previa, a four-film marathon kicking off on October 4 at Instituto Cervantes Intramuros, alongside Mensaje en una botella and Mariposas negras.

Play Video

If you want to explore Latin American stories

PELÍCULA>PELIKULA, by the way, isn’t limited to Spain. The lineup also includes Brazil’s Cyclone, Argentina’s Mensaje en una botella, Costa Rica’s Tengo sueños eléctricos, and Peru’s Vino la noche.

If you want to explore Spanish-language cinema from different countries, cultures, and perspectives, these are worth checking out.

Play Video

If you want to support Filipino and international short films

Don’t skip “Encuentros en el cine: En corto”, the festival’s showcase of five short films from the Philippines, Chile, Spain, and Mexico.

The Filipino shorts in the roster include Agapito, a film following bowling alley pin setters that’s being campaigned for Oscars 2027 consideration, and Elenita, Elena, Elaine, a visually experimental short that was previously screened at this year’s Cinemalaya. The program also includes Chile’s Voz de trompeta, Spain’s Gilbert, and Mexico’s ¡Abre las piernas!

The shorts screen on October 11 at 5 pm, offering a mix of Filipino and international perspectives.

Play Video

And if you just want to pick something randomly…

That works, too.

From family and friendship to identity, migration, history, adventure, and more, ‘Película>Pelikula’ has plenty of stories to discover. You don’t need to speak Spanish to enjoy Spanish cinema.

Check the full schedule on Instituto Cervantes de Manila’s Facebook page, and see where your chosen film takes you. – Rappler.com

This piece was written by Rappler volunteer Betina Andrea Santiago. Betina is a visual storyteller whose work centers on childhood nostalgia and pressing social realities. She enjoys exploring how visual media can drive empathy and is eager to use cinema to spark meaningful dialogue. A graduating Film major from the University of the Philippines Diliman, she aims to produce human-centered stories that give voice to everyday communities.

World.title: Verdict on Sara Duterte may be out December 16 — Senate court spokesman
World.content:
NOT ENEMY. Senate impeachment court spokesman Reginald Tongol urges House prosecutors to focus their energy on building up their case.

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court may issue its verdict in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte as early as December 16, spokesperson Reginald Tongol said Friday, October 2.

In a virtual press briefing, Tongol said the trial remains “aggressively” ahead of schedule despite the suspension of proceedings, and that the court could finish the case before the Senate goes on its holiday recess.

The court cut short the hearing on Thursday, October 1, and suspended the proceedings slated for October 2, after granting the defense counsel’s request to defer the testimony of Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura over confidentiality issues.

The trial resumes on Monday, October 5, with Buenaventura taking the witness stand.

According to Tongol, the prosecution’s decision to drop some of its witnesses has expedited the proceedings, saving the court 27 trial days. He also said the House prosecution panel is expected to finish presenting its witnesses on Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth by next week.

If the prosecution formally drops the bribery charges against Duterte, it may proceed with its formal offer of exhibits. The defense will then be asked to comment on the prosecution’s formal offer before presenting its own witnesses.

The defense has been allocated 30 trial days for its presentation of witnesses. Tongol said that if the defense uses all 30 days, the senator-judges could issue their verdict by December 16.

“If the defense consumes all 30 days they requested, then the verdict may come by December 16,” Tongol said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Under the pre-trial order, the prosecution listed 57 witnesses to be presented in 62 trial days. The defense panel said it will present 45 witnesses in 30 trial days. – Rappler.com

World.title: Progella, Pagara turn back China for PH’s maiden Asian Games beach volleyball medal
World.content:
DUO. Beach volleyball players Khylem Progella and Sofiah Pagara of the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.

Khylem Harl Progella and Sofiah Shanine Pagara complete a thrilling come-from-behind win over China to give the Philippines its first-ever beach volleyball medal in the Asian Games

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines captured a breakthrough Asian Games medal in beach volleyball as the duo of Khylem Harl Progella and Sofiah Shanine Pagara escaped with a bronze on Friday, October 2.

Progella and Pagara completed a thrilling come-from-behind 13-21, 23-21, 15-13 win over China’s Cao Shuting and Don Jie in the battle for bronze at the Hekinan Ryokuchi Beach Court in Japan.

Only in their early 20s, the Alas Pilipinas duo displayed steely resolve against their older Chinese foes, bouncing back from a first-set blowout and saving match point en route to giving the country its first medal in the sport, which debuted in the Asian Games in 1998.

The Philippines teetered on the brink of defeat when China grabbed a 20-19 lead in the second set, but Pagara scored on a drop shot that knotted the score and sparked a 4-1 run that sent the match into a decider.

China once again led 12-11 in the third set, only to fall short again as Progella and Pagara clinched four of the next five points to nail the bronze.

Progella, 20, and Pagara, 20, redeemed themselves after kissing their golden aspirations goodbye following a straight-sets defeat to Thailand in the semifinals.

That marked the Filipinas’ only loss as they went unbeaten in the preliminary round with a 3-0 record, swept Hong Kong in the round of 16, and edged top seed Japan in the semifinals.

Earlier in the tournament, Alas Pilipinas’ other beach volleyball tandem of Sisi Rondina and Bernadeth Pons crashed out of the quarterfinals.

Rondina and Pons, the reigning Southeast Asian Games champion, absorbed a narrow 21-17, 12-21, 15-13 loss to Thailand’s Taravadee Naraphornrapat and Worapeerachayakorn Kongphopsarutawadee on Wednesday, September 30. – Rappler.com

World.title: Linking Sara Duterte to China: What Trillanes’ testimony would have been about
World.content:
SONNY. Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV files cyberlibel and perjury complaints against lawyer Levito Baligod and 18 'ex-Marines' who accused him of bribery schemes, at the Department of Justice on March 5, 2026.

Trillanes claims that the 'Chinese government and corporations' sent hundreds of millions of pesos to companies or organizations associated with Vice President Duterte

MANILA, Philippines – Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV alleged on Friday, October 2, that entities tied to Vice President Sara Duterte received hundreds of millions of pesos in funds from the “Chinese government and corporations.”

Trillanes made the charges against the Vice President in his press conference after he was unceremoniously dropped from the prosecution’s lineup of witnesses in the impeachment trial.

The former senator said that Cale88, a food company, received P319 million in cash remittances from the Chinese government. Cale88 was founded by Duterte’s husband Mans Carpio, whose name appears in Duterte’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN).

Trillanes did not provide documents to back up his claim, but said they will be revealed in the coming days.

“You’d be shocked by this. She is the Vice President. There are national security implications, and that’s prohibited. You cannot accept [something] from a foreign government, especially [if you are] a high-ranking official,” Trillanes said.

Play Video

He raised supposed red flags in the operations of the company, from a low monthly electricity bill that doesn’t match the operations of a corporation, to its meager cash balance despite millions of pesos in sales.

Trillanes also claimed that China donated P150 million to Tapang at Malasakit Alliance for the Philippines, an entity whose board of trustees purportedly include the Vice President and Taguig Mayor Lani Cayetano, wife of trial senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano.

Rappler has reached out to Duterte’s spokesperson Paolo Panelo for comment, but we have yet to receive a response. This story will be updated once we do.

Companies linked to Sara Duterte

Trillanes’ other allegations focused on the corporate records of companies linked to Duterte.

He said the SEC records of Timesquare Bee Foods and later Gencorp contained the allegedly fictitious name Ang Hai Peng. That person has no birth, marriage, and death certificates, no tax identification number, and no passport.

He noted that the foreign name later vanished from SEC records and was replaced by the new controlling entity JTC Group of Companies, owned by the Dutertes’ business partner Jaime T. Cruz. Cruz was a special envoy to China when Rodrigo Duterte was president.

Trillanes claimed that Cruz and Ang incidentally share the same birthday.

“They are one person. I am one hundred percent person that [Ang Hai Peng] is nonexistent,” he said.

Trillanes also flagged the Vice President’s supposed undeclared time deposits in her SALN. Bank records obtained by Trillanes showed that Duterte’s peso time deposits ballooned from P53 million in 2007 to P94 million in 2009, yet her declared cash on hand and in bank remained at P2 million.

The former lawmaker also rehashed previous allegations that the Duterte family received P181 million from businessman and alleged drug lord Sammy Uy.

Dropped as a witness

The prosecution team was supposed to call Trillanes to the witness stand, but later abandoned the plan without providing a clear reason. Our sources said some prosecutors were caught off-guard and were in the dark when lead prosecutor Jinky Luistro made the surprise announcement at impeachment court.

Trillanes said his decision to withdraw was made to relieve the prosecution of the pressure it was facing, but he declined to explicitly identify the individual behind the supposed pressure. When asked about it on Friday, he sidestepped the question and took a swipe at presiding officer Chiz Escudero.

“You should have asked him: why did the presiding officer not issue a subpoena [to me]?” Trillanes said of Escudero.

Escudero previously suggested to the prosecution that the Anti-Money Laundering Council and the bank witnesses be presented first before Trillanes. – Rappler.com

World.title: Carlo Paalam takes home Asian Games silver after narrow loss to home bet
World.content:
FIGHT. Boxer Carlo Paalam in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.

Carlo Paalam falls short of becoming the first Filipino boxer to win an Asian Games gold medal since 2010 as he absorbs a split decision loss to home bet Rui Yamaguchi of Japan in the men's 55kg final

MANILA, Philippines – Carlo Paalam came oh-so-close to ending the Philippines’ 16-year drought for a boxing gold medal in the Asian Games.

Paalam settled for silver in the men’s 55kg division following a split-decision loss to home bet Rui Yamaguchi of Japan in the final at the Nishio Gymnasium on Friday, October 2.

Yamaguchi clinched the first two rounds as he earned the nod of three of the five judges by scores of 29-28, 29-28, 29-28, with the other two scoring it 30-27, 29-28 in favor of Paalam.

The defeat prevented the Olympic silver medalist from becoming the first Filipino boxer to rule in the Asian Games since Rey Saludar won the men’s 52kg crown in the 2010 Guangzhou, China, edition.

Paalam unanimously won the third and final round, but that hardly changed the outcome as Yamaguchi — the reigning Asian champion — pulled through for the gold.

The pride of Cagayan de Oro suffered the same fate as fellow Olympic medalist Eumir Marcial, who fell short of the men’s 80kg title in the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China, after a contentious unanimous decision loss to home fighter Tuohetaerbieke Tanglatihan.

Still, Paalam eclipsed his bronze finish in 2018 in Jakarta, Indonesia, where he competed in the 49kg class.

The 28-year-old also saved the Philippines from what could have been its first-ever medal-less campaign in Asian Games boxing after teammates Nesthy Petecio, Aira Villegas, Junmilardo Ogayre, Norlan Petecio, and Riza Pasuit all suffered exits.

Paalam assured himself of a medal by edging China’s Zhang Jiamao in the quarterfinals, then advanced to the gold-medal bout by scraping past reigning world champion Makhmud Sabyrkhan of Kazakhstan in the semifinals. – Rappler.com

World.title: [In This Economy] The nothing burger that is the Maharlika Investment Fund
World.content:
While Maharlika is earning money, its reliance on short-term placements and investments in established businesses leaves the promised additional development benefits unclear

At least some Filipinos must be wondering: whatever happened to the Maharlika Investment Fund, which is being managed by the Maharlika Investment Corporation (MIC)?

Well, we know for a fact that the three-year term of MIC’s first president, Rafael “Joel” Consing Jr., is nearly up. It’s been reported that Finance Undersecretary Ma. Angela “Angel” Ignacio is being considered to succeed Consing. The possible change has been linked to supposed dissatisfaction with the fund’s performance (aside from Consing’s reported health issues).

Recall that when President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed the fund into law on July 18, 2023, then-finance secretary Benjamin Diokno called it a “game-changing measure.” We were promised faster infrastructure development, more foreign investment, and high-quality jobs. But how much of that promise has materialized?

Where the money went

According to MIC’s unaudited financial disclosure for the first half of 2026, cumulative deployed capital had reached P24.7 billion by June 30. That’s only about a third of the P75 billion originally contributed by the Land Bank of the Philippines and the Development Bank of the Philippines.

MIC still held P53 billion in cash and cash equivalents, down from P71.1 billion at end-2025. In addition, another P50 billion subscribed by the national government remained unreleased.

The largest recent investment was a P15-billion short-term loan to Petron to finance fuel imports and operating needs, against the backdrop of the US–Iran war and the global oil shock this year. MIC says the loan supports fuel security and carries prevailing interest rates.

That could be useful during an energy crisis, but exactly what financing gap required Maharlika’s involvement? Petron already has other funding arrangements, as the MIC itself acknowledges. The public deserves evidence of the additional fuel supplies or other benefits enabled by this particular loan.

Before this, MIC also acquired additional shares of port operator Asian Terminals in the first half of 2026. Buying shares from existing owners gives Maharlika a claim on future profits. The transaction itself doesn’t finance the construction of new ports, however, and any subsequent improvements in capacity or logistics need to be demonstrated separately.

Meanwhile, MIC exited its short-term financing of Makilala Mining on June 5 by transferring the loan to Equinaire Holdings. MIC reported a 12.5% net annualized return in dollars or approximately 25% in pesos. That deserves credit, although the annualized figures should not be mistaken for the percentage earned over the actual holding period.

Then there’s the much-publicized grid deal announced in January 2025. The proposed major investment through Synergy Grid and Development Philippines, which holds an indirect interest in the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines, remained delayed.

Other initiatives are still underway. A July agreement with the Philippine National Oil Company, for instance, covers exploring a petroleum storage project in Bataan targeted for 2028.

What the profits show

To its credit, Maharlika seems somewhat profitable. MIC reported P1.24 billion in net income for the first half of 2026 and separately announced a P1.376-billion dividend remittance to the national government in June.

But if you dive deeper, you’ll see that the income comes from mainly cash and short-term placements that generated P1.14 billion in interest. Funds awaiting investment were placed primarily with government financial institutions.

In short, a large amount of money taken from state banks is just earning interest through placements primarily with state financial institutions.

Sure, this preserves liquidity or the ability to access money quickly — at least while deals are evaluated. But earning deposit interest hardly strengthens the rational of why we had to have Maharlika in the first place. It’s not exactly the promised game-changer.

Also, the headline P2.09 billion in portfolio returns includes P1.446 billion in unrealized gains, or increases in investment values that have not been realized through a sale. That’s roughly 69% of the total. Those gains can easily reverse when prices fall.

Running the institution also costs money, of course: operating expenses reached P170.8 million in the first half of 2026, including P111.8 million for professional services. Those costs need to be justified by returns and public benefits beyond what existing institutions could deliver.

Did you know that the president and CEO of MIC earns a salary of P2.5 million per month? Is it worth it, given MIC’s performance? And exactly how much are the other officials and directors earning?

The original problem

Of course, investment institutions take time to build. Pressuring managers to spend faster could produce worse or overly risky deals, and the unreleased government contribution reflects funding processes beyond MIC’s sole control.

But this brings us to Maharlika’s original problems. Recall that it didn’t create an extra P75 billion of national wealth or “surplus.” What it did, instead, was merely transfer resources from existing public institutions into a new investment vehicle. Those resources have alternative uses, including supporting the state banks’ development lending.

The value of the best forgone alternative is what economists like me call “opportunity cost.” Maharlika’s returns must be assessed against that opportunity cost, with allowance for the risks taken and the expense of running the fund.

Back in June 2023, 21 faculty members of the University of the Philippines School of Economics, myself included, published “Maharlika Investment Fund: Still beyond repair.” We questioned the fund’s unclear rationale, its competing financial and development objectives, and whether it could attract enough additional investment to justify the resources committed to it.

More than three years later, our concerns seem to be borne out. While Maharlika is earning money, its reliance on short-term placements and investments in established businesses leaves the promised additional development benefits unclear.

Likewise, the government must show what additional development Maharlika enables. How much private capital joined projects because of its involvement? Which investments would otherwise have lacked financing? What measurable improvements have reached consumers and communities?

At the very least, Congress should require a public accounting of each investment’s cost, realized earnings, risks, and development results. Large acquisitions and loans should also come with a clear explanation of why existing banks or government agencies couldn’t achieve the same objectives more effectively.

In conclusion, more than three years on, the Maharlika Investment Fund has turned out to be a nothing burger. I’m afraid that an upcoming change in leadership won’t resolve many of its fundamental problems. But as the current administration winds down, expect President Marcos to harp on its purported successes anyway. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

World.title: Tokayev Calls for Responsible AI Development, Stronger Technology Cooperation at AI & Digital Bridge 2026
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for responsible artificial intelligence development, stronger international technology cooperation and greater support for innovation as Kazakhstan advances its transition to a digital economy.

Speaking at the AI & Digital Bridge 2026 international forum on Oct. 1, Tokayev said AI is rapidly transforming industry, finance, education, science and public administration, making responsible development and effective regulation increasingly important, reported Akorda.

Kazakhstan’s digital transformation

Tokayev said Kazakhstan is creating the conditions for a fully digital state. Last year, the country’s IT services exports exceeded $1 billion, while Kazakh digital solutions are used in more than 100 countries.

He proposed compiling a list of industrial AI challenges based on real economic needs and launching an AI Challenge involving Kazakh and international teams. The most effective solutions would subsequently be introduced into production.

“If we strive to build a strong technological foundation for our country, we must provide real support to innovative startup companies and implement advanced projects,” Tokayev said.

Balanced AI regulation

Tokayev highlighted the need for a balanced, risk-based approach to AI regulation. Kazakhstan has already established a legal framework for digital transformation, including the Law on Artificial Intelligence and the Digital Code.

“We must not regulate this sphere to such an extent that promising teams, developments and capital begin to leave for other jurisdictions,” he said.

According to Tokayev, stricter requirements should apply where AI affects security, citizens’ rights and vital interests, while regulation should not unnecessarily constrain innovation.

Human capital and responsible AI

Tokayev stressed that scientists, engineers and entrepreneurs must support technological development. He identified the recently opened Qazaq AI Research University (QAIRU) as an important institution for developing Kazakhstan’s scientific and engineering capacity.

He also emphasized that AI should complement, not replace, human intellectual abilities.

“Artificial intelligence is not a replacement for human intellectual abilities, but only an auxiliary tool in the process of learning and cognition,” Tokayev said.

President Tokayev called for responsible use of AI, citing cybersecurity, data protection, information reliability, algorithmic transparency and accountability among the key issues requiring attention.

“Artificial intelligence should not create new dividing lines. Technological barriers will only increase the gap between countries and slow our development,” he said.

Tokayev concluded that Kazakhstan has established a foundation for a new technology-driven economy and called for international cooperation in research, investment, technology and talent development.

World.title: Why Dimash in Jakarta Matters for Kazakhstan
World.content:
A concert can fill a venue, but some concerts can do more. If a global cultural figure such as Dimash Qudaibergen were to take the stage in Jakarta, the opportunity for Kazakhstan could extend well beyond the venue itself.

Dimash has an international audience that crosses borders. Bringing him to Jakarta can connect that global audience with Indonesia, while creating a meeting point for Dears from different countries. For some of these audiences, Jakarta may be more than a concert destination: it can become their first meaningful encounter with Indonesia—and, through Dimash, with Kazakhstan.

That is what makes the Jakarta opportunity interesting for Kazakhstan. It is not simply about bringing an artist to Indonesia, but about leveraging the attention around him to create new connections with Kazakhstan’s culture, tourism and wider economic opportunities.

The strategic question is not how many people will attend the concert, but what Kazakhstan can build around the attention it creates—and what Indonesia can enable beyond the concert itself.

The platform and its ecosystem

As a platform, Indonesia is particularly relevant because of the scale of its domestic market and its regional connections. It provides access to a large population and a network of audiences, businesses and institutions, while Jakarta offers an entry point to Southeast Asia.

Indonesia also has an established MICE and international events ecosystem, with capacity to host major international artists in stadiums of up to 80,000 people. Its MICE infrastructure and supporting services can accommodate audiences from different countries and turn an international concert into a broader experience.

Within this ecosystem, Dimash provides the central attraction and brings an established international audience. Kazakhstan’s public and cultural institutions can use the attention to introduce the country, while businesses and creative industries can explore opportunities beyond the performance.

The opportunity is not to turn the concert into a trade fair, but to be present when attention is concentrated. Dimash creates the attention, Indonesia provides the platform, and the ecosystem around the concert can determine how far that opportunity travels.

More than a stage: Indonesia as a destination

For an international audience, travelling to Indonesia can become part of the concert experience. Its diverse destinations and experiences allow Dears to combine the concert with more than the performance. The platform therefore extends beyond the venue—from travel and accommodation to experiencing Indonesia.

For Kazakhstan, this creates an opportunity. Indonesia hosts the concert and provides the destination ecosystem around it, making it easier and more appealing for international Dears to travel to see Dimash. Dimash gives people a reason to come; Indonesia gives them reasons to stay and explore.

What Kazakhstan can leverage

Dimash gives Kazakhstan something it cannot easily create: a human connection with an international audience. A Jakarta performance can provide an organic entry point for Kazakhstan’s culture and identity, making the country more visible through his music and artistic expression. The opportunity is not to turn the concert into a diplomatic event, but to use the attention it creates as an entry point for greater visibility and access to Kazakhstan.

The connection can work in both directions. For Indonesian audiences, Kazakhstan offers something distinctive: a four-season destination within Asia. In a tropical country accustomed to two seasons, mountains, snow and winter landscapes have traditionally been associated with Europe. Kazakhstan offers a different possibility—an experience that feels culturally distinctive and closer to home.

Kazakhstan has been gaining attention among Indonesian travellers, with its visa-free access and distinctive seasonal, cultural and historical attractions drawing interest from the travel industry. In December 2025, the Kazakhstan Embassy in Jakarta and ASITA brought together more than 40 Indonesian travel companies, airlines and business representatives to explore ways to increase tourist flows to Kazakhstan.

Dimash could add another layer to this emerging connection. He can introduce Kazakhstan to more Indonesian audiences through a cultural relationship they already understand, while the country offers something different from the Indonesia they know.

The opportunity extends beyond tourism. Kazakhstan can introduce its contemporary identity through its creative and cultural industries. The international audience surrounding the event can also create space for cultural exchange and new connections between the two countries.

Finally, Jakarta offers Kazakhstan a way to extend its reach beyond the Indonesian market. As a major regional centre, it brings together audiences and stakeholders from across the region. A cultural presence in Jakarta can therefore give Kazakhstan wider regional visibility and create connections beyond Indonesia.

The strategic value of Indonesia is that it can provide a platform from which Kazakhstan can extend cultural visibility, tourism interest, creative connections and regional engagement.

These opportunities, however, depend not only on what Kazakhstan can leverage, but also on how Dimash and his management build a lasting connection with the Indonesian audience.

An investment in the Indonesian market

For Dimash and his management, Indonesia is not simply an established market. Building a stronger presence in a country of Indonesia’s scale requires an investment in audience development.

That investment should not be measured only by the immediate return from one concert. A major presence can introduce Dimash to audiences who may not yet know him while mobilising the existing international community. By connecting with Indonesian artists, influencers and other local voices with established audiences, Dimash and his management can strengthen their initial presence in the Indonesian market.

The event can therefore serve not only as a performance but as a starting point for building a stronger, longer-term relationship with the Indonesian audience. This is ultimately why bringing Dimash to Jakarta matters: the value of the opportunity lies not only in the concert itself, but in the platform that the concert can activate.

The value lies in what happens around the stage: new audiences discovering Kazakhstan, international Dears experiencing Indonesia, cultural and economic connections being created, and new regional connections. Dimash can open the door, but Kazakhstan can decide what lies beyond it. The concert may last one night. The connections created through the platform can travel much further.

The author is Imbuh Sulistyarini, a lecturer at the Department of Management, Faculty of Economics and Business, Universitas Indonesia (FEB UI).

World.title: CAMCA Forum in Baku Prioritizes Connectivity and Economic Integration
World.content:
BAKU – Regional connectivity, shifting geopolitical dynamics and the forces shaping Central Asia, Mongolia, the Caucasus and Afghanistan were among the key themes on the first day of the CAMCA Regional Forum, which kicked off in Baku on Oct. 1.

The forum opened with a historical perspective from Dr. Frederick Starr, the chairman of Central Asia-Caucasus Institute, who emphasized the role of people in driving greater interconnection across the region.

Cooperation in transport, trade, tourism and business has expanded significantly, while stronger regional institutions are needed to support this growing connectivity, Starr said.

Regional focus

The importance of connectivity was underscored by Azerbaijan’s Minister of Economy Mikayil Jabbarov, who described Central Asia as one of Azerbaijan’s most dynamically growing trading partners over the past five years.

The Middle Corridor, linking Central Asia and the South Caucasus with markets in Europe and Asia, was a major focus of discussion. A 2023 World Bank assessment found that a combination of investments and efficiency measures could triple trade flows along the route and halve travel times by 2030.

“For us, the next stage of regional integration should go beyond moving goods across borders. We should increasingly produce together, building regional value chains in sectors where our economies have complemented strengths and our major companies and financial institutions are already working in and present at markets of each other. We believe that confidence is measured by delivery, not by signatures,” said Jabbarov.

He noted that investments in Middle Corridor infrastructure serve as evidence of the region’s commitment to long-term development. Plans for green energy and the Black sea cable could also strengthen regional linkages.

“Peace is a very clear economic asset,” said Jabbarov. “Capitalization of the entire region and each country has grown significantly as a result of this process turning regional connectivity into something that can benefit the whole South Caucasus and Central Asian region because a more connected region is a more stable one,” he added.

A broader geopolitical perspective came from Sadiq Safoev, the First Deputy Chairman of the Senate of Uzbekistan’s Oliy Majlis, who said that Central Asia’s position at a crossroads was not a new phenomenon. “For Central Asia, perhaps, it’s a destiny to be at a crossroads,” he said, while arguing that the wider world is also undergoing a period of profound change.

Safoev said the region could transform from a landlocked into a “land linked” one as new transport and economic connections emerge.

At the same time, the speaker pointed to fragmentation in different parts of the world and said regional forces could encourage greater cooperation within Central Asia.

CAMCA network expands

The debates on transformation were followed by a focus on the people and networks behind these changes.

“We see the CAMCA network representatives are in the midst, drivers, not just observers, but drivers of this very change that we are seeing in our region today,” said Svante Cornell, director of the Central Asia-Caucasus Institute.

The CAMCA network itself is also expanding. Managing director Tamar Kekenadze announced plans to host the next CAMCA forum in Uzbekistan in June 2027.

“Our number has increased to 350 now. We created this forum decades ago so that we continue creating friendships, networks, among not only these 10 countries, but beyond, because every one of you who are here today, we know that you care about this region and about the shared future of this region,” she said.

Kekenadze also shared plans to launch a CAMCA TV channel.

Another development highlighted at the forum was the launch of the CAMCA Talking, a magazine founded by network members Aizhan Zhantayeva, Fidan Huseynli and Laura Demessinova.

The magazine provides a platform for voices from the CAMCA region to discuss transformations while honoring the people and communities driving change.

World.title: Kazakhstan Celebrates 35 Years Since Aubakirov Made Space History
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan marks the 35th anniversary of Toktar Aubakirov’s historic spaceflight on Oct. 2. His mission made him the first Kazakh to travel into space, marking a significant milestone in the country’s space history.

In 1991, Aubakirov launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard the Soyuz TM-13 spacecraft with Soviet cosmonaut Alexander Volkov and Austrian researcher Franz Viehböck. The crew traveled to the Mir space station, where Aubakirov spent around a week before returning to Earth on Oct. 10.

The mission was notable both politically and technically. For Austria and Kazakhstan, it marked their first national representatives’ journey into space. The crew also had an unusual composition, with Volkov serving as commander and Aubakirov and Viehböck as research cosmonauts.

Aubakirov’s preparation for the mission took around five months, drawing on his experience as a test pilot.

From May 20 to July 10, 1991, he trained under Kazakhstan’s visiting expedition program as a research cosmonaut alongside Valery Korzun and Alexander Alexandrov for a mission planned for November. However, shortages of launch vehicles and spacecraft, along with efforts to reduce costs, led to changes in the mission plan. Aubakirov was included in the Soviet-Austrian crew for the Austromir-91 program as a research cosmonaut.

During the mission, Aubakirov conducted five scientific experiments. The crew studied sandstorms in the Aral Sea region and carried out medical and biological research. They also examined the behavior of metal melts under microgravity, with samples returned to Earth for further study.

The mission also included testing specialized food products developed for spaceflight, including freeze-dried versions of traditional Kazakh foods such as airan, irimshik and meat.

Aubakirov later recalled that he had initially been reluctant to accept an offer to become a cosmonaut. He was first approached about a spaceflight in 1985 but declined because he wanted to continue his work as a test pilot. He accepted the offer in 1991.

Recalling the launch of Soyuz TM-13, Aubakirov described seeing Earth from orbit as one of the mission’s most memorable moments.

“I saw the Earth. We were leaving her, and she was leaving us. It was an indescribable sight. I was amazed by such beauty. Our Earth is indescribably beautiful,” he said.

Aubakirov’s flight came during a period of major political change. Kazakhstan declared its independence from the Soviet Union on Dec. 16, 1991, more than two months after the mission. Earlier, on Aug. 31, 1991, Kazakhstan declared the Baikonur Cosmodrome and the surrounding territory its property. The launch also coincided with steps to establish Kazakhstan’s own national space institutions.

From Mir to new space research

More than three decades later, Aubakirov continues to take part in discussions about Kazakhstan’s space research.

In 2025, he visited the National Space Center in Astana for the completion of the SANA-1 project, Kazakhstan’s first long-duration crew-isolation experiment designed to simulate conditions of a space mission.

The experiment examined the physiological, cognitive and emotional adaptation of an all-female engineering crew.

During the visit, Aubakirov reflected on the broader role of space research and its connection to Kazakhstan’s future.

“Space, as a boundless, bottomless and endless expanse, offers great opportunities to study our past and, most importantly, our future,” he said.

Aubakirov highlighted that such projects demonstrate the scientific potential Kazakhstan can draw on as it develops its space and research capabilities.

World.title: Kazakhstan Ranks 55th in Global Index Measuring AI and Human Skills
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranked 55th out of 98 countries in the 2026 AI-Human Skills Synergy Index, presented as part of Coursera’s Global Skills Report 2026, reported the Ministry of Science and Higher Education’s press service.

The new index measures how actively learners develop artificial intelligence skills alongside human competencies needed to apply them effectively, including critical thinking, leadership, communication and complex problem-solving.

According to Coursera’s methodology, the index combines data on skills acquisition, the breadth of competencies studied and the extent to which AI skills are developed alongside human skills. It also incorporates data from the Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index, which assesses countries’ capacity to use AI based on factors including government policy, infrastructure, human capital and the development of the AI sector.

Commenting on Kazakhstan’s approach to AI education, Minister of Science and Higher Education Sayasat Nurbek highlighted the role of the national AI-Sana program.

“When Kazakhstan launched the national AI-Sana program, we understood that access to digital courses alone was not enough. For systemic change, it was important to create conditions in which acquired knowledge is integrated into the educational process and put into practice,” Nurbek said.

The minister said the program currently brings together 100 universities to implement courses, monitor results and regularly update content in response to the rapid development of AI technologies.

“At the same time, we pay particular attention to developing the digital and pedagogical competencies of teachers,” he said, adding that more than 1,200 educators have already learned modern online teaching methods and participated in the development of 35 original courses.

According to Nurbek, the approach aims not only to expand access to AI-related knowledge but also to prepare students for changing labor market requirements.

Kazakhstan’s result indicates continued interest among active digital learning users in both technical AI competencies and the human skills needed to apply them in practice. Such skills are becoming increasingly relevant as AI is incorporated into education, professional activities and everyday workplace tasks.

At the same time, the AI-Human Skills Synergy Index should be considered in the context of its methodology. Coursera’s data primarily reflects learning activity among platform users and does not directly measure the skill levels of a country’s entire population.

The result therefore provides an international measure of AI and human-skills development among participants in digital learning, while also indicating broader global trends in workforce competency development.

World.title: Nazarbayev University Moves Into Top 400 in World University Rankings
World.content:
ASTANA – Nazarbayev University has moved into the 376–400 group in the latest Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings, improving its position by another 100 places and retaining its top ranking among universities in Kazakhstan and Central Asia.

The university has risen by 200 positions over the past two years. It was ranked in the 501–600 group in 2024, moved to 401–500 in the following edition and has now entered the 376–400 range.

The latest edition of the THE rankings includes a record 2,297 universities from 118 countries and territories, 106 more institutions than the previous year. Against this larger field, Nazarbayev University moved from the top 23% of universities globally two years ago to the top 17%.

Research remains a key strength

THE evaluates universities across five areas: teaching, research environment, research quality, international outlook and industry engagement.

Nazarbayev University improved its performance across almost all of the areas in the latest ranking, with research quality remaining its strongest indicator. According to the university, its research performance is comparable with that of the University of Geneva, the University of Arizona and the University of Rochester.

“First of all, I would like to congratulate the entire NU community and Kazakhstan on this result. For the first time, a Kazakh university has reached this level in one of the leading global university rankings. This is an important achievement not only for our university, but also for the country’s higher education system,” NU President Waqar Ahmad said.

Kazakhstan is represented by 10 universities in the latest THE ranking. Among them are Asfendiyarov Kazakh National Medical University, ranked 1,201–1,400, Al-Farabi Kazakh National University and Satbayev University, both in the 1,401–1,600 group.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and UAE to Explore New CASA Rail Route to Pakistani Ports
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have agreed to jointly study a new railway route connecting Central Asia with Pakistan’s seaports, the Prime Minister’s press service reported on Sept. 30.

The transport ministries of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan and the UAE Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure signed a memorandum of understanding on cooperation under the CASA railway project.

The proposed Kazakhstan–Uzbekistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan (CASA) railway would create a new transport link between Central and South Asia, potentially opening additional opportunities for international freight, trade, logistics and investment cooperation.

Feasibility studies planned

Under the memorandum, the three countries intend to conduct technical and economic studies and analytical assessments of the project. They will also examine the feasibility of developing the required railway infrastructure and related facilities.

The initiative brings together the existing railway infrastructure and transit potential of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan with the UAE’s experience in transport infrastructure, logistics and large-scale investment projects.

The parties said the cooperation is intended to move the CASA project toward practical development and help determine the most suitable implementation mechanisms. They also discussed establishing a joint working group to comprehensively examine the project’s technical, economic and financial aspects and coordinate further steps.

World.title: Middle Corridor Investments Could Triple Trade, Add 2 Million Jobs by 2040, Report Finds
World.content:
ASTANA – Strategic investment in the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route could more than triple trade along the route, cut travel times in half and create two million additional jobs by 2040, according to a new report published by the World Bank on Sept. 28.

The route, also known as the Middle Corridor and referred to by the World Bank as the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, is emerging as an increasingly important trade link between Asia and Europe through Central Asia, the South Caucasus and Türkiye.

The route combines rail, road and shipping across the Caspian and Black seas, connecting countries along the corridor with one another and with wider global markets. Its position also gives it a broader role as an overland link between East Asia and Europe.

The report identifies nine countries along the route: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Türkiye, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, with a combined population of nearly 200 million people. Armenia is included even though it is not yet directly connected to the corridor, as physical links are expected to be developed in the 2030s, within the report’s 2023-2040 timeframe.

Key findings

The report projects that stronger transport links could raise GDP across the nine countries along the corridor by 3.3%. This is equal to $58 billion at current levels of economic activity, as well as boost employment by 2.9%.

It identifies 16 priority infrastructure projects worth a combined $25.1 billion. Three-quarters are already underway or expected to begin soon, suggesting that a lack of infrastructure may no longer be the corridor’s biggest long-term constraint.

Kazakhstan accounts for several of the 16 priority projects identified in the report. They include the $1.4 billion Moiynty-Kyrgyz railway line, the $1.2 billion Bakhty-Ayagoz railway and border crossing, the $550 million Darbaza-Maktaaral railway, a $315 million Almaty bypass line, a $310 million expansion of Aktau Port and a $212 million upgrade of the Altynkol-Zhetigen railway. Together, the projects are intended to expand rail capacity, ease bottlenecks around major hubs and strengthen Kazakhstan’s connections to both the Caspian Sea and markets to the east and south.

An additional $30 billion will be required for what the report describes as “enabling” investments. This includes better road and rail connections to local economies, logistics hubs and inland terminals that can speed up cargo movement. Investment is also needed in locomotives, railcars, cargo-handling equipment and digital systems to keep goods moving efficiently across the network.

With major projects already moving forward, the harder challenge will increasingly be how efficiently the route is managed and how well countries coordinate operations across borders.

“Total trans-Caspian volumes are expected to increase by about 3.6 times, from 8.8 million tons in 2023 to 32.1 million tons by 2040. The Eastern gateway, consisting of the main entry and exit points along the corridor’s eastern flank, is projected to grow at a similar pace, increasing from 28.5 million tons to 105.7 million tons, and the Western gateway is expected to expand from 12.1 million tons to around 35.0 million tons over the same period,” said the report.

Beyond infrastructure

The report examines how stronger trade corridors can cut logistics costs, draw investment, improve productivity and create jobs. It assesses the economic potential of the Trans-Caspian route, identifies the main constraints limiting its performance and sets out recommendations for turning it into a stronger driver of regional growth.

The report indicates that if governments combine infrastructure spending with reforms to customs, logistics and other trade procedures, freight volumes could quadruple and travel times could fall by as much as two-thirds. Those gains would come from easing transport bottlenecks, making supply chains more reliable and expanding market access in the nine countries positioned along the route.

The stakes have grown as disruptions to global supply chains, geopolitical tensions and climate-related risks increase pressure on existing trade routes. Growing obstacles to trade across Eurasia have pushed the Middle Corridor higher on the policy agenda and accelerated investment by countries along the route, often with support from international financial institutions.

Many of the countries along the route are also major producers of energy, critical minerals, raw materials and food products.

A stronger route could therefore do more than carry transit cargo. The report notes it could help countries reduce their exposure to external disruptions while turning growing freight flows into domestic investment, business growth and jobs. Rising regional trade, particularly among developing economies, gives governments another reason to accelerate development of the Trans-Caspian route.

“The Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor can become a powerful driver for faster growth, economic diversification, poverty reduction, and expanded private investment for the countries along the corridor,” said World Bank Vice President for Europe and Central Asia Antonella Bassani.

From bulk cargo to containers

Immediate actions highlighted by experts cover expansion and modernization of railways, roads, ports, border crossings and inland logistics hubs along the route. The report emphasizes that is especially important because bulk commodities such as grain, fertilizer, construction materials and fuel account for 92% of freight currently crossing the Caspian Sea. For these goods, available capacity and low transport costs are critical.

The report stresses that the Middle Corridor’s biggest strategic challenge is to become a genuinely attractive route for container cargo, not just bulk goods.

“The most pressing, yet by its nature long-term, priority for the TCTC is to become a competitive, resilient option for containerized trade; this will require transformational changes to boost corridor performance,” reads the report.

Most of the investment is needed before 2030 to ease existing bottlenecks, the report says. Further upgrades will likely be required in the 2030s as new capacity constraints emerge.

Priority actions

The operational challenge is considerable. According to the report, depending on the route, a shipment traveling from origin to destination may cross four or five borders, change railway gauge twice, move between rail and ships up to four times and enter or leave customs transit systems up to 10 times.

Experts note the corridor also remains difficult to manage because responsibility is spread across a wide range of actors, including rail operators, shipping companies, ports, customs agencies and national and regional institutions. Differences in income levels, market integration and decision-making structures add another layer of complexity.

“Making this system work efficiently is among the most daunting development challenges in global logistics,” reads the report.

The World Bank proposes four broad steps to improve how the corridor is governed and operated.

One proposal is to replace fragmented paperwork systems with a shared digital platform where transport and trade data can be submitted once and used across the route. It also recommends closer integration between rail and Caspian shipping, potentially through a joint rail-and-shipping operator that could manage container traffic across both modes.

Another priority is stronger coordination among corridor countries so they can track delays, identify bottlenecks and respond to problems together. The report also says state-owned railways, ports and shipping companies need stronger governance and more commercial operating models to improve efficiency and financial performance.

“Realizing the corridor’s full potential will depend on practical improvements that make freight movement faster, more predictable, and easier to manage across borders,” said World Bank Regional Director of Infrastructure, Europe and Central Asia Charles Cormier.

He said better connected railways, ports, logistics hubs and digital systems, combined with stronger coordination among countries and operators, could make the corridor more competitive and strengthen its role in regional development.

Stakes of investing in the corridor are substantial as well as the benefits. The report describes the route for Central Asian countries as a “lifeline connection to global markets for all freight, as well as an enabler, in conjunction with complementary policies beyond transportation and logistics alone, of long-term economic diversification.”

Besides creating opportunities in transport, logistics services, the route also offers new channels for economic diversification, including via enabling new sectors, such as agro-processing, mining and extractives and minerals processing, light manufacturing, and digital logistics.

In that sense, the World Bank positions the Middle Corridor’s next phase as depending not simply on building more infrastructure, but on turning national railways, ports, border crossings and shipping services into a corridor that functions as a single, reliable trade system.

The World Bank’s earlier report on the Middle Corridor focused on Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, and Georgia to identify priority measures that can transform this multimodal rail and maritime corridor into a vital and dependable trade route.

The findings come against the backdrop of more than three decades of cooperation between Kazakhstan and the World Bank Group. Over 33 years, the bank has supported more than 50 projects in the country worth over $8 billion, including in transport, education, environmental protection, green technologies and digitalization, according to the Kazakh government.

World.title: ‘We will decide in the coming months’: Pashinyan on choosing model for Armenia’s new nuclear power plant
World.content:
Pashinyan on building a new nuclear power plant in Armenia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has announced a change in the government’s position on the technology and design of a new nuclear power plant.

“I have said dozens of times before that we do not need anything more [powerful] than a modular nuclear power plant. That was our position. But now we have to understand that a modular plant will most likely not be enough to meet our needs,” Pashinyan said.

He explained that the government changed its position because of the construction of AI factories. Armenia now needs to import electricity to meet their power requirements.

Discussions continue over which technology would best suit the new nuclear power plant. The Armenian government expects to make a decision on the issue by the end of 2027.

A day earlier, the prime minister met a delegation led by Alexey Likhachev, director general of the state-owned Rosatom corporation. They discussed proposals from the Russian side.

Armenia is currently working to extend the operating life of the Metsamor nuclear power plant until 2036. Russia has taken part in efforts to extend the plant’s operating life and modernise it throughout this period. The plant originally entered service in 1977.

At the same time, Yerevan is discussing the construction of a new nuclear power plant with several countries, including the US. The prime minister has repeatedly said in recent months that the nuclear power issue is not a geopolitical choice for Armenia: “We will choose the proposal that serves us best.”

Pashinyan does not rule out accepting the Russian proposal

Speaking about the upcoming decision on the technology for the new nuclear power plant, the prime minister stressed that before Armenia signed memorandums of understanding with the US on 8 August 2025, Armenia had a surplus of electricity.

“We had to think about where to direct this surplus energy. A year later, Armenia had become a country with an electricity deficit,” he said.

According to Nikol Pashinyan, this resulted from the construction of two AI factories in Armenia during that period:

“The point is that, given the scale of the investment projects already approved, Armenia has faced an electricity deficit. In other words, these projects are fully absorbing the surplus we have. So we need to decide what to do next.”

The prime minister said the government would make a decision in the coming months. Pashinyan also said that Armenia could accept the proposal put forward by Russia:

“It is quite possible that building a 1,000 MW plant will prove to be the most logical solution. However, I cannot say for certain at this stage because experts are still assessing the issue.”

“The unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW” — Likhachev

Rosatom director general Alexey Likhachev told journalists some details of Russia’s proposal after talks in Yerevan. Likhachev said Armenia would continue to rely on nuclear energy for decades to come. Russia therefore plans to “formulate the most competitive proposal” for building a new reactor unit in the coming months.

“And in our view, this unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW,” Likhachev said.

According to him, the proposal involves a VVER-1000 reactor, a pressurised water reactor with a capacity of 1,000 MW.

The head of Rosatom stressed that this proposal is “the best currently available on the global market”. He added that Rosatom has built and continues to build VVER reactors of this type in India and Iran:

“They combine very high economic efficiency, namely a low cost of electricity, with all the necessary Generation III+ safety systems.”

Details of talks with Rosatom director general in Yerevan

The Armenian prime minister’s office said Pashinyan and Likhachev discussed:

work to extend the operating life of the existing second reactor unit at the Armenian Nuclear Power Plant;

Russia’s proposals for building a new reactor unit.

At the same time, the prime minister told Likhachev that the Armenian government was continuing to consider proposals from other international partners.

Pashinyan stressed that the final decision would depend solely on economic considerations. These would include price, quality, safety, construction timelines and guarantees.

The statement also said Alexey Likhachev described cooperation with Armenian partners as constructive. The Rosatom chief also provided detailed information about the construction of not only large VVER reactors, but also small and medium-sized reactors.

Pashinyan on building a new nuclear power plant in Armenia

World.title: ‘Delicate issue’: how Abkhazia’s authorities are trying to ease situation of lawyer Irakli Bzhinava, arrested in Russia
World.content:
Abkhazia’s president, Badra Gunba, is discussing the fate of Abkhaz lawyer Irakli Bzhinava, who is being held in a Russian detention centre, with Moscow. Authorities have opened two criminal cases against him. Gunba says the issue requires a delicate approach.

At a meeting of the Consultative Council of political parties and civil society organisations, the president said Abkhaz authorities were working with their Russian counterparts on Bzhinava’s detention conditions. The foreign ministry and consular service are also providing the necessary support, including to his lawyers.

“State authorities are dealing with this issue. I personally discuss it with my colleagues through my own channels, and certain services are also involved,” the president said.

According to Gunba, the issue requires a delicate approach because it concerns another country’s laws. At the same time, he said, the Abkhaz side is not stepping back from the situation and continues to discuss it through various channels.

Irakli Bzhinava, who holds dual Abkhaz and Russian citizenship and lives in Russia, was detained on 5 February 2026 and has remained in pre-trial detention ever since.

According to the case materials, the authorities brought the charges over a social media post that Bzhinava published on 23 December 2022. The post concerned an agreement to transfer a famous state dacha in Abkhazia to Russia. Bzhinava criticised the agreement, arguing that it violated Abkhaz law.

Bzhinava initially faced charges of “criminal intent to make public calls for activities directed against the security of the Russian Federation”, which carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

However, in mid-September, Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a second criminal case against Bzhinava. The new charges accuse him of “publicly justifying the terrorist Shamil Basayev online” and carry a prison sentence of up to seven years.

Despite the more serious charges, Irakli Bzhinava was allowed to meet his mother for the first time in seven months in detention. According to civil society activist Kadir Argun, who is collecting signatures in support of Bzhinava, the meeting provided his family with “enormous support and moral strength during a difficult time”.

Irakli Bzhinava enjoys fairly broad support in Abkhazia, with local politicians and public figures regularly calling on the republic’s authorities to provide him with comprehensive assistance.

Abkhazia’s ombudswoman Anas Kishmaria has also formally appealed to her Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, asking her to help improve Bzhinava’s detention conditions and take personal oversight of the case.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Four Georgian citizens and people linked to country’s occupied regions hit by UK sanctions
World.content:
Georgian citizens under UK sanctions

The UK has announced a new package of sanctions against Russia, imposing restrictions on 31 individuals, organisations and vessels.

The UK has added four Georgian citizens to its sanctions list: journalist Nikoloz Mzhavanadze, who lives in Russia; pro-Russian businessman and Solidarity for Peace party chairman Mamuka Pipia; party member Giorgi Iremadze; and pro-Russian analyst Paata Abuladze. According to the British government, the sanctions target these individuals for spreading Kremlin disinformation.

The sanctions list also includes three people linked to Georgia’s occupied regions of Abkhazia and so-called South Ossetia. They are Marat Kambolov, the so-called president of the occupied Tskhinvali region; his predecessor Alan Gagloev; and Russian political strategist Sergei Tolmachev.

Media reports say Sergei Tolmachev helped run the election campaign of Badra Gunba, the so-called president of occupied Abkhazia.

According to the UK government, the sanctions target actions that threaten Ukraine’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence.

“Russia’s aggression against Ukraine forms part of a broader pattern of disregard for the sovereignty, territorial integrity and internationally recognised borders of neighbouring states. This includes Russia’s ongoing occupation of the Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

The UK condemns Russia’s attempts to cement its illegal control over Georgia’s occupied regions, including through the so-called ‘presidential elections’ held in South Ossetia on 18 September and subsequent steps towards de facto annexation.

The UK firmly supports Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders and continues to hold Russia accountable for its actions,” the statement says.

The broader package of sanctions announced on 1 October also targets Russian sources of revenue, including the so-called “shadow fleet” and Kremlin disinformation networks, as well as individuals involved in crimes against Ukraine’s civilian population.
