World.title: What Azerbaijan needs to do to benefit from Middle Corridor: World Bank recommendations
World.content:
Benefits for Azerbaijan from the Middle Corridor

Developing the Middle Corridor through 2040 will require more than $55 billion in investment. However, building new railways and ports alone will not guarantee faster cargo deliveries. A World Bank report published on 28 September also stresses the need to simplify border procedures, coordinate rail and maritime transport, and reform state-owned transport companies.

For Azerbaijan, the key question is how much revenue the country can generate from cargo transit across the Caspian Sea and how it can integrate these shipments into the local economy. According to World Bank estimates, developing the corridor could increase the country’s GDP by 0.43 per cent in the long term, or by about $326 million.

In April, we analysed growing demand for the Middle Corridor and constraints on the Caspian route, while in June we examined 10 priority projects proposed to increase cargo volumes. The new report adds separate estimates of Azerbaijan’s investment needs and the potential economic impact. Our June list did not include any projects directly linked to Azerbaijan, while the World Bank report specifically identifies additional investment in the country’s rail and logistics infrastructure.

The new document builds on the World Bank’s 2023 study. It extends the forecast period to 2040 and covers more countries and types of cargo.

Where does the Middle Corridor run?

The Middle Corridor is a transport network connecting Asia and Europe through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Turkey. Different sections of the route carry cargo by rail, sea and road.

One of the main routes runs from China through Kazakhstan to the ports of Aktau and Kuryk. From there, cargo crosses the Caspian Sea to the Port of Baku in Alat. It then travels through Azerbaijan by rail along the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars line to Georgia. From there, it continues to Turkey or reaches Europe via Georgia’s ports and the Black Sea. The route through the port of Turkmenbashi connects Turkmenistan and other Central Asian countries to this transport network.

The report covers Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Turkey and Uzbekistan. The Middle Corridor currently does not pass directly through Armenia. The World Bank included the country in its calculations on the assumption that relevant transport links could emerge in the 2030s.

Asian-European trade routes. Solid orange lines show the land sections of the Middle Corridor, orange dashed lines show planned extensions, and blue lines show maritime routes. Source: Alam and Blancas, World Bank, 2026, Map O.1. CC BY 3.0 IGO.

What is the $55 billion needed for?

According to the World Bank, more than $25 billion will be needed by 2040 to develop the core physical infrastructure. This includes railways, ports and transport links between them.

Another $30 billion will be needed for additional investments required to operate the corridor and integrate it with local economies. This includes spending on access roads, logistics centres, inland terminals, locomotives and railcars, cargo-handling equipment and digital systems.

This figure does not represent costs that Azerbaijan will have to cover on its own, nor does it refer to a World Bank loan. It is an estimate of the total investment needed along the entire route.

Of the 16 most important infrastructure projects identified by the World Bank, 75 per cent are already under way, while governments have included the remainder in their plans. The report therefore notes that the main task at the next stage may be to improve service quality and the efficiency of transport operations.

What specific projects are planned for Azerbaijan?

The report identifies three areas for additional investment in Azerbaijan, totalling $1.16 billion.

Completing the ongoing modernisation of the Baku-Alat-Boyuk-Kesik railway line will cost an estimated $260 million. Upgrading power supply and signalling systems should improve the efficiency of the corridor’s main section in Azerbaijan.

The report allocates $300 million to developing a network of dry ports. These inland terminals collect, store and transfer cargo between different modes of transport. The list includes the Boyuk-Kesik border crossing, Baku and a southern transport hub that could serve a proposed route to Kars through Azerbaijan and Armenia.

Another $600 million would go towards further expanding the Baku-Alat-Boyuk-Kesik railway line in the 2030s. The latter two projects remain at the preliminary feasibility study stage. The figures therefore do not represent funding under contracts that authorities have already signed. The list also does not cover all of Azerbaijan’s costs related to developing the Middle Corridor.

Alat port capacity and the Caspian Sea’s declining water level

According to the report, the Port of Baku increased its container-handling capacity from 100,000 to 150,000 TEUs in 2025 by improving the efficiency of its existing infrastructure. TEU is a unit of measurement equivalent to a standard 20-foot container. The port handled 107,000 TEUs that year, using about 71 per cent of its container capacity.

At the same time, the port’s overall cargo-handling capacity stood at 55 per cent utilisation. This distinction matters: spare capacity across the port as a whole does not mean that the container and ferry terminals face no congestion.

The World Bank points to another problem: since the port moved to Alat in 2018, authorities have not carried out dredging in the entrance channel or the approach areas leading to the berths. The falling level of the Caspian Sea requires urgent action. Draft restrictions can prevent ships from loading to full capacity and reduce the port’s actual throughput.

What is slowing cargo transport?

According to the World Bank’s analysis, container cargo spends the most time waiting at ports. One reason is poor coordination between train and vessel schedules.

The report proposes creating a single operator to integrate container services run by the railway companies of Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan and Turkey with Caspian Sea shipping operated by ASCO and Kazakhstan’s Kazmortransflot. This would allow operators to coordinate shipments along the entire route.

Document processing also takes considerable time. According to an example in the report, a container shipment between Asia and Europe may require 10 entry and exit procedures under customs transit regimes, five railway consignment notes and two maritime cargo documents. The World Bank recommends introducing a single digital T3 document combining transport, transit and trade data. To use it, countries would need to recognise each other’s documents, agree on data-sharing procedures and establish carriers’ responsibilities.

What conditions are needed to achieve the expected benefits?

According to the World Bank, investment and better services could more than triple cargo volumes along the route by 2040 and halve delivery times. Deeper trade and transport reforms could quadruple cargo volumes and cut delivery times by two-thirds compared with 2023.

The report estimates that, in the long term, the combined GDP of the nine countries could grow by 3.3 per cent, while employment could rise by 2.9 per cent. For Azerbaijan, the corresponding figures stand at 0.43 per cent and 0.66 per cent.

The report suggests that turning Azerbaijan’s geographic position into an economic advantage requires more than simply moving cargo through the country. Local businesses need access to the route, along with reliable transport and competitive logistics services. Planning should account for infrastructure costs, operating expenses and expected cargo volumes together. The World Bank also stresses that the report does not assess projects as ready for financing.

Benefits for Azerbaijan from the Middle Corridor

World.title: ‘Copper is to us what oil is to other countries’ – expert on Armenia’s mineral wealth
World.content:
Assessment of Armenia’s mineral resources

“Armenia does not have major oil or gas deposits with significant reserves. Instead, it can rely on substantial reserves of copper, molybdenum and gold, as well as rare elements and critical minerals. Gold, silver, copper, molybdenum and polymetals such as lead and zinc are currently in greatest demand. However, so-called critical minerals are gradually becoming increasingly important,” geologist Arshavir Hovhannisyan says.

The head of the Mineral Resources Department at the Institute of Geological Sciences of Armenia’s National Academy of Sciences says the terms “critical minerals” and “rare-earth elements” are sometimes confused in Armenia. He explains that critical minerals are elements, mainly metals, that are particularly important for a country’s industrial development, especially in high-tech sectors.

“Rare elements and rare-earth elements are among critical minerals. Copper, for example, is a critical mineral because neither batteries nor electric motors can function without it, but it is not a rare element,” he told Armenpress agency.

Copper, gold and silver reserves, but copper is key

“Copper is the queen of metals, the most important metal.

“We also talk about the importance of lithium, but it is likely to be replaced in the foreseeable future. Lithium is a rather unsuitable chemical element for use in batteries. It is highly flammable, performs poorly at high and low temperatures and has a limited number of charging cycles, after which it becomes unusable.

“Scientists are now looking for alternatives to lithium. Sodium and potassium are the most likely candidates. China is already producing sodium batteries using extremely cheap raw materials.

“Sodium, along with chlorine, is one of the main components of table salt, and Armenia has vast reserves of it. Yerevan is largely situated on salt deposits. The Ararat Valley, from Armavir to Arzni, lies entirely on salt deposits. If necessary, Armenia would have no difficulty obtaining extremely cheap raw materials.

Gold and silver can also be used in electrical equipment. The only element for which there is currently no substitute is copper.

“Copper is to us what, say, oil is to some other countries.”

Armenia’s copper reserves could last decades

“Reserves will be depleted in around 50-100 years unless we discover new deposits in the meantime. I think new deposits could be found because we have done virtually nothing in this area for about 35 years.

“Deposits that were not considered particularly promising during the Soviet period may now attract interest. First, technologies for extracting metals from ore have advanced. Second, the price of copper on the global market is rising rapidly.

According to Bloomberg estimates, by 2030-2040 global demand for copper will reach a level requiring 10-15 new mines to be brought into operation every year.

“I mean mines comparable in size to the large Kajaran deposit.

“According to various estimates, producing a conventional passenger car requires 10-15kg of copper, while an electric vehicle requires more than 50kg. Tens of millions of electric vehicles are produced each year. Simple arithmetic therefore gives an idea of how much pure copper will be needed for the automotive industry alone, with production volumes expected to continue growing.

“There are also other sectors where copper is essential, including electrification, modern technologies and the infrastructure supporting them.”

Oil and gas not worth considering

“The geodynamic processes that took place over tens of millions of years in the territory where Armenia is now located have left virtually no prospect of large hydrocarbon reserves.

“A large number of deep wells were drilled in Voghjaberd for research purposes, and similar exploration was carried out in Armavir. Some traces were found, including small amounts of gas. These are remnants of deposits that once existed, as well as accumulations formed more recently, over the past 30 million years. Given the geology and location, these cannot be large volumes.

“There is little reason to expect oil and gas deposits to be discovered in Armenia in the future.

Small deposits could potentially be found at great depths. But even finding them would be extremely costly, as numerous wells would have to be drilled.

“Even then, it would not be clear whether the gas discovered would last a month, an hour or a year. In any case, the volumes would be so small that they are hardly worth considering.”

Areas where rare elements could be found

“Demand for rare-earth elements and other minerals has risen sharply worldwide, along with their prices. They are in high demand in modern high-tech manufacturing.

“They attracted little interest in the past, but technologies have changed. We need to understand what resources we have.

We cannot say there is no chance of Armenia having rare-element reserves. There are geological areas in the country that could contain them.

“Further research is needed to establish this. Our institute has a dedicated group studying rare-earth elements, funded by a grant from the Science Committee. The research does not have an industrial or applied research component and is purely scientific, but the fact that it is being conducted is itself a positive development.

“The research covers potential mineralisation of lithium, selenium, tellurium and rhenium. Meanwhile, more than 20 other rare-earth elements have not previously been studied.

“Some have been identified incidentally during other research. As demand for them grows, we will have to explore them, whether we want to or not. If the state does not do so, the private sector will.”

Investment needed to explore new deposits

“Armenia is indeed very rich in mineral resources, both metallic and non-metallic. Kajaran, Sotk, Agarak and Teghut are all located within a relatively small area covering around 30-35% of the country. Moreover, Kajaran is among the world’s 10 largest mines by scale.

“The difficulties are related not to geology but to the terrain. In many cases, mines are located at altitudes of around 3,000 metres, in hard-to-reach areas, and deposits are often relatively small.

The chances of discovering new large deposits comparable in scale to Kajaran or Zod [Sotk] are very low. The chances of finding medium-sized and small deposits are higher.

“Exploration of new deposits will become possible if the state creates the necessary conditions for investment and also invests itself. At the very least, this would give us a clearer picture of the rare elements and critical minerals in Armenia’s subsoil. This would then be followed by detailed exploration and reserve estimates, an even more labour-intensive and costly process.”

World.title: From self-defence to political statements: how former Georgian PM Garibashvili’s ‘prison’ letters have evolved
World.content:
Analysis of former Georgian PM’s “prison” letters

Former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili has published his eighth letter from prison, which differs significantly from his previous seven. In the letter, Garibashvili looks back on his political career and presents himself to the public as a successful prime minister. The text effectively serves both as a political report and a statement of leadership ambitions.

In the letter, the former prime minister seeks to show that in 2021 he led the government out of a deep political and economic crisis and improved the country’s situation through his work.

At the end of the letter, he asks the public whether the situation has improved or deteriorated since he resigned. Although he does not directly name current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, the question clearly challenges his administration.

“Almost three years have passed since then [my resignation], and I want to ask the people: has the situation in the country improved or deteriorated, both in domestic and foreign policy?”

About former PM Giorgi Gakharia

Garibashvili begins his account with February 2021, when he returned as prime minister for a second time after Giorgi Gakharia resigned. He says Georgia faced several serious challenges at once: a political crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, a shortage of vaccines, an economic downturn, a large budget deficit, rising public debt and a weakening lari.

In his view, Gakharia abandoned the country and the ruling team under these circumstances. Garibashvili’s position on Gakharia echoes the Georgian Dream party’s narrative:

“Gakharia left the country and the team in the middle of an acute crisis, committing an act of unexpected betrayal by resigning. The government stood on the brink of collapse, the ruling party had lost morale, the team was divided, and the party’s approval rating had fallen to 35–37%.”

Garibashvili portrays his return as, essentially, a rescue operation for the government. He says that after taking office as prime minister, he strengthened the team, stabilised the situation, reopened the country and the economy, secured vaccine supplies and lifted restrictions introduced during the pandemic.

The former prime minister stresses that the government abandoned what he calls a “Covid dictatorship” and gave people complete freedom to choose whether to get vaccinated.

“In the shortest possible time, we restored balance, strengthened the team and stabilised the situation. Together with the team, we took bold, decisive, effective and — at the time — risky steps.”

In his view, these measures secured Georgian Dream’s victory in the 2021 local elections. Garibashvili credits himself not only with helping the party clear the 43 per cent threshold and win 47 per cent of the vote, but also with preventing a potential revolutionary scenario after Mikheil Saakashvili returned to Georgia.

“We prevented destabilisation and an attempted revolution involving Saakashvili, put all destructive forces in their place and brought the political crisis to an end.”

Showcasing economic results

A significant part of the letter focuses on economic indicators. Garibashvili claims that Georgia’s economy grew by 30 billion lari (about $11,516,310,000) during his three years as prime minister. He says the economy recorded double-digit growth in 2021 and 2022, putting Georgia first among EU member and candidate countries in terms of growth.

Garibashvili lists the following among his government’s achievements:

cutting the budget deficit from 9 per cent to 2.8 per cent;

reducing public debt from 60 per cent to 38 per cent of GDP;

stabilising the lari exchange rate at between 2.6 and 2.7;

bringing inflation below the target level;

reducing unemployment and poverty to historic lows;

creating tens of thousands of new jobs;

raising pensions and salaries for public-sector workers.

The former prime minister attributes lower medicine prices to the opening of the Turkish pharmaceutical market and the introduction of a reference pricing system for medicines.

EU candidate status and the issue of being “dragged into war” with Russia

Garibashvili also devotes considerable attention to foreign policy. Here again, he echoes Georgian Dream’s rhetoric. He says Georgia faced intense pressure after the war between Russia and Ukraine began, but his government managed to protect the country from the threat of war and destabilisation.

“From the very first days of the war between Russia and Ukraine, despite enormous pressure, we firmly and uncompromisingly defended our country’s national interests, preventing destabilisation and the real threat of war.”

Garibashvili thus repeats one of Georgian Dream’s key political arguments: after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia faced the risk of being dragged into the conflict.

The former prime minister lists his foreign visits and diplomatic initiatives in the letter. These include applying for EU membership, developing strategic relations with China, signing free trade agreements with several countries, mediating between Azerbaijan and Armenia, and hosting a meeting of the three countries’ prime ministers in Tbilisi.

Garibashvili considers Georgia’s achievement of EU candidate status in December 2023 his main foreign policy accomplishment.

“Without bowing to anyone — either inside the country or abroad — and solely through our uncompromising defence of our country’s national interests and the joint efforts of our team, we secured EU candidate status in December 2023.”

The letter says these results came without political subordination to external forces.

Approval ratings and resignation

Garibashvili claims he left office with high levels of public support. According to him, in January 2024, approval of the government’s performance and support for Georgian Dream both reached 60 per cent.

“Thanks to the results we achieved — and, most importantly, thanks to democratic methods — we politically neutralised the entire radical opposition, leaving no one with any grounds for criticism or complaint.”

Garibashvili presents not only his government’s record but also the neutralisation of the opposition as a political achievement. He effectively equates this “democratic success” with the ruling party’s dominance and the opposition’s removal from the political arena.

The letter does not explain why Garibashvili resigned as prime minister at a time when, according to his own account, the government enjoyed high approval, the economy was growing and the opposition had suffered political defeat.

From self-defence to political statements: analysis of former Georgian PM’s “prison” letters

Garibashvili’s eight letters form a coherent political narrative. At first, he sought to protect himself and his family. He later accused the authorities of orchestrating political persecution. He subsequently began raising questions about the government’s actions and several other issues. In his eighth letter, he defends his political legacy and criticises the current government. Political analysts say the latest letter points to political ambitions on Garibashvili’s part.

The first stage — Ivanishvili loyalty and self-preservation

In his first letters, Garibashvili described the pressure against him as the main source of the conflict. He said he did not plan to return to politics, but the authorities demanded that he admit guilt to new corruption charges, fearing a “one per cent risk” that he might return to politics.

He firmly reaffirmed his loyalty to Bidzina Ivanishvili, while holding him personally responsible if anything threatened his family.

“I am not fighting or battling anyone — I am only defending myself and my family!”

Garibashvili took a defensive position, seeking to show that he had not chosen this confrontation and that the authorities had forced him to defend himself.

The second stage — accusing specific individuals

In his subsequent letters, it became clearer who exactly Garibashvili was targeting with his criticism. His focus shifted from Ivanishvili to Prime Minister Kobakhidze and former regional development minister and former State Security Service chief Mamuka Mdinaradze. Garibashvili accused both of them of organising the pressure against him.

By presenting the situation this way, the former prime minister clearly left the door open to reconciliation with Ivanishvili. He continued to describe Ivanishvili as someone for whom he had “enormous love, respect, boundless gratitude and absolute loyalty”, while placing the blame for what was happening on people around him.

The third stage — systemic accusations

In his fifth and sixth letters, Garibashvili broadened the scope of the conflict. He publicly questioned the circumstances surrounding the death of human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze and linked the incident to other suicides that occurred while Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze held power.

The convicted former prime minister later accused the government as a whole of conducting systematic propaganda, using investigations for political purposes, and trying to link Garibashvili to the United National Movement or foreign agents.

Garibashvili moved beyond his own criminal case, criticising the government’s methods and presenting himself as a victim of political persecution.

The fourth stage — creating an alternative to the current government

In his seventh letter, Garibashvili claimed that the authorities had arrested him to destroy his political future. He accused the government of creating an atmosphere of endless chaos, crisis and impoverishment.

The most significant point came when he compared Georgian Dream with Mikheil Saakashvili’s administration:

“You are already following in Saakashvili’s footsteps and bringing back the methods of governance used by the National Movement…”

For years, Georgian Dream has built its political identity around contrasting itself with Saakashvili’s rule. Garibashvili’s accusation that the current government uses the same methods therefore directly challenges the ruling team’s legitimacy.

Analysts say the eighth letter takes a more political tone than his previous statements in his own defence.

Garibashvili has not officially announced a return to politics. However, the logic of his letters points towards a political comeback.

World.title: ‘Transparent and competitive, but also cause for concern’: PACE report on Armenia’s elections
World.content:
PACE report on Armenia’s elections

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe’s election observation mission has published a report on the parliamentary elections, which took place in Armenia on 7 June.

“The elections were competitive, and citizens had a genuine choice between different political forces and alternatives,” the report says.

Observers also found the process well organised and transparent, with no serious incidents.

At the same time, they identified several serious problems. In particular, they expressed concern over a post-election dispute involving the invalidation of voting results at polling stations 10/51, 35/65 and 12/13. PACE experts believe that if officials had counted those votes, the opposition Prosperous Armenia party could have crossed the four per cent threshold and won seats.

Meanwhile, the Central Election Commission said the annulment of the results at these polling stations did not affect the election outcome. It therefore decided not to hold repeat voting there. However, PACE described the decision as “unsatisfactory, given the significance of its consequences”.

“A perfectly acceptable option would have been to hold repeat voting at the relevant polling stations. The CEC rejected this without providing serious justification. Authorities should base such an important decision on strong, transparent and verifiable grounds. Unfortunately, that did not happen,” said Swiss politician Damien Cottier, one of the report’s authors.

Armenian journalists also noted that MPs from the ruling party and the opposition selectively presented PACE’s assessment to the public. They quoted and highlighted the parts of the document that supported their respective positions.

“Politicians often resort to such tactics. In English, there is an expression for this: cherry-picking. Politicians select and present only the findings that portray them in a positive light, while ignoring or downplaying the negative ones,” Factor TV said in a report.

Main concerns

“Interference by the Russian Federation and foreign information operations in a Council of Europe member state have reached unprecedented levels,” the report says.

According to the PACE mission, Russia used economic restrictions and tough diplomatic rhetoric to influence the election results in favour of the pro-Russian opposition.

The report also identifies the following problems:

abuse of administrative resources,

biased coverage on public television and by key opposition media outlets,

some Karabakh Armenians being unable to vote because bureaucratic delays prevented them from obtaining Armenian citizenship,

unprecedented external interference and geopolitical pressure.

PACE recommendations

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe has called on Armenia to amend its electoral code:

“The law should clearly require repeat voting whenever the fundamental right of a political force to have representation [in parliament] comes into question. It should also establish a clear threshold and procedures for such cases.”

The observation mission also recommends that the Armenian authorities take the following steps:

strengthen the resilience of the electoral process and democratic institutions, particularly by increasing national capacity to identify and counter Russian information operations and economic pressure tools;

broaden the range of people who can challenge electoral disputes in court, extend appeal deadlines and introduce more flexible remedies for violations;

ensure the independence of the process for appointing members of electoral commissions;

fully regulate the use of administrative resources and effectively punish any abuse of them;

end the selective prosecution of opposition figures and guarantee compliance with all procedural rules in election-related court proceedings;

guarantee the right of all political forces to hold peaceful assemblies;

simplify documentation requirements for displaced people and vulnerable groups of voters, and speed up the citizenship and registration processes.

PACE said it stood ready to work with the Armenian authorities to address all these issues.

Ruling party and opposition representatives on the report

Hayk Konjoryan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction and deputy speaker of parliament, emphasised that the report described the elections as “well organised”. He also highlighted the following points from the document:

voters had a genuine choice between political alternatives,

observers gave the electoral process a positive assessment at the vast majority of polling stations they monitored.

Konjoryan also highlighted the PACE observers’ assessment that the elections took place amid major geopolitical transformations. They described the scale of external interference in Armenia’s affairs as “unprecedented and alarming”.

The deputy speaker also pointed to the report’s description of the economic restrictions and political pressure that outside actors imposed on Armenia during the pre-election campaign. The report explicitly says that the goal was to influence voters and encourage them to vote for opposition forces.

“According to the report, the election results show that society demonstrated its democratic resilience despite unprecedented external pressure and the shortcomings identified. The PACE report says that the elected authorities received a clear mandate from the people, which they must now carry out with honour,” Konjoryan concluded.

Narek Karapetyan, head of the opposition Strong Armenia faction, focused on other points in the report. He highlighted the following problems identified by European parliamentarians:

“On unlawful detentions

The number of searches and arrests of opposition politicians, activists and candidates has increased significantly.

The observation mission stressed that these measures undermined electoral fairness and had a significant chilling effect on the opposition’s election campaign.

On administrative resources

The ruling party used official government platforms, public infrastructure and administrative levers to support its campaign. This significantly distorted the campaign environment and prevented opposition forces from competing on an equal footing.

On pre-election bribery

While law enforcement agencies promptly launched high-profile investigations into alleged vote-buying and illegal campaign financing by opposition factions, they dealt with similar allegations and complaints against ruling-party representatives far less thoroughly or more slowly.

On election fraud

“Prosperous Armenia” could have crossed the four per cent threshold for entering parliament, won seats and deprived the ruling party of its three-fifths majority.”

“A one-sided approach”: Factor TV’s assessment

Journalists from Factor TV examined the report itself as well as MPs’ comments.

In their view, Konjoryan and Karapetyan presented diametrically opposed interpretations of the same document:

ruling-party MP Hayk Konjoryan completely ignored the parts of the report that criticise the authorities and highlight abuses of administrative resources and shortcomings in the electoral process.

opposition MP Narek Karapetyan focused only on accusations against the authorities, while ignoring sections that confirm the legitimacy of the elections and document external pressure.

“Both sides present only the half of the truth that suits them. But even combining these two perspectives does not provide the full picture. For example, the report contains statements that criticise both the authorities and the opposition.”

The document says:

“Extreme polarisation in society and mass protests created a tense domestic political environment. Years of confrontation and ongoing [unfinished] legal and institutional reforms have weakened confidence in the possibility of achieving political change through institutions and elections.”

The journalists concluded that each side highlighted passages criticising its opponents while leaving out criticism of its own political force.

PACE report on Armenia’s elections

World.title: Iranian ambassador calls history of Georgian Queen Ketevan “controversial”, sparking criticism in Georgia
World.content:
Scandal over Iranian ambassador’s remarks in Georgia

Iranian ambassador to Georgia Seyed Ali Mojani has announced the publication of his own research on Georgian Queen Ketevan. His remarks about the need to “re-examine” history have drawn criticism from a Georgian historian and MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party. The dispute centres on the ambassador’s references to different historical accounts without specifying which generally accepted facts he is questioning.

What did the ambassador write?

Mojani, a historian by profession, posted a photograph on Facebook showing the facade of the Iranian embassy with an image of Queen Ketevan projected onto it. He wrote that, for him, the image symbolises a historical memory surrounded by “numerous conflicting accounts that persist to this day”.

The ambassador promised to publish the findings of his preliminary research soon. The study will focus on Queen Ketevan and draw on Georgian and Iranian sources. Mojani stressed that it would not represent Iran’s official position but rather his personal perspective as a historian, which could be refined or revised in the future.

Mojani has not yet published either the study itself or the sources he intends to use.

Why did the post spark criticism?

Queen Ketevan was tortured to death in the Iranian city of Shiraz in 1624 on the orders of Shah Abbas I. Historical sources and academic studies document her martyrdom. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates Ketevan as a saint and commemorates her on 26 September.

Against this backdrop, some interpreted Mojani’s reference to “conflicting accounts” as a suggestion that the ambassador was questioning the history of Ketevan’s martyrdom.

Historian and lecturer Giorgi Javakhishvili believes the ambassador’s statement goes beyond his diplomatic mandate. According to him, “Queen Ketevan’s martyrdom is a fact.” Javakhishvili also accuses Mojani of disregarding the methodology and ethics of historical research.

Georgian Dream MPs react

Nikoloz Samkharadze, chairman of parliament’s Foreign Relations Committee, urged the ambassador to “stick to diplomatic protocol and refrain from delving into history”. Samkharadze said he would discuss the incident with Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili when she returns to Georgia.

MP Irakli Kadagishvili said Mojani’s statement had nothing to do with the embassy’s work, stressing that the ambassador should perform his duties within the scope of his authority.

MP Aluda Gudushauri expects the foreign ministry to respond, noting that “no one can change or distort the true course of our history — reality is what it is and what we know it to be”.

The ambassador’s previous statements

Mojani’s posts have sparked controversy in Georgia before. On 31 March, he wrote that “countries that willingly or unwillingly surrender their space and territory to foreign adventurers sooner or later pay the price within their own borders”. The ambassador did not name any specific country, but some analysts and politicians interpreted the post as a threat against Georgia.

World.title: Saida Mirziyoyeva meets Donald Trump as US-Uzbekistan ties deepen
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 2. Today, Saida Mirziyoyeva, head of the Presidential Administration of Uzbekistan, met with U.S.President Donald Trump and conveyed warm wishes from Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in Washington, D.C.

This was reflected in the statement posted by the Head of the Presidential Administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva, on her social media account.

“It was a great honor to meet with President of the United States Donald Trump and convey to him the best wishes from President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev,” she said in her post.

The meeting comes as Uzbekistan and the United States continue to expand political and economic engagement. Mirziyoyeva also serves as co-chair of the American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council, which was established to strengthen investment and business ties between the two countries.

Recent bilateral cooperation has focused on energy, critical minerals, mining, infrastructure, finance, artificial intelligence, and digital technologies, with both sides pursuing additional investment and joint projects.

The meeting comes amid deepening U.S.-Uzbekistan relations, particularly in trade, investment and strategic economic cooperation. During her recent visit to New York for the 81st UN General Assembly, Mirziyoyeva held meetings with U.S. officials and business representatives. She also co-chairs the American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council, launched in 2026 to strengthen commercial ties between the two countries. In June, Washington and Tashkent announced an early harvest of trade commitments and agreed to accelerate negotiations toward a Reciprocal Trade and Investment Agreement.

World.title: Samruk-Energy raises renewable generation forecast accuracy to 86%
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 2. Samruk-Energy has increased the accuracy of renewable power generation forecasts to 86% through an artificial intelligence-based system, Head of the Digitalization and AI Office Aizek Zhupankhan said at AI & Digital Bridge 2026 in Astana.

“Considering the growth in the share of renewable energy sources - if I am not mistaken, from 7% to 15% by 2035 - high-quality forecasting is becoming more important than ever, since the balance of the entire energy system depends on it. At Samruk-Energy, we managed to increase forecast accuracy to 86%. The project is currently in pilot operation, after which we plan to scale it to all our renewable energy facilities,” Zhupankhan said.

He noted that artificial intelligence is also being used by Samruk-Energy for predictive diagnostics, computer vision, digital twins and other applications aimed at improving the efficiency and reliability of power generation.

Furthermore, Zhupankhan added that at Ekibastuz GRES-1, Kazakhstan’s largest power plant, the company is connecting 56,000 sensors that generate almost 81 million signals per day. The data is analyzed by an AI system to identify developing equipment defects before failures occur, while a digital twin helps determine optimal operating modes and maintenance timing.

Samruk-Energy is also using AI-powered video analytics at its main facilities. According to Zhupankhan, the system analyzes data from thousands of cameras in real time and detects safety violations, including the absence of helmets and personal protective equipment, access to hazardous areas, falls, smoke, and fires.

Following the deployment of the system, the company reduced the number of safety violations at its main facilities by 87%, he said.

The company is also using drones for aerial monitoring, including automated measurement of coal stocks at its thermal power plants. The process, which previously took up to 10 days, can now be completed in no more than 20 minutes, Zhupankhan said.

World.title: Central Bank of Azerbaijan records 36% growth in FX reserves
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 2. As of October 1, 2026, the foreign exchange reserves of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA) stood at $15.363 billion.

This was announced in a report published by the press service of the CBA.

According to the report, the Central Bank’s foreign exchange reserves increased by $62.1 million, or 0.41%, compared to September 1, 2026.

Over the past year, the CBA’s foreign exchange reserves grew by $4.053 billion, or 35.8%.

Thus, as of October 1, 2025, the Central Bank’s foreign exchange reserves totaled $11.310 billion. As of September 1, 2026, this figure reached $15.301 billion.

Consequently, from the beginning of October last year to the beginning of October this year, the Central Bank’s foreign exchange reserves increased by more than $4 billion.

The information also reveals indicators related to the dynamics of the monetary base in Azerbaijan.

In addition, it is noted that as of October 1, 2026, the monetary base in Azerbaijan stood at 24.818 billion manat ($14.6 billion).

This figure is 579.1 million manat ($340.7 million), or 2.39%, higher than on September 1, 2026.

At the same time, the country’s monetary base increased by 3.277 billion manat ($1.9 billion), or 15.2%, over the past year.

For comparison, as of October 1, 2025, Azerbaijan’s monetary base stood at 21.541 billion manat ($12.6 billion). As of September 1, 2026, the monetary base stood at 24.239 billion manat ($14.2 billion).

Thus, there was growth in both the Central Bank’s foreign exchange reserves and the country’s monetary base on both a monthly and annual basis.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan sees opportunities to expand investment ties with Turkmenistan
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the National Investment Agency under the President of the Kyrgyz Republic

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 2. Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan have opportunities to expand economic and investment cooperation, Head of the National Investment Agency under the President of Kyrgyzstan Ravshanbek Sabirov said at the Turkmenistan Investment Forum 2026 (TIF 2026) in Ashgabat.

According to the National Investment Agency, Sabirov attended the opening ceremony of the forum on October 1. He highlighted prospects for strengthening direct dialogue between government agencies and businesses of the two countries.

"New opportunities are emerging for our countries to develop investment cooperation. Strengthening direct dialogue between government agencies and businesses, implementing joint projects and expanding mutual investments can provide additional momentum to the economic ties between the two countries," he said.

According to Ravshanbek Sabirov, Kyrgyzstan continues to improve its investment legislation and investor support mechanisms, develop public-private partnerships and digital tools for project support.

Promising areas include artificial intelligence, creative industries, renewable energy, infrastructure and transport and logistics projects.

Priority areas of cooperation between Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan also include trade and economic ties, energy, oil and gas supplies, the textile industry, transport and logistics, and tourism.

The expansion of direct business contacts and implementation of joint initiatives create additional opportunities for businesses and contribute to strengthening regional economic ties.

World.title: Flydubai 'hero' pilot says praying gave him courage
World.content:
The "hero" Indian pilot who fought off a mid-flight attack from his co-pilot has described the harrowing ordeal from hospital in a talk with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Captain Smit Machchhar, appearing from an Abu Dhabi hospital bed, told Mr Modi that he opened the cockpit door while he was still being attacked on the floor.

Captain Smit Machchhar has worked in the airline industry for more than a decade, according to his LinkedIn profile. (Supplied: Israel Foreign Ministry)

"I had so many wounds. I had fallen down," he said from the hospital, his head bandaged and tubes in his nose, before breaking down as he recalled the attack in a nearly 10-minute-long video released by the prime minister's office on Friday, local time.

"I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn't get up … then passengers would lose their lives," he told Mr Modi.

"I knew that the aircraft was going down … I had fallen to the ground. I told myself that the door is right there, just open it. I managed to do it and people entered."

Mr Machchhar was stabbed by his co-pilot in an alleged attempt to crash the flydubai plane on Wednesday.

The jet plunged nearly 14,000 feet (4,267 metres) in less than 30 seconds in the incident.

The flight bound for Tel Aviv was carrying 174 people and was forced to divert to Tabuk in north-western Saudi Arabia for an emergency landing.

Mr Machchhar said that during those difficult moments, he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a Hindu devotional hymn dedicated to Lord Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.

"Lord Hanuman gave me courage," he told Mr Modi.

Co-pilot attempted to crash plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv, Netanyahu says The plane was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

Mr Machchhar, who is married and has two children, has worked for flydubai for about four years, according to his LinkedIn profile.

Before joining the airline, he spent 11 years with SpiceJet, an Indian low-cost carrier, where he served as a senior commander and line training captain.

He logged more than 9,750 flying hours with SpiceJet.

ABC/AP/REUTERS

World.title: Breaking: Former Liberal politician Bruce Baird dies aged 84
World.content:
Former Liberal politician Bruce Baird has died aged 84.

Mr Baird was father to former NSW premier Mike Baird and journalist Julia Baird.

The NSW Liberal Party recognised Mr Baird in a statement on Friday.

"Bruce was a party stalwart and a greatly respected politician, serving the people of NSW in the state and federal parliaments," a spokesperson said.

"We offer our deepest condolences on behalf of all members to his family at this difficult time."

Baird quit politics in 2007. (ABC News)

After a career in state politics, Baird went on to represent the federal seat of Cook in the Sutherland Shire in NSW from 1998 to 2007.

The seat was later won by former prime minister Scott Morrison.

Baird retired prior to general elections in 2007, when he expressed his disappointment that he was never made a minister in the Howard Liberal government.

"I have no regrets and in politics you have to learn to roll with the punches," he said at the time.

Baird was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia in 2010.

World.title: Bookkeeper admits defrauding $2.8m from farming family
World.content:
As a pioneering Far North Queensland farming family battled cyclones, floods and an outbreak of Panama disease, a trusted employee was secretly stealing millions of dollars behind their backs.

The Johnston family of Tully, south of Cairns, thought of Michelle Kathleen Lawson as their friend and devoted bookkeeper.

But the District Court in Cairns heard Lawson, 53, used her trusted position to fund a "lavish" lifestyle through payments to her own bank account and those of her husband and son.

As members of the Johnston family started new businesses, Lawson would begin defrauding them, hiding payments on the books under the names of false employees, the court heard.

Police charged Lawson with fraud in 2024. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

Lawson pleaded guilty to seven counts of fraud, spanning a six-year period and totalling about $2.8 million.

The court heard the former justice of the peace and one-time treasurer of the local business chamber spent the money on horses, cars, holidays, property, her own business and extra tuition for her children.

'Felt like a death'

Lawson's crimes have devastated the Johnstons, who invited her to their weddings and once congratulated her for buying a clothing boutique with her sisters, unaware their money helped fund it.

The Johnstons congratulated Lawson for buying a boutique on Tully's main street. (ABC News: Dominic Cansdale)

In a victim impact statement, Jill Johnston, 81, recounted how she thought a family meeting at her home in June 2023 was to sign papers for a succession plan.

Instead, the matriarch was told what Lawson, who ran the family businesses' finances for 18 years, had done.

"It has felt in many ways like a death," Mrs Johnston's statement said.

"I carry a deep sense of guilt that I did not detect the fraud.

"I checked the bank statements and asked questions, but still I did not see it."

Lawson's fraud continued as a Panama disease outbreak forced the Johnstons to stop producing bananas. (ABC News: Casey Briggs)

The court heard Lawson wanted to return to work soon after her son's birth, so Mrs Johnston arranged for a cot to be placed in the business's air-conditioned office.

Lawson also declined an offer to have someone cover her while she took her daughter on the horse show circuit, the court heard.

"She insisted she would keep doing the wages herself because she did not want to have to fix someone else's mistake," Mrs Johnston said in her statement.

"I now understand why she did not want anyone else looking at her work.

" In the more than three years since this has come to light, Michelle has never apologised to me or my family. "

Mrs Johnston's children Paul, Anthony, Stephen and Melanie also made statements outlining how Lawson's betrayal had generational consequences.

The court heard Lawson cost the family the chance to employ more staff, pay for machinery and chemicals outright, and stymied plans to buy a neighbouring property.

"It's a bitter pill to swallow as I view that farm every day on my way to work," Paul Johnston's statement said.

Cyclone Yasi flattened banana crops around Tully in 2011. (ABC Rural: Nikolai Beilharz)

Stephen Johnston said the family resolved to take civil action to recover money from Lawson, who discussed the hardships of farming while skimming from the businesses.

" We owed it to my mother and the life's work of my late father [Mort] not to let what was taken simply disappear. "

Lawson appeared from jail

The court heard the Johnstons managed to recover almost $1.5 million through civil action, but the legal fees and forensic accounting to do so cost about $500,000.

Defence counsel Kelly Goodwin told the court Lawson had a "traumatic" upbringing marked by domestic violence, alcohol abuse and the death of her father.

Mr Goodwin tendered a six-page letter from Lawson and some character references, telling the court Lawson accepted responsibility.

Lawson appeared at her plea hearing on a video link from the Townsville Women's Correctional Centre, where she has been remanded for more than two years since voluntarily having her bail revoked.

Judge Joshua Treviño KC is due to sentence Lawson on Wednesday.

World.title: Woman who stopped Adelaide beach brawl speaks out
World.content:
A woman who tried to stop a brawl on an Adelaide beach before being pelted with bottles has spoken publicly for the first time.

Earlier this week, videos emerged online of several fights at Glenelg and Henley Beach on Tuesday, with hundreds of teenagers spectating.

In several clips, a bystander tried to break up two males wrestling at Glenelg Beach, but she was hit with bottles and copped boos when she stepped up.

Kate, whose name we have changed for her safety, is sharing her experience for the first time since that footage circulated online.

She was at the beach with her daughter and her friend when she first noticed dozens of people running toward a gathering, which she soon realised was people watching a fight.

Kate has spoken of having bottles thrown at her by onlookers. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

"I wasn't thinking, really. I just thought, 'I've got to try and stop this'," she said.

"It was so loud … we're not talking 50 kids here, we're talking 200.

" Some were yelling out, 'I wanna see blood, I wanna see blood'. "

Kate said she felt she had no choice but to try and protect other beachgoers.

When she broke up the altercation, the fighters got up and told her they were "mucking around".

But she said the crowd egged on the violence.

"No-one could probably really hear me in the end because there was so much booing happening," she said.

Kate said the situation escalated when several bottles were thrown at her direction, leaving her with bruises.

A video image from social media captures Kate intervening in the Glenelg beach fight. (Supplied: TikTok)

"Then the other one threw something at me, and I did pick up the bottle, and I said: 'Enough'. I was doing my mum's voice," she said.

"What scared me too [is] there was a mother with little kids sitting right at the front."

Kate said she had reported it to police.

Public disorder operation starts early

On Wednesday, SA Police said it was looking to identify the "level of organisation" behind the fights and find those responsible.

As of this morning, no charges had been laid and the investigation remains ongoing.

Police said they were called after large crowds gathered at both Glenelg and Henley Beach, but most people had scattered by the time they arrived.

In the wake of recent incidents, a police operation to prevent street crime and public disorder along Adelaide's western beaches, originally planned to start at the end of the month, was brought forward to today.

Loading...

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas on Thursday condemned the fights but said government cannot "eradicate idiocy".

"When young people decide to beat each other up, it is completely unacceptable behaviour and we should all be uncompromising in our desire to see it leave our society," he said.

Police Minister Michael Brown today vowed police would maintain a strong presence over summer.

"The public need not be concerned about this particular issue because I can assure you that SAPOL are certainly investigating on a regular basis," he said.

However, it is not enough peace of mind for Kate, who said she will avoid busy beaches during the hotter months.

Fights at Adelaide's beaches were shared on social media and are now the subject of police investigation. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

"I just don't want my daughter to see stuff like that either … it's not good," she said.

Kate had a serious message for the people fighting too, warning they could have been seriously injured.

"These kids have got to think before doing anything," she said.

World.title: Man charged after toy poodle suffers broken jaw in alleged attack
World.content:
A man is facing 14 charges after allegedly snatching and breaking the jaw of a toy poodle on the NSW Central Coast.

Daniel Galea has been charged with a range of offences including aggravated cruelty upon an animal, robbery, resisting and assaulting a police officer, attempting to drive under the influence of drugs and possessing a prohibited weapon.

He also stands accused of destroying or damaging property and breaching bail.

The 44-year-old has been under police guard in the Wyong Hospital but faced a bail court hearing today and will now undergo a mental health assessment.

Tania Gorry says she was left traumatised after her dog was snatched, then allegedly attacked. (Supplied: Tania Gorry)

Noraville woman Tania Gorry told the ABC she was walking her dog Bella along Toukley foreshore on September 29, when a man grabbed the dog and locked himself and the animal in a car.

"I couldn't fight him, I just couldn't," she said.

"I hung on for dear life but he got the lead out of my hands."

Man tasered as dog rescued

A NSW Police Media statement said officers tried to rescue the dog as it was being attacked.

"The man allegedly seriously injured the dog and refused to comply with police directions," the statement read.

" Officers smashed the front windows of the vehicle and deployed Tasers and OC spray to effect the arrest of the man. "

Four officers were taken to hospital for lacerations to their arms and hands allegedly suffered during the arrest.

Toy poodle Bella suffered a broken jaw, spending several days in intensive care after surgery. (Supplied: Tania Gorry)

ICU and a broken jaw

Bella the toy poodle was taken to a veterinary clinic, needing surgery for a fractured jaw and a haematoma to her eye.

The dog spent three days in intensive care, with vets concluding she was also allegedly strangled.

Ms Gorry said her vet bill was likely to exceed $18,000.

A social media fundraising campaign saw donations reach the target in a matter of days.

Bella the toy poodle before the dog was snatched by a stranger and allegedly attacked, suffering a broken jaw. (Supplied: Tania Gorry)

"I'm so grateful to the outpouring of all the people who are showering love and support and donations," Ms Gorry said.

The 58-year-old said she was also injured during the ordeal, suffering bruising and injuries to her hand, wrist, knee, ribs and abdomen.

But Ms Gorry said her focus was solely on the dog, which is being fed through a tube as it recovers.

Bella was picked up from the vet today and is recovering at home. (Supplied: Tania Gorry)

"I'm just so grateful to God that she's alive," she said.

This morning, Bella the dog was discharged by the vet clinic and has returned home.

World.title: Perth man accused of letting toddler steer car appears in court
World.content:
A 30-year-old man who allegedly let a toddler steer a car while sitting unrestrained on his lap through suburban streets in Perth's north has appeared in court on reckless driving charges.

Police said Jake Douglas Smith uploaded a video to social media which appeared to show a young child on his lap while driving a Toyota Hilux in Alkimos on September 11.

The child appeared to "have control" of steering the vehicle, police allege.

The 30-year-old was arrested the next day at an address in Morley.

Jake Douglas Smith allegedly let a child steer his car while sitting on his lap. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

The video shows the child's hands on the steering wheel and the back of their head, as the car is driven through a residential area.

It then mounts a curb and stops on a front lawn.

When the car stops, a man can be heard excitedly saying, "say hello, yeah I did it, a three-year-old driving the car!"

The video was captioned "3 year old driving a Hilux what a legend".

Bail extended

Mr Smith represented himself when he appeared in the Joondalup Magistrates Court on Friday and asked the magistrate for an adjournment.

When Magistrate Raelene Johnston asked the prosecution whether Mr Smith had a record, the court was told he was on a conditional suspended imprisonment order.

No further details were provided.

Jake Douglas Smith represented himself in court. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Mr Smith's bail was extended until his next hearing later this month.

When asked by a reporter outside the court whether he uploaded the alleged video to social media, Mr Smith said he was "not too sure".

World.title: Rogue OpenAI agent accessed second NSW government website
World.content:
OpenAI says a rogue agent accessed a second New South Wales government website in June, with authorities only informed of the "misalignment" this week.

The Premier's Department said the model entered a National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) web application containing historical information and data on fires.

It said investigations have not found any unauthorised access to personal information.

In a statement, the department said the incident is understood to have happened in June, but OpenAI did not notify the government until yesterday.

"The NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) is working with Cyber Security NSW and its technology service provider to investigate the matter and assess its impact," the statement said.

OpenAI to face inquiry Australia is looking to impose a dual notification requirement under tougher new standards enforced after OpenAI's breach of a Medicare website.

A spokesperson for OpenAI confirmed the incident had taken place in June, but that no personal information had been accessed when a "model" had gone "beyond its intended use".

"After being made aware of this activity … we conducted an urgent internal technical and legal review to understand the nature of the activity against the research being carried out," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"As soon as that review was complete, we briefed the NSW Premier's Office and notified the Australian Signals Directorate.

"We sent a technical notification through the appropriate NSW Government channel and obtained details for the relevant NPWS contacts."

The spokesperson added the company followed up by providing a technical briefing and resources in line with its commitment to assisting where "misaligned activity has occurred".

"If our review identifies additional agencies, we will notify them promptly with the information available and keep them updated as we establish further facts."

'Not a malevolent company'

The NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR) revealed an OpenAI agent accessed a public crime mapping tool to research public crime statistics last week.

NSW Premier Chris Minns said at the time that incident was concerning.

"The mere fact the agent was told not to access the information — it's not a malevolent company, they weren't attempting to steal confidential information — and they did it anyway, that's the power of artificial intelligence," he said.

"That's the battle that we'll have to contend with, because whilst this might have been contained to semi-public information that wasn't privacy related, it may get to the point where that information is released."

Mr Minns says the BOCSAR data incident is concerning. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

It also comes after OpenAI apologised for breaching an Australian Medicare portal, with company saying it wanted to "rebuild trust with the Australian people".

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last week revealed that an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics reporting service portal on June 18.

The agent gained access to both public and non-public data, but no personal Medicare details were breached.

OpenAI said the incident occurred during a training exercise of an "internal-only OpenAI model", with the bot gaining access to non-public access to Services Australia Medicare's Statistics Reporting Service.

It then ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and statistics, as well as wrote files, according to the company.

World.title: NRLW needs its own CEO, says legend Ali Brigginshaw
World.content:
In her final press conference before retirement, rugby league legend Ali Brigginshaw has called on the NRL to create a separate chief executive for the women's game.

As she prepares for a fairytale finish hoping to win back-to-back premierships with Brisbane, Brigginshaw knows the NRLW still has much growing to do.

At today's official pre-grand final press conference, the Bronco was asked to put herself at the desk of newly crowned executive chairman Peter V'landys.

"If there's someone in charge of the [women's] game, maybe someone that plays the game, not me, maybe Millie," Brigginshaw joked about her fellow retiring grand finalist, the Roosters' Millie Elliott.

"Just someone that knows the game and what we've been through.

"We try to shape our game exactly [how] the men do, but there's nothing saying we have to just follow in those footsteps.

"We can go in a different direction, we can do what we want to do and what's best for the [NRLW] players and the staff."

Ali Brigginshaw was given a guard of honour for Brisbane's last home game. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

The women's game is currently managed by the chief executive of the NRL. In contrast, the AFLW has always had its own dedicated leadership, currently headed by Laura Kane.

It was not the only major innovation suggested at today's fan event, with tributes to Brigginshaw also on the agenda.

"She will be remembered in the game for such a long time, and I really hope that they name an award after Ali," Broncos coach Scott Prince said.

The 2020 Dally M medallist has captained her state and country and now leaves behind a legacy that even her fiercest rivals admire.

"Ali's been a pioneer of our game for a very long time now, and I've been really lucky to know Ali for a number of years and play with her and experience her as a leader as well," Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly said.

Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly paid credit to the retiring Ali Brigginshaw. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

She also shared plenty of praise for her own retiring teammates Corban Baxter and Elliott, the 2022 Dally M medallist.

"[Millie] never stops; she's always putting her best foot forward. She promotes the game in such a positive and respectful light that so many young girls look up to.

"Corban, she's the most humble, beautiful human that I think has just put such a landmark on this game."

Meanwhile, the Roosters will make a last-second decision on winger Jayme Fressard as she races the clock to have her shoulder right for grand final day.

The Blues representative picked up a shoulder injury in last week's win over Canberra and did not return to the field after half-time.

A final decision will be made after the captain's run tomorrow, with coach John Strange rating Fressard a "50-50" chance of playing.

"A little niggle, a few fitness tests to still get through, but hopefully looking good," Strange said.

"I just really want to be present this week and do everything that I need to do to be the best athlete as possible."

World.title: ‘I’ll try and teach him a couple of things’: Lachie Neale becomes a Magpie, could make Nick Daicos even more dominant
World.content:
Triple-premiership Lion and two-time Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale has officially joined Collingwood on a three-year deal.

The Lions will receive a compensation pick in return for Neale, a free agent, while the Pies are expected to complete the trade for star forward Jesse Hogan and for the transfer of club legend Scott Pendlebury on Monday.

A source familiar with the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Hogan, who has to be traded because he is not eligible for free agency at the Giants, would likely be swapped for a fourth-round pick. The Magpies have Sydney’s fourth-round choice this year.

Jesse Hogan will give the Pies a genuine focal point deep inside their forward 50. Getty Images

Pendlebury, who is headed to the Gold Coast on a four-year deal (two playing, two coaching), is also likely to be traded for a fourth-round pick from the Suns. This would avoid Gold Coast diluting their compensation for Ben King, who is headed to the Hawks as a free agent.

The Magpies have also been linked with Richmond’s Jayden Short, but sources told this masthead Collingwood and Richmond are yet to have any formal discussions. He is contracted for a further two years.

The Suns have targeted young Hawk Aidan Schubert for a separate deal that would compliment the club’s exchange of King as a free agent. Schubert, who has shown promise at Box Hill, has little prospect of a regular AFL game next year, given King’s arrival, the re-contracting of Calsher Dear for two more years, the four-year commitment of seasoned key forward Mitch Lewis, and veteran star Jack Gunston continuing on.

World.title: The budget ChatGPT rival that could change AI
World.content:
TechnologyAI The budget ChatGPT rival that could change AI James Titcomb October 2, 2026 — 7:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Diogo Almeida was one of the fathers of ChatGPT, but he believes his creation has failed to deliver. “It’s not leading to an AI-based economic revolution, which is what the early people really wanted,” he told an audience earlier this year. TypeSafe chief Diogo Almeida is taking on OpenAI. Rather than simply lament his failure, Almeida has done something about it. In the last week, Jev – his low-cost AI system – has become a viral sensation, prompting rumours of a $US10 billion ($14.4 billion) valuation, as well as a string of copycats. Jev’s developer, TypeSafe, says the system is both hundreds of times cheaper and faster than the “frontier” models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, and designed for use by machines, rather than humans.



Almeida – recognisable by a trademark pink fluffy coat that he says he purchased on Temu for $US20 – believes Jev could displace ChatGPT and Claude, and upend the two trillion-dollar companies. He is now at the vanguard of a wave of low-cost AI systems that, if successful, could rewrite the rules of the booming AI industry. Related Article Opinion

AI I owe an AI panic sceptic a beer. But she was only half right David Swan Technology editor Almeida, a maths genius raised in Manila in the Philippines, worked at the Google Brain AI lab before joining OpenAI, interrupted by an 18-month sabbatical – much of which he spent playing fantasy video games. At OpenAI, he pioneered the training technique known as reinforcement learning from human feedback, in which bots improve based on how humans rate their answers. The procedure was used to create ChatGPT, which launched in 2022 as the first AI system able to hold a conversation and answer questions.



But chatbots like ChatGPT, which produce results in text, place extraordinary demands on computing resources. “Language models” such as ChatGPT or Claude produce complex strings of text to reason through questions, and queries can take several seconds or even minutes for a response. Humans might be willing to wait a few seconds for a chatbot answer. But increasingly, AI’s users are other machines: a customer service system deciding where to route email complaints; an automated recruitment system screening CVs; or a bank’s compliance software assessing transactions for fraud. For these cases, tolerance for delay is lower. Loading Jev, released this month, produces answers in nanoseconds. Instead of answering with words, it responds with numbers, for example assigning a probability that a bank payment is fraudulent. This makes it orders of magnitude faster and cheaper than rival systems. At a time when corporate customers are seeking to rein in staff spending on AI systems, TypeSafe says Jev delivers results 194 times faster and 445 times cheaper than the best OpenAI and Claude systems. One demo shows the model working fast enough to control the video game Doom. In the real world, the concept could be applied to controlling robots fast enough for them to become useful.



Since the system was released, incessant demand has forced it to suspend sign-ups, and reports have suggested the company’s $US200 million valuation could rise to $US10 billion. Almeida has said investors are “battering down our door”. Vercel, a company that provides software development tools, says Jev became the fastest-adopted AI model in its history after launch. Related Article Opinion

AI Billion-dollar losses but worth $2.9 trillion? The mind-boggling maths of AI Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Jev’s own staying power is up for debate. Within days, a cluster of copycat systems has emerged built on the same idea (one, unimaginatively, is called “Kev”). But if a swath of AI usage moves from expensive frontier systems to fast, budget models, it could puncture the investment case for OpenAI and Anthropic, both of which are planning to go public in the coming months. HSBC’s analysts said that the system had the potential to deliver a market sell-off similar to the DeepSeek market crash at the start of last year, which sent shares in Nvidia, AMD and Google tumbling on fears that it would lead demand for computing resources to crater.



“The prospect of a new class of AI models that are much cheaper and faster could lead to a resurgence of market fears about AI monetisation,” they said, although they added that those fears would be misplaced. Almeida has predicted that his system will lead to a massive expansion in AI usage. Jev comes from the Jevons paradox, the phenomenon named after the British economist William Stanley Jevons, who observed that when coal use became more efficient, demand for it went up. If the same is true when it comes to AI, then Jev could keep the boom alive. The expensive models it replaces might be collateral damage – Almeida’s earlier creation among them. World.title: ‘We need a Netflix series’: Calisthenics competitors warm up for their grand final day
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life ‘We need a Netflix series’: Calisthenics competitors warm up for their grand final day Carolyn Webb October 2, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Sophie Day tells people that her hobby is calisthenics, the recurring issue is that the response is usually “What’s that”? “We need a Netflix series to put us on the map,” Day says, promising that a documentary capturing their hard-slog rehearsals, the backstage drama and impeccable hair, make-up and spray tans would be “a good watch”. Rachel Fenton (left), a Regent Calisthenic College senior coach, pictured with performer Sophie Day in her freearm costume in St Kilda. Joe Armao A physically demanding team sport that was invented locally and runs in families, calisthenics combines dance with acrobatics, marching and use of apparatus such as rods and clubs. The standards and sacrifices required at the senior level can be brutal.



Day has driven a round trip of 220 kilometres from her home in Geelong to Boronia, where her team trains, three times this week, to attend practice. Sometimes training with her team, Regent Calisthenic College, lasts for up to four hours meaning she gets home at 11.30pm. But Day is hoping her efforts will pay off on Sunday at the Palais Theatre in St Kilda, where Regent will take on five other clubs in the calisthenics state championships, in the most elite level, CaliChamp. Siena Tainsh with her partner, North Melbourne AFL player Zane Duursma, at the 2024 Brownlow Medal night. Getty Images It’s the calisthenics equivalent of the AFL grand final. The rivalry is fierce and expectations sky-high, but sometimes things happen that are out of your control. At last year’s event, Siena Tainsh, from Ceres Calisthenics Club – a model and girlfriend of North Melbourne AFL footballer Zane Duursma – injured her knee while performing on stage. (Tainsh has recovered and will compete this Sunday.)



Calisthenics combines dance with acrobatics, marching and use of apparatus such as rods and clubs. From left to right, Darci Gurney, Jayna Soh and April Henwood from Regent Calisthenic College. Joe Armao Unlike mainstream sports like AFL where players earn six and seven-figure salaries, elite calisthenics participants do it for the love, and have day jobs. Day, who has been a calisthenics girl since she was five, works as a police custody officer and estimates she spends about $3000 annually to take part in the sport. Regent Calisthenic College team member Sophie Day, pictured at her day job is a police custody officer. Having moved to Geelong from Mount Gambier in 2021, Day joined Regent, despite the long drives, after admiring the passion and artistry of the club’s routines, which she watched online.



Brooke Synnott, Regent’s co-principal, said her club was “probably in the best position” to win on Sunday since its revival in 2009 after a 12-year closure. Sophie Day competing in calisthenics in Mount Gambier, South Australia, age five, as a child, circa 2008. Regent was runner-up at last year’s state championships. And out of the three major senior competitions so far this year, Regent has won one, and came second in another. Brooke’s grandmother, the late Enid Feltham, founded Regent in Balwyn, in Melbourne’s east, in 1939, and taught for 58 years before retiring. In the last 20 of those years, Enid’s daughter Diane Synnott coached the senior team to 18 wins at the then pinnacle South Street competitions in Ballarat.



But by 1997 the pair were exhausted, says Brooke, and folded the club. Then aged 16, Brooke says she was “devastated” but forged a successful career in dance and musicals. In 2009, Brooke and Diane decided to reopen Regent. Brooke said she wanted to try teaching and also says it was “in the blood”. Family tradition: Regent Calisthenic College founder Enid Feltham (centre), pictured in 2012 with her daughter, Diane Synnott (left), and granddaughter Brooke Synnott (right). Brooke said a win this Sunday “would be hugely satisfying for everyone who has been with us since we reopened”.
