World.title: Mental health watchdog secretly puts a line through vital investigations
World.content:
Victoria’s mental health watchdog stopped investigating systemic issues including the availability of beds for young patients and the illegal use of restraints after successive state government cuts to its powers, budget and staff. Outraged mental health groups have warned of major safety issues for vulnerable Victorians and are demanding the state government explain who is now overseeing the mental health system, after an investigation by The Age uncovered a prolonged undermining of the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission (MHWC). Hundreds of pages of confidential documents outline the impact of budget cuts and legislative overhauls inside the MHWC, culminating in its December 2025 decision to scale back investigations into systemic failings that impact thousands of vulnerable people relying on Victoria’s psychiatric services. In recent months, The Age has laid bare a system in crisis, with two recent youth suicide clusters, services failing to meet their targets for admitting acutely mentally unwell patients, escalating violence against workers, and the resignation of the fly-in, fly-out boss of the state’s flagship youth mental health service. The MHWC was established in 2022 as an independent watchdog to monitor the government’s progress in implementing the mental health royal commission’s recommendations, as well as systemic issues and complaints about mental health services. Legislation demanded it be headed by four independent commissioners.



An Instagram post from the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission on April 28, 2026 – the day an act of parliament eliminated the role of the commissioners. But changes to that legislation introduced to parliament on December 4, 2025, sought to replace the MHWC’s independent leaders with a single minister-appointed commissioner. New laws also limited the watchdog’s remit to investigate the government’s post-royal commission reforms and systemic failings, and instead required it to focus on complaints about individual health services. When the soon-to-be-axed commissioners met on December 18, 2025 – a fortnight after the legislative amendments were introduced to parliament – they literally put a line through major systemic issues they understood they were losing jurisdiction to examine. Internal records from that meeting, seen by The Age, reveal the commissioners and executives discussed their diminishing capabilities and how they would reprioritise the issues they would continue to scrutinise, and those that would instead be placed on a watch list or ignored altogether.



“Legislative changes are likely to see the remit of the MHWC focus on systemic issues arising from complaints and investigations (ie focus on service providers) likely be set out in a ministerial letter of expectations provided to the Commission by the Minister for Mental Health,” the MHWC’s December 18 meeting heard. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Rewritten mental health report scrubs critical findings, doubles progress “The commission has a legislative and moral obligation to review these issues and progress those that warrant further exploration and align to the commission’s review function as set out in the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022. “Changes within the MHWC including budget constraints mean very limited resourcing will be available to support process to identify and prioritise systemic issues or conduct systemic reviews or inquiries.” Through its “Interim Approach to Addressing Systemic Issues”, the meeting worked through the MHWC’s list of priority systemic issues and put a line through seven major areas it believed it no longer had the power to examine.



Those scrubbed out included: the rollout of new dedicated mental health beds for young people, particularly in rural areas; pay disparities between mental health workers amid a workforce crisis; the impact of working with children check requirements for drug and alcohol workers; and the use of restrictive practices outside the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act. The commissioners were left with a colour-coded table of priorities, including a purple “short list” of issues they deemed suitable for inquiries in the next six to 12 months. They included difficulties accessing alcohol and drug services; patients being chemically restrained; and the misuse of hospital “code grey” security procedures. Issues listed as blue were consigned to a “watching brief” rather than receiving immediate examination. They included the availability of existing inpatient mental health beds for young people; services not taking carer complaints seriously; legal risks when patients or staff are harmed; a review of Koori mental health liaison officers; the frequency of patients being discharged into homelessness; the use of code greys to prevent patients “absconding”; and follow-ups for people denied access to mental health services. The priority list also included a teal category for ad hoc issues – such as requiring all mental health services to hold security camera footage for longer – which would generate a simple response, such as a letter.



The final green category would see direct requests receive an immediate response, such as endorsing another organisation’s campaign or providing a comment. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health ‘Genuine life and death’: Emergency departments pushed to the brink by mental health surge Even when it did have full powers to investigate any systemic issue the MHWC failed to launch a single own-motion investigation, the watchdog conceded in its 2024-25 annual report. As a consequence, it had pledged to identify a list of appropriate issues to examine. After their remit was cut, the commissioners’ “Interim Approach to Addressing Systemic Issues” was intended to scale back that list further to hold the fort from December until the health minister appointed a permanent mental health commissioner. But within a month, the MHWC’s ability to safeguard even the parts of the system it still had jurisdiction over was also buckling.



At their January 29, 2026 governance meeting, MHWC leaders shared concerns that high vacancy rates in the complaints and resolutions team were impacting performance standards, as each resolution officer dealt with between 25 and 30 cases. Mitigation controls had been put in place to address “psychosocial risks” for those staff, the meeting heard. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health ‘Not what the royal commission intended’: The missing mental health windfall Brief notes from the ensuing discussion “voiced that is not a reasonable expectation for complaints and resolutions staff to continue to meet the benchmarks and performance standards set for the previous larger staffing levels”. “AB [commissioner Anabel Brebner] emphasised the need of temporary revised benchmarks and clear messaging to staff on expectations in the current state,” the discussion notes continued. The meeting resolved to notify the Department of Health it had moved its benchmarks to reflect its diminishing situation, and that “there is no expectation set on current staffing levels to absorb additional work to the current workload”.



When The Age this week questioned the MHWC about scaling back investigations, it conceded it had “navigated a period of significant organisational and governance change following the introduction of the new legislative framework, alongside the impacts of broader fiscal pressures across the public sector”. In a statement, the MHWC maintained it upheld its independent role while adapting to forced changes and remained focused on handling complaints; monitoring and reporting on system performance; and reporting on the implementation of the royal commission’s recommendations. Victoria’s new Mental Health and Wellbeing Commissioner Jennifer Black – who took up her role this week after being appointed by Health Minister Ingrid Stitt – said she was focused on working with the state government to ensure the commission was well-placed to deliver its functions and drive change. “The commission plays an important role in protecting rights, and it is vital that it is positioned to effectively perform its core functions, to support positive outcomes for all Victorians who access the public mental health and wellbeing system,” Black said.



A Department of Health spokesperson said the MHWC remained an independent and critical part of Victoria’s mental health oversight framework. Mental Health Victoria chief executive Phillipa Thomas. “Recent changes strengthen leadership and accountability, focusing the commission on where it can have the greatest impact – safeguarding rights, resolving complaints and helping improve the mental health system,” the spokesperson said. Victorian Mental Illness Awareness Council chief executive Vrinda Edan said some of the sector’s biggest problems were systemic and not necessarily visible through individual complaints. “What’s important to us is the consequence for independent oversight. Whatever the underlying reasons for the changes, any reduction in the capacity to identify and report systemic problems should be taken seriously,” Edan said.



Phillipa Thomas, the chief executive of peak body for public and private health providers Mental Health Victoria, said the latest revelations raised concerns about the MHWC’s ability to respond to complaints, with some of the issues on short lists “alarming”. “These documents clearly foreshadow planning for the removal of mechanisms for independent oversight and accountability of royal commission implementation and contradicts reassurances provided to the sector,” she said. Mental Health Legal Centre chief executive Charlotte Jones said revelations that the MHWC kept a waiting list of systemic issues, rather than immediately acting or launching investigations into matters it was aware of, showed it needed an overhaul. “Where are these investigations which should have helped prevent incidents and recommendations to raise standards? A budget of $750,000.00 per inquiry without any detail as to how this was assessed – and we can only recall one report,” Jones said. “They were as siloed as the system they were working in. These failures highlight why we need an adult safeguarder who oversees the safeguards in the system to check these are working.” If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636.

World.title: Forget your Mazda 3: All the cool girls want old cars now
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsCars Forget your Mazda 3: All the cool girls want old cars now Susannah Guthrie October 2, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bonnie didn’t know she had a dream car until she first laid eyes on it. The 27-year-old Pilates instructor, who has chosen to withhold her surname for privacy reasons, had previously driven a series of small hatchbacks that were perfectly serviceable, if a little forgettable. “I was driving a Mazda 3, and there was nothing wrong with it, but I was sick of it,” she recalls. “I’d been talking to my partner for a while about what I wanted in a car, and I couldn’t really verbalise it. But when I saw the Pajero, I knew it was my dream car.” Bonnie, 27, and her beloved 1991 Mitsubishi Pajero.



She fell head over heels for a bright red short-wheelbase Mitsubishi Pajero that’s older than she is. The two-door, diesel-powered 4WD from 1992 has a manual transmission and not much else. “When I bought it three years ago, it didn’t have seats or carpet on the floor, and the speedometer and the tachometer didn’t work,” Bonnie laughs. “It still doesn’t even have airbags.” While her friends drive modern SUVs with cruise control and blind-spot monitoring, Bonnie says she wouldn’t trade her vintage ride for all the mod-cons in the world. “Honestly, I don’t think I was a very good driver in the past, and now, having a connection to my car, I’m a much better driver,” she admits. “Because I really enjoy it, I’ve asked my partner lots of questions about how it works and how to fix things. He’s taught me how to service it, so I do that on my own too.”



Bonnie is one of an increasing raft of young women opting for old, off-road-focused cars over modern SUVs, hatchbacks and electric vehicles. In June, a headline in The Wall Street Journal declared, “The Expensive Accessory Every ‘Hot Girl’ Wants: An Old, Loud SUV”, with journalist Chavie Lieber pointing to the booming market for secondhand Ford Broncos and Land Rovers, driven by affluent young women. It turns out a similar phenomenon is playing out in Australia, but swap Ford Broncos for Toyota LandCruisers and “affluent young women” for savvy creatives with a thirst for serious adventure. An antidote to ‘disposable culture’ Stuart Amm, owner of Sydney-based restoration company Aussie Motor Group, has witnessed this trend in real time over the last two years, and says young female owners now account for roughly 25 per cent of his company’s work.



“Specifically for women, they’ve been exposed to the car scene via social media, and they see the beauty, the design and the story of these vehicles and want to be involved,” Amm says. Related Article Electric vehicles Looks like a Porsche and priced like a Kia? This may be the most talked-about new car in Australia “They love to continually refine and update their vehicles, so they’re falling into that pattern of the old-school revhead, but coming at it from a different angle.” Amm says his female customers tend to be successful business owners with a creative background who are heavily involved in their car’s design and customisation. Most recently, Amm worked with Ngoc Dang, the owner of Melbourne-based events company Ed&Ed Studio, to customise her 2015 Land Rover Defender.



“One of the biggest things that drew me to my car was that it was a manual, and it’s really difficult to buy a manual car new,” Dang explains. “But the first time I actually drove it, I was like, ‘What was I thinking?!‘. It has such a heavy clutch, and it’s clunky to drive, but you get used to it. Those are the things that make you feel like you’re really driving.” While Dang has kept the manual transmission, she’s worked with Amm to add Apple CarPlay and sound dampening so she can take work phone calls on the go, and has had the interior fitted out in a striking caramel-coloured leather. “I don’t think I’ve stopped – the best thing about the Defender is you can continually keep working on the small details.” Amm concurs: “These cars are the antidote to disposable culture. And there’s something beautiful about bringing something back to new – there’s a pride there.”



It doesn’t hurt that cars like the Defender or Toyota LandCruisers are just as capable as they are aesthetically pleasing. “It’s a cool car to take to the beach or to your highlands farm, but it looks just as good parked outside a hotel next to a modern Range Rover – they cross worlds really well,” Amm says. Jaycee Wilson and “Saltee the Troopy”. @shannonkellycreative Going off-road and offline For Madelyn Holmes, a 31-year-old photographer from Queensland, it was this duality that kick-started her love affair with vintage Land Rovers.



“My original interest was photography and nature, and I realised that 4WDs are the perfect way to access the more remote locations,” she says. “It’s great to have a capable vehicle, but they’ve also got such a character to them, and they’re photogenic too,” she says. For Holmes, the bare-bones design was a plus rather than a minus, allowing her to disconnect from her screen-heavy lifestyle. “I work in photography and graphic design, and I’m surrounded by cameras and phones and computers, so I like that it’s stripped back.” Holmes is a seasoned Land Rover enthusiast – she’s owned three in total and currently runs a 2015 Defender 110 and a 1973 Land Rover Series III – but says she’s faced backlash from male enthusiasts not ready to welcome young women into the fold.



“At the start of my experience in Land Rover world, I had a lot of people saying ‘Wow, I really like your boyfriend’s car,’” she recalls. Related Article Collecting Why Gen Z wants a slice of this multimillion-dollar ’90s hobby “When I was trying to buy my Series III I had some people push back and say, ‘I’m not going to sell this car to you,’ purely based on my profile picture and name.” Holmes started her popular Instagram account @ladyinalandy as a tongue-in-cheek response to the sexist comments. In reality, it’s younger buyers like Holmes that are seeing models like the Land Rover Defender and Toyota LandCruiser hold their value incredibly well on the used market.



Impressively, a 2012 Land Rover Defender on average retains more than 100 per cent of its original value when sold on today’s used market, according to data from automotive intelligence firm AutoGrab. Toyota LandCruisers are a similarly solid buy, with data showing two-to-four-year-old models are regularly selling for the same amount as they cost new. For Jaycee Wilson, a LandCruiser Troop Carrier or “Troopy” was the only option when buying her first car. “I fell in love with Troopy because I saw the possibility and capability. I grew up camping and my family is very outdoorsy, so I wanted something that could take me anywhere and that I could sleep in – like a little house on wheels,” she explains. Jaycee Wilson says while her troopy wasn’t the most sensible choice in first car, she wouldn’t change a thing. @shannonkellycreative



The Sunshine Coast local purchased her 2006 LandCruiser Troop Carrier from a French tourist when she was just a 17-year-old with freshly minted P-plates. She worked with her father, a cabinet maker, to slowly turn it into the portable home of her dreams, complete with a fridge, oven, pop-up tables, a pantry and even a bathroom with outdoor shower. Looking back on her early days as a novice driver, Wilson admits the Troopy “wasn’t the most sensible choice of car”. “It’s pretty big for a first car. I’m quite limited as to where I can park a lot of the time – underground carparks are always a no for me. And it’s not the most economical car to run,” she admits. “I don’t see it as a sacrifice though, I’d much rather have the experiences I’ve had.”



The ultimate statement purchase Wilson has driven her car – nicknamed “Saltee the Troopy” in full – almost 400,000km in four years. Like Bonnie, she’s learned to service the car herself and has grown accustomed to the manual roll-down windows (which occasionally require WD-40) and the air con system, which sporadically breaks down. “I definitely get a lot of comments and reactions to my car,” she admits. “People are surprised that it’s actually my car and I’ve done all the stuff to it myself.” Thankfully, the reactions have been overwhelmingly positive. “I have my Instagram handle on the back, so lots of people post and tag me if they see me on the road,” she says.



However, the best interactions are always with other young women her age. “My favourite is that I get a lot of car-fulls of young girls driving past me,” Wilson explains. “I’ll look over and they’re waving at me, and then I’ll see they’re holding up messages on their phone saying things like, ‘WE LOVE YOUR CAR!’” That, Amm says, is perhaps the crux of the trend – the ability to stand out from an increasingly homogenous crowd. “I still think a big part of this anybody can buy a brand-new SUV, but a restored classic makes a bigger statement,” he says.



“Generally, most people will look at that and say, ‘Now that’s cool’.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Bruce Baird, the Liberal stalwart who fought for refugees, has died aged 84
World.content:
The former Liberal politician Bruce Baird, who served in state and federal parliaments and played a key role in securing the Sydney 2000 Olympics, has died while on an overseas trip. He was 84. Several sources close to Baird have confirmed the keen ocean swimmer died in Singapore after a fall on his way home from a European holiday. Former NSW and federal Liberal MP Bruce Baird has died aged 84. James Alcock / AFR Baird is the father of former NSW premier Mike Baird, who led the state from 2014 to 2017, journalist Julia Baird and Steve who works in the not-for-proft sector. His wife Judy died in 2021. As the state MP for the now-abolished seat of Northcott, Baird was instrumental in winning the Olympics for Sydney while at Macquarie Street, where he was minister for tourism, roads, environment and transport.



He was elected Northcott in 1984, and held the seat for 11 years, before moving to federal politics when he was elected to the southern Sydney seat of Cook in 1998. He represented the electorate for nine years, retiring before the 2007 election and making way for future prime minister Scott Morrison to take the seat. Mike Baird greeting his father, Bruce, on NSW state election day in 2015. Andrew Meares Former premier Nick Greiner and Baird embrace in 1993 after the announcement Sydney would host the 2000 Olympic Games. Fairfax Archives Baird was never a minister in federal parliament. He was overlooked for a frontbench position in the Howard government because of his stance on asylum seekers, which went against then prime minister John Howard’s policy at the time, as well as his closeness to Howard’s treasurer and nemesis, Peter Costello.



In his valedictory speech, according to a report in the publication Sydney Anglicans in 2007, Baird paid tribute to a young man called Adnan, who was the first of 50 asylum cases that Baird became personally involved with. Baird with former NSW premier Nick Greiner in 1992. Fairfax Former prime minister John Howard and Baird in federal parliament in 2005. Fairfax Baird took the case to then immigration minister Phillip Ruddock who used his ministerial powers to grant Adnan refugee status. The young Iranian went on to study engineering and was a translator for his Farsi-speaking congregation at Guildford Anglican Church. “This for me illustrates why a compassionate approach is so important,” Baird told his parliamentary colleagues.



Before his political career, Baird’s was assistant trade commissioner at the Australian embassy in Germany in the early 1970s, followed by a three-year stint as trade commissioner in New York. Bruce Baird was a regular swimmer at the Bold and the Beautiful swim squad, which swims between Manly Beach and Shelly Beach. James Brickwood Baird swam in the “Bold & Beautiful” swim squad, which regularly exercised in the waters off Manly and Shelly Beach. He was described as a “great mate” to those in the group by squad organiser Peter Anthony. “Bruce was a much-loved part of our swim community and a wonderful friend to so many of us,” Anthony told members on Friday. “Our thoughts are with his family and everyone who loved him.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: The budget ChatGPT rival that could change AI
World.content:
TechnologyAI The budget ChatGPT rival that could change AI James Titcomb October 2, 2026 — 7:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Diogo Almeida was one of the fathers of ChatGPT, but he believes his creation has failed to deliver. “It’s not leading to an AI-based economic revolution, which is what the early people really wanted,” he told an audience earlier this year. TypeSafe chief Diogo Almeida is taking on OpenAI. Rather than simply lament his failure, Almeida has done something about it. In the last week, Jev – his low-cost AI system – has become a viral sensation, prompting rumours of a $US10 billion ($14.4 billion) valuation, as well as a string of copycats. Jev’s developer, TypeSafe, says the system is both hundreds of times cheaper and faster than the “frontier” models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, and designed for use by machines, rather than humans.



Almeida – recognisable by a trademark pink fluffy coat that he says he purchased on Temu for $US20 – believes Jev could displace ChatGPT and Claude, and upend the two trillion-dollar companies. He is now at the vanguard of a wave of low-cost AI systems that, if successful, could rewrite the rules of the booming AI industry. Related Article Opinion

AI I owe an AI panic sceptic a beer. But she was only half right David Swan Technology editor Almeida, a maths genius raised in Manila in the Philippines, worked at the Google Brain AI lab before joining OpenAI, interrupted by an 18-month sabbatical – much of which he spent playing fantasy video games. At OpenAI, he pioneered the training technique known as reinforcement learning from human feedback, in which bots improve based on how humans rate their answers. The procedure was used to create ChatGPT, which launched in 2022 as the first AI system able to hold a conversation and answer questions.



But chatbots like ChatGPT, which produce results in text, place extraordinary demands on computing resources. “Language models” such as ChatGPT or Claude produce complex strings of text to reason through questions, and queries can take several seconds or even minutes for a response. Humans might be willing to wait a few seconds for a chatbot answer. But increasingly, AI’s users are other machines: a customer service system deciding where to route email complaints; an automated recruitment system screening CVs; or a bank’s compliance software assessing transactions for fraud. For these cases, tolerance for delay is lower. Loading Jev, released this month, produces answers in nanoseconds. Instead of answering with words, it responds with numbers, for example assigning a probability that a bank payment is fraudulent. This makes it orders of magnitude faster and cheaper than rival systems. At a time when corporate customers are seeking to rein in staff spending on AI systems, TypeSafe says Jev delivers results 194 times faster and 445 times cheaper than the best OpenAI and Claude systems. One demo shows the model working fast enough to control the video game Doom. In the real world, the concept could be applied to controlling robots fast enough for them to become useful.



Since the system was released, incessant demand has forced it to suspend sign-ups, and reports have suggested the company’s $US200 million valuation could rise to $US10 billion. Almeida has said investors are “battering down our door”. Vercel, a company that provides software development tools, says Jev became the fastest-adopted AI model in its history after launch. Related Article Opinion

AI Billion-dollar losses but worth $2.9 trillion? The mind-boggling maths of AI Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Jev’s own staying power is up for debate. Within days, a cluster of copycat systems has emerged built on the same idea (one, unimaginatively, is called “Kev”). But if a swath of AI usage moves from expensive frontier systems to fast, budget models, it could puncture the investment case for OpenAI and Anthropic, both of which are planning to go public in the coming months. HSBC’s analysts said that the system had the potential to deliver a market sell-off similar to the DeepSeek market crash at the start of last year, which sent shares in Nvidia, AMD and Google tumbling on fears that it would lead demand for computing resources to crater.



“The prospect of a new class of AI models that are much cheaper and faster could lead to a resurgence of market fears about AI monetisation,” they said, although they added that those fears would be misplaced. Almeida has predicted that his system will lead to a massive expansion in AI usage. Jev comes from the Jevons paradox, the phenomenon named after the British economist William Stanley Jevons, who observed that when coal use became more efficient, demand for it went up. If the same is true when it comes to AI, then Jev could keep the boom alive. The expensive models it replaces might be collateral damage – Almeida’s earlier creation among them. World.title: ‘We need a Netflix series’: Calisthenics competitors warm up for their grand final day
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life ‘We need a Netflix series’: Calisthenics competitors warm up for their grand final day Carolyn Webb October 2, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Sophie Day tells people that her hobby is calisthenics, the recurring issue is that the response is usually “What’s that”? “We need a Netflix series to put us on the map,” Day says, promising that a documentary capturing their hard-slog rehearsals, the backstage drama and impeccable hair, make-up and spray tans would be “a good watch”. Rachel Fenton (left), a Regent Calisthenic College senior coach, pictured with performer Sophie Day in her freearm costume in St Kilda. Joe Armao A physically demanding team sport that was invented locally and runs in families, calisthenics combines dance with acrobatics, marching and use of apparatus such as rods and clubs. The standards and sacrifices required at the senior level can be brutal.



Day has driven a round trip of 220 kilometres from her home in Geelong to Boronia, where her team trains, three times this week, to attend practice. Sometimes training with her team, Regent Calisthenic College, lasts for up to four hours meaning she gets home at 11.30pm. But Day is hoping her efforts will pay off on Sunday at the Palais Theatre in St Kilda, where Regent will take on five other clubs in the calisthenics state championships, in the most elite level, CaliChamp. Siena Tainsh with her partner, North Melbourne AFL player Zane Duursma, at the 2024 Brownlow Medal night. Getty Images It’s the calisthenics equivalent of the AFL grand final. The rivalry is fierce and expectations sky-high, but sometimes things happen that are out of your control. At last year’s event, Siena Tainsh, from Ceres Calisthenics Club – a model and girlfriend of North Melbourne AFL footballer Zane Duursma – injured her knee while performing on stage. (Tainsh has recovered and will compete this Sunday.)



Calisthenics combines dance with acrobatics, marching and use of apparatus such as rods and clubs. From left to right, Darci Gurney, Jayna Soh and April Henwood from Regent Calisthenic College. Joe Armao Unlike mainstream sports like AFL where players earn six and seven-figure salaries, elite calisthenics participants do it for the love, and have day jobs. Day, who has been a calisthenics girl since she was five, works as a police custody officer and estimates she spends about $3000 annually to take part in the sport. Regent Calisthenic College team member Sophie Day, pictured at her day job is a police custody officer. Having moved to Geelong from Mount Gambier in 2021, Day joined Regent, despite the long drives, after admiring the passion and artistry of the club’s routines, which she watched online.



Brooke Synnott, Regent’s co-principal, said her club was “probably in the best position” to win on Sunday since its revival in 2009 after a 12-year closure. Sophie Day competing in calisthenics in Mount Gambier, South Australia, age five, as a child, circa 2008. Regent was runner-up at last year’s state championships. And out of the three major senior competitions so far this year, Regent has won one, and came second in another. Brooke’s grandmother, the late Enid Feltham, founded Regent in Balwyn, in Melbourne’s east, in 1939, and taught for 58 years before retiring. In the last 20 of those years, Enid’s daughter Diane Synnott coached the senior team to 18 wins at the then pinnacle South Street competitions in Ballarat.



But by 1997 the pair were exhausted, says Brooke, and folded the club. Then aged 16, Brooke says she was “devastated” but forged a successful career in dance and musicals. In 2009, Brooke and Diane decided to reopen Regent. Brooke said she wanted to try teaching and also says it was “in the blood”. Family tradition: Regent Calisthenic College founder Enid Feltham (centre), pictured in 2012 with her daughter, Diane Synnott (left), and granddaughter Brooke Synnott (right). Brooke said a win this Sunday “would be hugely satisfying for everyone who has been with us since we reopened”. World.title: Mental health watchdog secretly puts a line through vital investigations
World.content:
Victoria’s mental health watchdog stopped investigating systemic issues including the availability of beds for young patients and the illegal use of restraints after successive state government cuts to its powers, budget and staff. Outraged mental health groups have warned of major safety issues for vulnerable Victorians and are demanding the state government explain who is now overseeing the mental health system, after an investigation by The Age uncovered a prolonged undermining of the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission (MHWC). Hundreds of pages of confidential documents outline the impact of budget cuts and legislative overhauls inside the MHWC, culminating in its December 2025 decision to scale back investigations into systemic failings that impact thousands of vulnerable people relying on Victoria’s psychiatric services. In recent months, The Age has laid bare a system in crisis, with two recent youth suicide clusters, services failing to meet their targets for admitting acutely mentally unwell patients, escalating violence against workers, and the resignation of the fly-in, fly-out boss of the state’s flagship youth mental health service. The MHWC was established in 2022 as an independent watchdog to monitor the government’s progress in implementing the mental health royal commission’s recommendations, as well as systemic issues and complaints about mental health services. Legislation demanded it be headed by four independent commissioners.



An Instagram post from the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission on April 28, 2026 – the day an act of parliament eliminated the role of the commissioners. But changes to that legislation introduced to parliament on December 4, 2025, sought to replace the MHWC’s independent leaders with a single minister-appointed commissioner. New laws also limited the watchdog’s remit to investigate the government’s post-royal commission reforms and systemic failings, and instead required it to focus on complaints about individual health services. When the soon-to-be-axed commissioners met on December 18, 2025 – a fortnight after the legislative amendments were introduced to parliament – they literally put a line through major systemic issues they understood they were losing jurisdiction to examine. Internal records from that meeting, seen by The Age, reveal the commissioners and executives discussed their diminishing capabilities and how they would reprioritise the issues they would continue to scrutinise, and those that would instead be placed on a watch list or ignored altogether.



“Legislative changes are likely to see the remit of the MHWC focus on systemic issues arising from complaints and investigations (ie focus on service providers) likely be set out in a ministerial letter of expectations provided to the Commission by the Minister for Mental Health,” the MHWC’s December 18 meeting heard. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Rewritten mental health report scrubs critical findings, doubles progress “The commission has a legislative and moral obligation to review these issues and progress those that warrant further exploration and align to the commission’s review function as set out in the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022. “Changes within the MHWC including budget constraints mean very limited resourcing will be available to support process to identify and prioritise systemic issues or conduct systemic reviews or inquiries.” Through its “Interim Approach to Addressing Systemic Issues”, the meeting worked through the MHWC’s list of priority systemic issues and put a line through seven major areas it believed it no longer had the power to examine.



Those scrubbed out included: the rollout of new dedicated mental health beds for young people, particularly in rural areas; pay disparities between mental health workers amid a workforce crisis; the impact of working with children check requirements for drug and alcohol workers; and the use of restrictive practices outside the Mental Health and Wellbeing Act. The commissioners were left with a colour-coded table of priorities, including a purple “short list” of issues they deemed suitable for inquiries in the next six to 12 months. They included difficulties accessing alcohol and drug services; patients being chemically restrained; and the misuse of hospital “code grey” security procedures. Issues listed as blue were consigned to a “watching brief” rather than receiving immediate examination. They included the availability of existing inpatient mental health beds for young people; services not taking carer complaints seriously; legal risks when patients or staff are harmed; a review of Koori mental health liaison officers; the frequency of patients being discharged into homelessness; the use of code greys to prevent patients “absconding”; and follow-ups for people denied access to mental health services. The priority list also included a teal category for ad hoc issues – such as requiring all mental health services to hold security camera footage for longer – which would generate a simple response, such as a letter.



The final green category would see direct requests receive an immediate response, such as endorsing another organisation’s campaign or providing a comment. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health ‘Genuine life and death’: Emergency departments pushed to the brink by mental health surge Even when it did have full powers to investigate any systemic issue the MHWC failed to launch a single own-motion investigation, the watchdog conceded in its 2024-25 annual report. As a consequence, it had pledged to identify a list of appropriate issues to examine. After their remit was cut, the commissioners’ “Interim Approach to Addressing Systemic Issues” was intended to scale back that list further to hold the fort from December until the health minister appointed a permanent mental health commissioner. But within a month, the MHWC’s ability to safeguard even the parts of the system it still had jurisdiction over was also buckling.



At their January 29, 2026 governance meeting, MHWC leaders shared concerns that high vacancy rates in the complaints and resolutions team were impacting performance standards, as each resolution officer dealt with between 25 and 30 cases. Mitigation controls had been put in place to address “psychosocial risks” for those staff, the meeting heard. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health ‘Not what the royal commission intended’: The missing mental health windfall Brief notes from the ensuing discussion “voiced that is not a reasonable expectation for complaints and resolutions staff to continue to meet the benchmarks and performance standards set for the previous larger staffing levels”. “AB [commissioner Anabel Brebner] emphasised the need of temporary revised benchmarks and clear messaging to staff on expectations in the current state,” the discussion notes continued. The meeting resolved to notify the Department of Health it had moved its benchmarks to reflect its diminishing situation, and that “there is no expectation set on current staffing levels to absorb additional work to the current workload”.



When The Age this week questioned the MHWC about scaling back investigations, it conceded it had “navigated a period of significant organisational and governance change following the introduction of the new legislative framework, alongside the impacts of broader fiscal pressures across the public sector”. In a statement, the MHWC maintained it upheld its independent role while adapting to forced changes and remained focused on handling complaints; monitoring and reporting on system performance; and reporting on the implementation of the royal commission’s recommendations. Victoria’s new Mental Health and Wellbeing Commissioner Jennifer Black – who took up her role this week after being appointed by Health Minister Ingrid Stitt – said she was focused on working with the state government to ensure the commission was well-placed to deliver its functions and drive change. “The commission plays an important role in protecting rights, and it is vital that it is positioned to effectively perform its core functions, to support positive outcomes for all Victorians who access the public mental health and wellbeing system,” Black said.



A Department of Health spokesperson said the MHWC remained an independent and critical part of Victoria’s mental health oversight framework. Mental Health Victoria chief executive Phillipa Thomas. “Recent changes strengthen leadership and accountability, focusing the commission on where it can have the greatest impact – safeguarding rights, resolving complaints and helping improve the mental health system,” the spokesperson said. Victorian Mental Illness Awareness Council chief executive Vrinda Edan said some of the sector’s biggest problems were systemic and not necessarily visible through individual complaints. “What’s important to us is the consequence for independent oversight. Whatever the underlying reasons for the changes, any reduction in the capacity to identify and report systemic problems should be taken seriously,” Edan said.



Phillipa Thomas, the chief executive of peak body for public and private health providers Mental Health Victoria, said the latest revelations raised concerns about the MHWC’s ability to respond to complaints, with some of the issues on short lists “alarming”. “These documents clearly foreshadow planning for the removal of mechanisms for independent oversight and accountability of royal commission implementation and contradicts reassurances provided to the sector,” she said. Mental Health Legal Centre chief executive Charlotte Jones said revelations that the MHWC kept a waiting list of systemic issues, rather than immediately acting or launching investigations into matters it was aware of, showed it needed an overhaul. “Where are these investigations which should have helped prevent incidents and recommendations to raise standards? A budget of $750,000.00 per inquiry without any detail as to how this was assessed – and we can only recall one report,” Jones said. “They were as siloed as the system they were working in. These failures highlight why we need an adult safeguarder who oversees the safeguards in the system to check these are working.” If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636.

World.title: Forget your Mazda 3: All the cool girls want old cars now
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsCars Forget your Mazda 3: All the cool girls want old cars now Susannah Guthrie October 2, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bonnie didn’t know she had a dream car until she first laid eyes on it. The 27-year-old Pilates instructor, who has chosen to withhold her surname for privacy reasons, had previously driven a series of small hatchbacks that were perfectly serviceable, if a little forgettable. “I was driving a Mazda 3, and there was nothing wrong with it, but I was sick of it,” she recalls. “I’d been talking to my partner for a while about what I wanted in a car, and I couldn’t really verbalise it. But when I saw the Pajero, I knew it was my dream car.” Bonnie, 27, and her beloved 1991 Mitsubishi Pajero.



She fell head over heels for a bright red short-wheelbase Mitsubishi Pajero that’s older than she is. The two-door, diesel-powered 4WD from 1992 has a manual transmission and not much else. “When I bought it three years ago, it didn’t have seats or carpet on the floor, and the speedometer and the tachometer didn’t work,” Bonnie laughs. “It still doesn’t even have airbags.” While her friends drive modern SUVs with cruise control and blind-spot monitoring, Bonnie says she wouldn’t trade her vintage ride for all the mod-cons in the world. “Honestly, I don’t think I was a very good driver in the past, and now, having a connection to my car, I’m a much better driver,” she admits. “Because I really enjoy it, I’ve asked my partner lots of questions about how it works and how to fix things. He’s taught me how to service it, so I do that on my own too.”



Bonnie is one of an increasing raft of young women opting for old, off-road-focused cars over modern SUVs, hatchbacks and electric vehicles. In June, a headline in The Wall Street Journal declared, “The Expensive Accessory Every ‘Hot Girl’ Wants: An Old, Loud SUV”, with journalist Chavie Lieber pointing to the booming market for secondhand Ford Broncos and Land Rovers, driven by affluent young women. It turns out a similar phenomenon is playing out in Australia, but swap Ford Broncos for Toyota LandCruisers and “affluent young women” for savvy creatives with a thirst for serious adventure. An antidote to ‘disposable culture’ Stuart Amm, owner of Sydney-based restoration company Aussie Motor Group, has witnessed this trend in real time over the last two years, and says young female owners now account for roughly 25 per cent of his company’s work.



“Specifically for women, they’ve been exposed to the car scene via social media, and they see the beauty, the design and the story of these vehicles and want to be involved,” Amm says. Related Article Electric vehicles Looks like a Porsche and priced like a Kia? This may be the most talked-about new car in Australia “They love to continually refine and update their vehicles, so they’re falling into that pattern of the old-school revhead, but coming at it from a different angle.” Amm says his female customers tend to be successful business owners with a creative background who are heavily involved in their car’s design and customisation. Most recently, Amm worked with Ngoc Dang, the owner of Melbourne-based events company Ed&Ed Studio, to customise her 2015 Land Rover Defender.



“One of the biggest things that drew me to my car was that it was a manual, and it’s really difficult to buy a manual car new,” Dang explains. “But the first time I actually drove it, I was like, ‘What was I thinking?!‘. It has such a heavy clutch, and it’s clunky to drive, but you get used to it. Those are the things that make you feel like you’re really driving.” While Dang has kept the manual transmission, she’s worked with Amm to add Apple CarPlay and sound dampening so she can take work phone calls on the go, and has had the interior fitted out in a striking caramel-coloured leather. “I don’t think I’ve stopped – the best thing about the Defender is you can continually keep working on the small details.” Amm concurs: “These cars are the antidote to disposable culture. And there’s something beautiful about bringing something back to new – there’s a pride there.”



It doesn’t hurt that cars like the Defender or Toyota LandCruisers are just as capable as they are aesthetically pleasing. “It’s a cool car to take to the beach or to your highlands farm, but it looks just as good parked outside a hotel next to a modern Range Rover – they cross worlds really well,” Amm says. Jaycee Wilson and “Saltee the Troopy”. @shannonkellycreative Going off-road and offline For Madelyn Holmes, a 31-year-old photographer from Queensland, it was this duality that kick-started her love affair with vintage Land Rovers.



“My original interest was photography and nature, and I realised that 4WDs are the perfect way to access the more remote locations,” she says. “It’s great to have a capable vehicle, but they’ve also got such a character to them, and they’re photogenic too,” she says. For Holmes, the bare-bones design was a plus rather than a minus, allowing her to disconnect from her screen-heavy lifestyle. “I work in photography and graphic design, and I’m surrounded by cameras and phones and computers, so I like that it’s stripped back.” Holmes is a seasoned Land Rover enthusiast – she’s owned three in total and currently runs a 2015 Defender 110 and a 1973 Land Rover Series III – but says she’s faced backlash from male enthusiasts not ready to welcome young women into the fold.



“At the start of my experience in Land Rover world, I had a lot of people saying ‘Wow, I really like your boyfriend’s car,’” she recalls. Related Article Collecting Why Gen Z wants a slice of this multimillion-dollar ’90s hobby “When I was trying to buy my Series III I had some people push back and say, ‘I’m not going to sell this car to you,’ purely based on my profile picture and name.” Holmes started her popular Instagram account @ladyinalandy as a tongue-in-cheek response to the sexist comments. In reality, it’s younger buyers like Holmes that are seeing models like the Land Rover Defender and Toyota LandCruiser hold their value incredibly well on the used market.



Impressively, a 2012 Land Rover Defender on average retains more than 100 per cent of its original value when sold on today’s used market, according to data from automotive intelligence firm AutoGrab. Toyota LandCruisers are a similarly solid buy, with data showing two-to-four-year-old models are regularly selling for the same amount as they cost new. For Jaycee Wilson, a LandCruiser Troop Carrier or “Troopy” was the only option when buying her first car. “I fell in love with Troopy because I saw the possibility and capability. I grew up camping and my family is very outdoorsy, so I wanted something that could take me anywhere and that I could sleep in – like a little house on wheels,” she explains. Jaycee Wilson says while her troopy wasn’t the most sensible choice in first car, she wouldn’t change a thing. @shannonkellycreative



The Sunshine Coast local purchased her 2006 LandCruiser Troop Carrier from a French tourist when she was just a 17-year-old with freshly minted P-plates. She worked with her father, a cabinet maker, to slowly turn it into the portable home of her dreams, complete with a fridge, oven, pop-up tables, a pantry and even a bathroom with outdoor shower. Looking back on her early days as a novice driver, Wilson admits the Troopy “wasn’t the most sensible choice of car”. “It’s pretty big for a first car. I’m quite limited as to where I can park a lot of the time – underground carparks are always a no for me. And it’s not the most economical car to run,” she admits. “I don’t see it as a sacrifice though, I’d much rather have the experiences I’ve had.”



The ultimate statement purchase Wilson has driven her car – nicknamed “Saltee the Troopy” in full – almost 400,000km in four years. Like Bonnie, she’s learned to service the car herself and has grown accustomed to the manual roll-down windows (which occasionally require WD-40) and the air con system, which sporadically breaks down. “I definitely get a lot of comments and reactions to my car,” she admits. “People are surprised that it’s actually my car and I’ve done all the stuff to it myself.” Thankfully, the reactions have been overwhelmingly positive. “I have my Instagram handle on the back, so lots of people post and tag me if they see me on the road,” she says.



However, the best interactions are always with other young women her age. “My favourite is that I get a lot of car-fulls of young girls driving past me,” Wilson explains. “I’ll look over and they’re waving at me, and then I’ll see they’re holding up messages on their phone saying things like, ‘WE LOVE YOUR CAR!’” That, Amm says, is perhaps the crux of the trend – the ability to stand out from an increasingly homogenous crowd. “I still think a big part of this anybody can buy a brand-new SUV, but a restored classic makes a bigger statement,” he says.



“Generally, most people will look at that and say, ‘Now that’s cool’.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

Walkability, world-class dining, cafes, markets, access to nature, waterside living, festivals, and vibrant nightlife – Melbourne’s inner-city suburbs offer plenty to enjoy. From South Yarra and St Kilda, to Carlton North and Richmond, here are five of the best homes for sale now in inner Melbourne. 680 Drummond Street, Carlton North VIC From the backyard of this inner-city home, you’d never know you’re only around the corner from Rathdowne Village’s restaurants, cafes and wine bars.



The deep backyard is filled with established greenery, creating an oasis you can enjoy from the pergola-covered deck that overlooks it and from the self-contained studio with a kitchenette at the rear. The main residence makes the most of the surroundings with its large, double-glazed windows, high ceilings and double doors that connect the open-plan living and dining to the pergola. Other highlights include the kitchen designed by Golden and a wine cellar. 48 Tivoli Road, South Yarra VIC



This solid brick Victorian home is located on one of South Yarra’s most revered streets and within walking distance of Vogue Shopping Centre, Como Centre and Cinemas, Toorak Road, South Yarra’s boutiques, Yarra River trails and South Yarra station. Renovated, the home honours its past with soaring high ceilings and sash windows, while updates such as an open-plan living area, hydronic heating and a primary bedroom with dual-zoned walk-in robes cater to contemporary living. Outside, landscaped gardens, a pool and a poolside terrace provide outdoor living space. 37 Dalgety Street, St Kilda VIC



A landmark in St Kilda’s architectural history, the largest of the three remaining homes that comprised Lansdowne Terrace has hit the market. Related Article Luxury property Our five favourite luxury homes by the coast for sale Built circa 1857, the tri-level residence has been renovated while retaining much of its period grandeur, evident in its large proportions, high ceilings, engineered oak floors, an arched hallway, elegant formal living and dining rooms, and marble open fireplaces. Outside, the wisteria-wrapped colonnaded walkway leads to the wraparound verandah, setting the tone for what’s inside. The property has five bedrooms, with one opening onto a roof terrace with city views.



12 Park Avenue, Richmond VIC This renovated Federation home sits on the city’s edge, close to the Yarra River, Burnley Park, and a range of schools. Behind the timeless façade, you will find an interior with quality finishes and natural light, designed for family living and entertaining. There are five bedrooms, with the option for a sixth, plus an entertainer’s kitchen with soft-close drawers, V-Zug appliances, a steam oven, a Qasair rangehood, and a Billi tap, plus secured gate access and carport parking for two cars.



Other features include Velux skylights throughout, electric blinds in the bedrooms, a battery-ready solar panel array, hydronic heating, and split-system heating and cooling throughout. Outside, there is a solar- and gas-heated swimming pool. 374 Montague Street, Albert Park VIC This dual-level c1890 Victorian has been renovated to give it a contemporary style.



Original features, including the facade, wide arched hallway and hardwood floor, remain, while a designer kitchen with integrated appliances showcases the modern updates. Highlights include Venetian plaster walls that extend through the living area to full-height stacked sliders, opening to the private decked courtyard with a built-in barbecue and established greenery.

World.title: Bruce Baird, the Liberal stalwart who fought for refugees, has died aged 84
World.content:
The former Liberal politician Bruce Baird, who served in state and federal parliaments and played a key role in securing the Sydney 2000 Olympics, has died while on an overseas trip. He was 84. Several sources close to Baird have confirmed the keen ocean swimmer died in Singapore after a fall on his way home from a European holiday. Former NSW and federal Liberal MP Bruce Baird has died aged 84. James Alcock / AFR Baird is the father of former NSW premier Mike Baird, who led the state from 2014 to 2017, journalist Julia Baird and Steve who works in the not-for-proft sector. His wife Judy died in 2021. As the state MP for the now-abolished seat of Northcott, Baird was instrumental in winning the Olympics for Sydney while at Macquarie Street, where he was minister for tourism, roads, environment and transport.



He was elected Northcott in 1984, and held the seat for 11 years, before moving to federal politics when he was elected to the southern Sydney seat of Cook in 1998. He represented the electorate for nine years, retiring before the 2007 election and making way for future prime minister Scott Morrison to take the seat. Mike Baird greeting his father, Bruce, on NSW state election day in 2015. Andrew Meares Former premier Nick Greiner and Baird embrace in 1993 after the announcement Sydney would host the 2000 Olympic Games. Fairfax Archives Baird was never a minister in federal parliament. He was overlooked for a frontbench position in the Howard government because of his stance on asylum seekers, which went against then prime minister John Howard’s policy at the time, as well as his closeness to Howard’s treasurer and nemesis, Peter Costello.



In his valedictory speech, according to a report in the publication Sydney Anglicans in 2007, Baird paid tribute to a young man called Adnan, who was the first of 50 asylum cases that Baird became personally involved with. Baird with former NSW premier Nick Greiner in 1992. Fairfax Former prime minister John Howard and Baird in federal parliament in 2005. Fairfax Baird took the case to then immigration minister Phillip Ruddock who used his ministerial powers to grant Adnan refugee status. The young Iranian went on to study engineering and was a translator for his Farsi-speaking congregation at Guildford Anglican Church. “This for me illustrates why a compassionate approach is so important,” Baird told his parliamentary colleagues.



Before his political career, Baird’s was assistant trade commissioner at the Australian embassy in Germany in the early 1970s, followed by a three-year stint as trade commissioner in New York. Bruce Baird was a regular swimmer at the Bold and the Beautiful swim squad, which swims between Manly Beach and Shelly Beach. James Brickwood Baird swam in the “Bold & Beautiful” swim squad, which regularly exercised in the waters off Manly and Shelly Beach. He was described as a “great mate” to those in the group by squad organiser Peter Anthony. “Bruce was a much-loved part of our swim community and a wonderful friend to so many of us,” Anthony told members on Friday. “Our thoughts are with his family and everyone who loved him.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Christopher Luxon walks back 'bizarre claim' about the Greens
World.content:
Christopher Luxon has walked back claims made by one of his ministers about the Greens, before then suggesting - wrongly - that they originated from the media.

Trade Minister Todd McClay, on Wednesday, accused the Green Party of "joining with foreign actors to attack New Zealand" in regards to a climate change complaint lodged with the European Commission.

The Greens quickly denied any involvement and McClay provided no evidence.

Asked for evidence on Friday, Luxon put the responsibility back on reporters to investigate whether the Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick had any involvement.

"That'd be up for you guys to accertain whether she has or hasn't," he said.

Luxon then suggested that the media had first raised the possibility of Swarbrick's involvement.

"I'm just saying that's not appropriate if that's the case. But equally, I'm sure she hasn't done that."

Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick. RNZ / Nick Monro

Told that the Green Party had not been involved, Luxon replied: "Great, great. That's good to hear. That's good that you've bottomed that out. Well done, well done... Good job."

In a statement, Swarbrick said McClay had provided "zero evidence" to support his "bizarre claim". She said Luxon's government was blaming everybody else for the consequences of its policy to "shred climate action".

"The worst absurdity of all of this is that the most fired up the government has got on climate action is trying to cover their tracks by attacking everyone else, instead of doing the responsible thing."

RNZ has asked McClay's office for evidence for his claim.

Trade Minister Todd McClay. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Luxon said he was not worried about the international complaint because New Zealand upheld its free trade obligations.

"It's very disingenuous to suggest otherwise. We take that incredibly seriously. We are a free trading nation. We respect our FTA agreements and what's in them, and we'll continue to do so.

"When any other country gets to 96.3 percent renewable electricity, then you might want to throw some stones at us.

"But until then, I'm not that interested in what Laura Clarke or anybody else says, frankly."

World.title: One person dead after falling from cliff at popular Coromandel beach
World.content:
One person has died after an incident at Cooks Beach on Friday afternoon.

Emergency services were called to Purangi Road about 5.50pm after a report that someone had fallen from a cliff.

In a post on social media, Cooks Beach Volunteer Fire Brigade said they immediately started medical treatment when they arrived.

"Our combined Cooks and Hahei crews worked extremely hard in very difficult and dangerous conditions, with ambulance crews, westpac and Police.

"Unfortunately, the person is deceased and our thoughts go out to the family," chief fire officer Brayden Jack said

A witness saw a rescue helicopter drop off a crewmember before returning 10 minutes later to airlift a stretcher from the base of Shakespeare Cliff.

St John had sent two local first response units, a helicopter, and a manager to the beach.

Cordons remain in place while emergency services personnel work at the scene.

The death will be referred to the Coroner.

World.title: Review into OmniHealth clinics launched after staff resignations
World.content:
The Primary Health Organisation (PHO) says a review into OmniHealth clinic services is being launched after seven staff resigned from Pahīatua Medical Centre.

The staff, who included a doctor and nurses, resigned in September claiming overwhelming workloads in a ballooning safety crisis.

OmniHealth is the parent company behind 16 medical centres and owns Tararua Health Group. It also provides services at Dannevirke Community Hospital, but it's currently on notice after a spot audit found the hospital was unsafe for patients due to staff shortages.

There's currently a 30-day freeze on any patient admissions, and Omni has a deadline to get more staff.

PHO chief executive Tony Wai told Checkpoint the a review was being done to ensure the concerns from Pahīatua Medical Centre were not "existing in other areas".

"I know there's been some staffing shortages which have been announced, but we recognise as well that like other clinics around the country, there are a number of staffing shortages, but we took prudent measures now to just do a review."

"At a minimum service level, we do see that they have to be open, they have to be seeing patients, they have to see patients within a certain timeframe, they have to maintain certain standards actually in there."

The staff that have resigned from Pahīatua Medical Centre have said they would not return unless OmniHealth was out of the picture.

Wai said OmniHealth was "taking some steps at the moment and there are other parties involved".

"It's not my role to say what will happen with those parties and what they will look to do. But we recognise that our role is to ensure that the clinic is safe for the meantime and that the changes are actually made to continue to issue on."

Wai said the review is to be done by a PHO team and will look at the Omni Health clinics within the PHO network.

He also acknowledged that OmniHealth chief executive Mark Wills was on the PHO board but said they had taken steps to ensure Wills was not part of any conversations that relate to the review.

"He is stood down from those matters as it relates to anything in relation to Omni or in relation to Tararua Health Group.

"We have asked him and each of the clinics that he's involved in to get the information back. So he is aware that the review's there and he's in no way influencing that part of it."

Once the information is received an internal assessment would take place but Wai said the review would likely not be publicised.

"Largely because this is about an assurance level for us and the individual providers."

World.title: 'Shedding tears for you': Tributes to late MP Adrian Rurawhe at tangi in Whanganui
World.content:
Audio player for " Some MPs pause campaigning to attend former Speaker's funeral " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics/1686307%2Fshedding-tears-for-you-tributes-to-late-mp-adrian-rurawhe-at-tangi-in-whanganui

Some MPs pause campaigning to attend former Speaker's funeral Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Politicians, whānau and iwi leaders have come together to pay their respects to former Labour MP and Speaker of the House Adrian Rurawhe.

Gathering for his tangi at Whangaehu Marae in Whanganui on Friday afternoon, a 100-strong delegation of political leaders from across the motu remembered Rurawhe as a "huge leader within Parliament", who conducted himself with "quiet resolve and real dignity".

Rurawhe's death was confirmed by his family on Wednesday.

Iwi leaders and Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po were welcomed to the marae first, followed by the political delegation led by Speaker Gerry Brownlee.

That delegation also included Labour leader Chris Hipkins, deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni and Māori caucus chair Willie Jackson. Te Pūoho Katene, who is contesting Te Tai Hauāuru - the seat Rurawhe held - also attended.

Shane Jones and Jenny Marcroft represented New Zealand First, Rawiri Waititi and John Tamihere attended on behalf of Te Pāti Māori, and Todd Stephenson attended on behalf of ACT.

Waititi speaks at the tangi. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

Former MPs Trevor Mallard, who Rurawhe succeeded as speaker, as well as Nanaia Mahuta and Poto Williams attended.

Following kōrero in te reo Māori, politicians from both sides of the House paid tribute to Rurawhe.

Hipkins said Rurawhe had not told Labour he was ill, because "he didn't want to get in the way".

"That's made the shock that much harder for many of our team," Hipkins said.

Brownlee paid tribute to Rurawhe as a speaker with "quite a different approach".

Brownlee told the tangi that Rurawhe had left a strong legacy. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

"He was able to use his gentle persona to terrify people," he joked.

"Adrian, your legacy is a strong one."

Jackson said he was a "quiet achiever" whose strength was underrated.

"He had lovely skills, in terms being calm and cool. But his big strength was he could... do the business. I mean, he kicked me out of the House, and that was one of the biggest shocks I got from him. I thought, 'what the heck's happened here?'"

Adrian Rurawhe quit politics earlier this year. VNP / Phil Smith

Jackson said Rurawhe was "almost universally" rated or loved across the House.

"He'd always stand his ground, if he knew he was right. He was terrific, incredibly underrated, undervalued at times. But to become the Speaker of the House, and then to become a great Speaker of the House, even better."

Katene said the party was searching for who would follow in Rurawhe's footsteps.

"Tēnei tō Pāti Reipa e tangi hotuhotu ana mōu," Katene said.

"Here is your party, the Labour Party, shedding tears for you."

Davidson attends Rurawhe's tangi on Friday. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

Green MP and Assistant Speaker Teanau Tuiono recalled that Rurawhe had ejected Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson from the House twice.

"Nōku anō te hē engari nōku te hōnore," Davidson said.

World.title: Going for gold: World panning championship takes over Cromwell
World.content:
Audio player for " Dozens of gold prospectors flock to Otago for world champs " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/regions/1686301%2Fgoing-for-gold-world-panning-championship-takes-over-cromwell

Dozens of gold prospectors flock to Otago for world champs Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

More than 150 high-speed prospectors have converged on Central Otago to prove their weight in gold.

The 49th annual World Gold Panning Championship is being held at Cromwell Racecourse, with competitors putting a centuries-old goldfields skill to the test.

Panners from more than 20 countries have been facing off over troughs of water and buckets of gravel, racing to extract minuscule flakes as accurately as possible.

Event coordinator Terry Davis said international visitors had embraced everything on offer, from fierce competition to warm spring weather and tours of local mining history.

An immense amount of work had gone into hosting the event, not least sourcing 20 tonnes of gravel and building water troughs that adhered to strict World Gold Panning Association codes, he said.

New Zealand's Sally Beverley competes in the panning with an unusual object event using a pāua shell. Katie Todd/RNZ

"It was a huge logistical nightmare getting it all together. There were a lot of things had to come together and they did come together," he said.

Event organiser and New Zealand competitor Megan Ide said the tournament had attracted top-tier international talent.

"It's a very high calibre of competitors. We've got a panner here, Ken Carlson, who actually designed the speed pan. I had a chat to him yesterday to get a few tips off him. He's won 39 championship medals in his panning career," she said.

The New Zealand competitors were putting on a powerful performance, Ide said.

"We've managed to qualify for quite a few semi-finals and finals, so the Kiwi contingent is holding their own."

A judge inspecting a competitor's vial of gold flakes at the World Gold Panning Championship. Katie Todd/RNZ

Davis said the week's festivities had included an opening parade, movie night and markets, and would finish with a hoedown.

Many of the competitors were camping at the racecourse, where there had also been novelty competitions such as "panning with an unusual object" - a pāua shell, he said.

Canadian competitor Jonathan Garner, who was attending his fifth world championship, said the event was as much about the global community as it was about panning.

"It's a good way to see the world and you have friends everywhere you go," he said.

"This year has been awesome. This is a little smaller and so it's given me a chance to meet many of these people who I've met before but get to know them on a more intimate basis."

World Gold Panning Association (WGA) president Sanjay Singh praised the execution of the New Zealand event.

World Gold Panning Association president Sanjay Singh travelled to Cromwell as part of the South African contingent. Katie Todd/RNZ

"From the proceedings, the processes and managing of the rules of the WGA, I can say the competition will get a tick from the rules committee," he said.

Singh, who travelled to the competition as part of a 19-person South African delegation, said he had been marvelling at the Kiwi hospitality.

"The reception, from the time we got to the airport up to now, has been phenomenal. People ask me which is the best part for me - the best part besides the competition is my interaction with New Zealand people."

The championship was due to conclude on Saturday with the finals and an afternoon medal ceremony.

World.title: Christchurch residents told to rely on instincts not sirens for tsunami evacuation
World.content:
Audio player for " Christchurch tsunami sirens to be removed " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/regions/1686212%2Fchristchurch-residents-told-to-rely-on-instincts-not-sirens-for-tsunami-evacuation

Christchurch tsunami sirens to be removed Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

New Brighton beach-goers have expressed concerns about Christchurch City Council moves to remove tsunami sirens but emergency managers say people must rely on their instincts rather than waiting for someone else to sound the alarm.

From 6 October Canterbury's city and district councils will move from the current three tsunami evacuation zones - red, orange and yellow - to a single blue tsunami evacuation zone.

The 45 sirens between Brooklands and Taylors Mistake will also be removed, with the city council instead urging people to rely on their own judgement in an emergency, and mobile phone alerts.

New Brighton's beach and playground was busy with people enjoying the warm spring weather on Friday but none of the dozen people spoken to by RNZ knew that the sirens were being removed and most did not understand the rationale.

Carol Williams, who works in New Brighton and lives nearby, said she was particularly concerned for the elderly and people who did not have a cellphones.

"I don't think its right. We have a large population down here of elderly people who might not have cell phones and they won't get their emergency alerts. Sirens need to stay," she said.

New Brighton visitor Pauline King shared Williams' concerns.

Nicole Hibbs and Pauline King often visit New Brighton, but had heard nothing about the tsunami sirens being removed. Pauline says she thinks they are important for anyone who doesn't have a cell phone. Rachel Graham/RNZ

"I don't think its a good idea because of the old people. The old people really need to hear the sirens. I think the sirens should go to let people know," King said.

Sam, who lives near the beach in North Canterbury, said she did not know whether to evacuate during the 2016 Kaikoura earthquake.

"I was back in bed and it wasn't until I heard the sirens I thought, 'oh we need to go', and at that point we also had people knocking on our doors. I'd probably urge them to keep it."

Christchurch City Council emergency manager Brenden Winder said an independent review of tsunami alert methods showed that sirens were not the best option.

"The sirens are being removed because they are unreliable. They rely on power, they are no good in the wind and people don't know what to do when they hear them. Our reports told us very clearly it was time to get rid of the sirens and be consistent with the rest of the country," he said.

"People will use the reminder - long and strong get gone - and they can receive emergency mobile alerts on their cellphone too."

Brenden Winder, Christchurch City Council Emergency Manager, says the tsunami sirens are now outdated. Rachel Graham/RNZ

Winder said the council would also put up signs in tsunami evacuation zones and embark on a public information campaign.

In April 2025 the bi-annual test of Christchurch's tsunami sirens did not happen because the person in Auckland who was supposed to activate them was waylaid by a car crash.

Winder said that was not the reason the sirens were reviewed but did point to a weakness in the system.

"While that was regrettable, in some ways it just reminded us of how fragile the system was. We certainly didn't plan for that to happen," he said.

"While the guy in Auckland was doing the right thing in the moment, it didn't help with the testing of the sirens but it did highlight the larger fragility of the arrangements that were in place."

Winder said technology has improved since the sirens were first introduced in 2016 and the mobile emergency alerts offered more comprehensive cover.

"The sirens met a need for a time but they were never across the whole region. They are only in Christchurch, not Banks Peninsula, so there are some equity challenges there. They are also costly and had coverage issues too, so it was time for the sirens to go."

Winder said the council had decided to remove the sirens altogether to ensure the message was simple.

World.title: 'I want to move': Papatoetoe community reels after three family members found dead
World.content:
Audio player for " Three people found dead at south Auckland home " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/regions_auckland/1685976%2Fi-want-to-move-papatoetoe-community-reels-after-three-family-members-found-dead

Three people found dead at south Auckland home Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

A sense of collective trauma hangs over Cambridge Terrace in Auckland's Papatoetoe, after a number of people - including children - saw a bloodied dead body on the doorstep of a suburban house on Thursday night.

When police arrived at the scene around 6.40pm on Thursday, they found another two bodies.

Police have since confirmed that those who died at the property were "three family members".

RNZ has been told by multiple sources that two children live at the property, but has not been able to confirm whether they are among the deceased.

'I don't want to stay here anymore'

The community is reeling from the deaths.

One resident, George, said he was "not really good at the moment" after seeing the body.

His seven-year-old daughter saw it as well.

"She was crying. That's why we came home."

RNZ / Felix Walton

Rachel, who is George's mother, said her family "didn't sleep well" after hearing three people had died.

"It's not safe here anymore... I'll be honest, I'm really scared.

"I don't want to stay here anymore, I want to move out. I want to find another place. Scary."

Royce Walker managed to prevent his granddaughter from seeing the body across the road.

"I thought it was a female lying on the concrete, but when I looked again it was a male. It's pretty freaky, saw the blood everywhere," he said.

"I am pretty shaken up, especially learning this morning about another two inside. That's very shocking. Never think it would happen so close to home, you know what I mean?

"It's very scary. I'm very just lost at the moment."

RNZ / Felix Walton

He described the property's residents as a good family who would regularly stop to chat.

Manukau Ward councillor Alf Filipaina, who served as a police officer for more than 38 years, has a message for those affected by what they saw on Thursday night.

"My humble suggestion, being in the police for quite a few years and seeing quite a few incidents that people should never see, is just to seek help for themselves as well. It's so important to do that. That'll be the message and just talk to each other about it as well because that'll help."

Deaths were an isolated incident, Police say

Police detectives and forensic teams spent all day at the property on Friday, a blue tent erected in front of the main entrance.

Authorities have released very little information about what happened at the house on Thursday night, and have declined requests to be interviewed.
