Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406082423112

Counties Manukau District Commander Shanan Gray released a short message on Facebook, in which he passed on his condolences to the family at the centre of the incident.

"I know the family at this time will be reeling at the loss of three family members. Police are working with the family to ensure that they have the necessary support wrapped around them," he said.

World.title: Young people call on politicians for more online gambling restrictions
World.content:
Audio player for " Politicians face grilling from young people calling for online gambling restrictions " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics/1685983%2Fyoung-people-call-on-politicians-for-more-online-gambling-restrictions

Politicians face grilling from young people calling for online gambling restrictions Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Election candidates have faced a grilling from young people calling for more restrictions for online gambling.

Three political hopefuls were asked what their parties would do about the harm it causes.

Many of the people they heard from felt pushed into action because they've grown up inundated by online ads for gambling outfits and have seen firsthand their mates gamble away meagre student incomes.

Faith Tupuhi has watched online gambling harm seeping into her community.

She studies at the University of Otago and said she's constantly surrounded with people using online pokies and sports betting apps.

Tupuhi is a co-designer of Touchgrass, a specialist youth digital wellbeing and screen addiction treatment service.

"Just putting the big spin-wheel up on the projector, and something called feast or famine."

"You put all your dinner money onto bets and you either feast for dinner, or famine."

At first, putting a few dollars on an online gambling app might seem harmless.

But Faith Tupuhi said it's led some students to gamble their weekly student loan payments, that they'd usually use to pay for rent or food.

Faith Tupuhi and Laga Jensen Bella Craig/RNZ

"One of the guys ended up trying to win back all his money [because] he lost all of the rent money."

"They were taken to the tribunal and that has ruined a lot of [his] friendships in the flat."

It's a story all too familiar for fellow University of Otago student Laga Jensen, who told Checkpoint online gambling has become normalised in Dunedin.

"It's just how normal it seemed, in the library, pre-drinks, afters, at full on street parties."

On Friday, at a community hall in Auckland's Greenlane, young people questioned election candidates about the issue, at a meeting put on by the Problem Gambling Foundation, Asian Family Services and Mapu Maia.

In the hot seat was The Green's Party's Ricardo Menéndez March, New Zealand First's Sheldon Eden-Whaitiri and National's Greg Fleming.

Young people put their questions to The Green's Party's Ricardo Menéndez March, New Zealand First's Sheldon Eden-Whaitiri and National's Greg Fleming. Bella Craig/RNZ

In response to a question asking the candidates their parties position on advertising, all candidates agreed that advertising should not be able to be targeted to people under 18 years old.

Sheldon Eden-Whaitiri said, "New Zealand First is very pragmatic that gambling does exist, but it shouldn't be targeting kids and children."

The Green Party's Ricardo Menéndez March said his party was committed to introducing a ban on online gambling s.

"s in my view and the marketing rules that exist right now only serve to actually benefit the companies that profit from the harm that it causes."

A new law passed this year means 15 offshore online casinos can have licenses to operate in Aotearoa.

National's Greg Fleming said the Online Casino Gambling Bill has been where the government focused on mitigating online gambling harm.

By law, online gambling companies must have a harm-prevention strategy, ensure users are at least 18 years old and stick to advertising restrictions.

But Melissa Thompson, Chief Executive of the Problem Gambling Foundation said the restrictions don't go far enough because they are not addressing volume or frequency.

"I think the advertising's the key, it's so visible, it's in young people's pockets, it's in their phones, it's on their desktops."

"[We need] really strong regulations around advertising for not just online casinos, but sports betting, some consistency across the board."

Sitaleki Tonga, from Mapu Maia told Checkpoint he'd also like to see stronger regulation in place for advertising.

"Even if you jump on a simple website like YouTube, you get like three to four ads coming on."

Sitaleki Tonga (right) Bella Craig/RNZ

"Even in live sports sometimes, you might [be watching] a team like the Warriors, but unfortunately sometimes it's advertised during half-time or pre-game."

Some people are exposed to online gambling through online gaming, through features such as loot boxes and using in-game currency.

Faith Tupuhi said she'd like to see gambling restrictions extend to gaming.

"I just don't think it is discussed as an issue as a whole, so just talking about it and understanding just how young kids are using it."

"We were finding 13, 16 and 9-year-olds all hopping on Roblox and on other online gaming apps, or using their older siblings."

A recent New Zealand Gambling Survey found that 44 per cent of young people aged 15-24 participated in gambling in the past year.

And Māori, Pacific and Asian communities were disproportionately affected by gambling harm.

World.title: Amy Shark to lead NRL grand final musical tribute to Jai Arrow
World.content:
An all-star ensemble of Australian musicians is set to take part in this weekend's NRL grand final pre-game entertainment.

Pop sensation Amy Shark is leading the performance, alongside members from Newcastle favourites and Better hit-makers The Screaming Jets, electronic duo Peking Duk, plus rock groups Grinspoon, and Teen Jesus and the Jean Teasers.

The all-Australian supergroup will soundtrack an on-ground tribute to South Sydney Rabbitohs player Jai Arrow, who told ABC earlier this week he knew "nothing" about plans for him to take a lap of honour around Stadium Australia on Sunday.

The ABC understands that Shark, who performed at the 2020 NRL grand final, and company will perform a series of cover songs, including the Gerry and the Pacemakers' song and Liverpool FC anthem You'll Never Walk Alone.

Each musician's appearance fee is reportedly being donated to motor neurone disease causes.

The Screaming Jets were among the acts speculated by fans to replace Tones And I. (Supplied: The Screaming Jets)

News of the supergroup musical tribute comes after the NRL's negotiations to secure Tones And I fell through, leaving the grand final without a pre-match entertainment headliner.

Why Tones And I won't appear at grand final Tones And I has broken her silence after the NRL declared it will forego a grand final tradition of pre-match entertainment.

The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the issue centred on the NRL's insistence that she perform her 2019 mega-hit Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.

However, the musician's team confirmed that prior commitments touring with Macklemore in the US left her unable to accept the offer when it was made in September.

"Nothing was signed or confirmed in writing," Tones and I's management said.

"Due to the last-minute nature and prior commitments by Tones, we were unable to accept the offer."

It sparked speculation over potential replacements for pre-match entertainment, including Silverchair frontman Daniel Johns ruling out rumours that the band would be reuniting to cheer on their home team, the Newcastle Knights

Jai Arrow was awarded the Provan-Summons Medal at the 2026 Dally M Awards for embodying the spirit of the game. (Getty Images: Don Arnold/WireImage)

Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC the money spent on pre-match entertainment — running close to $1 million — could be put to better use.

"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend $1 million on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.

"You spend money to get outcomes, and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to play with their mates, gear etc, to play rugby league."

Peter V’landys said money set aside for pre-match entertainment would be invested in junior rugby league. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

V'landys also said the league would be donating $100,000 to Arrow's family, following the Rabbitohs player's departure from the NRL earlier this year after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease.

The grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop star Teddy Swims last year, and previous acts such as Billy Idol and Tina Turner.

"Our game sells itself," said V'landys.

"People come to watch rugby league. They don't come to watch a pop concert."

World.title: How Assefa ran third fastest marathon ever despite 'destroyed' Achilles
World.content:
Right up until the 40km mark of the Berlin Marathon at the weekend, Tigst Assefa was well on track to regain her world record.

After 10km, the Ethiopian star was already over a minute in the lead of a race that quickly became a challenge between her and the clock.

By the 30km mark, the noted fast-finisher was running inside world record pace and flying.

"She was on [target] to run 2:09:30, 2:09:40," Assefa's representative Gianni Demadonna told The Associated Press on Tuesday.

Tigst Assefa was flying through the first 30km of the race, running well under world record pace. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

Official World Marathon Majors social media accounts were excitedly posting "this is on" with Assefa 20 seconds under the existing world record time, set by controversial Kenyan Ruth Chepng'etich.

Chepng'etich's record is 2:09:56 from the 2024 Chicago Marathon, but she hasn't raced since July 2025 after admitting to a doping violation.

She is currently serving a three-year ban. There is no suggestion that Chepng'etich doped in Chicago and that record still stands.

Assefa was within touching distance of eliminating Chepng'etich from the record books.

But, within sight of the Brandenburg Gate at just 2 kilometres remaining, Assefa began to grimace, then started to limp and hobbled to the line.

She eventually finished 68 seconds shy of Chepng'etich's record.

Assefa suffered 'complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon'

Assifa's finishing time of 2:11:04 was the third-fastest in history and gave the Olympic silver medallist her third career victory in Berlin, in a new course record.

But incredibly, it was later revealed that the 29-year-old had suffered a "complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon" and has since undergone surgery.

According to her team, Assefa had felt pain in her Achilles from the 31st kilometre, but pushed on regardless, before complete disaster struck with just 2km to go.

Tigst Assefa was unable to stand after crossing the line. (Getty Images: picture alliance/Andreas Gora)

The Achilles tendon connects your calf muscles to your heel bone and lifts the heel when the calf muscle contracts.

"Your Achilles is basically a spring to propel yourself forward," Zoe Russell, a specialist sports and exercise physio as awarded by the Australian College of Physiotherapists, told ABC Sport.

"It transfers your load to propel you forward.

"Tendon experts around the world sort of suggest that a painful tendon doesn't often rupture because it just can't sustain the load.

"You don't typically hear this story of how they're running along, they're sore and then it pops."

How can you run with a ruptured Achilles?

Associate Professor Peter Malliaras, a physiotherapist and clinical researcher at Monash University, told ABC Radio National's Health Report in 2022 that an Achilles tendon rupture "is quite a catastrophic injury".

"It will prevent you from pretty much doing everything in your daily functions; including walking, running, driving, for a fair period of time," he said.

Tigst Assefa could barely struggle to her feet. (Getty Images: Anadolu/Halil Sagirkaya)

Demadonna claimed that Assefa "completely destroyed the tendon" by the end of the race, running the final 500 metres without it.

"She was no longer able to run, because when she was going to put her foot on the ground she had no power," Demadonna said.

Adidas one-run-and-done shoe sets new mark in sport's arms race Adidas's new running shoe helped Ethiopia's Tigst Assefa take more than 2 minutes off the marathon world record in Berlin at the weekend — but if you want to get hold of the one-run-and-done shoe, you'd better start saving.

Yet Assefa was still able to finish the race, running along at a fair lick too, despite being unable to push off with her forefoot.

One reason for her ability to keep moving forward could be found in the super shoes she was wearing, with the integrated carbon plate essentially providing some of the spring instead.

"It could have helped her keep going, yes," Russell suggested.

"Those carbon plates will allow you to transfer your load a bit easier."

Nevertheless, Assefa collapsed soon after crossing the line in clear distress before support arrived, including Ethiopian long-distance running legend Haile Gebrselassie.

Quick surgery vital

She was immediately flown to Munich by private jet courtesy of her sponsor, Adidas, where Demadonna said she underwent "very complex surgery" on Monday.

Without knowing the exact details of the rupture, or the exact surgery technique used, Russell said a time frame for a return would be impossible to guess, but noted that quick surgery was essential.

"Things can move quickly, really quickly in elite sport," she said.

"I've had athletes get an appointment with a surgeon within 20 minutes, half an hour of the injury.

Tigst Assefa was aided by four-time Berlin winner Haile Gebrselassie to leave the finishing area. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

"When you've got means and connections at the elite level, things can move very quickly — and you do want to move fairly quickly with an Achilles rupture because it is constantly under tension. When it ruptures, it actually retracts back.

"So if you're waiting weeks for surgery, it means that your muscles actually start to suffer the effects of de-conditioning and it retracts, which makes for a technically harder surgical process because you've got to pull it and put it all on tension and then stitch it up.

"For an elite athlete, you'd want to get it in two or three days, whereas in the general population, you'll probably get away with getting it within a week."

In a statement, Assefa's coach Gemedu Dedifo said that she "successfully underwent surgery" within 24 hours.

"Tigst is a champion," the statement read.

"We believe in her strength, courage and determination.

"We look forward to seeing her recover and return to the track and roads."

Assefa vows to return

Assefa sent a message from her hospital bed via the Berlin Marathon organisers, defiantly promising to return to break the record.

"My surgery went well," she said in a statement.

"I am overwhelmed by the tremendous support I have received from all over the world. From the bottom of my heart, I would like to thank everyone for their incredible support and concern.

"I will definitely come back to Berlin, and then I will break the world record."

Tigst Assefa holds the women's only world record. (Getty Images: Xinhua/Li Ying)

No marathon has seen more world records than Berlin, with 13 set at the race since 1974 thanks to its largely flat profile with just 73 metres of elevation gain and 79 metres of elevation loss over the 42km.

Assefa set one of those world records in 2023, running 2:11:53 to become the first woman to set a record on the course since Sydney Olympic champion Naoko Takahashi did so in 2001.

Assefa already holds the women's only world record, having run 2:15:41 to win the 2026 London Marathon in April.

Races where men and women start at the same time, as is the case in Berlin, tend to be faster for women, who are able to benefit from male pacemakers who can block the wind and reduce fatigue earlier in the race.

World.title: Roosters blow as Watson ruled out of NRL grand final
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters have suffered a significant blow ahead of the NRL grand final, with hooker Connor Watson ruled out of the match.

In a cruel blow, Watson will miss Sunday's decider against his former club Newcastle and become the first player to sit out a grand final as a result of a concussion.

Watson was dazed and was taken from the field moments after coming on in the Roosters' preliminary final win over the Dolphins.

Under the NRL's protocol, players diagnosed with a category-one concussion, as Watson was, face a mandatory stand-down period of 11 days.

The Roosters had indicated that Watson was testing well leading into Thursday when the 30-year-old met with an independent specialist.

But on Friday the club confirmed the utility had failed to receive clearance to line up in the grand final.

The outcome means Watson has played his last game for the Roosters with the popular utility heading to St George Illawarra next season before linking up with the PNG Chiefs in 2028.

Connor Watson has played 127 games for the Roosters in the NRL. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Watson's absence likely forces Roosters coach Trent Robinson's hand when it comes to his bench, with hooker Benaiah Ioelu the most obvious man to come into Easts' 19-man squad.

Five things to know ahead of the NRL and NRLW grand finals The final day of the NRL and NRLW season is almost here, with the grand finals being held this Sunday. Here's everything you need to know.

Ioelu has played mostly off the bench through his 17-game NRL career, starting just once in five appearances this season, and would act as cover for Reece Robson.

"I don't think it takes too much to work out what plan B is, but we have got some really good hookers," Robinson said on Thursday.

"Benaiah Ioelu played some great footy for us this year. He brings a lot of energy to us as well so he will come into consideration then."

Newcastle, meanwhile, are also expected to face a tough decision leading into Sunday's decider as they weigh up a replacement for suspended number nine, Phoenix Crossland.

Harrison Graham has excelled as a bench option at hooker for the Knights, but coach Justin Holbrook, who doesn't have to name his final team until 90 minutes before kick-off on Sunday, has the option of also starting Thomas Cant or Diesel Hagan.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Neale switches to Collingwood, Greene joins Cats in AFL free agency
World.content:
Lachie Neale has sealed his high-profile switch to Collingwood, with Brisbane teasing the dual Brownlow medallist on his way out the door.

The AFL approved Neale signing a three-year deal with the Magpies on Friday afternoon, closing out the first day of free agency.

The 33-year-old ball-winner leaves as an unrestricted free agent after the Lions clinched a third-straight flag with their stunning seven-point grand final victory over Fremantle.

Brisbane chairman Andrew Wellington poked fun at Neale's switch to the "dark side" at the club's best and fairest event, where he finished third behind Will Ashcroft and Josh Dunkley.

"Take a last look at Lachie, because he's going tomorrow to have some teeth removed and a bit more ink," Wellington joked on Thursday night, drawing laughter from the crowd.

Departing coach Chris Fagan hailed Neale's perseverance after stepping down as captain in January following the public breakdown of his marriage and almost missing the grand final through suspension.

"As we all know, he's been under a fair bit of pressure, but it's never shown out on the field," Fagan said.

"[We] wish you all the best at your new club and with the rest of your life and whatever happens to you."

The Lions have been handed a second-round draft compensation — currently pick number 39 — with Neale reportedly raking in about $900,000 a season.

Toby Greene has signed a three-year deal with Geelong. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Jason McCawley)

Earlier, Toby Greene became the first major AFL free agency domino to fall, with Greater Western Sydney to receive a second-round draft pick for losing their former captain to Geelong.

The Cats lodged paperwork on Friday to land the inaugural Giant as an unrestricted free agent.

Greene, a triple All Australian and dual club champion, booted 450 goals across his 15-year, 282-game tenure for GWS.

The 33-year-old cited family reasons for returning to his native Victoria and reuniting with his close mate and former Giants forward Jeremy Cameron at the Cattery on a lucrative three-year deal.

The Giants will receive a second-round draft selection as compensation, currently slated at number 26.

Earlier, key forward Joel Amartey's switch from Sydney to Carlton was confirmed as the free agency period opened.

The Swans will receive draft compensation for losing the unrestricted 27-year-old, who was an emergency during finals after failing to convince coach Dean Cox following a partial Achilles tear.

Melbourne's 2021 premiership vice-captain Jack Viney is poised for a move with two years remaining on his contract after meeting with West Coast.

After being sidelined through injury for all but one game this season, the 32-year-old was told by coach Steven King there would likely be limited opportunities for him in the Demons midfield.

"Footy's gone that way mate," Viney told 10 News at Perth Airport on Thursday.

"So took a bit to process early days, but we're here now, so we'll make the best of the opportunity … it [a deal] will get done."

Neale set to join Magpies Collingwood says it "looks forward" to Lachie Neale joining the club in 2027 after it is announced he is leaving the Brisbane Lions.

Young Hawthorn forward Calsher Dear, meanwhile, has opted to stay at the Hawks on a two-year deal after weighing up a potential move to the Dees.

The 21-year-old, son of late 1991 Norm Smith medallist Paul Dear, burst onto the scene in his debut season with 25 goals from 17 appearances in 2024.

But the emerging tall has struggled to hold his spot through injury and internal competition, adding just 14 games in 2025 and 2026.

"We are very excited about what the future holds for Calsher with a strong pre-season under his belt and greater continuity into 2027 and beyond," Hawks list manager Mark McKenzie said.

Hawthorn's key forward selection squeeze is set to worsen in 2027, with Gold Coast's restricted free agent Ben King expected to join Jack Gunston, Mitch Lewis, Mabior Chol and Dear.

AAP

World.title: NRLW grand final marks end of era
World.content:
One year after the greatest and most controversial grand final in the NRLW, we're right back where we were 12 months ago.

Once again the Roosters will face Brisbane, with the Broncos all that stands between the Tricolours and a perfect season.

But while the season seems to be ending in the same place, the changes in the two sides, plus those that loom in the near future, make this game feel like the end of an era.

Controversial try decides NRLW premiership Brisbane and the Roosters played one of the greatest games in NRLW history, but the controversial winning try to Mele Hufanga shapes as a football mystery that might never be solved.

Roosters Millie Elliott and Corban Baxter will retire after the match, while New South Wales Origin prop Rima Butler is bound for Wests Tigers.

But where they limped into the decider last year, without injured halfback Tarryn Aiken and winger Taina Naividi after she broke down at the club's final training session, this time they're fully loaded.

The Broncos have not quite been the dominant force they were last year but they showed their class downing the Gold Coast in last week's preliminary final and have extra motivation of their own.

Ali Brigginshaw, one of the icons of the NRLW's early years, will be playing her last game before hanging up the boots.

Throw in lingering feelings from last year's 22-18 Broncos victory, which was sealed by a contentious try to Brisbane centre Mele Hufanga with three minutes left, and the stakes could not be higher.

The Roosters are determined to run towards the bad memories, having watched a replay of the match together before the season began.

"We're building on the feelings from last year," five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher said.

"It was a big theme of our pre-season camp.

"We watched it all together and it was really hard. There were a lot of people getting emotional but it was dead silent. It was so eerie.

"We all feel the hurt and the pain from last year. We won't let it happen again. We've worked so hard to fix those little things that went wrong last year."

After another undefeated regular season, that grand final loss is the only time the Roosters have had their colours lowered in the past two years, giving them 30 wins from their last 31 starts.

The Roosters have humbled their opponents this year. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

It meant they'd forgotten what defeat could even feel like. While they'll keep talk about it to a minimum this week, there's no doubt it hangs over them like a spectre.

"At the time, it was a weird feeling because the result was disappointing, but there was a lot of things in the lead-up that didn't go our way," hooker Keeley Nizza said.

"That's rugby league though and we still had the opportunity to win it but we didn't. The way we rallied together and played well regardless of the result, it brought us closer together.

"We won't speak about it too much, so it won't need to be brought up. It's always with us. Every year there's a new squad and a new feel, but we won't forget."

That possibility of a new squad in 2027 is why the match feels like the end of something.

Elliott is a Test and Origin mainstay, Baxter has played for the club since 2019, Butler has blossomed since joining Newcastle, and each of them leaves a serious hole in the roster with their departure.

Millie Boyle is one of three key players appearing in their last game for the Roosters. (Getty Images: Matt King)

The Roosters have done an excellent job identifying and progressing talent through their women's program, but all three are exceptionally difficult to replace.

While the club will be a premiership threat for some years to come, this game could mark the end of the club as a historically dominant force.

The combined impact of the departing trio makes them just a little more like everyone else, which could make this their last chance at the elusive perfect season.

Brisbane have already felt the pinch hurting the Roosters now. They have eight changes from last year's grand final, including Hufanga, who left for the Warriors.

But they did welcome in Blues halfback Jesse Southwell, and with her and Brigginshaw calling the shots, the Broncos attack is sure to fire.

Plus the defending premiers boast newly minted three-time Dally M and two-time Karyn Murphy Medal winner Tamika Upton, who's won three of the past four premierships across two different clubs.

Brigginshaw's last 'last' in NRLW grand final Ali Brigginshaw and fellow OGs Julia Robinson and Chelsea Lenarduzzi are hoping to join Broncos royalty with a fifth NRLW premiership.

Given her record in big matches, she's sure to put her stamp on the game and is good enough to win it almost on her own, meaning the result is well and truly up for grabs.

The Roosters were in imperious form to end the regular season, winning their last four regular season games by a combined total of 200 points to 34, but any thought of catching them complacent was ended in the preliminary final against Canberra.

The gallant Raiders gave a fine account of themselves in an intensely physical encounter, and the 20-10 Roosters win has them primed to hit their straps when it matters most.

"That's the sorest I've felt all year," Kelleher said.

"We absolutely bashed each other up on that field for 70 full minutes."

"We showed our mindset, that we could go through the grit and the arm wrestle. It's the perfect lead in to a grand final."

World.title: Piastri likens track to 'sandpaper' as F1 returns to Malaysia
World.content:
Formula 1 is heading back to Malaysia's Sepang International Circuit after a nine-year hiatus this weekend, with more than half the drivers on the grid unfamiliar with a track that is hosting the rescheduled Bahrain Grand Prix.

After making its first appearance on the calendar in 1999, Sepang has not hosted a Formula 1 race since 2017 after the Malaysian government said it could no longer justify the costs given the declining returns.

But it is making its F1 comeback after owners Liberty Media said it would host the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, relocating the race from Sakhir due to the Iran war and the situation in the Middle East.

Russell wins Azerbaijan GP after Piastri disaster in Baku George Russell has claimed a nail-biting victory in Baku, holding off Max Verstappen by just 0.196 seconds to secure his third victory of the season.

The 5.543-km long circuit combines long straights with several high-speed corners, with this week's race set to be held over 56 laps.

Only 10 of the 22 drivers have previously raced in Malaysia, leaving world champion Lando Norris and his McLaren teammate Oscar Piastri among those who will be learning the track for the first time.

Tyre supplier Pirelli has warned teams to expect challenging conditions, describing Sepang's surface as "relatively abrasive" with roughness comparable to Bahrain.

Piastri said the track "looks like sandpaper" and he too expected a lot of tyre degradation.

"I don't know how much racing or track running there's been recently. And anything that has been, the rain probably washes it off every afternoon anyway," Piastri said.

"So it's going to be a pretty tough weekend for everyone."

Thunderstorms are far from unusual in Malaysia, where the tropical climate regularly produces heavy afternoon showers and lightning storms.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli said Sepang's notorious abrasive surface could prove a welcome surprise should F1 finally get its first wet race of the season in Malaysia.

The young Italian, who has enjoyed a charmed run of dry conditions throughout his title charge, reckons the Malaysian circuit's rough tarmac would make it the ideal venue to test the sport's 2026 cars in challenging weather.

"I think this track will be quite OK in the wet … The surface is so open, there's actually not a lot of standing water unless it pours down," Antonelli told reporters, adding that it was the "roughest track tarmac" he had ever seen.

"But if it rains normally, then it would probably be the best track to try these cars for the first time in the rain because the tarmac is so open that the water just doesn't sit on top of the surface. It actually goes in between the stones. So it makes less risk of aquaplaning."

Reuters

World.title: Australia calls Maddinson and Harper into Test squad
World.content:
Nic Maddinson is within touching distance of a remarkable return to the Test team, after Cameron Green's abdominal strain left him in doubt for the series opener against South Africa.

Selectors confirmed on Thursday night that Maddinson had been called into the Test squad after not featuring in Australia's red-ball side for almost 10 years.

Sam Harper has also been drafted in as a back-up wicketkeeper, with a finger fracture now officially ruling Josh Inglis out of the first Test in Durban starting next Friday.

Inglis was hurt while playing in the series-opening ODI against South Africa last week, with further scans back home in Perth revealing a fracture.

Cameron Green is in doubt for the first Test after being injured in the Potchefstroom ODI against South Africa. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

There are now similar concerns around Green following the third ODI in Potchefstroom on Wednesday after he hurt his abdomen trying to pull a ball while batting in Australia's dead-rubber win.

Australian medical staff will now keep close watch on the allrounder, who will be "assessed further" in the coming week.

Regardless, the latest abdominal injury will raise question marks over Green's ability to bowl, after having not done so yet in a game on this tour.

The one bit of good news for Australia is opener Matt Renshaw has been cleared of a wrist injury after being hurt while fielding in the final ODI.

But the injuries do leave Australia's line-up for the first Test largely up in the air with up to two spots in the top-six unclear if Green is not fit.

Inglis had stood a chance of coming into the side for Marnus Labuschagne if selectors had opted to drop the Queenslander for the series opener.

Australia Test batter Nic Maddinson reveals testicular cancer diagnosis Former Australia batter Nic Maddinson has revealed he underwent chemotherapy for testicular cancer.

Maddinson could now fill one of those roles, with Cooper Connolly the other reserve batter in the Test squad.

Maddinson last played a Test on Boxing Day in 2016, and has since overcome a battle with testicular cancer to restart his cricket career.

The 34-year-old did not play a first-class match last summer, but struck 126 for NSW in a one-day match against Victoria last week.

Harper looms as another option, after being called into his first Australian squad at age 29.

The Victorian was the second-leading run-scorer in last summer's Sheffield Shield with 677 at 35.63 and is fresh off hitting a century for Australia A against India A in Pudcherry.

"Sam gives us wicketkeeping cover as Josh continues his recovery, while Nic provides flexibility throughout the batting order," chief selector George Bailey said.

Australia will play an intra-squad warm-up match in Potchefstroom this weekend, before moving to Durban on Monday to commence preparations for the first of three Tests.

AAP

World.title: Pallister and Short continue winning form at short course title
World.content:
Lani Pallister and Sam Short, Australia's stars of the pool in 2026, have continued their terrific year with more success at the national short course championships in Sydney.

The pair, who had already scooped a hatful of Commonwealth and Pan Pacific titles, made it five Australian titles between them in a week at Olympic Park Aquatic Centre.

They are intent on ending their year with more gold at the world short course championships in Beijing in December.

Pallister, having already lifted the 200 metre and 1,500m freestyle titles, powered to victory over 400m on the penultimate night of racing on Thursday, as did Short, who had already won the 800m.

Forrester breaks 17yo record Jenna Forrester has never competed at the short course world championships, but winning a silver and a gold in the same evening, also beating a 17-year-old a national record, has put her in pole position to do so.

Short was in an imperious mood as he took the 16-lap title in 3 minutes and 35.16 seconds, easily inside the Beijing qualifying time of 3:39.14, which convinced him the world record of 3:32.25 was sure to fall at the famed Water Cube venue that hosted the 2008 Olympic swimming program.

"I think that's gone in a couple of months at [the] world short course," Brisbane star Short said.

"I haven't swum much short course … in some ways it keeps you hungry."

Former short course 400m world champion Elijah Winnington, though, was just outside the time needed, as he clocked 3:39.24 to finish runner-up.

Pallister was in a class of her own as she prevailed in 3:54.55, the fastest women's time ever recorded in Australia, shaving 0.03 seconds off the old mark set by Ariarne Titmus six years ago.

Runner-up Jenna Forrester, who won 400m individual medley gold in a national record, was 0.65 seconds outside of qualifying time.

In the women's 50m, Iona Anderson continued her breakthrough year by completing her sweep of the backstroke events, clocking 25.88 seconds as she got closer to Kaylee McKeown's Australian record of 25.35 seconds.

AAP

Tech.title: Apple’s reportedly developing a smart home camera that doesn’t record video
Tech.content:
They’re also building home security products, both first-party and third-party home security products. And the biggest thing is a program called J450. And this is an offshoot and a companion product to the J490 smart home display. And these are little cameras that you can put around your house. They have very low frame rate. It looks like a cylinder. It looks like a metal giant, you know, chapstick.

And what does that mean? No video recording. So it’s a sensor that cannot actually pull in real video footage. It’s analyzing your environment in your home and around your home simply using AI.

Tech.title: Google’s new Guided Vision feature can help you read the fine print
Tech.content:
Guided Vision is launching in Gemini Live on compatible Android devices today to use AI to give real-time audio descriptions of anything you point your phone’s camera at. By sharing your camera in Gemini Live, you can have Google’s AI help with things like reading small text, describing your surroundings, finding or identifying objects around you, and describing details on specific objects.

Like the VoiceOver Live Recognition feature Apple has added to the iPhone and Vision Pro, it’s designed for people who are blind, have low vision, or want assistance in specific situations. In addition to the Gemini app, Guided Vision is also available in Google TalkBack, or users can set up an accessibility shortcut for it in the Settings app on devices running Android 9 and above, after it was announced in a recent set of Pixel updates.

You can also ask follow-up questions about whatever you’re looking at, like asking Gemini to read off the expiration date on an item it helped you find. Google says Gemini will give you audio cues to help line up your camera if you ask about something that’s not in the shot. However, Google cautions users not to rely on Guided Vision for things like “navigation, safe-travel guidance, or obstacle detection,” or as a replacement for a cane or mobility aid.

Tech.title: Android Central ‘will continue’ despite laying off its staff
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Android Central, a blog focused on the Android ecosystem, laid off its staff yesterday, but owner Future confirms to The Verge that the site will continue publishing.

Yesterday, four of the six staffers on Android Central’s staff page posted publicly about the layoffs, including Shruti Shekar, Derrek Lee, Harish Jonnalagadda, and Nicholas Sutrich, and former senior editor Namerah Saud Fatmi updated her LinkedIn to indicate that her tenure at Android Central had ended. Both Lee, the site’s managing editor, and Sutrich confirmed that all remaining staff were laid off.

The former staffers weren’t told whether the site would shut down. Today, new posts have been published to the site, though they are from the site’s freelance contributors rather than the previous full-time staffers.

“Future will continue to publish Android Central. We’ll share further information about the future of the site in due course,” Future spokesperson Nicole Martineau tells The Verge, adding: “We will not be providing any further comment at this time.”

Android Police, another Android-focused blog, also laid off at least two staffers recently. The site currently lists an editorial team of four people. Valnet, which owns Android Police and previously purchased The Verge’s sister site Polygon, didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Steam Deck 2: Is AMD Gainsborough the chip Valve’s been waiting for?
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Steam Deck, ROG Ally, and more: all the news about the handheld PC gaming revolution

The Steam Deck is four and a half years old, and handheld gamers are eagerly awaiting a Steam Deck 2 — but Valve has consistently said it needs a new chip with a “generational leap” in performance and efficiency before building the sequel.

There’s some reason to believe that chip has now broken cover: AMD Gainsborough. But I’m a tad skeptical.

As leaker Moore’s Law is Dead and IT Home report, the latest AMD drivers have leaked the codename for a previously unknown chip: an “AMD Gainsborough.” The first Steam Deck chip was named “Aerith” after Final Fantasy VII’s heartbreaking love interest, and Gainsborough is her last name. Plus, the chip appears to be a semi-custom one (read: designed for a specific customer) on TSMC’s relatively recent N3P process.

IT Home checked import/export records and found that AMD’s already been shipping test equipment for the Gainsborough chip for validation, suggesting that a potential customer might already be testing to see if it’s suitable for their device.

Image: NBD Data via IT Home

Those import records also show the Gainsborough chip will be fairly small, with an FF6 package measuring 25mm by 25mm. Today, leaker Gotou_3rd seemingly revealed that AMD’s next handheld chips, the Ryzen Z3 and Z3 Extreme, will also be 25mm by 25mm chips. Gotou also published a possible fragment of an AMD slide deck that suggests the Z3 is targeting 15 watts, the same power envelope as the Steam Deck and Steam Deck OLED:

Image via Gotou_3rd

This isn’t quite enough to tie Gainsborough specifically to a Steam Deck 2, though.

First, a semi-custom chip doesn’t always wind up in its originally intended gadget. It’s long been rumored that the Steam Deck’s own semi-custom chip wasn’t originally designed for the Steam Deck, but rather a Magic Leap headset, and that it was shopped around for tablets (including this canceled Microsoft tablet, the story goes) before Valve took advantage. There are portions of the original Steam Deck’s chip that went entirely unused.

Second, you should know that “Aerith” (Steam Deck), “Sephiroth” (Steam Deck OLED) and “Gainsborough” are not Valve’s codenames. When I visited Valve’s headquarters in late 2023, I commented on this Aerith wafer hanging on the wall — and Valve designers told me they didn’t really want the Final Fantasy codenames. AMD was the one that chose them.

The Aerith wafer I saw at Valve HQ. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Some extra evidence that Valve isn’t tied to those names: When Microsoft and Asus picked the “Ryzen Z2 A” chip for the vanilla $500 Xbox Ally, they were choosing an “Aerith Plus” chip.

Third, 25mm by 25mm might be small, but it’s actually large for a Steam Deck! The original Steam Deck’s “Aerith” chip, before it shrunk to remove the unused components in its “Sephiroth” revision, reportedly measured 19mm by 19mm. But perhaps Gainsborough is efficient, and perhaps it’s more affordable if this apple doesn’t fall too far from AMD’s 25mm x 25mm Ryzen Z3 tree.

Lastly, Valve was still figuring out “how and when” to do a Steam Deck 2 as of last month, after it would have theoretically received these Gainsborough chips. But I guess Valve might just be trying not to overpromise, after this year’s RAM-forced hardware delays.

Tech.title: Judge dismisses antitrust lawsuits over Google’s AI Overviews
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A federal judge has dismissed a pair of antitrust lawsuits filed by Chegg and Rolling Stone parent company Penske Media Corporation, which accused Google of driving away web traffic with its AI-powered search features, as reported earlier by Reuters. US District Judge Amit Mehta takes Google’s side in a ruling on Wednesday, writing that PMC and Chegg’s claims don’t stand up to antitrust law.

In lawsuits filed last year, Chegg and PMC accused Google of abusing its monopoly power by coercing publishers into supplying content for AI Overviews for free, or risk disappearing from search results. The publishers alleged Google’s practices diverted traffic away from their sites, hurting their revenue.

Judge Mehta, who made a landmark antitrust ruling against Google in 2024, disagrees with Chegg and PMC’s claims. “Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search ​traffic if they make their content available for free,” Mehta writes. “But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works.”

Related Google reportedly tests paying publishers for AI search results

Mehta adds that the court is not “unsympathetic to the situation publishers now find themselves in,” but writes that antitrust rules can’t replace a legislative body’s decision to address the economic impact of “new innovation.”

Disclosure: The Verge is part of Penske Media.

Tech.title: Sony brings AI graphics upscaling to the regular PS5
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sony is launching a new AI upscaling technology specifically for the regular PS5. The new tech, called Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), is a “new performance tier of AI upscaling” that’s a result of Sony’s Project Amethyst work with AMD, according to a blog post.

Sony says that PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR), which is available on the PS5 Pro, “remains the gold standard,” and in Digital Foundry’s early hands-on with the tech, it does seem that QSSR isn’t as fast as PSSR because the PS5 doesn’t have dedicated machine learning silicon. As a result, you should probably expect closer to an upscaled 1440p resolution on PS5 instead of the upscaled 4K on PS5 Pro.

”On PS5 Pro, developers almost uniformly output to 4K and adjust render resolution beneath it,” Sony principal graphics R&D engineer Daniel Craig told Digital Foundry. “On PS5, teams have to be more flexible, tuning not just render resolution, but also their intermediate and final presentation targets depending on the graphics mode.”

But Craig also said that QSSR is “fundamentally a drop-in replacement for titles that already support PSSR” after only a few days of tuning, making it likelier that PS5 developers will take advantage. The tech will be “offered broadly to all PlayStation developers,” Sony says.

Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei will be the first games to take advantage of QSSR, and are getting patches today to offer the tech as “an additional graphics option on PS5.” (Ghost of Yōtei Complete Edition also launches today.) Here are a couple videos from Sony showing off how QSSR looks in those games, and it appears to make graphics a little bit sharper:

Digital Foundry writes that “the potential here is remarkable: low resolution and poor upscaling have impacted so many titles in this generation, but QSSR could make a big difference.”

Tech.title: Can VR glasses save VR?
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

I’m pretty sure I won’t be buying the $1,299 Meta VR Glasses. That’s too rich for my blood in today’s economy, and my feelings about Meta are… conflicted. But I want you to understand that Meta just changed the game. We’ve had glasses, but we’ve never had glasses like this.

The Meta VR Glasses are not an opaque VR headset. They are not a pair of transparent AR glasses. They might be the best of both. After playing with the Meta VR Glasses, Valve’s Steam Frame, the Apple Vision Pro, and the Google / Xreal Aura back to back, I think they’re the first design that could convince regular people to give VR a chance.

It’s not because they look like glasses. It’s not just that they’re five times lighter than a typical headset at around 100 grams. It’s certainly not the $1,300 price tag, even if that’s much less than a $3,700 Vision Pro.

It’s about what you see and feel — and what you don’t see and feel — when you put Meta’s VR Glasses on your head.

You aren’t fully enclosed. You aren’t isolated. Because the Meta VR Glasses are glasses, not goggles, you have real peripheral vision. You see a live video feed of your room in the center, thick “rims” around that, then an actual naked-eye view of your surroundings around those rims. Even when you’re in a game, you still have peripheral vision.

I know people who aren’t comfortable in VR at home because they can’t afford to feel isolated from their kids or pets. I’ve personally never felt comfortable wearing headsets on a plane or train or in a park because I don’t like being surrounded by strangers I can’t easily see.

Women have told me VR is a nonstarter because they have long hair or wear makeup. Many headsets balance their weight by sandwiching your head between a back strap and a front cushion, and they don’t want to deal with the hassle of a high ponytail or smears every time they strap in.

Glasses are a potential solution, resting on your ears and floating before your eyes instead of pushing on your head. For years, the industry has suggested headsets will eventually make way for glasses.

But typically when we talk about glasses, they’re transparent. We’re imagining indistinguishable-from-eyeglasses spectacles that let you see the real world in all its glory, then magically make virtual objects appear within the entirety of the frame.

Today’s transparent-display glasses have made leaps and bounds, but they’re not there yet. While the basic lenses might look like glasses and give you a glasses-like field of view, the displays inside the glasses light up a much smaller area. When I sweep my head left or right, up or down, I see virtual objects disappear even when I’m still looking roughly in their direction.

In 2013, I briefly wore Google Glass — a tiny screen above my right eye with a postage stamp-sized 15-degree diagonal field of view. In 2015, I tried Microsoft’s HoloLens, with a 34-degree field of view. Four years later, HoloLens 2 achieved 52 degrees diagonally, the Xreal One Pro glasses I’ve been testing offer 57 degrees, and the Xreal Aura will finally push transparent glasses to 70 degrees diagonal this fall.

Oh look, it’s me from 2013. Guy had no idea what he was getting into. Photo: Google

But even with the Aura, 70 degrees diagonal is more like 60 degrees horizontal by 40 degrees vertical. Humans have roughly 120 degrees of binocular vision alone, and VR headsets like the Meta Quest 3 and Steam Frame offer around 110 degrees horizontal so you can feel like a virtual world is all around you.

Transparent glasses are also, well, transparent. Glasses like the Aura have to make their projected light compete with the real world while still letting you see through. That often means projectors right up against your brow. Virtual objects can seem ghostly unless you activate electrochromic lenses, which turn the clear lenses dark at the push of a button, blocking your view of the world.

Even then, you can see games, movies, and virtual desktops far better in a VR headset, where virtual light and real light don’t have to compete. You see the real world through what’s called “passthrough vision” — a live camera feed — with virtual objects realistically appearing at the correct depth and blocking real-life objects behind them.

The Steam Frame is one of the smallest, lightest, and most comfortable standalone VR headsets, but it’s still goggles. Photo: Kelsey McClellan / The Verge

That’s how the Steam Frame, Meta Quest, and Apple Vision Pro all work. But again, they weigh four to eight times as much and are fully enclosed. What if there were a lighter, open-air set of glasses that used passthrough vision instead of transparent lenses? You see where I’m going with this.

Instead of 60 degrees horizontal by 40 degrees vertical, the Meta VR Glasses offer 70 degrees by 66 degrees, and let me tell you, it feels like a bigger difference than it sounds. But the difference isn’t just the raw field of view — it’s that my real and virtual fields of view are the same. Anywhere I look inside the lenses, virtual objects can fill that frame, instead of getting abruptly cut off where the display part of the transparent display ends.

It also doesn’t hurt that the VR Glasses offer much higher angular resolution than most AR or VR devices (37ppd), making it easier to read text.

What you don’t get at 70 degrees by 66 degrees is full immersion. Some nerds like me will argue that the Meta VR Glasses don’t offer true VR, because it’s hard to feel like you’re “there” if you see so much less of your game. But it didn’t feel like I had tunnel vision, either, and it helps that the headset can track your hands far outside your field of view.

Wearing the Meta VR Glasses was the first time I thought to myself: Is there such a thing as “enough” field of view? I’ll always want more, but maybe the problem with virtual reality isn’t about feeling immersed. The industry’s problem is convincing enough people that it’s worth wearing any sort of headgear at all.

The 1-pound Steam Frame was a step in the right direction, but it’s still just for obsessives like me. Quarter-pound VR glasses that let you see your real world clearly will be a much easier sell. Even if you don’t plan to buy a $1,300 set from Meta, I suspect other companies are about to copy Meta’s homework.

When it announced the VR Glasses, Meta called it “a new era for virtual reality,” and in an interview, VP of wearables Alex Himel told my colleague Victoria Song that “the future of everything we’re doing is a pair of augmented reality glasses.”

As of February, it sounded like more goggles were still coming from Meta — but if the VR Glasses do well, I wouldn’t be surprised if it stops making headsets in the future.

Tech.title: Microsoft’s Office and Teams chief is leaving
Tech.content:
Team,

In 1996, as a college freshman, I taught myself to code so a few friends and I could help other students find a place to live around campus. I didn’t know much. I did know the internet was about to change how people found things, and I wanted to be as close to that as possible.

In 2009, Jeff Weiner made me his first hire at LinkedIn. I’ve spent the nearly 18 years since working on a much bigger version of that same idea: helping people find opportunity, and then helping them do great work once they have it.

This has (obviously) been the best professional experience of my life.

As a product manager, I got to build dozens of features that are still around today (some good, some not so good!). When I became CEO in 2020, the world was months into a pandemic that changed what work even meant. Nobody hands you a playbook for that. This team wrote one anyway. Since then, LinkedIn has passed a billion members and nearly tripled its business, and every bit of that belongs to the people who built it.

Last year, Satya asked me to help build the future of M365. Once again, the old rules didn’t apply. AI was rapidly changing how professionals work, and the world’s largest productivity suite needed to lead the way. That meant figuring out what Copilot, and the future of work, should look like as one ecosystem.

We still have a ways to go, but the progress over the past year has been inspiring to watch. A lot of talented people set aside their own roadmaps to make that happen. Thank you. I know it wasn’t easy.

Satya, thank you. When LinkedIn joined Microsoft, you gave us room to build, and then trusted many of us with a lot more. I’ve learned more from you than I can fit in an email, and I’m grateful for the friendship that came with it.

All of which made this a hard decision. I know what it would take for me to lead the next phase of this work well: being in Redmond full time, every day. But my life and my family’s life are here in the Bay Area. My wife Leigh gives her time to more local organizations than I can keep track of. Our youngest daughter just started high school, and our dog Buddy remains deeply committed to the trails on the Peninsula!

I thought about this for a long time. It’s the right call. The work now goes to leaders who are set up to take it further. I can’t wait to see what they do with it.

Over the years, people have asked me what’s kept me so energized and motivated in this work. I think the answer is that I got to spend my career working where doing good and doing well are the same thing. In technology, that’s the best place to operate.

Most companies start by focusing on doing well, so doing good becomes a compromise. It’s the last slide of the PowerPoint, or a separate .org. But when doing good is built into the product itself, it becomes a real competitive advantage. When we build valuable products, people find jobs, they hire, they learn skills, they start companies, they run companies. That creates value for members, customers and the world. And for our business too.

Not many companies get to work this way, and not many people get the chance to build something like it. We do.

That matters more now than it ever has. Technology will continue to touch every job on the planet, and the people building it will decide what kind of world it helps create. I can’t think of a better group to figure that out than the people reading this note.

Thank you for the best 18 years I could have asked for.

RR

Tech.title: Robotaxi operators will face fines for blocking first responders
Tech.content:
Autonomous vehicle (AV) technology companies like Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox will have to provide first responders with local, on-the-ground support when their robotaxis cause problems under a new California law. The companies could also face penalties if a robotaxi blocks police or firefighters for more than 30 minutes.

Senate Bill 1246, which was signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom, sets a series of new rules for AVs designed to improve safety and response times when they become disabled or interfere with emergency responders. The law also creates ways to hold these companies accountable if they don’t.

The law follows a string of high-profile incidents in California in which robotaxis broke down and disrupted traffic, drove into crime scenes, or impeded first responders.

The bulk of those incidents involved Waymo, the largest robotaxi operator in the U.S. , which has about 4,000 autonomous vehicles in its commercial fleet across the country. About 1,200 of those are in the San Francisco Bay Area. A TechCrunch investigation earlier this year identified a number of incidents in which Waymo relied on first responders to manually drive its vehicles when they encountered problems.

Those incidents prompted state and federal lawmakers to call for stricter rules governing robotaxis, particularly how they behave around first responders. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) even sent a letter to AV developers demanding that they come up with “solutions” to the problem.

This new California law attempts to address those concerns, at least in the state.

“California has embraced autonomous vehicles, but we cannot embrace innovation at the expense of public safety. When an autonomous vehicle crashes, breaks down, blocks a roadway in an emergency, or gets in the way of law enforcement or first responders, there must be clear accountability,” said state Senator Dave Cortese, who introduced the bill.

Under the law, AV developers can only employ remote drivers who are based in the United States and those drivers must hold a U.S. driver’s license. The requirement is meant to address concerns around how companies use remote operations when autonomous vehicles run into trouble.

The term “remote operations” has been interpreted very broadly and there is still little known about the methods AV companies use. The “remote drivers” term in the law is far more specific. It refers to a human who directly operates or drives the vehicle from afar. Tesla is the only company that has publicly stated that it has remote operators who can take direct control of its robotaxis.

Other companies, including Waymo, have said they use forms of remote assistance, in which the self-driving system remains in control and a human employee can provide guidance or send software commands if needed. Waymo has a global network of remote assistance staff, including in the Philippines, and operates command centers in Arizona and Michigan. Zoox’s remote operations teams are based in the United States, according to the company.

The law will also require AV companies to notify cities, towns, and other local jurisdictions about the location and status of vehicles during system-wide failures and to provide “local incident technicians” who can assist with AV accidents and obstructions. Companies cal also be fined if an AV blocks first responders during an emergency for more than 30 minutes.

Companies including Waymo and Zoox have said they will comply.

“We are grateful for the amendments made to the bill, which ensure autonomous vehicle operators can still feasibly serve Californians,” a Waymo spokesperson said in an emailed company statement. “Waymo is committed to making roads safer in California and continually improving our service.”

The law goes into effect in July 2028. The California Department of Motor Vehicles, which regulates autonomous vehicles in the state, will set guidelines on certain aspects of the new law, including required response times.

Tech.title: The founder’s guide to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Everything you need to know
Tech.content:
TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is built around one question: How do you build an enduring company in the AI era? Our programming and speaker lineup reflect that, based on the feedback we’ve gotten from the community and the reality on the ground.

Last year at Disrupt, we spoke with founders about their experiences and discovered the results of their attendance firsthand. One founder saw a 3x oversubscription rate after their confirmation for Startup Battlefield and more than 100 investor inbounds helping fuel conversations about a future fundraising round. Another founder had nearly 30 back-to-back conversations with investors who flocked to them after a pitch onstage and followed them to their booth.

That’s not the exception at Disrupt — that’s the point. And those opportunities aren’t just available for Battlefield finalists. Every conversation in the Expo Hall or in a Side Event can create an opportunity for your startup. For years, whether it’s been held in New York, San Francisco, or elsewhere, Disrupt has brought together thousands of founders, investors, startup team members, and tech leaders.

We’re keeping that mission alive at SF’s Moscone West, this October 13-15 with a packed lineup of speakers, more than 200 expert sessions, a wealth of organized and serendipitous networking opportunities, and most of all, the chance to be in the same room as the person who could change your nascent idea for a company or your current startup’s trajectory.

This guide is for the founders out there who are just learning about Disrupt, who need a refresher, or are skeptical of whether it’s worth it. TechCrunch has been around for more than 20 years; we can take it. And before you dive in, we have two discounts that run up until Disrupt begins you should be know about. Founders can bring a team member along for 50% off their ticket by following this link, or you can help laid off members of your network find their next opportunity at Disrupt with our steep discount of Expo+ passes.

The reality of what makes Disrupt, Disrupt

If you’re asking Claude or ChatGPT if TechCrunch Disrupt is worth it, you’re not alone. The reality is that Disrupt is a unique event, and it’s happening at a unique time for the startup community.

This year’s Disrupt isn’t about predicting the future of AI; it’s about building companies in it. Across six editorially curated stages, founders will hear practical lessons from the CEOs, investors, engineers, and operators shaping the next decade of technology.

Whether you’re raising your first round, scaling your team, or deciding how AI changes your product, every session is designed to answer one question: “What can I take back to my company on Monday morning?”

The founders Disrupt empowers

Disrupt works a bit differently, depending on where you are in your founding journey, with different tracks you can follow to make the most of the three days:

Pre-seed and idea stages

You’re here to pressure-test your thesis, meet your first angel or pre-seed investors, and figure out who else is building in your space. Prioritize the Builders Stage, the Startup Battlefield semifinalist pitches, and the Expo Hall, along with roundtables tied to your industry and conversations you’ll want to learn more from.

Early revenue or actively raising

You’re here for capital and validation above all else, and your time is valuable. Prioritize our investor-matchmaking tools and the connections that come with your Founder Pass, including the networking tools in our app. You also get access to the Deal Flow Café, where we foster one-on-one conversations between founders and investors.

And when your schedule isn’t packed with dealmaking, learn from VC perspectives and fundraising-focused sessions at the Builders Stage.

Scaling, hiring, in search of partnerships

You’re here in search of talent, strategic partners, and market visibility. Those same networking tools and opportunities can help you meet potential hires and partners and deepen those connections or make new ones. Disrupt’s Side Events aren’t to be missed — there’s one for every industry, interest, or post-event vibe you could be looking to find.

The Startup Battlefield winner’s reveal packs the Disrupt stage and is each year’s capstone event. But it’s the lead-up to that $100,000 check and the deluge of attention the winner receives that’s the most valuable for founders attending Disrupt.

The 200 startups chosen on August 20 to compete go through a rigorous prep process and get the opportunity to pitch onstage in front of top-tier VCs and the Disrupt crowds. You’ll also get to watch those pitches, take notes, learn from the peaks and valleys, and potentially meet the teams behind the ideas and innovations. It could be in a follow-up meeting or just walking through the halls of Moscone.

And if that all leaves you inspired, here’s an insider tip: Most Battlefield participants, and several winners, have gone through the process multiple times.
